title: Hyperíōn
text: Name: Hyperíōn (hyperion) Greek / original script form: Ὑπερίων Pantheon: greek Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: He who goes above (from ὑπέρ) Original script (Greek): Ὑπερίων Transliteration: Hyperíōn Pronunciation: /hy.pe.rí.ɔːn/ — 'hü-peh-REE-ohn' — round the lips for Hy- (the ü of German 'über'), strike the accent hard on -rí-, and let the final -ōn ring long. text: Name: Rꜥ (ra) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: egyptian Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Sun (from Egyptian rꜥ) Etymology: Original script (Hieroglyphs): 𓂋𓂝𓇳 Transliteration: Rꜥ Provenance: The name is written rꜥ (𓂋𓂝) with the sun-disk (𓇳) as a determinative/rebus for 'sun'. Egyptologists vocalise the name as Ra or Rꜥa, but the hieroglyphs record only rꜥ. text: Name: Ꜣst (isis) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: egyptian Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Throne (Egyptian ꜣst) Original script (Hieroglyphs): 𓊨𓏏𓆇 Transliteration: Ꜣst Provenance: The Egyptian name is written 𓊨𓏏𓆇 in hieroglyphs. text: Name: Bꜣstt (bastet) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: egyptian Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: She of the ointment jar (Egyptian bꜣstt) Original script (Hieroglyphs): 𓎯𓏏𓏏𓁐 Transliteration: Bꜣstt Provenance: The Egyptian name is written 𓎯𓏏𓏏𓁐 in hieroglyphs. title: Quetzalcōātl
text: Name: Quetzalcōātl (quetzalcoatl) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: nahuatl Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Feathered serpent Original script (Colonial Nahuatl (Latin script)): Quetzalcōātl Transliteration: Quetzalcōātl Provenance: Nahuatl was recorded by Spanish and native scribes in Latin alphabets from the sixteenth century onward. The name is a compound: quetzalli 'precious green feather' + cōātl 'snake'. Macrons mark long vowels in scholarly Classical Nahuatl orthography. The Unicode restoration Quetzalcōātl preserves vowel length; there is no indigenous logographic spelling for the personal name. Pronunciation: /két͡saɬˈkoː(w)aːt͡ɬ/ — 'ket-SAHL-KOH-wahtl' — the 'tl' at the end is one sound, the 'z' is like 'ts,' and the whispered 'l' in 'zal' is Nahuatl ɬ. Phonemes: Quet-: Voiceless velar stop [k] plus [e], then the affricate [t͡s]. In Classical Nahuatl, qu before e/i is /k/ (not /kw/), and tz is /t͡s/. -zal-: Open [a] plus voiceless alveolar lateral fricative [ɬ] — the Nahuatl l is a 'whispered l,' not the English approximant. -cō-: Voiceless velar stop [k] plus long back rounded [oː]. Classical Nahuatl had no /u/ sound; the macron marks vowel length. -ātl: Long open [aː] plus lateral affricate [t͡ɬ] — final -tl is a single Nahuatl sound, not separate t + l. Pronunciation note: Classical Nahuatl had no /u/; qu before e/i is /k/ and cu is /kw/. The long vowels ō and ā are preserved in the PUNICODEX restoration, and the final -tl is a lateral affricate [t͡ɬ], not English 'tuhl.' The [w] glide between ō and ā is common in natural speech but optional. Tier 1: the two macrons preserve reconstructed vowel length. Sources: Andrews Introduction to Classical Nahuatl, Karttunen An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl, Wiktionary Nahuatl. title: Cōātlīcue
text: Name: Cōātlīcue (coatlicue) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: nahuatl Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: She of the serpent skirt Pronunciation: /koː.aːˈtɬiː.kwe/ — 'koh-AH-tlee-kweh' — the 'tl' is one crisp sound, and the macrons stretch the o, a, and i into long vowels. Phonemes: Cō-: Voiceless velar stop [k] followed by long open-mid [oː]. In Classical Nahuatl, c before back vowels is /k/; the macron marks vowel length. -ā-: Long open front [aː], a held vowel that distinguishes the first element of the compound. -tlī-: Lateral affricate [tɬ] plus long close front [iː]; the -tl is a single Nahuatl sound, not English t + l. -cue: Voiceless velar stop [k] plus rounded [we], the Nahuatl labiovelar sequence. Pronunciation note: Classical Nahuatl vowel length is the key prosodic feature preserved here. The name is transparently composed of cōātl ('snake, serpent') and īcue ('her skirt'), a possessive form of cueitl 'skirt.' The final labiovelar [kwe] is not a diphthong in English terms but a velar stop followed by a labial glide. Tier 1: the three macrons preserve reconstructed long vowels in the first, second, and fourth syllables. title: Huītzilōpōchtli
text: Name: Huītzilōpōchtli (huitzilopochtli) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: nahuatl Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Left-handed hummingbird Pronunciation: /wiː.t͡si.loːˈpoːt͡ʃ.tɬi/ — 'weet-see-loh-POCH-tlee' — the 'tz' is 'ts,' the 'ch' is as in 'church,' and the final -tli is one released sound. Phonemes: Huitz-: Rounded [w] plus long close front [iː], then alveolar affricate [t͡s] — the beginning of huītzilin, the Nahuatl word for 'hummingbird.' -ilo-: Close front [i], alveolar lateral [l], and short [o]: the -il- tail of huītzilin plus the ligature -o- that joins it to ōpōchtli in the compound. -pōch-: Voiceless bilabial stop [p] plus long back rounded [oː] plus voiceless postalveolar affricate [t͡ʃ]; ōpōchtli means 'left-handed,' also associated with the south. -tli: Lateral affricate [tɬ] plus close front [i], the absolute suffix closing the noun. Pronunciation note: The etymology is debated. The most widely accepted analysis takes huītzilin 'hummingbird' + ōpōchtli 'left/south,' joined by the ligature -o-, with a possible interpretation of the hummingbird as the soul of the warrior returning from death. Tier 1: the three macrons preserve the long vowels of huītzilin and ōpōchtli (per Karttunen), distinctive features the ASCII form loses. title: Ẹṣù
text: Name: Ẹṣù (eshu) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: yoruba Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Divine trickster Original script (Yoruba (modern Latin orthography)): Ẹ̀ṣù Transliteration: Ẹ̀ṣù Provenance: Yoruba has been written in the Latin alphabet since the 1840s, with diacritics for tone and vowel quality. The underdot marks the open vowels /ɛ, ɔ/ and the postalveolar fricative /ʃ/; these are the obligatory phonemic marks. Tone marks (grave low, acute high) are fully written in dictionaries but routinely omitted in everyday Yoruba writing. The owned Unicode form preserves the underdots and the tone marks the domain could carry; the fully tone-marked dictionary form is documented in the variants and here. Pronunciation: /ɛ̀.ʃṹ/ — eh-SHOON — start low on 'eh', rise to a bright, slightly nasal 'SHOON'. Phonemes: Ẹ-: Open-mid front unrounded vowel [ɛ] with low tone, written with a dot below in standard Yoruba orthography. -ṣu: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] with dot below, followed by close back rounded vowel [u] with high tone; nasalised in many dialects. Pronunciation note: Ẹṣu is Tier 1: the dots below ẹ and ṣ are distinctive features the ASCII form loses, the dot below ẹ marking the open [ɛ] vowel. The name is often wrongly conflated with the Christian devil; in Yoruba religion he is a necessary divine functionary, not an evil being. Tone conventions for the name vary between dictionaries (Èṣù / Èṣú); written Yoruba routinely omits tones. title: Dažbog
text: Name: Dažbog (dazhbog) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: slavic Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Giving god Original script (Church Slavonic / East Slavic Cyrillic): Дажбог Transliteration: Dažbog Provenance: The name is attested in East Slavic chronicles as Дажьбогъ (Dažĭbogŭ) and in the Primary Chronicle. It is usually analyzed as daždĭ 'rain, gift' + bogŭ 'god', hence 'giving god' or 'rain god'. The modern Unicode restoration Dažbog uses the caron ž; the medieval Cyrillic spelling includes the reduced jer vowels ь and ъ. The Cyrillic form is not registrable in .com; the Latin transliteration Dažbog is. Pronunciation: /ˈdaʒ.boɡ/ — 'DAHZH-bog' — crisp 'dah', then the 'zh' sound of 'measure', and end with 'bog' as in 'god' (which is what the word means). Phonemes: D-: Voiced alveolar stop [d], as in English 'day'. -a-: Short open front [a], the first unstressed syllable in the compound. -ž-: Voiced postalveolar fricative [ʒ], the Slavic 'zh' sound written with a caron. -bog: Voiced bilabial stop [b], open-mid back rounded [ɔ], and voiced velar [ɡ]; means 'god'. Pronunciation note: Dažbog is Tier 1: the caron on ž preserves the distinctive Common Slavic fricative, a feature the ASCII form loses. The h in the lexicon's ASCII form is silent, reflecting an older East Slavic spelling convention (Daždbog / Dadzbog) that was later simplified. We do not invent an etymology beyond the attested compound 'giving god'. title: Typhōn
text: Name: Typhōn (typhon) Greek / original script form: Τυφῶν Pantheon: greek Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Whirlwind, smoke Etymology: Cognates: τῦφος (Greek); τυφώς (Greek); typhoon (English) Original script (Greek): Τυφῶν Transliteration: Typhōn Provenance: The Greek form Τυφῶν is written in the Classical Greek alphabet. Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek. Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form. The Unicode restoration Typhōn encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name. Pronunciation: /tyˈpʰɔːn/ — "tee-FOHN" — but the first vowel is like French "tu," and the second is long and breathy, like a storm that does not end quickly. Phonemes: Ty-: Short upsilon [y] — a rounded, front vowel like French "u" — the whirlwind's first breath. -phōn: Aspirated phi [pʰ] followed by long omega [ɔː] and nu; the name roars and sustains. Pronunciation note: Typhōn is Tier 1 because the Greek Τυφῶν contains both stress and length: the circumflex over the omega marks a long vowel that also carries the pitch peak. The single character ῶ encodes both features, and the macron form Typhōn preserves the long vowel while implying the original stress position. The name sounds like what it describes: a long, smoky exhalation. The form is attested throughout the Codex Regius poems (Reginsmál, Fáfnismál) and in Vǫlsunga saga; Cleasby-Vigfusson (s.v. Fáfnir) and Zoëga's Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic record the name and connect it with the notion of 'the embracer' (cf. faðmr, 'embrace'). The medial -fn- was pronounced with a voiced fricative, [vn] — hence the approximation 'FAHV-neer'. title: Ḥkꜣ
text: Name: Ḥkꜣ (heka) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: egyptian Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Magic, first work Etymology: Original script (Hieroglyphs): 𓎛𓂓𓏛 Transliteration: Ḥkꜣ Provenance: The Egyptian name is written 𓎛𓂓𓏛 in hieroglyphs. Hieroglyphs combine logograms, phonograms, and determinatives; the exact function of each sign depends on context. Egyptian writing does not record vowels; the vocalised form is a modern convention reconstructed from Coptic and Greek evidence. The Unicode restoration Ḥkꜣ uses Egyptological alef/ayin and other registrable characters; the hieroglyphic form is not registrable in .com. Pronunciation: /ħaˈkaːʕ/ — 'heh-KAH' — start with a strong, throaty h, then a sharp ka held slightly longer at the end. Phonemes: Ḥ-: Voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ], a dry h pronounced deep in the throat — the breath of a god before speech. -e-: Short unstressed vowel, reconstructed from Coptic ϩⲓⲕ (hik). -kaː-: Long vowel before the ka-radical; the word contains the root of ka, the vital essence, because magic activates life. -ʕ: Final alef (ꜣ), leaving the name open like an incantation that has not yet ended. Pronunciation note: Heka is Tier 1 because the restoration preserves the Egyptological alef ꜣ and the underdotted ḥ — distinctive letters the ASCII form loses. The ḥ marks a consonant English lacks; it is not 'h' as in 'house' but a voiceless fricative produced at the back of the throat, giving the name its hissing, authoritative sound. title: Tlāltēcuhtli
text: Name: Tlāltēcuhtli (tlaltecuhtli) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: nahuatl Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Lord of the earth Pronunciation: /tɬaːɬˈteː.kʷet͡ɬi/ — 'TLAH-lteh-KWEH-tlee' — begin with the single 'tl' sound, hold the first and second vowels long, and treat the final -tl as one release. Phonemes: Tlāl-: Lateral affricate [tɬ] plus long open [aː]; tl- is a single Nahuatl initial, and ā marks vowel length. -tē-: Voiceless alveolar stop [t] plus long close-mid [eː], the honorific or lordly element. -cuhtli: Voiceless velar stop [k] plus rounded [we], then lateral affricate [tɬ] plus close front [i]; -cuhtli is the reverential suffix meaning 'lord.' Pronunciation note: The name is a straightforward compound of tlālli ('earth') and tēcuhtli ('lord'). The honorific suffix is not gender-exclusive in Nahuatl; Tlāltēcuhtli is depicted as both male and female, and sometimes as a toad-like being. Tier 1: the macrons on ā and ē preserve reconstructed vowel length. title: Ọrúnmìlà
text: Name: Ọrúnmìlà (orunmila) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: yoruba Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Heaven knows who will succeed Original script (Yoruba (modern Latin orthography)): Ọ̀rúnmìlà Transliteration: Ọ̀rúnmìlà Provenance: Yoruba has been written in the Latin alphabet since the 1840s, with diacritics for tone and vowel quality. The underdot marks the open vowels /ɛ, ɔ/ and the postalveolar fricative /ʃ/; these are the obligatory phonemic marks. Tone marks (grave low, acute high) are fully written in dictionaries but routinely omitted in everyday Yoruba writing. The owned Unicode form preserves the underdots and the tone marks the domain could carry; the fully tone-marked dictionary form is documented in the variants and here. Pronunciation: /ɔ̀.rúɱ.mì.là/ — aw-ROON-mee-LAH — low 'aw', high 'ROON', then low 'mee-LAH'. Phonemes: Ọ-: Open-mid back rounded vowel [ɔ] with low tone, written with a dot below. -rú-: Voiced alveolar tap or trill [r] plus close back rounded vowel [u] with high tone. -ɱì-: Voiced labiodental nasal [ɱ] before [m], with close front vowel [i] in low tone. -là: Voiced alveolar lateral approximant [l] followed by open [a] with low tone. Pronunciation note: Ọrúnmìlà is Tier 1: the dot below ọ and the acute and grave accents that preserve Yoruba tones are distinctive features the ASCII form loses. The dot below ọ marks the open [ɔ] vowel. title: Ọṣọọsì
text: Name: Ọṣọọsì (ochosi) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: yoruba Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: The hunter — orisha of the hunt, the forest, and deliberate strategy (standard Yoruba Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì; Cuban Ochosi, Brazilian Oxóssi) Original script (Yoruba (modern Latin orthography)): Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì Transliteration: Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì Provenance: Yoruba has been written in the Latin alphabet since the 1840s, with diacritics for tone and vowel quality. The name Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì is the standard orthography of the hunter orisha known in Brazil as Oxóssi. The underdots distinguish /ɔ/ and /ʃ/ from their plain counterparts; tone marks carry lexical tone (low–high–low–low). The Unicode restoration Ọṣọọsì preserves the underdots and the final low tone; the ASCII form loses all of them. Pronunciation: /ɔ̀.ʃɔ́.ɔ̀.sì/ — aw-shaw-AW-sih — the dotted ọ is the open 'aw' of 'law'; ṣ is 'sh'; the tones run low-high-low-low. Pronunciation note: The name in standard Yoruba orthography is Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì, fully tone-marked; the owned form Ọṣọọsì keeps the underdotted vowels (ọ, the open o) and the long double-o while following the diaspora convention that leaves tone marks implicit — the spelling carried across the Santería and Candomblé worlds. Abraham's Dictionary of Modern Yoruba lists him as the god of hunters; the etymology is debated, though the ọ̀ṣọ́ element suggests swiftness. Tier-1 by rule: the underdots and the ṣ are distinctive letters the ASCII "Ochosi" cannot carry. title: Mjǫllnir
text: Name: Mjǫllnir (mjolnir) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: norse Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: The grinder Original script (Younger Futhark): ᛘᛁᚢᛚᚾᛁᚱ Transliteration: miulnir Provenance: ᛘ (maðr) writes /m/ ᛁ (ís) writes both /i/ and /e/ ᚢ (úr) writes the rounded back vowels /u, o, ø, ǫ, y/ and /w/ The spelling miulnir is a normalized phonetic reconstruction; Younger Futhark does not distinguish voiced/voiceless stops or separate short and long vowels Pronunciation: /ˈmjɔlː.nir/ — 'MYAWL-lnir' — begin with the mj of 'music', sound the vowel like the short rounded 'o' of 'hot', and hold the ll double before the final '-nir'. Phonemes: Mj: The onset cluster [mj], m followed by a palatal glide, as in English 'music'; the anglicized Mjolnir keeps the spelling but usually drops the glide ǫ: Short open-mid back rounded [ɔ], written o-ogonek; the rounded 'o' of 'hot', held short — distinct from both o and ó ll: Long or geminated alveolar lateral [lː], written double in Old Norse to show length; hold it like the ll of Italian 'bella' Pronunciation note: Mjǫllnir is Tier 1: the o-ogonek ǫ (the short rounded [ɔ] of Old Norse) and the geminate ll are features the ASCII form loses — this is the normalized dictionary form (Cleasby–Vigfusson, s.v. 'Mjöllnir'; Zoëga, s.v. 'Mjǫllnir'), with the living Icelandic Mjölnir as the attested modern variant. The etymology is genuinely disputed: proposals connect the name to Old Norse mala, 'to grind' ('the grinder'), to mjǫll, 'new snow' ('the shining one'), and to the Slavic lightning word seen in Russian mólnija, and the scholarship has settled on none of them. title: Wꜣḏyt
text: Name: Wꜣḏyt (wadjet) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: egyptian Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: The green one Original script (Hieroglyphs): 𓇅𓏏𓆗 Transliteration: Wꜣḏyt Provenance: The Egyptian name is written 𓇅𓏏𓆗 in hieroglyphs. Hieroglyphs combine logograms, phonograms, and determinatives; the exact function of each sign depends on context. Egyptian writing does not record vowels; the vocalised form is a modern convention reconstructed from Coptic and Greek evidence. The Unicode restoration Wꜣḏyt uses Egyptological alef/ayin and other registrable characters; the hieroglyphic form is not registrable in .com. Pronunciation: /waˈd͡ʒiːt/ — 'WAD-jeet' — start like 'wad', then 'jeet' with a long 'ee' and a crisp final t. The middle consonant may also be pronounced as a sharp emphatic 't' in stricter reconstructions. Phonemes: W-: Labial-velar approximant [w], as in English 'we'. -a-: Short open vowel; the alef ꜣ in the spelling colours or lengthens the vowel but is not pronounced as a separate consonant here. -d͡ʒ-: Voiced postalveolar affricate [d͡ʒ], the conventional Egyptological reading of ḏ (d-with-line-below, U+1E0F); Coptic evidence later points to a /t/ reflex, as in Coptic ⲟⲩⲱⲧ 'green'. -iː-: Long close front vowel in the final syllable. -t: Voiceless alveolar stop [t]; the final -t is the feminine marker. Pronunciation note: The name Wꜣḏyt derives from the Egyptian word for 'green/blue' (wꜣḏ), recorded in Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache I, 263–268. Hieroglyphs write only the consonants w-ꜣ-ḏ-y-t; the vowels are uncertain. The ꜣ functions as a vowel carrier or glottal onset, and the ḏ (palatal/ejective in earlier Egyptian, later merging toward /t/) is represented in PUNICODEX by the registrable d-with-line-below (U+1E0F). title: Amitābha
text: Name: Amitābha (amitabha) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: buddhist Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Of unmeasured splendour; infinite light; the Buddha of the Pure Land Sukhāvatī. Original script (Devanagari): अमिताभ Transliteration: Amitābha Provenance: Sanskrit Amitābha is written अमिताभ in Devanagari. The compound is a-mita ('unmeasured') + ābha ('light, splendor'), hence 'of unmeasured splendor, infinite light'. IAST macrons and subscript dots encode length and aspiration; the acute on the domain label is a typographic convention. The Unicode restoration Amitābha is registrable in .com; the Devanagari form is not supported in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /ə.ˈmɪ.taː.bʱə/ — 'uh-MEE-tah-bhuh' — the 'bh' is aspirated like 'b-huh' in one sound; the 'tā' is held long. Phonemes: A-: Short open vowel [ə], the Sanskrit prefix a- meaning 'without, un-' -mi-: Short close front [ɪ] plus voiced bilabial nasal [m]; part of the root mā, 'to measure' -tā-: Long open [aː], the feminine noun-forming suffix; the macron marks length -bha: Voiced aspirated bilabial stop [bʰ] plus short [ə]; bha means 'light, splendor' Pronunciation note: Amitābha is Tier 1 because the medial ā is long. The name is a standard Sanskrit bahuvrīhi compound: a-mita ('unmeasured') + ābha ('light, splendor'). In East Asian Buddhism he is also known as Amitāyus, 'Infinite Life,' the two names emphasizing light and longevity. text: Name: Baꜥal (baal) Greek / original script form: Βαάλ Pantheon: canaanite Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Canaanite storm and fertility god; the title "Lord" (baʿlu) was also applied to local deities Etymology: Cognates: בַּעַל (Baʿal) (Hebrew); 𐤁𐤏𐤋 (Bʿl) (Phoenician); بَعْل (Baʿl) (Arabic) Original script (Ugaritic): 𐎁𐎓𐎍 Transliteration: Baꜥal Provenance: The name is written 𐎁𐎓𐎍 in the Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet. Pronunciation: /baʕ.al/ — 'BAH-ahl' — the middle consonant is a deep, throaty 'ʿ' (like Arabic ع), not a glottal stop or silent letter. Phonemes: ba-: Plain voiced bilabial [b] plus open [a]; the word means 'lord, owner, husband' across Semitic languages. -ʕal: Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ] plus [a] and [l]. The pharyngeal is the signature consonant; we render it with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for registrability. Pronunciation note: Baꜥal is technically a title ('Lord') that became a name. title: Ašeratu
text: Name: Ašeratu (aseratu) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: phoenician Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: She who treads on the sea Original script (Phoenician): 𐤀𐤔𐤓𐤕 Transliteration: Ašeratu Provenance: The name is written 𐤀𐤔𐤓𐤕 in the Phoenician abjad. Phoenician writing records consonants only; vowels are supplied by modern scholars from cognate languages. The final vowel markings in the transliteration are inferred from older Northwest Semitic case endings. The Unicode restoration Ašeratu is registrable in .com; the Phoenician form is not in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /ʔa.ʃe.ˈra.tu/ — 'ah-she-RAH-too' — begin with a slight catch in the throat, then 'she' with a crisp sh, roll or tap the r, and end with 'rah-too'. Phonemes: ʔa-: Glottal stop [ʔ] followed by open [a]; the initial aleph of the Canaanite name (not a pharyngeal ʿayin, so the registrable form uses plain A). -še-: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] plus mid front [e]. The š reflects the Phoenician/Canaanite sibilant; Ugaritic wrote the same consonant as ṯ (probably [θ]). -ra-: Tapped or trilled [r] plus open [a]. -tu: Voiceless alveolar stop [t] plus close back rounded vowel [u], the final nominative case vowel of the divine name in Ugaritic and Phoenician. Pronunciation note: Reconstruction follows the Phoenician/Ugaritic nominative form ʾAšeratu. The initial consonant is a glottal stop (aleph), not a pharyngeal, so the PUNICODEX form uses plain A rather than Egyptological Ain. The medial š marks the Canaanite/Phoenician reflex of Proto-Semitic *ṯ, while Ugaritic retains the older ṯ (probably [θ]); the final -u is the case vowel, dropped in Hebrew Asherah. Tier 1: the caron on š preserves a distinctive Semitic phoneme — a distinctive diacritic the ASCII form loses. title: Libyē
text: Name: Libyē (libye) Greek / original script form: Λιβύη Pantheon: greek Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: The African continent (etymology uncertain) Etymology: Original script (Greek): Λιβύη Transliteration: Libyē Provenance: The Greek form Λιβύη is written in the Classical Greek alphabet. The Unicode restoration Libyē encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name. Pronunciation: /li.ˈbýː.ɛː/ — 'lee-BOO-ay' — the middle vowel is tight and rounded like French u, and the final 'ay' is held long. Phonemes: Li-: Voiced alveolar lateral [l] plus short close front [i]; the first syllable is unstressed -by-: Voiced bilabial stop [b] plus front rounded [y], the Greek upsilon sound before a front vowel -ē: Long close-mid front [ɛː], the Greek eta; the macron marks length, giving the word its Tier-1 status Pronunciation note: Libyē is Tier 1 because the final eta is long. text: Name: Aígyptos (aigyptos) Greek / original script form: Αἴγυπτος Pantheon: greek Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: From Egyptian Ḥwt-kꜣ-ptḥ ("House of the Ka of Ptah") Etymology: Original script (Greek): Αἴγυπτος Transliteration: Aígyptos Provenance: The Greek form Αἴγυπτος is written in the Classical Greek alphabet. title: Ṛta
text: Name: Ṛta (rta) Pantheon: sanskrit Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Cosmic order, truth — the Vedic principle of rightness that governs gods and nature (ṛta) Etymology: Cognates: aṣ̌a (avestan); rītus (latin) Original script (Devanagari): ऋत Transliteration: Ṛta Provenance: Sanskrit Ṛta is written ऋत in Devanagari. Each aksara combines a consonant with an inherent or explicit vowel. IAST diacritics preserve length, retroflexion, and aspiration lost in plain ASCII. The Devanagari form is not used as the primary domain because Indic scripts are not in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /r̩.tɐ/ — 'RIH-tuh' — the first syllable is a voiced r that carries the vowel, almost like 'rurr' clipped short; the t is crisp. Pronunciation note: IAST Ṛta uses the underdotted ṛ for the syllabic r vowel. It is never personified in the Vedic corpus; it is the impersonal principle by which sun, moon, sacrifice, and morality all hold together. Devanagari ऋत is one of the most philosophically charged short words in Sanskrit. title: Bꜣ
text: Name: Bꜣ (ba) Pantheon: egyptian Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: The soul, personality, or manifestation of a person. One of the five components of the Egyptian soul. Etymology: Original script (Hieroglyphs): 𓅡𓏤 Transliteration: Bꜣ Provenance: The Egyptian name is written 𓅡𓏤 in hieroglyphs. Hieroglyphs combine logograms, phonograms, and determinatives; the exact function of each sign depends on context. Egyptian writing does not record vowels; the vocalised form is a modern convention reconstructed from Coptic and Greek evidence. The Unicode restoration Bꜣ uses Egyptological alef/ayin and other registrable characters; the hieroglyphic form is not registrable in .com. Pronunciation: /baːʕ/ — 'BAH-ah' — but close the final syllable with a soft catch in the throat, as if the name itself were a wing-beat. Phonemes: B-: Voiced bilabial stop [b], as in English 'bone' — the sound of manifestation taking shape. -aː-: Long open vowel reconstructed between the consonants; Egyptian hieroglyphs do not write vowels, so the length is inferred from Coptic and Semitic parallels. -ʕ: Final ꜣ (Egyptian alef), representing a voiced pharyngeal fricative or glottal catch — the breath that keeps the name open at the back of the throat. Pronunciation note: Egyptian is written without vowels. The transliteration Bꜣ uses Gardiner's ꜣ (reversed glottal stop / alef) for the final guttural. The dot under ḥ in other entries marks a voiceless pharyngeal fricative; here the ꜣ marks a voiced counterpart or a glottal catch. The ba is Tier 1 in the PUNICODEX system because the restoration preserves the Egyptological alef ꜣ — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. title: Kꜣ
text: Name: Kꜣ (ka) Pantheon: egyptian Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: The vital essence, life force, or double of a person. Created at birth and surviving death. Pronunciation note: The ka is Tier 1 because the restoration preserves the final Egyptological aleph (ꜣ) — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. title: ʾAṯiratu
text: Name: ʾAṯiratu (athiratu) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: canaanite Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: ‘Lady of the Sea’ — the Ugaritic mother of the gods (rbt ʾaṯrt ym), consort of ʾIlu and intercessor for Baʿlu, KTU Original script (Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet): 𐎀𐎘𐎗𐎚 Transliteration: ʾaṯiratu / ʾaṯirtu Provenance: The Ugaritic alphabet writes the name in four signs: ʾa-ṯi-ra-tu. The normalized vocalization ʾAṯiratu follows the KTU convention; the shorter form ʾAṯirat (without final -u) is also common in modern scholarship. The Greek tradition renders her name Ἀσερά (Philo of Byblos); the Hebrew Bible knows her as ʾăšērāh (Asherah), and the Phoenician form shifts ṯ → š as Ašeratu. The Unicode restoration ʾAṯiratu preserves the glottal onset and the interdental ṯ; the domain aṯiratu.com carries the registrable ṯ. Pronunciation: /ʔaθ.i.ˈraː.tu/ — ah-thi-RAH-too — the th is the soft interdental of English 'thin'; the stress and the long ā fall together on the third syllable. Pronunciation note: Ugaritic writes the name 𐎀𐎘𐎗𐎚 — four signs, a-ṯ-r-t, in alphabetic cuneiform. The second consonant is the letter ṯ: a voiceless interdental fricative /θ/, the 'thin' sound English keeps and most later Semitic languages lost. In Phoenician and Hebrew the sound shifted to š, which is why the same goddess appears as Ašeratu in Phoenician and ʾĂšērāh in the Hebrew Bible. The restoration ʾAṯiratu keeps the Ugaritic consonant exactly where the tablets put it, marks the glottal onset ʾalep, and carries the nominative case-vowel -u; the scholarly Latin convention 'Athirat' inserts an h that no Ugaritic sign writes. Character breakdown: a (undefined), t (undefined), h (undefined), i (undefined), r (undefined), a (undefined), t (undefined), u (undefined) Sources: Die keilalphabetischen Texte aus Ugarit; Michael D. Coogan, Stories from Ancient Canaan; John Day, Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan

title: ꜥAsherah
text: Name: ꜥAsherah (asherah) Greek / original script form: Ἀσερά Pantheon: canaanite Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Canaanite mother goddess, consort of Ēl and patroness of childbirth Etymology: Cognates: אֲשֵׁרָה (ʾĂšērāh) (Hebrew); 𐤀𐤔𐤓𐤕 (ʾšrt) (Phoenician); أَثِيرَة (ʾaṯīrah) (Arabic) Original script (Ugaritic): 𐎀𐎘𐎗𐎚 Transliteration: ꜥAsherah Provenance: The name is written 𐎀𐎘𐎗𐎚 in the Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet. Ugaritic ʿayin is rendered with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for DNS registrability. Long vowels are reconstructed from Hebrew and Akkadian cognates and marked with macrons. The Unicode restoration ꜥAsherah is registrable in .com; the Ugaritic cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /ʔaθeːra/ — 'ah-THAY-rah' — start with a slight catch in the throat, then a long 'thay' (the 'th' of 'thin') and a soft 'rah'. Phonemes: ʔa-: Glottal stop [ʔ] followed by open [a]; in some reconstructions the initial consonant is a pharyngeal ʿ rather than a glottal stop. The Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) marks this debated point. -ṯē-: Voiceless interdental fricative [θ] — Ugaritic ṯ, as in English 'thin' (cf. ṯlṯ, 'three') — plus long [eː], marked by macron; the length is inferred from Hebrew and Aramaic reflexes. -ra: Tapped or trilled [r] plus final [a], a feminine ending. Pronunciation note: The initial consonant of the Ugaritic name is disputed: some read it as a glottal stop (ʾ), others as a pharyngeal (ʿ). We follow the lexicon's use of Egyptian Ain (ꜥ) as the registrable compromise. The long ē is marked with a macron to preserve the length implied by Hebrew and Aramaic cognates; stress falls on the long middle syllable. title: Ōkeanós
text: Name: Ōkeanós (okeanos) Greek / original script form: Ὠκεανός Pantheon: greek Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: The great river encircling the world Etymology: Original script (Greek): Ὠκεανός Transliteration: Ōkeanós Provenance: The Greek form Ὠκεανός is written in the Classical Greek alphabet. Pronunciation note: Ōkeanós is Tier 1 because the Greek Ὠκεανός carries both stress (acute on the final ό) and a long vowel (the initial omega). The ideal form Ōkeanós is difficult to register; Okeanos is the standard form used here. title: Trengtreng
text: Name: Trengtreng (trengtreng) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: mapuche Tier: Tier 2 Meaning: Mapuche thunder and war god Etymology: Pronunciation: /tɾeŋˈtɾeŋ/ — TRENG-TRENG — a rattling, drum-like reduplication that mimics successive thunderclaps. Phonemes: tɾeŋ: Alveolar onset followed by close-mid [e] and a velar nasal [ŋ]; the first syllable of the reduplicated thunder name. -: Reduplication divider; the name is doubled to intensify sound and power. tɾeŋ: Repeated syllable, producing the rattling, drum-like effect of rolling thunder. Pronunciation note: Trengtreng is a reduplicated, onomatopoeic Mapuche name for thunder; reduplication is a productive device for intensification in Mapudungun. Because the Latin alphabet renders all of its sounds without diacritics, the Unicode restoration coincides with the ASCII form, so the name is Tier 2 by tradition rather than by restored marks. title: Aša
text: Name: Aša (asa) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: zoroastrian Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Truth, righteousness, and the cosmic order. The central ethical and metaphysical principle of Zoroastrianism. Etymology: Cognates: ṛtá (sanskrit) Original script (Avestan): 𐬀𐬴𐬀 Transliteration: Aša Provenance: The Avestan form 𐬀𐬴𐬀 writes the sounds of the Avesta phonetically. Long vowels and special fricatives have distinct Avestan letters. The Unicode restoration preserves length and the postalveolar/velar nasal distinctions in a registrable Latin form. The Unicode restoration Aša is registrable in .com; the Avestan script is not in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /aʃa/ — "AH-shah" — two level syllables, with a crisp "sh" in the middle and no stress thrown onto either vowel. Phonemes: a-: Open unrounded vowel [a], the first breath of the name — short, clear, and level. -š-: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ], like English "sh" but sharper; the caron marks the sound that separates Avestan from ordinary "sa". -a: Final open vowel [a], equal in weight to the first; Avestan vowel quantity is real, and the name balances on the two. Pronunciation note: Aša is Tier 1 because the registrable form Aša preserves the postalveolar š (caron) — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The Avestan original was likely pronounced with a level or slightly rising pitch on an open [a], but standard scholarly transliteration does not encode Avestan accent. The š is not decorative: it distinguishes the name from ordinary "asa" and points back to the Avestan letter 𐬴 (še). Character breakdown: a (undefined), s (undefined), a (undefined) Sources: Altiranisches Wörterbuch; Christian Bartholomae, Altiranisches Wörterbuch

title: Vāc
text: Name: Vāc (vac) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: sanskrit Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Speech personified — the Vedic goddess of sacred utterance (Vāc) Etymology: Cognates: vōx (latin); ἔπος (greek) Original script (Devanagari): वाच् Transliteration: Vāc Provenance: Sanskrit Vāc is written वाच् in Devanagari. Each aksara combines a consonant with an inherent or explicit vowel. IAST diacritics preserve length, retroflexion, and aspiration lost in plain ASCII. The Devanagari form is not used as the primary domain because Indic scripts are not in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /ʋaːtʃ/ — "VAHCH" — one long syllable, like "watch" but with the vowel drawn out and a crisper final "ch." Phonemes: V-: Labiodental approximant [ʋ], softer than English v; the lips almost meet but do not buzz. -ā-: Long open back vowel [aː], held roughly twice the length of short a; the macron is the vowel's length, not stress. -c: Voiceless palatal affricate [tɕ] or [tʃ], like English "ch" but more forward on the palate; the virāma marks that no vowel follows. Pronunciation note: Vāc is Tier 1 because the registrable form Vāc preserves the long ā (macron) — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. Vedic Sanskrit was pitch-accented, but the position of the accent in Vāc is not normally encoded in transliteration. The virāma on the Devanagari च् indicates the consonant is final, making the name a single closed syllable: vāc. Character breakdown: v (undefined), a (undefined), c (undefined) Sources: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā; Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary; Arthur A. Macdonell, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary

title: Hén
text: Name: Hén (hen) Greek / original script form: ἕν Pantheon: greek Tier: Tier 2 Meaning: Greek neuter of εἷς, "one"; philosophically "The One" in Neoplatonism. Etymology: Cognates: εἷς, μία, ἕν (greek); semel (latin); same (english) Original script (Greek): ἕν Transliteration: Hén Provenance: The Greek form ἕν is written in the Classical Greek alphabet. Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek. Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form. The Unicode restoration Hén encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name. Pronunciation: /hɛ́n/ — 'HEN' — with a slight initial h and a rising pitch on the first, only syllable. Phonemes: h-: Rough breathing [h], the audible breath that precedes the vowel in classical Greek. -é-: Short epsilon with acute pitch stress [ɛ́], the prosodic peak of the word. -n: Voiced alveolar nasal [n], closing the syllable. Pronunciation note: Hén is Tier 2: the Greek ἕν preserves only the acute pitch stress on the first syllable and has no long vowel. It is an Accent-Preserving Tier-2 name. Variants: owned: hén; ascii: hen Character breakdown: h (undefined), e (undefined), n (undefined) Sources: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon; Etymological Dictionary of Greek; Plato, Dialogues

title: Nirmātā
text: Name: Nirmātā (nirmata) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: sanskrit Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Creator, maker, architect (from Sanskrit निर्मातृ) Original script (Devanagari): निर्माता Transliteration: Nirmātā Provenance: Sanskrit Nirmātā is written निर्माता in Devanagari. Each aksara combines a consonant with an inherent or explicit vowel. IAST diacritics preserve length, retroflexion, and aspiration lost in plain ASCII. The Devanagari form is not used as the primary domain because Indic scripts are not in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /nɪr.ˈmaː.taː/ — 'neer-MAH-tah' — stress the long middle syllable, roll the 'r' lightly, and hold both final vowels long. Phonemes: nir-: Voiceless alveolar nasal [n] plus short close front [ɪ] and retroflex tap [r]; the prefix nir- carries the sense of 'out, forth, away' -mā-: Long open [aː], the root mā meaning 'to measure, build, fashion' -tā: Voiceless alveolar stop [t] plus long open [aː]; the agent suffix -tṛ/-tā means 'one who makes' Pronunciation note: Nirmātā is Tier 1 because both ā vowels are long. The name is a transparent Sanskrit agent noun, not a personal divine name in classical Hinduism, but it captures the abstract principle of the divine maker. Character breakdown: n (undefined), i (undefined), r (undefined), m (undefined), a (undefined), t (undefined), a (undefined) Sources: Monier-Williams Sanskrit-English Dictionary

title: Liwyāṯān
text: Name: Liwyāṯān (leviathan) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: canaanite Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Coiled sea serpent Original script (Hebrew): לִוְיָתָן Transliteration: Liwyāṯān Provenance: The name is written לִוְיָתָן in the Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet. Ugaritic ʿayin is rendered with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for DNS registrability. Long vowels are reconstructed from Hebrew and Akkadian cognates and marked with macrons. The Unicode restoration Liwyāṯān is registrable in .com; the Ugaritic cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /liwjaːˈθaːn/ — 'liw-yah-THAHN' — 'liw' rhymes with 'live'; the middle 'yah' is long and stressed; the final 'th' is soft as in 'think', and the last 'a' is drawn out. Phonemes: li-: Alveolar lateral [l] followed by short [i], the hireq under ל. -wə-: Labio-velar approximant [w], the waw functioning as a consonant, with a short vocal sheva [ə]. -yā-: Palatal approximant [j], the yod functioning as a consonant, followed by long [ɔː], the qamets gadol under י. -ṯān: Voiceless interdental fricative [θ] — spirantized taw without dagesh — plus long [ɔː], the qamets gadol under ת, and final [n]. Pronunciation note: BHS points the name לִוְיָתָן (Job 3:8). The form is a nominal derivative from l-w-h 'to twist, turn' with the -ān suffix; the medial waw and yod are consonantal, yielding the sequence [liwjaː-]. Both qamets vowels are long [ɔː]. The taw lacks dagesh and is therefore spirantized [θ] in the Tiberian tradition. The Ugaritic cognate ltn (KTU 1.5 i 1–3) is vocalized by scholars as /lītan-/ or /lōtanu/. HALOT s.v. לִוְיָתָן; TDOT s.v. Leviathan; Day, Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan, 105–6. Character breakdown: l (undefined), e (undefined), v (undefined), i (undefined), a (undefined), t (undefined), h (undefined), a (undefined), n (undefined) Sources: Ugaritic Textual Corpus; Corpus Inscriptionum Semiticarum

title: ꜥnḫ
text: Name: ꜥnḫ (ankh) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: egyptian Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Life; Egyptian ankh sign Original script (Hieroglyphs): 𓋹 Transliteration: ꜥnḫ Provenance: The Egyptian name is written 𓋹 in hieroglyphs. Hieroglyphs combine logograms, phonograms, and determinatives; the exact function of each sign depends on context. Egyptian writing does not record vowels; the vocalised form is a modern convention reconstructed from Coptic and Greek evidence. The Unicode restoration ꜥnḫ uses Egyptological alef/ayin and other registrable characters; the hieroglyphic form is not registrable in .com. Pronunciation: /ˈʕaːnax/ — 'AH-nakh' — say 'ah' from the back of the throat, then 'nakh' with the final consonant like Scottish 'loch' (not a hard English k). Phonemes: Ꜥ-: Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ], the Egyptological Ain (U+A725, small letter; U+A724 is the capital Ꜥ) used as a registrable stand-in for the original guttural; deeper than English 'a' and pronounced far back in the throat. -aː-: Long open vowel reconstructed between the consonants; Egyptian hieroglyphs do not write vowels, and the quality is inferred from Coptic ⲱⲛϩ (ōnh) and from Semitic cognates. -n: Alveolar nasal [n], as in English 'no'. -ḫ: Voiceless velar fricative [x], like the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch' or German 'Bach'; Egyptology also allows a voiced [ɣ] in some periods. Pronunciation note: Hieroglyphic writing records only the consonants Ꜥ-n-ḫ; the vowels are reconstructed from Coptic ⲱⲛϩ and from comparative Semitic evidence. The Ꜥ is a voiced pharyngeal fricative and the ḫ is a voiceless velar fricative, neither of which English possesses. In the PUNICODEX system the Egyptological Ain ꜥ (U+A725, small letter; U+A724 is the capital Ꜥ) serves as the only registrable DNS stand-in for the pharyngeal; this is a Tier 1 restoration that preserves a distinctive consonant the ASCII form loses. Sources: Allen, Middle Egyptian (2014), pp. 18–19, 30; Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, s.v. ꜥnḫ; Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache I, 170–171; Hoch, Semitic Words in Egyptian Texts (1994), on Egyptian–Semitic velar and pharyngeal correspondences. Character breakdown: a (undefined), n (undefined), k (undefined), h (undefined) Sources: A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian; Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar: Being an Introduction to the Study of Hieroglyphs

title: Nḫt
text: Name: Nḫt (nekhet) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: egyptian Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Strong, mighty, victorious Original script (Hieroglyphs): 𓈖𓎛𓏏 Transliteration: Nḫt Provenance: The Egyptian name is written 𓈖𓎛𓏏 in hieroglyphs. Hieroglyphs combine logograms, phonograms, and determinatives; the exact function of each sign depends on context. Egyptian writing does not record vowels; the vocalised form is a modern convention reconstructed from Coptic and Greek evidence. The Unicode restoration Nḫt uses Egyptological alef/ayin and other registrable characters; the hieroglyphic form is not registrable in .com. Pronunciation: /ˈnaxt/ — 'NAKHT' — one syllable, with the 'kh' like Scottish 'loch' (not 'k'). Phonemes: N-: Alveolar nasal [n], as in English 'no'. -a-: Short open vowel; Egyptian hieroglyphs do not write vowels, so the vowel quality is inferred from Coptic and from Semitic transcriptions. -ḫ-: Voiceless velar fricative [x], like the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch'; written with h-breve (U+1E2B). -t: Voiceless alveolar stop [t]; the final consonant of the root. Pronunciation note: The Egyptian root nḫt means 'strong, mighty, victorious'. Hieroglyphs record only N-ḫ-t; the vowel is reconstructed from Coptic ⲛⲟϭ and from the pattern of Egyptian triliteral nouns. The ḫ is a voiceless velar fricative. In PUNICODEX the Nḫt spelling uses the registrable h-breve (U+1E2B) as a Tier 1 restoration — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses; the ASCII fallback is 'nakht'. Sources: Allen, Middle Egyptian (2014); Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, s.v. nḫt; Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache II, s.v. nḫt; Hoch, Semitic Words in Egyptian Texts (1994), on Egyptian ḫ in Semitic orthography. Character breakdown: n (undefined), e (undefined), k (undefined), h (undefined), e (undefined), t (undefined) Sources: A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian; Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache (Erman-Grapow)

title: Mōšeh
text: Name: Mōšeh (moses) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: canaanite Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Hebrew prophet and lawgiver Original script (Hebrew): מֹשֶׁה Transliteration: Mōšeh Provenance: The name is written מֹשֶׁה in the Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet. Ugaritic ʿayin is rendered with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for DNS registrability. Long vowels are reconstructed from Hebrew and Akkadian cognates and marked with macrons. The Unicode restoration Mōšeh is registrable in .com; the Ugaritic cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /moːˈʃɛh/ — 'moh-SHEH' — the first vowel is long and steady like 'mow'; the second syllable is short and crisp, ending in a soft breath. Phonemes: mō-: Bilabial nasal [m] followed by long [oː], the Tiberian holam under מ. -šeh: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] — Hebrew shin, marked by the upper right dot — plus short [ɛ], the segol under ש; the final ה is silent in Masoretic reading, often transcribed only as a breath. Pronunciation note: BHS points the name מֹשֶׁה (Exodus 2:10). The first vowel is a long holam [oː]; the second is a short segol [ɛ]. The Tiberian tradition preserves the final he as a silent mater, not as a pronounced consonant. The name lacks the Tiberian pharyngeals aleph [ʔ] and ayin [ʕ]. HALOT s.v. מֹשֶׁה; TDOT s.v. Moses; Khan, The Tiberian Pronunciation Tradition of Biblical Hebrew (2020). Character breakdown: m (undefined), o (undefined), s (undefined), e (undefined), s (undefined) Sources: Brown, Driver & Briggs, A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament

title: Dāwîḏ
text: Name: Dāwîḏ (david) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: canaanite Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Second king of Israel Original script (Hebrew): דָּוִד Transliteration: Dāwîḏ Provenance: The Masoretic spelling דָּוִד (Dāwîḏ) is preserved in the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia. The first dalet carries a dagesh (דּ) because it follows a silent shewa at the beginning of the word, marking the stop /d/. The vav (ו) with qāmeṣ and ḥīreq points indicates the diphthongal sequence /awī/. The name is traditionally explained as from the root d-w-d 'beloved', though some scholars connect it to a Northwest Semitic theophoric element. Pronunciation: /dɔːˈwiːð/ — 'daw-EEDH' — draw out the first 'aw' like 'dawn'; the middle sound is 'wee' with a glide; the final consonant is a soft 'th' as in 'this'. Phonemes: dā-: Voiced alveolar plosive [d] — dalet with dagesh — followed by long [ɔː], the qamets gadol under ד. -wî-: Labio-velar approximant [w], the waw functioning as a consonant, plus long [iː] from the hireq-yod combination. -ḏ: Voiced dental fricative [ð] — spirantized dalet without dagesh. Some reading traditions keep the final consonant plosive [d], so the exact realization is uncertain. Pronunciation note: BHS points the royal name דָּוִד (1 Samuel 16:13). The initial dalet carries a dagesh (plosive [d]) and a long qamets [ɔː]; the medial waw functions as a consonant [w] with hireq [iː]; the final dalet is spirantized [ð] in Tiberian because it lacks dagesh, though the phonetic realization of a final fricative is debated. HALOT s.v. דָּוִד; TDOT s.v. David. Character breakdown: d (undefined), a (undefined), v (undefined), i (undefined), d (undefined) Sources: R. C. Abraham, Dictionary of Modern Yoruba

title: Šəlōmōh
text: Name: Šəlōmōh (solomon) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: canaanite Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Third king of Israel, builder of the Temple Original script (Hebrew): שְׁלֹמֹה Transliteration: Šəlōmōh Provenance: The name is written שְׁלֹמֹה in the Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet. Ugaritic ʿayin is rendered with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for DNS registrability. Long vowels are reconstructed from Hebrew and Akkadian cognates and marked with macrons. The Unicode restoration Šəlōmōh is registrable in .com; the Ugaritic cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /ʃəloːˈmoː(h)/ — 'shuh-LOH-moh' — start with a quick 'shuh'; both later 'o' sounds are long and steady, like 'show'. Phonemes: šə-: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] — Hebrew shin, marked by the upper right dot — with a short vocal sheva [ə]. -lō-: Lateral approximant [l] followed by long [oː], the holam under ל. -mō(h): Bilabial nasal [m] plus long [oː], the holam under מ; the final ה is silent, a mater lectionis for the long vowel. Pronunciation note: BHS points the name שְׁלֹמֹה (1 Kings 1:1). The initial shewa is vocal (šəwa naʿ) because it opens the word; the two holams are long [oː]. The final he is silent. Modern Israeli Hebrew flattens the vowels to [o] and often elides the shewa, but the Tiberian tradition distinguishes length. HALOT s.v. שְׁלֹמֹה; TDOT s.v. Solomon. Character breakdown: s (undefined), o (undefined), l (undefined), o (undefined), m (undefined), o (undefined), n (undefined) Sources: R. C. Abraham, Dictionary of Modern Yoruba

title: Nōaḥ
text: Name: Nōaḥ (noah) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: canaanite Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Builder of the ark Original script (Hebrew): נֹחַ Transliteration: Nōaḥ Provenance: The name is written נֹחַ in the Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet. Ugaritic ʿayin is rendered with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for DNS registrability. Long vowels are reconstructed from Hebrew and Akkadian cognates and marked with macrons. The Unicode restoration Nōaḥ is registrable in .com; the Ugaritic cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /ˈnoːaħ/ — 'NOH-ahkh' — stress the first syllable and hold the 'o'; the final syllable is a quick 'ah' followed by a throaty 'kh' as in Scottish 'loch'. Phonemes: nō-: Alveolar nasal [n] followed by long [oː], the holam under נ. -aḥ: Short [a] from the furtive patah, pronounced before the final voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ] — Hebrew ḥet. Some traditions render ḥet as a uvular [χ]. Pronunciation note: BHS points the name נֹחַ (Genesis 5:29). The patah under the final ḥet is a furtive patah (pataḥ ganuv): it is pronounced as a short [a] before the guttural, and the word stress remains on the long holam (hence 'NOH-ahkh', not 'no-AHKH'). The ḥet is a voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ] in Tiberian, though Modern Hebrew merges it with [χ]. HALOT s.v. נֹחַ; TDOT s.v. Noah. Character breakdown: n (undefined), o (undefined), a (undefined), h (undefined) Sources: R. C. Abraham, Dictionary of Modern Yoruba

title: Qāyīn
text: Name: Qāyīn (qayin) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: canaanite Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: First son of Adam and Eve Original script (Hebrew): קַיִן Transliteration: Qāyīn Provenance: The name is written קַיִן in the Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet. Ugaritic ʿayin is rendered with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for DNS registrability. Long vowels are reconstructed from Hebrew and Akkadian cognates and marked with macrons. The Unicode restoration Qāyīn is registrable in .com; the Ugaritic cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /qaˈjiːn/ — 'kah-YEEN' — the first consonant is a deep 'k' made at the back of the throat (like Arabic qāf); the second syllable is a long 'yeen'. Phonemes: qa-: Voiceless uvular plosive [q] — Hebrew qof — followed by short [a], the patah under ק. -yīn: Palatal approximant [j], the yod as consonant, plus long [iː] from the hireq-yod combination, ending in alveolar nasal [n]. Pronunciation note: BHS points the name קַיִן (Genesis 4:1). The first vowel is a short patah [a] in the Masoretic pointing, although the qāṭīl-pattern form historically had a long *ā (reflected in the PUNICODEX macron convention Qāyīn); the second vowel is a long hireq-yod [iː]. The qof is a uvular [q], distinct from kaf. HALOT s.v. קַיִן; TDOT s.v. Cain. Character breakdown: q (undefined), a (undefined), y (undefined), i (undefined), n (undefined) Sources: R. C. Abraham, Dictionary of Modern Yoruba

title: Hāḇel
text: Name: Hāḇel (habel) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: canaanite Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Second son of Adam and Eve Original script (Hebrew): הֶבֶל Transliteration: Hāḇel Provenance: The name is written הֶבֶל in the Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet. Ugaritic ʿayin is rendered with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for DNS registrability. Long vowels are reconstructed from Hebrew and Akkadian cognates and marked with macrons. The Unicode restoration Hāḇel is registrable in .com; the Ugaritic cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /ˈhɛvɛl/ — 'HEH-vel' — both vowels are short 'e' as in 'bed'; the 'v' is soft, and the stress falls on the first syllable. Phonemes: hĕ-: Voiceless glottal fricative [h] — Hebrew he — followed by short [ɛ], the segol under ה. -vel: Voiced labiodental fricative [v] — Hebrew vet without dagesh, fricative [β]/[v] — plus short [ɛ], the segol under ב, ending in [l]. Pronunciation note: BHS points the name הֶבֶל (Genesis 4:2). The Tiberian/Masoretic pronunciation is Hevel [ˈhɛvɛl], with two short segol vowels and a fricative bet (vet). The PUNICODEX display form Hāḇel follows the Greek/Latin conventional spelling (Ἅβελ / Abel) rather than the Masoretic vocalization; the macron on ā is not supported by the Tiberian pointing. HALOT s.v. הֶבֶל; TDOT s.v. Abel. Character breakdown: h (undefined), a (undefined), b (undefined), e (undefined), l (undefined) Sources: R. C. Abraham, Dictionary of Modern Yoruba

title: Lóng
text: Name: Lóng (long) Greek / original script form: 龍 Pantheon: chinese Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Chinese dragon Original script (Chinese characters): 龍 Transliteration: Lóng Provenance: The Chinese character 龍 (simplified 龙) represents the dragon, a central cosmological creature in Chinese religion and imperial symbolism. Modern Mandarin reading is lóng (second tone), written in Pinyin with an acute accent. Old Chinese reconstructions include *C-rjoŋ or *mə-roŋ (Baxter-Sagart); the initial consonant cluster is debated. The Unicode restoration Lóng preserves the Mandarin tone mark; the ASCII form loses tone and therefore meaning-distinctive information. Pronunciation: /lʊŋ˧˥/ — LUHNG — the 'o' is like the 'oo' in 'book', and the tone rises from mid to high, as in a questioning intonation. Phonemes: lóng: Single syllable with voiced alveolar lateral approximant [l], final [ʊŋ] (close-mid back rounded vowel + velar nasal), and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). Pinyin 'o' before 'ng' corresponds to IPA [ʊ]. Pronunciation note: 龍 denotes the Chinese dragon, an emblem of imperial authority, fertility, and cosmic yang force. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is lóng (Tone 2), as recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) and standard Mandarin dictionaries. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese form as *[m]-roŋ (GSR 1193a). The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Lóng preserves the citation rising tone of the second tone; in connected speech the contour may be compressed, but the lexical tone remains Tone 2. Character breakdown: l (undefined), o (undefined), n (undefined), g (undefined) Sources: Chinese folklore; Chinese classical texts

title: Wújí
text: Name: Wújí (wuji) Greek / original script form: 無極 Pantheon: taoist Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: The primordial state of emptiness Original script (Chinese characters): 無極 Transliteration: Wújí Provenance: The name is written with the Chinese characters 無極. Each character is a logogram that encodes meaning and historical pronunciation. Hanyu Pinyin with tone marks preserves Mandarin pronunciation; the ASCII form loses tone. The Unicode restoration Wújí is the registrable form because hanzi are outside the .com IDN table. Pronunciation: /u˧˥ tɕi˧˥/ — WOO-JEE — both syllables carry a rising tone (mid to high), like a gentle question on each half. Phonemes: wú: Syllable beginning with labio-velar glide [w] (written 'w' in Pinyin), high back rounded vowel [u], and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). jí: Syllable with unaspirated alveolo-palatal affricate [tɕ], high front vowel [i], and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). Pinyin 'j' is always [tɕ] before front vowels. Pronunciation note: 無極 (Wújí) means 'Limitless' or 'Ultimate Nothing', the undifferentiated state before the emergence of Tàijí in Zhou Dunyi's Taijitu shuo. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is wú (Tone 2) + jí (Tone 2), per the Hanyu Pinyin scheme and the Unihan Database (kMandarin). Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct 無 as *ma (GSR 0103a, 'not have') and 極 as *[g](r)ək (GSR 0910e, 'extreme'). The Unicode restoration Wújí preserves the parallel rising tones of both syllables. title: Yīnyáng

text: Name: Bifrǫst (bifrost) Greek / original script form: — Pantheon: norse Tier: Tier 1 Meaning: Trembling pathway (from bifa, to shake, + rǫst, league) Original script (Younger Futhark runes): ᛒᛁᚠᚱᚬᛋᛏ Transliteration: bifrǫst Provenance: The name Bifrǫst is recorded in the Poetic and Prose Eddas in medieval Icelandic manuscripts. Younger Futhark inscriptions do not preserve the name directly; the runic spelling is a scholarly reconstruction. ᛒ = b, ᛁ = i, ᚠ = f, ᚱ = r, ᚬ = ǫ (rounded back vowel), ᛋ = s, ᛏ = t. The Unicode restoration Bifrǫst preserves the normalized Norse spelling; the runic form is displayed as the original script. Pronunciation: /ˈbif.rɔst/ — 'BIV-rost' — stress the first syllable; let the f pass as a soft breath between the lips, almost a 'v'; say the ǫ as a short, open 'aw' cut in half, not the long 'oh' of the English Bifrost. Phonemes: f: A soft bilabial fricative [β] between vowels, made with both lips rather than the teeth; lighter and voiced compared with the English 'f' ǫ: Short open-mid back rounded [ɔ], the o-ogonek; it is the u-umlaut of a, written ö in Modern Icelandic, and is never the long vowel st: A true final cluster [st]; the r before it is a full alveolar trill and no vowel is inserted between the s and the t Pronunciation note: Cleasby–Vigfusson (s.v. bifrǫst) glosses the name 'the trembling way,' from bifa 'to shake, tremble' and rǫst 'a league, a distance to be traversed'; Zoëga (s.v.) gives the same etymology and records the alternate name Ásbrú 'the Æsir-bridge.' The Eddic codex reads Bilrǫst, with bil 'moment, lapse of time,' and editors still debate which compound is original; Snorri's Bifrǫst is the form that prevailed. The o-ogonek ǫ is a distinctive atomic letter that the ASCII form loses, so the restoration is Tier 1 under the mechanical rule. The name is simply the common noun máni, 'moon', raised to a person — the same word that gives mánaðr, 'month'. title: Maiden of Battles
text: Maiden of Battles: War, Hunt, and Ferocious Loyalty ꜥAnat is the maiden who refuses the domestic sphere . In the Ugaritic texts she is neither wife nor mother but a singular force: a warrior who wades knee-deep in the blood of her enemies, a huntress of the open country, and the most faithful ally of Baꜥal. Her title btlt — 'maiden' — marks her as marriageable, yet mythologically she remains unattached, unpredictable, and absolutely devoted to her brother. Divine Warfare: She fights both armies and cosmic foes, wielding bow, spear, and sword; KTU 1.3 ii describes her battle fury in graphic detail. The Hunt: She ranges mountains and heights in search of game or vengeance; her pursuit of Aqhat turns the hunt into tragic myth. Loyal Sister: Baꜥal's most passionate advocate; she confronts El, avenges Baꜥal's death, and restores the storm to the world. Unbound Feminine Power: A young woman operating in male-coded spheres without condemnation — a figure of autonomous, even terrifying, agency. Symbols: Bow — The peerless bow of Aqhat — she would kill for it, and the land paid the price (KTU 1.17–19); Spear and sword — The blade she turned on Mot itself, splitting death like a stalk of grain (KTU 1.6 ii); Lion — Her leonine ferocity; Day reads her as Ugarit's Mistress of Animals (JNES 51, 1992); Dew and rain — Baꜥal's cleansing gift after battle — war purified by the storm's water (KTU 1.3 ii) ꜥAnat's mythology is preserved chiefly in the Ugaritic Baꜥal Cycle and the Epic of Aqhat. She is not a fertility goddess in the usual sense; she is force itself, concentrated in a young woman's body, and her stories turn on violence, loyalty, and the refusal to accept limits. The Battlefield: Wading Knee-Deep in Blood The most famous portrait of ꜥAnat is a battlefield after the killing is done (KTU 1.3 ii). She stands in her house, her garments spattered, and boasts over her work: 'heads rolled beneath her like balls, the hands of warriors flew over her like locusts.' In exultation she fastens the severed heads to her back and hangs the men's hands on her belt, then sits down to her own victory rite — she slaughters her captives 'beneath her like lambs.' When the gore is spent she washes herself, not in water alone but in the dew of heaven that Baꜥal, the Rider on the Clouds, sends down upon her. The scene appalls and fascinates in equal measure: war here is not grim duty but ecstasy, and the dew that cleanses her comes from her brother, binding her violence to the storm's life-giving water. Destruction and fertility are the two hands of one goddess. Vengeance: The Sowing of Mot When Mōt swallows Baꜥal, ꜥAnat becomes the myth's destroyer of death itself. She ranges the earth searching for her brother; finding him dead, she gives him burial on Zaphon and turns her full ferocity on the god who took him (KTU 1.6 ii). She seizes Mot and works him like a harvest: 'with a sword she splits him, with a sieve she winnows him, with fire she burns him, with millstones she grinds him, in a field she scatters him.' Every verb is a verb of threshing — splitting, winnowing, grinding, scattering — so that the annihilation of death is cast as the harvest it had interrupted. Baꜥal returns, and the rains return with him. The portrait redeems the earlier horror: the ferocity that seemed an excess on the battlefield proves to be the world's repair mechanism. Only an unbounded love, the myth says, is equal to an unbounded appetite — and only a sister could do this work. Epic of Aqhat: The Bow and the Refusal The Epic of Aqhat turns on a gift and a refusal. Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs gives the young hero Aqhat a bow without equal, and ꜥAnat covets it. She offers him silver and gold; he refuses. She offers him the one prize gods cannot truly give — 'years like Baꜥal's, life like the sons of El' — and Aqhat answers with a line the tradition never forgave: bows are for men, not for women. Enraged, the goddess flies to the Sutean warrior Yatpan and, in a disguise the poem savors, orders Aqhat's death. The plan miscarries catastrophically: the marvelous bow is shattered, the land is cursed with drought, and Aqhat's sister Pughat — the poem's quiet, formidable heroine — sets out after Yatpan. The text breaks off before her revenge is complete. Even so, the poem's judgment is plain in its ruined harvest: to deny a goddess her due, whether her honor or her weapon, is to let the whole world dry out. Hymn: Mistress of the Highlands A single fragmentary hymn (KTU 1.13) opens a quieter window on the goddess: the poet sings of Anat the maiden , of the beauty and bounty of the highlands where she roams. Though badly broken, the tablet shows her invoked in blessing — a guardian of her devotees and a power of the open country rather than the city wall, matching her role in the Aqhat epic as a huntress of mountain and steppe. Peggy Day's study of the goddess read her as Ugarit's Mistress of Animals , heir to a Bronze Age tradition of the woman who stands among lions and controls the game, and the fragment coheres with that reading. The hymn matters because almost everything else we have of ꜥAnat is violence; here, at the edge of a broken tablet, is the goddess invoked the way a patron is invoked — for protection, for plenty, for the favor of one who has never learned to be mild. Syncretism: In Egypt, ꜥAnat was worshipped as a war goddess alongside her sister Aštart, especially at Tanis and Memphis; she appears on scarabs and in the Egyptian pantheon as ꜥnt(t). Greeks and Romans later identified her with Athena/Minerva in her martial aspect. Some scholars have argued for an early equation with the Mesopotamian Ishtar/Inanna, since both are young, autonomous warrior goddesses, but the Ugaritic texts treat ꜥAnat as a distinct Levantine figure. In the Hebrew Bible, place names such as Anathoth preserve her memory without endorsing her cult. Cultural legacy: The name ꜥAnat echoes across millennia in unexpected ways. The Israelite town of Anathoth (Jeremiah's birthplace) carries her name. Medieval Jewish folklore remembered her in the figure of the warrior woman, and modern Levantine archaeology has recovered countless amulets and plaques bearing her image. In contemporary literature, film, and Neopagan practice, Anat resurfaces as an icon of untamed female power — a goddess who will not be domesticated, who fights for those she loves, and who makes the boundaries between love and violence uncomfortably thin. Extended meditation: ꜥAnat disturbs the modern imagination because she refuses our categories. She is a young woman and a killer, a sister and an avenger, a goddess of life-giving rain and of blood-soaked battlefields. In a world that still struggles to imagine female power without apology, she stands as a difficult ancestor: not a nurturer, not a consort, but a self-possessed force. Yet her loyalty is unmistakable. Everything she does for Baꜥal — confronting El, destroying Mot, mourning in the wilderness — she does out of love that does not negotiate. To meditate on ꜥAnat is to meditate on the sacredness of rage rightly aimed, on the ferocity that protects rather than merely consumes. She asks us: What would you fight for, without limit, without consent, because it is yours? Original script note: The name is written in Ugaritic alphabetic cuneiform as 𐎓𐎐𐎚 (ʿ-n-t). The first sign is ʿayin, a voiced pharyngeal fricative absent from English and from standard Latin transcription. Because the standard IPA ʿ is blocked at the DNS root, PUNICODEX represents it with the Latin Capital/Small Letter Egyptological Ain (ꜥ / U+A724), preserving visual recognition while remaining registrable.

title: Lady of the Sea
text: Lady of the Sea: Mother of the Gods, Consort of Ēl ꜥAsherah is the great mother of the Canaanite pantheon , the consort of Ēl and the goddess whose very treading calms the sea. Unlike the fierce maiden ꜥAnat, she moves through the myths as queen mother, intercessor, and source of divine legitimacy. Where Ēl is the distant father, Asherah is the active power broker who knows how to approach him. Mother of the Gods: Called qnyt ʾilm, 'Creatress of the Gods'; the seventy sons of Asherah populate the divine court. Lady of the Sea: Her epithet rbt ʾaṯrt ym links her to the Mediterranean, to fishing, and to the cosmic waters tamed by her presence. Royal Intercessor: It is Asherah who petitions Ēl on Baꜥal's behalf, securing permission for the storm-god's palace. Domestic Sovereignty: Spindle, weaving, and nursing imagery mark her as the divine model of women's work raised to cosmic scale. Symbols: Spindle — Her attribute in Ugaritic iconography; symbol of feminine labor and cosmic order; Sea — The waters she treads and tames, source of fertility and commerce for coastal Ugarit; Tree or pole — The biblical ʾăšērâ, a wooden cult object that may represent her presence or be her symbol; Donkey — The beast she rides when approaching Ēl's tent in the Baꜥal Cycle ꜥAsherah does not star in the great combat myths; she rules by relationship. Her appearances in the Baꜥal Cycle show a goddess who can approach the high god, sway his decisions, and guarantee the succession of kings. She is the still center around which the violent younger gods revolve. KTU 1.4: The Queen Mother's Journey In KTU 1.4, Baꜥal longs for a palace but cannot win Ēl's approval directly. He turns to Asherah. She prepares herself with care — bathes, anoints herself, harnesses her donkey, saddles the ass — and travels to Ēl's tent at the source of the two divine rivers, in the midst of the sea's flood. There she prostrates herself, flatters the high god's wisdom ('your decree, Ēl, is wise; your wisdom is everlasting'), and asks that Baꜥal be granted a house 'like the gods'. Ēl laughs with delight, welcomes her, and consents — but not before she has reminded him of what refusal would cost the divine household. Without her diplomacy, Baꜥal would remain homeless, and the cosmos without a storm-god enthroned. The myth means that even the high god's decrees pass through domestic channels: cosmic order is negotiated, not commanded. KTU 1.3–1.4: Creatress of the Gods Asherah is repeatedly called qnyt ʾilm , 'Creatress of the Gods' (KTU 1.3 v 25–26; 1.4 i 23; iii 26) — and the epithet's very ambiguity is revealing, since qny can mean both 'create' and 'acquire, beget': either reading makes her the founder of the divine line. The 'seventy sons of Asherah' (KTU 1.4 vi 46) are the divine council itself — seventy being the round number of totality, so that the phrase is simply another name for the pantheon's full court. When Baꜥal later disappears into Mot's realm and heaven's throne stands empty, it is to her that the gods turn: 'let one of the sons of Asherah occupy his throne.' The crisis of Baꜥal's death is thus staged as a succession question inside her family. The myth means the pantheon is matrilineal at its root: the high god sits above it, but the mother of the gods owns its membership. KTU 1.23: Nurse of the Divine In KTU 1.23, the 'Birth of the Gracious Gods', Asherah stands in the background of a sacred-marriage and birth narrative. The fragmentary lines seem to open with a hieros gamos — Ēl, aroused by two goddesses on the seashore, begets the gracious gods Šaḥar and Šalim, Dawn and Dusk — and Asherah's presence frames the household into which they are born: the newborn gods drink and are suckled, and kings may be called her nurslings. The text is ritual through and through — birth, blessing, suckling performed as liturgy — so that her maternity here is not backstory but ceremony: the community re-enacts divine nursing to secure its own fertility and the king's legitimacy. The myth means the goddess's breast is a political institution — nourishment, once divine, becomes the charter of dynasty. Epithet: The Lady and the Sea Her full title, rbt ʾaṯrt ym , 'Lady Asherah of the Sea', has been read two ways — 'Lady Asherah of the Sea' or 'Lady Asherah who treads on the sea' — and both may be true at once. Ugarit's position explains the title's force: the city lived from the sea, its purple dye, timber, and grain shipped to Cyprus, Egypt, and the Aegean, so a Lady of the Sea is patroness of the entire economy. But the older mythic hearing is eschatological: in the Hebrew Bible's reworking of Canaanite myth, it is still the sea that must be tamed before order can be built, and it is still a female power who stands between the waters and the world. Asherah is therefore a boundary-goddess: she walks where land and water meet and brings the wild under domestic sovereignty. The myth means the sea — commerce and chaos at once — has a mistress, and civilization is her dowry. Syncretism: ꜥAsherah's influence spread far beyond Ugarit. In Hittite treaties she appears as Ašertu, the consort of Elkunirša. In Egypt she was identified with Hathor and venerated under the name Qudshu, 'Holiness.' In Israel and Judah she became the most controversial divine figure of the Bible: the Queen of Heaven, consort of Yahweh in some inscriptions and folk religion, condemned by prophets and reformers. She was later flattened into a mere wooden pole (the ʾăšērâ) by Deuteronomistic polemic. Modern archaeology — especially the Kuntillet ʿAjrud inscriptions — has reopened the question of whether Israelite religion once knew her as God's wife. Cultural legacy: ꜥAsherah is the hidden goddess of the Hebrew Bible. Wherever the prophets rage against 'the Asherah' or the women bake cakes for the Queen of Heaven, they testify to her persistent hold on popular devotion. Her suppression shaped Western monotheism, yet her symbols — the tree, the pole, the nursing mother — survived in folk religion and, some argue, in the very figure of the Shekhinah and the Virgin Mary. Today she is reclaimed by feminist theologians and Neopagans as the divine feminine exiled from the Western canon. Extended meditation: ꜥAsherah teaches a theology of mediation. She is not the storm on the mountain; she is the one who persuades the high god to let the storm have a house. Her power is relational, domestic, and therefore easy to overlook — yet without it, the cosmos loses its cohesion. In an age that often mistakes loudness for authority, Asherah reminds us that influence can be quiet, patient, and rooted in care. She is the queen mother, the wet nurse of gods, the one who walks between sea and shore. To remember her is to remember that the divine feminine was never absent from the ancient Near East; it was edited out later, and what has been edited out can be read back in. Original script note: Ugaritic writes her name 𐎀𐎘𐎗𐎚 (ʾ-a-ṯ-r-t). The third sign, ṯ, represents the voiceless interdental fricative /θ/, as in English 'thin' (cf. ṯlṯ, 'three'); later Semitic reflexes shift it to š. The initial consonant may be glottal stop (ʾ) or pharyngeal (ʿ); the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) is used here as a registrable stand-in. The macron over ē marks the long vowel inferred from Hebrew אֲשֵׁרָה.

title: She of the Womb, Queen of Heaven
text: She of the Womb, Queen of Heaven: Love, War, Fertility, and the Morning Star Aštart is the Phoenician Venus — a goddess in whom love and war are not opposites but twin faces of the same radiant power. She is 'she of the womb,' the planet Venus as deity, and the Queen of Heaven invoked by women across the Levant. In Ugarit she stands just behind ꜥAnat in the warrior-huntress pair; in Phoenicia and Egypt she becomes one of the most widely traveled goddesses of antiquity. Venus and the Stars: The morning and evening star; her celestial body marks the boundaries between day and night, human and divine. Love and Desirability: She governs sexual attraction, fertility, and the life-giving power of the womb; her cult emphasized renewal. Warrior and Huntress: KTU 1.92 casts her as a huntress in the wilderness; in Egypt she rides chariots and battles enemies beside the king. Queen of Heaven: The title invoked by Jewish women in Egypt (Jeremiah 44) and by Phoenician devotees across the Mediterranean. Symbols: Dove — The bird of love and the soul, companion of her Venus aspect — carried west by Phoenician ships; Lion — Her war aspect's ferocity; she shares the leonine grammar of Ishtar and the Qudshu plaques; Horse and chariot — Her Egyptian persona — the naked, scimitar-bearing goddess of the war-chariot; Pomegranate — 'She of the womb' — fertility, blood, and renewal gathered in one fruit Aštart's mythology is more dispersed than centralized. She appears in Ugaritic texts as a huntress and member of Ēl's household, but her full fame comes from Phoenician, Egyptian, and later Greco-Roman cult. She is the goddess who crosses borders as easily as the Phoenician ships that carried her. Ugarit: Aštart the Huntress KTU 1.92 is the only Ugaritic literary text in which Aštart is the protagonist, and it is short and partly broken. The goddess arms herself and goes out into the šd , the open country, where she hunts and fells game; she then returns to serve the meat at the table of her father Ēl and of Yarikh, the moon god. Johannes de Moor's edition titled it Athtartu the Huntress , and it remains the clearest window on her Ugaritic personality — not yet the queen of a great city cult, as she would become at Sidon, but a divine huntress of the wilderness, a goddess of the between places where game runs and boundaries blur. The text has been connected with the ritual hunt known from Emar on the Euphrates, suggesting a seasonal rite lay behind the poem. Even in fragments the figure is vivid: the armed maiden of the steppe, bringing home the kill for the high god's table. Ugarit: In the Household of Ēl In KTU 1.114 — the tale of Ēl's drunken banquet — Aštart appears at the high god's table alongside ꜥAnat, her constant companion in the Ugaritic sources. The two goddesses are the most animated members of Ēl's household: they feast, they stagger home with the incapacitated father of gods, and they share his appetite and his lack of ceremony. The scene is comic, but the pairing is theologically pointed. Where later traditions split the dangerous feminine into separate deities — a love goddess here, a war goddess there — Ugarit kept Aštart and ꜥAnat together as sister powers, appetite and ferocity dining at the same table. Both are called btlt , 'maiden'; both refuse the settled roles of wife and mother. The household of Ēl — the Bible's arch-foe — is here simply a family: loud, tipsy, and fond of its unruly daughters. Phoenicia: Queen of Heaven Aštart's Phoenician career turned her into a civic sovereign. At Sidon she presided over one of the Levant's greatest sanctuaries, honored in royal inscriptions from the ninth century onward; at Tyre she stood beside Melqart as the city's divine pair. Her title Queen of Heaven — mlkt šmym — became so beloved that it outlived her cult: in Jeremiah 44, Jewish refugees in Egypt tell the prophet to his face that their wives, daughters, and they themselves have kept baking cakes for the Queen of Heaven, 'as we and our ancestors... did in the towns of Judah.' Farther west, the gold tablets of Pyrgi record a joint dedication of the Caeretan sanctuary to Uni — usually identified with Aštart — and the local king. Her cult traveled Phoenician trade routes from Carthage to Kition to Sicily, making her one of the most widely worshipped goddesses of the first millennium BCE. Egypt: The Warrior of the Nile New Kingdom Egypt adopted the Levantine goddess with enthusiasm. From the reign of Amenhotep II onward, Aštart — ꜥa-set-ir-ti — appears as a goddess of horses and chariotry, shown with the naked body, Hathoric wig, and raised scimitar of the Asiatic war goddess, protecting the pharaoh in his chariot and trampling his enemies. At Tanis and Memphis her cult flourished; Ramesside tradition could identify her with the leonine Sakhmet, and her image spreads across Delta scarabs and temple reliefs. A late Egyptian tale — the so-called Astarte Papyrus, its leading women nameless in what survives — dramatizes the Sea's demand for tribute from the gods, a plot scholars have long compared with the Ugaritic Baꜥal Cycle; whether Aštart stood at its center is debated. Either way, the papyrus shows how deeply her mythic world had been naturalized on the Nile by the end of the Bronze Age. Syncretism: Aštart is the West Semitic face of the older Mesopotamian Ištar, and the two names almost certainly share a common ancestor, though the exact historical path is debated. The Greeks identified her with Aphrodítē in matters of love and with Ártemis in matters of hunting; the Romans made her their Venus. In Egypt she merged with Sakhmet and Hathor.
