Pinyin Nézhā combines the special proper-name reading né (Tone 2) of 哪 — preserved only in this name, the ordinary interrogative reading being nǎ — with 吒 zhā (Tone 1), as recorded in the standard dictionaries and the Unihan Database. The name is a medieval transcription of Sanskrit Nalakūvara, so no Old Chinese reconstruction applies. The tone-marked restoration Nézhā maps directly to the registrable domain form: the display keeps both diacritics (é and ā, both registrable IDN characters), and no apostrophe is required anywhere in the name.

title: Goddess of the Cold Moon
text: Goddess of the Cold Moon: Immortality, Exile, Reunion Chángé is the woman who swallowed forever and paid for it with the earth. Wife of the archer Hòuyì, she came into possession of the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West — and drank it. Whether to keep it from a treacherous disciple or out of her own longing, the sources divide; what they agree on is the result: she rose through the night until the moon received her, and there she remains, in the Guǎnghán Palace — the Palace of Vast Cold. The Moon: Her dwelling and her domain; the full moon of Mid-Autumn is read as her face, brightest and roundest when mortal eyes seek reunion. The Archer Hòuyì: Her husband, who shot down nine of the ten suns and received the elixir of immortality from Xīwángmǔ — the gift that divided them forever. The Palace of Vast Cold: The Guǎnghán Palace (廣寒宮), her luminous and solitary court on the moon, shared with the Jade Rabbit and the woodcutter Wú Gāng. Reunion under the Full Moon: The Mid-Autumn Festival (中秋節): mooncakes, moon-gazing, and the gathering of families — the night her separation sanctifies mortal togetherness. Symbols: The full moon — Her dwelling and her face; completeness, distance, and the reunion it mirrors; The Jade Rabbit — Her companion (玉兔), who pounds the elixir of immortality with mortar and pestle — labor without end in her service; Mortar and pestle — The ceaseless preparation of the elixir she carried to heaven; The cassia tree — The self-healing tree Wú Gāng chops forever beside her palace — punishment and persistence in a single image; The mooncake — The round pastry of Mid-Autumn, cut and shared as an edible likeness of the moon she rules Chángé's story is short and inexhaustible: one ascent, endlessly retold. The early sources preserve a bare skeleton — an elixir, a flight, a moon — and two thousand years of poets, painters, and festival-goers have hung their longing on it. Huainanzi, Lǎnmíng xùn: The Elixir of Immortality The core myth, fixed in the Lǎnmíng xùn 覽冥訓 chapter of the Huáinánzǐ (c. 139 BCE), begins with the archer Hòuyì, who had shot down nine of the ten suns and so received from Xīwángmǔ, Queen Mother of the West, the elixir of immortality. Chángé took it and floated up to the moon, where she became its goddess. The sources divide on her motive: in some versions she drinks to keep the elixir from Féngméng, Hòuyì's treacherous disciple; in others she drinks out of her own longing for deathlessness. Scholarship preserves both strands rather than adjudicating between them — the myth holds theft and sacrifice in suspension, and it is precisely the undecidability that has kept two thousand years of readers arguing on her behalf or against it — the earliest Chinese debate about a woman's motives that is still open. Naming Taboo: From Héng'é to Chángé The goddess was originally 姮娥 Héng'é . Under the Han, her name was altered to avoid the naming taboo on the personal name of Emperor Wen, Liú Héng 劉恆: the graph 姮 was replaced by the synonymous 常, and Héng'é became Chángé. It is a rare case where imperial censorship is legible inside a divine name itself — a goddess renamed so that a mortal emperor's name could remain unspoken. The change also shows how the myth lived inside institutions rather than outside them: not a fossil preserved in a book, but a name people actually said, and therefore a name the court could edit. Every modern recitation of 'Chángé' quietly repeats a two-millennium-old act of deference — the goddess has been carrying an emperor's taboo on her own identity ever since. Lunar Folklore: The Jade Rabbit and the Woodcutter Her court on the moon is small and eternal. The Jade Rabbit (玉兔) stands at her side, pounding the elixir of immortality with mortar and pestle — the same work, night without end. Beside the palace grows a cassia tree that heals every wound the moment it is struck; the woodcutter Wú Gāng was condemned to fell it, and so he chops forever at a trunk that will not fall. Companionship, labor, and futility share one silver landscape. The two figures are the goddess's household gods of persistence: one works usefully forever, the other pointlessly forever, and the moon keeps both. Folk religion rarely states its theodicy outright, but here it is drawn plainly — the wheel of toil turns under every sky, even the coldest one, and the only comfort is that someone is there while it turns. Festival: The Mid-Autumn Moon At the full moon of the eighth lunar month, China keeps the Mid-Autumn Festival (中秋節). Families gather, mooncakes are cut into wedges like the phases returning to round, and eyes turn upward to the brightest moon of the year — to her. Sū Shì's famous lyric of 1076 closes with the wish that, though a thousand miles apart, we may share chánjuān 嬋娟 — the lovely one, the moon, her. The festival reads her exile backward: the goddess who can never come home becomes the patroness of everyone who can. It is the myth's final inversion — the coldest palace in heaven underwriting the warmest night on earth, and loss itself converted, once a year, into an instrument of reunion: the goddess of distance presiding over the one night no one is meant to spend apart. Syncretism: The rabbit in the moon is older than any single nation's telling of it. Buddhist tradition carried the śaśajātaka — the tale of the rabbit who offered itself as food and was set in the moon as a reward — from India into East Asia, and scholars commonly link the Chinese moon rabbit to this transmission, though the Jade Rabbit's elixir-pounding is China's own elaboration. Taoist religion absorbed Chángé into its celestial bureaucracy, where she is often identified with the sovereign of the yin luminary (太陰). Japan received the moon rabbit without the elixir: there he pounds mochi instead, and the autumn moon-viewing custom ( tsukimi ) echoes Mid-Autumn without keeping its goddess. Korea's harvest festival Chuseok and Vietnam's Tết Trung Thu share the same full-moon night of cakes, lanterns, and family gathering — the festival traveled further than the myth, and in each harbor took local form. Cultural legacy: Chángé has been China's shorthand for beautiful distance since the poets claimed her. Sū Shì's Mid-Autumn lyric closes with the wish that, though a thousand miles apart, we may share chánjuān 嬋娟 — the lovely one, the moon, her. The Mid-Autumn Festival remains one of the great holidays of the Chinese world, and the mooncake its edible emblem. In 2020 the animated film Over the Moon carried her to global audiences as a pop-diva goddess still waiting for Hòuyì. Most remarkably, she has gone back: China's lunar exploration program is named for her, and the probes Chángé 1 through 6 (2007–2024) orbited the moon, landed on it, achieved the first landing on its far side (Chángé 4), and returned samples to earth (Chángé 5 and 6). No other deity in this lexicon has been so literally restored to her own heaven. Extended meditation: Chángé teaches that every ascent is also a departure. She took the one thing everyone is told to want — endless life — and found that it cost the one thing that makes life bearable: the person she left below. The myth refuses to resolve her motive, and that refusal is its honesty; we have all swallowed things half in longing and half in self-defense, and only later learned which. Her moon is the most beautiful object in the Chinese night precisely because it is the far side of reunion — the light by which the separated recognize one another. To name a domain Chángé is to claim that paradox: the cold palace and the warm festival, the exile and the homecoming, the goddess who cannot return and the probes that returned for her. It is a name for anyone who understands that distance is not the opposite of devotion but, too often, its price. Original script note: The original script is 嫦娥, written identically in traditional and simplified Chinese; the earlier form of the name is 姮娥, altered under the Han naming taboo on Emperor Wen's personal name. Pinyin Chángé (Tone 2 + Tone 2) is the Modern Standard Mandarin reading, recorded in the Unihan Database and standard dictionaries. The apostrophe is part of standard Hanyu Pinyin orthography, separating the two syllables so the name cannot be misread as a single syllable or wrongly divided; the display form Chángé keeps it, while the registrable domain label drops it, since IDN labels cannot contain an apostrophe — the tone-marked vowels alone carry the restoration into the domain system.

title: Archer of the Nine Fallen Suns
text: Archer of the Nine Fallen Suns: Precision, Deliverance, the Spared Light Hòuyì is the divine archer of Chinese myth, the hero who stood between heaven's excess and the earth's survival. In the age of the sage-emperor Yáo, the ten suns — three-legged crows, sons of Dìjùn and the sun-mother Xīhé — rose all at once instead of taking their appointed turns. Rivers dried, crops failed, and monsters crawled out of the scorched wilderness. Hòuyì drew his great bow and shot nine suns from the sky, sparing one so that day and night, sowing and harvest, could keep their order. His story is a hinge between worlds: the same bow that cleared the earth of monsters also won him the elixir of immortality from Xīwángmǔ, the Queen Mother of the West — the elixir his wife Chángé would ultimately take, fleeing to the moon. The archer who saved the earth lost heaven, and Chinese myth has never stopped telling both halves of that story. The Divine Bow: The great bow and its arrows are heaven's instruments of correction — not conquest, but the precise removal of what has grown excessive. The Ten Suns: Ten three-legged crow-suns, sons of Dìjùn and Xīhé, once took turns crossing the sky; their simultaneous rising nearly ended the world. Slayer of Monsters: With the suns subdued, Yi cleared the earth of the beasts the drought had unleashed: Yàyǔ, Záochǐ, Jiǔyīng, Dàfēng, the serpent Xiūshé, and the boar Fēngxī. The Elixir: Xīwángmǔ's gift of immortality, earned by the archer's service — and lost when Chángé drank it and rose to the cold palace of the moon. Symbols: The great bow and arrows — Heaven-sent precision; the power to correct cosmic disorder without destroying the cosmos; The three-legged crow — The true form of each sun; nine were shot down, and the tenth still crosses the sky; The Fusang tree — The cosmic mulberry at the eastern edge of the world where the ten suns roosted between journeys; The elixir of immortality — Xīwángmǔ's reward and the pivot of loss — the gift that carried Chángé to the moon; The spared sun — Measured judgment; the hero preserves the order he restores rather than abolishing it The cycle of Hòuyì is the great Chinese myth of cosmic correction: a heaven that gives too much, an earth that suffers for it, and one archer whose arrows restore the mean. Its episodes run from the scorched world of the ten suns to the cold moon where his wife still dwells — and to the darker coda in which the master dies by his student's hand. Shanhaijing · Huainanzi: The Shooting of the Nine Suns In the reign of Emperor Yáo, the ten suns — three-legged crows roosting in the Fusang tree, sons of Dìjùn and the sun-mother Xīhé — abandoned their orderly rotation and rose together. The earth burned: rivers dried, crops withered, and the people starved. Yáo called on Hòuyì, the divine archer, who climbed to the heights and loosed his arrows. One by one nine suns fell from the sky in their crow forms, and the tenth — spared at Yáo's prayer, or the archer's own measure — resumed its solitary, lawful journey. The myth is told across the Shān Hǎi Jīng tradition, given its fullest early form in the Huáinánzǐ (139 BCE), and interrogated with wonderful skepticism in the Chǔ Cí poem Tiān Wèn ('Why did Yì shoot down the suns? Why did the crows shed their feathers?'). The myth teaches that the world can be saved not by abolishing light but by restoring its measure — and that one well-aimed arrow can outweigh a cosmos of excess. Huainanzi: The Clearing of the Monsters The drought had loosed terrors on the world, and the Huáinánzǐ lists the archer's second labor in its characteristic catalogue: he slew Yàyǔ, the man-eating beast of the wilds; Záochǐ in the waters of Chouhua; Jiǔyīng, the nine-headed monster of the Xiong river; the great wind-bird Dàfēng in the marshes of Qingqiu; the giant serpent Xiūshé at Lake Dongting; and the monstrous boar Fēngxī in the mulberry groves of Sanglin. When the last beast fell, 'the people of all within the seas rejoiced, and the ten thousand things came to life.' Only then could the people plow in peace. The second labor teaches that the hero's work is never finished with the wonder: after the miracle, the ordinary world must still be made safe for ordinary life — and Chinese myth, unusually, gives us the inventory. Cosmic correction, the list insists, is mostly administration. Huainanzi · later tradition: The Elixir and the Flight of Chángé For his service, Xīwángmǔ, the Queen Mother of the West, granted Hòuyì the elixir of immortality. He brought it home — and there the story turns. His wife Chángé took the elixir and rose to the moon, leaving the archer mortal and alone on the earth he had saved. The earliest tellings are strikingly spare about her motive; later tradition filled the silence with variants — she stole it, she drank it to keep it from the archer's treacherous disciple Féngméng, she swallowed both halves meant to be shared. On the moon she keeps company with the cassia tree and the jade rabbit, and the Huáinánzǐ already records that 'Chángé went to the moon' and became a toad. The Chángé sequel became the myth every Chinese child knows first, and the Mid-Autumn Festival still gathers families to look for her. The cycle's hinge is this: the archer who measured the suns could not measure his own household, and the elixir passed to the one he loved — heaven's justice arriving sideways. Mengzi 7B.24: The Betrayal of Féngméng The darker strand of the cycle is preserved already in the Mèngzǐ, which records that Féngméng (逢蒙) studied archery under Yì and, once he had learned all that Yì could teach, killed his master — in the fuller later accounts, clubbing him to death with a peachwood staff. The Mèngzǐ itself weighs how far Yì shared the blame for trusting such a man, and Chinese moralists have debated the lesson ever since. The student murders the teacher the moment the teaching is complete — and the cycle refuses to let its hero end on the pyre of his own glory. The tradition asks the harder question — what did the master teach, that the lesson could not survive its teacher? — and answers it unsparingly: mastery without loyalty unmakes both, and even the archer of the suns could not shoot his way out of a student's ambition. The gods gave him a bow for monsters; they gave him no defense against gratitude turned. Syncretism: Hòuyì's myth traveled with Chinese civilization itself. In Japan the story of the archer and the ten suns was known through Chinese texts and pictorial art, where it informed depictions of solar catastrophe alongside native Amaterasu lore; Korea received the cycle through the same classical canon, and its own founding archer figure Jumong — whose very name is glossed as 'skilled archer' — shows how deeply the archer-hero type resonated on the peninsula. Vietnamese tradition likewise absorbed the ten-suns narrative through Chinese literature. Within China, Taoist tradition folded Yì into its cosmology of solar regulation and immortality elixirs, while the Queen Mother of the West, his benefactor, rose to become one of the highest deities of the Taoist pantheon. Scholars have long noted the parallel with other great archers — Apollo's plague-bringing arrows in Greece, Rama's bow in India — but the Chinese version is distinctive: the archer's target is not a rival god but disorder itself. Cultural legacy: Hòuyì never left the Chinese imagination. The shooting of the suns is among the first myths Chinese children learn, retold in primers, animated films, and television dramas, and the Chángé sequel anchors the Mid-Autumn Festival, when families gaze at the moon where the archer's wife is said to dwell. Modern China has written the pair onto the sky itself: the national lunar exploration program is named Chángé, and its missions are spoken of as the moon goddess finally receiving visitors — a deliberate bridal of myth and engineering. The idiom of 'shooting the suns' survives as a metaphor for cutting down excess and correcting what has grown monstrous. In art, from Han dynasty tomb reliefs to contemporary illustration, the archer drawing his bow against a wheel of suns remains one of the most recognizable images in the Chinese visual canon. Extended meditation: Hòuyì teaches the hardest lesson of heroism: that power must know when to stop. Nine arrows were justice; a tenth would have been annihilation. The archer's greatness lies not in what he destroyed but in the one sun he spared — the judgment that the world needs light, only not too much of it. Chinese thought found in this a parable of the mean: excess, even of a good thing, is the true monster, and correction, not eradication, is the hero's work. And yet the myth refuses him a clean triumph. The savior of the earth loses immortality, loses his wife, and in the darker telling dies at the hand of his own student. To name a domain Hòuyì is to claim that double inheritance: the steadiness to draw the bow against a burning sky, and the humility to accept that even perfect aim cannot hold everything it wins. Original script note: The original script is 后羿, identical in traditional and simplified Chinese (the character 后 'sovereign' must not be confused with 後 'after', which simplifies to 后 — in the archer's name it is the archaic title, 'lord'). Pinyin Hòuyì (both syllables Tone 4) is the Modern Standard Mandarin reading, recorded in the Unihan Database and standard dictionaries. The registrable Unicode restoration uses the tone-marked Pinyin Hòuyì rather than the hanzi because PUNICODEX renders the original characters in the temple's 'Original Script' card while keeping the domain label pronounceable and internationally registrable; the name carries no apostrophe, so the display form and the domain form differ only in the tone marks. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese reading of 羿 as *N-ŋ(r)ik-s.

title: Kings of the Four Seas
text: Kings of the Four Seas: Crystal Palaces, Rain by Mandate, the Bureaucracy of Water Lóngwáng , the Dragon King, is not one god but a crowned office — the royal administration of water. Four brothers hold the Four Seas in crystal palaces beneath the waves; the Jade Emperor decrees each rain by amount and hour, and the Dragon King delivers it exactly. A king in his own water, a clerk in heaven's: sovereignty won by accountability. The Four Seas: Four royal brothers divide the encircling oceans — East, South, West, and North — each ruling tides, storms, and every creature of his sea from a crystal palace below the waves. Rain by Mandate: Rainfall is paperwork: the Jade Emperor decrees the amount and the hour, and the Dragon King executes the order exactly — to alter either is treason against heaven. The Sea Treasury: The crystal palace hoards the wealth of the waters — pearls, coral, and the Rúyì Jīngū Bàng, the iron pillar that once pinned the seas, until the Monkey King claimed it for a staff. Kingship under Heaven: The Dragon King is sovereign in his own water and a subject above it — a king who kneels to the celestial bureaucracy and answers with his life for every misplaced drop. Symbols: Crystal palace — The underwater court (龍宮, Dragon Palace) — sovereignty, hidden wealth, and the ordered world beneath the chaos of the sea; Rúyì Jīngū Bàng — The compliant gold-banded staff, an iron pillar that once pinned the seas — the tameable measure of the waters, taken from the East Sea treasury by Sūn Wùkōng; Dragon robe and royal crown — Enfeoffed kingship within the celestial bureaucracy — the Dragon King rules as a peer of heaven's administration, not as a free lord; Rain clouds and tidal bore — The waters he commands — rain, rivers, lakes, and tides delivered by decree, withheld in drought, unleashed in flood; Shrimp soldiers and crab generals — The aquatic retinue of the Dragon Palace — the sea's own creatures enrolled as a court, a mirror of the imperial administration below the waves The Dragon Kings stand at the crossing of two Chinas: the literary China of the great Ming novels, where they are foils, creditors, and comic bureaucrats, and the living China of the village temple, where they were the address to which a drought-stricken county sent its prayers. The same figure is mocked in the novel and begged in the field. Journey to the West: The Jìng River Dragon King's Wager The great cautionary tale of the celestial bureaucracy survives in Journey to the West (ch. 9). The Dragon King of the Jìng River wagers with the Chang'an fortune-teller Yuán Shǒuchéng over the coming day's rain; the diviner names the hour and the inch, and when the Jade Emperor's decree arrives it matches exactly. Unwilling to lose the bet, the king secretly shaves the allotted rain and delays its fall by an hour. The difference is trifling, and it does not matter: for editing heaven's paperwork he is condemned to death, with the mortal minister Wei Zheng appointed as executioner. His ghost then haunts the Tang emperor who had promised to save him — an embarrassment that drags the entire plot of the novel into motion. The myth's arithmetic is merciless. In a cosmos run as an administration there are no small alterations, and the smallest forgery is treason. Investiture of the Gods: Nézhā and the Third Prince In the Investiture of the Gods (ch. 12–13), the boy Nézhā, bathing where the river meets the East Sea, churns the water with his magic Red Armillary Sash until the crystal palace of Āo Guǎng trembles on its foundations. The Dragon King sends his yaksha enforcer and then his third son, Āo Bǐng; the child kills them both and plucks out the prince's sinews to make a belt. Robbed of an heir, Āo Guǎng demands justice of heaven and of Li Jing's town alike; and faced with the choice between his family and his child's life, Li Jing hesitates. Nézhā answers with the terrible arithmetic of filial duty — cutting himself apart, returning his flesh to his mother and his bones to his father, so that the debt dies with him. The Dragon King wins the confrontation and loses everything he came for: his son is not restored, and the story every Chinese child knows is not his. The myth's sympathy lies entirely with the child. Journey to the West: The Sea-Pinning Iron Needing a weapon worthy of himself, Sūn Wùkōng descends to Āo Guǎng's treasury and waves aside every blade and spear the court can offer ( Journey to the West , ch. 3). What he takes instead is a fixture of the deep: the Rúyì Jīngū Bàng, the Compliant Gold-Banded Staff, a black iron pillar thirteen thousand five hundred catties heavy that once pinned the seas and measured the flood-waters of the world. To the Dragon King it was obsolete hardware; to the Monkey King it shrinks to a needle behind the ear and grows to a pillar that props up heaven. The other three Dragon Kings, summoned to help, can only add golden armor, cloud-walking shoes, and a phoenix-feather cap while their brother's treasury walks out the door. To the water's own government the staff was the sea's measure; to the rebel it became the measure of the rebel — and the East Sea never got it back. Folk Religion: Parading the King in the Sun Dragon King temples (龍王廟) once dotted farming China, and when the rains failed the county did not pray — it petitioned. Processions, offerings, and rain-letters addressed the local king as a magistrate who had neglected his district; ethnographers of North China recorded what came next in extreme drought: the king's lacquered effigy was carried from his shrine and paraded through the burning fields, or set in the sun before his own temple door, so that he might feel on his own scales the heat his villages were dying of. Some communities threatened to leave the statue outdoors, or unroofed, until the rain came. It is a theology of astonishing literalness — the god made answerable by exposure, his comfort held hostage to his performance. Few traditions anywhere have written accountability so plainly into ritual: sovereignty over water is a mandate, and mandates, the farmers knew, are reviewable by the ruled. Syncretism: The Dragon Kings are among the clearest cases of Buddhism and native Chinese religion merging into a single figure. Native Chinese water-dragon and river-god cults are ancient, but the named kings with submarine palaces, retinues, and treasuries owe much to the Indian nāgarājas — serpent kings of the waters — carried into China with the translated sūtras; Chinese translators rendered nāga as lóng (dragon), and the eight nāga kings of Buddhist scripture became native sea-kings. The relative weight of the Indian import against the older Chinese cult remains a matter of scholarly debate. Taoism then absorbed the kings wholesale into its celestial administration as rain officials answerable to the Jade Emperor. From China the figure travelled with the culture: in Japan the dragon kings appear as ryūō , kin to the sea-god Ryūjin of the undersea palace; in Korea as Yongwang , propitiated by fishing and farming villages alike; in Vietnam as Long Vương , guardian of waters and of the nation's own dragon genealogy. Cultural legacy: The Dragon King never fully retired. His temples still stand along China's coasts and rivers, and rain-processions to the local king persisted in the countryside into the twentieth century. In literature and performance he is a permanent stock character: every adaptation of the Journey to the West — opera, film, television, animation — must eventually send someone down to the crystal palace, whether to borrow a weapon or to wreck the court. The feud with Nézhā alone has carried him through a century of Chinese animation, from the 1979 feature Nézhā Nào Hǎi ( Nezha Conquers the Dragon King ) to the 2019 blockbuster Ne Zha , where the dragon clan's grievance drives the plot. In the modern idiom the Dragon King's palace remains a byword for fabulous drowned wealth, and the figure himself endures wherever Chinese fantasy needs a throne beneath the sea. Extended meditation: The Dragon King teaches that water is governed, not merely unleashed. In the Chinese imagination even rain is paperwork: every shower has an issuing authority, an amount, an hour, and a signature. This is not a failure of wonder but a different kind of wonder — the conviction that the wildest force in the farmer's world can be brought under seal and ledger, and that the price of that order is absolute accountability. The Jìng River king lost his head for a trifle of water and an hour's delay, because in a cosmos run as an administration there is no such thing as a small alteration. To name a domain Lóngwáng is therefore to claim the throne under the waves: the palace where treasure and law are kept together, where the sea's own creatures wear the robes of ministers, and where a king may be sovereign of all he surveys and still answer for every drop. It is the oldest Chinese lesson about power — that it is real only when it is answerable. Original script note: The original script is 龍王 in traditional Chinese and 龙王 in simplified. The Pinyin reading Lóngwáng — two Tone-2 (rising) syllables — is the Modern Standard Mandarin citation form, recorded in the Unihan Database (kMandarin) and standard dictionaries. The tone-marked restoration keeps both acute accents as the display form; the registrable domain maps the accented vowels to their ASCII base letters, giving longwang . No syllable-boundary apostrophe is required: the segmentation lóng·wáng is unambiguous, so the display and domain forms differ only in the tone marks. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese forms as *[m]-roŋ (龍) and *[ɢ]ʷaŋ (王).

title: The Western Paradise
text: The Western Paradise: The Peaches of Immortality, Mount Kūnlún, and the Taming of a Wilderness Goddess Xīwángmǔ , the Queen Mother of the West, has the strangest biography of any great Chinese goddess: in the oldest text she is a tiger-toothed power of plague on Mount Kūnlún; by the Han she is enthroned in the western paradise; by the Tang she hosts the Peach Banquet and guards the elixir. The wilderness was never banished from her — it was enthroned. Mount Kūnlún: Her paradise stands on Mount Kūnlún at the western edge of the world, the axis where heaven leans down to meet the wild earth. The Peaches of Immortality: The pántáo ripen once every three thousand years; to taste one is to step outside death's jurisdiction — which is why the Monkey King could not resist them. Tiger's Teeth, Leopard's Tail: Her archaic form keeps its claws: the Shān Hǎi Jīng gives her a tiger's teeth and a leopard's tail, the regalia of a mistress of plague and calamity. Sovereign of Yin and the West: In mature Taoist theology she rules yin, the west, and all goddesses, balanced against Dōngwánggōng's yang and east — the two poles of a complete cosmos. Symbols: The shèng headdress — Her ancient insignia of authority — the distinctive headdress she wears even in her oldest, wildest images; Tiger's teeth and leopard's tail — The zoomorphic vestiges of her primordial form, marking her dominion over plague and calamity; The Peaches of Immortality — Sovereignty over death itself — fruit that ripens once in three thousand years and frees the eater from mortality; Mount Kūnlún — The western paradise at the edge of the world, where her palace and orchards stand; The tallies — The tokens her Han-era devotees carried from commandery to commandery as pledges of her protection and long life Xīwángmǔ's myths trace an arc no other Chinese deity matches: from wilderness terror to the most gracious sovereign of the Taoist heavens. Each age kept something of the last, so that the serene hostess of the Peach Banquet still carries the teeth and tail of the mountain power she once was. Shan Hai Jing: The Fearsome Portrait Her oldest portrait is the strangest. In the Classic of Mountains and Seas , compiled from Warring States to Han materials, the Queen Mother "has the form of a human, the tail of a leopard, the teeth of a tiger, and is good at whistling; her tangled hair is bound with a sheng headdress" (ch. 2, Xishan jing). A later stratum adds her office — she "presides over the calamities of heaven and the five punishments" (ch. 16, Dahuang xi jing), seated on Mount Kūnlún with three azure birds to fetch her food. She is not yet a queen in any courtly sense. She is the numinous danger of the far west itself: the lands where the sun goes down, source of plague and of everything the settled world cannot control. Later ages would dress her in silk and seat her among goddesses — but the earliest text keeps her wild, and the wildness never entirely left the throne. Huainanzi: The Elixir for Hòuyì It is from Xīwángmǔ that immortality flows. The Huainanzi records that Hòuyì, the archer who shot down the nine excess suns, "begged the elixir of undying from the Queen Mother of the West" — and that his wife Héng'é stole it and fled to the moon, where she became the moon's goddess (her name later softened to Cháng'é under a Han emperor's name-taboo). Versions disagree about the theft — greed, fear, or rescue of the elixir from unworthy hands — but they agree on the source: no one in the Chinese cosmos rises beyond death except through the Queen Mother's treasury. The same storehouse reappears in every later system: her peaches ripen once in three thousand years; her banquet seats the assembled immortals; her garden is raided in every retelling of the Monkey King. Sovereignty over the boundary between life and death was her first office and remained her last — whether she wore a leopard's tail or a phoenix crown. Book of Han: The Movement of 3 BCE The Queen Mother was never only a goddess of mirrors and palace ladies. In 3 BCE — recorded in the Book of Han (ch. 11, Annals of Emperor Ai) — her cult ignited across the empire: crowds in more than twenty commanderies passed her tally-tokens (chóu) from hand to hand, sang and danced in the streets, wore her tokens, and converged on the capitals "thousands strung together", awaiting the fulfilment of her promise. The movement alarmed the court enough to be entered in the dynastic history — one of the earliest documented popular religious movements in China, three centuries before the organized Daoist church. The tallies were small pieces of wood, and their passing was the whole theology: a pledge, from the goddess of the west, that the world as it was could not last. The chroniclers record the phenomenon and not the promise. The crowds, clearly, knew what they were waiting for. Journey to the West: The Theft of the Peaches Once in three thousand years the Peaches of Immortality ripen in the Queen Mother's orchard, and once in three thousand years she hosts the pántáohuì , the Peach Banquet, for the assembled immortals, gods, and buddhas of the three religions. In Journey to the West (ch. 5) the task of guarding the orchard is given, with fatal optimism, to Sūn Wùkōng — who samples the fruit systematically, dining on the 3,000-year, 6,000-year, and 9,000-year trees alike, and then crashes the feast itself in a disguise borrowed from a serving goddess. It is one of literature's great heists, and its comedy rests on real theology: the peaches are the most tightly held treasure in heaven, ripening on a schedule longer than recorded history, and the Queen Mother is their unanswerable custodian. The Monkey King's appetite did what no god could. It made her orchard — and her three-thousand-year patience — the most famous garden in Chinese fiction. Mu Tianzi Zhuan: The Hostess at the Jasper Pool Before she was a Taoist sovereign she was a royal hostess. The Mu Tianzi Zhuan (Account of King Mu) — a Warring States text unearthed in 281 CE from a Wei royal tomb — sends King Mu of Zhou to her Jasper Pool (Yáochí) at the western edge of the world. There she receives the traveling king as an equal: she sings to him in the text's archaic verse — "white clouds in the sky, the road long, mountains between us; may you not die, and come again" — and he answers in kind before turning his eight-horse team east. The scene is her earliest humane portrait, and it fixed two things: the title by which Taiwanese temples still know her, Golden Mother of the Jasper Pool, and her oldest character — not empress, not bureaucrat, but the hostess at the end of the road, inviting the greatest traveler of the age to live long enough to come back. Every later banquet descends from that first cup of wine at the edge of the world. Syncretism: The Queen Mother travelled with Chinese letters and liturgy across East Asia. In Japan she is read Seiōbo , appearing in painting, garden imagery, and the literary imagination as the hostess of the western orchard; in Korea she is Seowangmo , present in folklore and shamanic song; in Vietnamese she is Tây Vương Mẫu , her name borne into the southern reception of the Taoist pantheon. Within China her deepest transformation was her absorption into organized Taoism, where she rose to the summit of the celestial hierarchy as sovereign of yin and the west, paired with Dōngwánggōng, the King Father of the East, as the balanced poles of the cosmos. Buddhist storytellers did not so much absorb her as borrow her orchard: the immortality peaches and the great banquet pass freely between Taoist and popular-Buddhist narrative worlds, and it is in that shared space that the Journey to the West stages her most famous scene. Cultural legacy: The Queen Mother never retired from the heavens. In Taoist temples across Taiwan and the diaspora she is venerated still, often under the title Golden Mother of the Jasper Pool, and her birthday is kept with festival observance. In art she rides phoenixes and cranes through centuries of painting, lacquer, and embroidery, and the immortal peach she tends became the standard emblem of longevity, pressed into birthday buns and painted onto porcelain as a wish for long life. The Journey to the West made her banquet immortal in another sense: every screen adaptation of the Monkey King's career — film, television, animation, games — must sooner or later raid her orchard. She remains what she has been since the Han mirrors first invoked her for blessing: the great goddess at the western edge of the world, holding the one treasure every mortal wants and no one may take uninvited. Extended meditation: Xīwángmǔ teaches that civilization does not destroy its wilderness; it enthrones it. The tiger-toothed power of the Shān Hǎi Jīng was not replaced by the serene hostess of the Peach Banquet — she was carried forward, wildness and all, into the highest seat of the Taoist heavens. The goddess who once sent plague became the goddess who grants endless life, and the two offices are not as far apart as they seem: both are sovereignty over the boundary between life and death, held by the same unanswerable hand. To name a domain Xīwángmǔ is to claim that whole arc — the west where the sun descends, the orchard where three thousand years ripen into a single fruit, and the promise whispered from tally to tally through the Han commanderies: that mortality is a border, and someone keeps the gate. Original script note: The original script is 西王母, written identically in traditional and simplified characters — none of the three graphs was altered in the twentieth-century simplification. Pinyin Xīwángmǔ (Tones 1-2-3) is the Modern Standard Mandarin reading, recorded in the Unihan Database and standard dictionaries: xī (west, Tone 1), wáng (sovereign, Tone 2), mǔ (mother, Tone 3). The registrable Unicode restoration uses the tone-marked Pinyin rather than the hanzi because PUNICODEX renders the original characters in the temple's 'Original Script' card while keeping the domain label pronounceable and internationally registrable; the tone marks ī, á, and ǔ carry the citation tones that plain ASCII drops.

title: Rainbow, Fire, Threshold
text: Rainbow, Fire, Threshold: The domain of Bifrǫst In the norse tradition, Bifrǫst is the burning rainbow that joins Miðgarðr to Ásgarðr — the trembling path, from bifa 'to shake' and rǫst 'a league, a distance to be traversed.' The gods themselves call it Ásbrú , the Æsir-bridge, and ride it daily to hold court beneath Yggdrasill. The name encodes a structure built to fail: strong beyond any other work, as Snorri insists, yet fated to shake, to burn, and at last to break beneath the sons of Muspell. Between its watchman's horn and its final shattering, the bridge is the measure of the distance between gods and everything else. The Trembling Way: From bifa 'to shake' and rǫst 'league, path': the bridge is a trembling span of three colors, made with more skill and cunning than any other structure. The Red Band of Fire: Snorri explains the red stripe as burning fire: the bridge is warded in flame so that frost-giants and mountain-giants cannot climb it into heaven. Heimdallr's Watch: At Himinbjǫrg, where the bridge reaches heaven's edge, Heimdallr keeps guard — hearing the grass grow, seeing a hundred leagues by night, holding the Gjallarhorn. The Breaking at Ragnarǫk: When the sons of Muspell ride over it toward the field of Vígríðr, the bridge shatters beneath them; the horses of the gods must swim the flood. Symbols: The red band — The stripe of burning fire within the rainbow that bars the giants from heaven; Gjallarhorn — Heimdallr's horn, kept at the bridge and winded to wake the gods at Ragnarǫk; Himinbjǫrg — 'Heaven's castle,' Heimdallr's hall at the bridge's head where it touches the sky; Urðr's well — The spring beneath Yggdrasil where the gods ride each day to sit in judgment; The horses of the Æsir — The steeds named in Grímnismál — Glad, Gyllir, Glær, Skeiðbrimir and the rest — that bear the gods over the burning span Bifrǫst is the one road between the worlds of gods and men, and every story told of it is a story about passage: who may cross, what the crossing costs, and what happens when the road itself gives way. Snorri describes it as the strongest of all constructions and yet builds its destruction into the end of the world. The poems of the Codex Regius, which read the name as Bilrǫst , already know that the bridge will break. Around it gather Heimdallr the watchman, the daily assize at Urðr's well, and the solitary figure of Þórr, who is forbidden the span and wades the rivers instead. Gylfaginning: The Bridge of Three Colors Gangleri asks how the gods pass from heaven to earth, and Hárr answers that they built Bifrǫst from earth to heaven: a bridge of three colors, very strong, and made with more skill and cunning than any other work. The red in the rainbow, Hárr explains, is burning fire, so that the frost-giants and mountain-giants cannot mount into heaven over the bridge. At the bridge's head, where it reaches the edge of heaven, stands Himinbjǫrg , the hall of Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods. He needs less sleep than a bird, sees a hundred leagues by night as by day, and hears the grass growing on the earth and the wool on the sheep. Beside him waits the Gjallarhorn , whose blast is heard in all worlds. The bridge is the strongest thing in the world, and it is guarded by the one god who never sleeps — the Edda's way of saying that the way between worlds is always open, and never safe. Grímnismál: The Daily Ride to Judgment Every day the Æsir ride up over Ásbrú — the Æsir-bridge — on their named horses, to sit in judgment at the ash Yggdrasill. But Þórr does not ride. Grímnismál says that he must wade the rivers Kǫrmt and Ǫrmt and the two Kerlaugar each day on his way to the doomstead, for the Æsir-bridge stands all aflame and the holy waters seethe. Snorri gives the same exception a physical cause: the thunder-god's passage, with the heat and weight of his thunder, would break the span. The strongest of the gods is thus the one who walks — the bridge that carries everyone else cannot carry him. The daily wading is Þórr's liturgy: the god of the common people keeps both feet on the ground, even on his way to judgment. Ragnarǫk: The Shattering at Vígríðr When the end comes, Heimdallr stands and winds the Gjallarhorn to wake the gods. Surtr advances from the south with fire, and behind him ride the sons of Muspell toward the field of Vígríðr . They ride over Bifrǫst, and the bridge breaks beneath them. The poets of the Codex Regius knew it already: Fáfnismál says that Bilrǫst breaks as the hosts ride across, and the horses must swim in the surge, and Grípisspá repeats the prophecy. The road between worlds is the first great work of the gods to fall — the connection is severed before the battle is even joined. That the bridge fails before the gods do is the Edda's hardest structural insight: connection is the first casualty of the end, and even Muspell's sons cross it only once. Völuspá: The Watchman's Hearing The bridge's safety rests on one insomniac. Völuspá says the seeress knows Heimdallr's hearing, hidden beneath the radiant holy tree, and remembers him drinking the good mead where he stands (stanzas 26–27); Hyndluljóð gives him nine wave-mothers (stanza 35). At Himinbjǫrg he keeps the Gjallarhorn, whose blast runs through all worlds (Gylfaginning). Lokasenna measures the cost of the post: Loki taunts the watchman as the whitest and most doomed of gods, fated to stand drenched and unsleeping at his door forever. Heimdallr answers — and keeps the bridge. The Edda's most eloquent structure is guarded by its least eloquent god: the bridge is only as real as the one who never stops listening for it. His nine wave-mothers make him a child of everything that moves, set to watch over everything that must stay. Syncretism: The burning rainbow has no attested continental Germanic counterpart — no Old English or Old High German source names the bridge, so Bifrǫst belongs to the Old Norse material alone, and any deeper common-Germanic pedigree is conjecture. Comparanda crowd around it nonetheless. In Greek tradition Iris is the rainbow made person, the messenger who moves between heaven and earth along the arc; in the Rig Veda the rainbow is Indra's bow (Indradhanush), a weapon hung in the sky; and the rainbow covenant of Genesis 9 was familiar to the Christian Icelanders who copied the Eddas, a juxtaposition that colors, though it does not explain, Snorri's red band of fire. In Finnic and Baltic folklore the Milky Way is a road of birds or souls, another shining path overhead. Later European folk belief kept the rainbow as a bridge and a boundary — the treasure at its foot, the impossibility of reaching its end — and modern popular culture, most openly Marvel's Einstein–Rosen 'Bifrost,' has translated the trembling way into a wormhole, which is the same intuition in newer physics: a bridge that burns, shakes, and cannot be trusted to hold. Cultural legacy: Wagner fixed the bridge in the modern imagination at the close of Das Rheingold : Donner's hammer summons the storm that clears the air, the rainbow appears, Froh names it as the way to the gods' new castle, and the gods process over it into Valhalla while Loge mutters that they are hastening toward their end — a reading of Bifrǫst's built-in doom that Snorri would have recognized. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century book illustration kept the burning arc as the standard emblem of the passage to Ásgarðr. Marvel's comics and films made Bifrost a household word, reimagining it as a wormhole guarded by Heimdall and gate-keeping travel between realms; games from God of War Ragnarök to Assassin's Creed Valhalla render it as the shimmering road between worlds. Modern heathen practice uses the rainbow bridge as a symbol of the live connection between Miðgarðr and the gods, while the unrelated 'Rainbow Bridge' poem of pet bereavement shows how far the idiom of the shining span has travelled from its Old Norse root. Restoring Bifrǫst in Unicode keeps the trembling in the name — the ASCII Bifrost has forgotten that the bridge shakes. Extended meditation: Some names are nouns; this one is a verb wearing the shape of a thing. Bifrǫst means the trembling way, and everything the tradition says about it honors that grammar: a bridge of fire and color that the gods trust daily and that is fated, precisely because it connects what must be kept apart, to fail at the last. To name a structure after its shaking is to admit that connection is always provisional — that the distance between heaven and earth is not abolished by the bridge but measured by it. Unicode restoration returns that admission to readable form. Original script note: The name is Old Norse Bifrǫst , transmitted in Latin-script codices; no runic inscription preserves it. In a normalized Younger Futhark rendering it would be written ᛒᛁᚠᚱᛅᛋᛏ , with ᛅ for the ǫ. The ǫ is the o-ogonek, the u-umlaut of a — a short open-mid vowel, written ö in Modern Icelandic — and it is the one distinctive feature the ASCII form destroys. The restored registrable form is bifrǫst.com (punycode xn--bifrst-zcc.com ); the ASCII fallback bifrost.com flattens the trembling vowel into a plain 'o'.

title: Thunder, Hallowing, Return
text: Thunder, Hallowing, Return: The domain of Mjǫllnir In the norse tradition, Mjǫllnir is the hammer of Þórr — the one treasure the gods cannot do without. Dwarf-forged and short in the haft from Loki's sabotage, it never misses its mark, never flies so far that it fails to return to the thrower's hand, and shrinks small enough to be hidden inside a shirt. With it Þórr holds the wall between Ásgarðr and the giants. Yet the hammer is not only a weapon. It is laid in the bride's lap to hallow the marriage, raised over the newborn, and lifted against the dead man's pyre — it blessed Baldr's burning ship. In the Viking Age men and women wore it in silver and iron around their necks, the heathen answer to the Christian cross, and it is worn again today. The Dwarven Forge: Wagered into being by Loki, forged by the dwarf brothers Sindri and Brokkr; a fly's bite at the bellows left the haft too short. The Stolen Hammer: Þrymr the giant buried it eight miles down and demanded Freyja as bride-price; Þórr won it back veiled as the bride. Hammer of Hallowing: The same weapon that shatters giants consecrates brides, newborns, and funeral pyres — destruction and blessing in one tool. The Worn Hammer: Viking-age smiths cast it by the hundred in silver and iron; the pendant answered the cross then and signifies heathen faith now. Symbols: The short haft — The flaw left by Loki's fly-form sabotage at the bellows — the defect that makes the hammer a one-handed weapon; The unerring throw — It never misses its target and never flies so far that it fails to return to the thrower's hand; The hidden hammer — It shrinks small enough to be kept inside the shirt — power carried unseen; Lightning made iron — The thunderbolt given haft and head, the storm wielded as a tool; The amulet — The pendant form worn across the Viking world, the heathen counterpart of the cross Mjǫllnir is the most famous weapon in the northern world and the busiest: no other treasure of the gods both kills and consecrates. Forged as the stake in one of Loki's wagers, it came out of Sindri's forge with a haft too short — and the gods judged it the best of all treasures anyway. The sources hand it four great stories: its flawed making, its theft, its duel, and its blessing of the dead god's pyre. Skáldskaparmál: The Wager and the Short Haft After Loki shears Sif's hair, he must replace it, and from the sons of Ívaldi he commissions hair of living gold, the ship Skíðblaðnir, and the spear Gungnir. Swaggering, he wagers his head with the dwarf Brokkr that Brokkr's brother Sindri cannot make three finer treasures. At the forge, Loki becomes a fly and bites Brokkr at the bellows — arm, then neck, and Brokkr does not falter; but the third bite lands on his eyelid, and blinded by his own blood for one stroke of the bellows, he mars the work. Out of the forge comes a hammer — with a haft too short (Skáldskaparmál, trans. Brodeur). Brokkr names its virtues to Óðinn, Þórr, and Freyr: swung, it never fails; thrown, it never misses; it returns to the hand of its own will; and it shrinks small enough to be kept inside the shirt. Only the short haft is held against it — and the gods judge it the best of all six treasures, 'for with it Þórr can defend us against the mountain-giants.' Loki, defeated by the very sabotage he taught, keeps his head only by a trick. The myth means the flaw in the gods' most trusted tool is the permanent signature of the adversary's interference. Þrymskviða: The Hammer in the Bride's Lap Þórr wakes one morning and the hammer is gone. Loki borrows Freyja's falcon-shape, flies to Jötunheimr, and hears Þrymr boast that he has buried Mjǫllnir eight leagues down — and that no one recovers it unless Freyja is brought to him as bride. Freyja's refusal shakes her hall and snaps the necklace Brísingamen, so Heimdallr proposes the unthinkable: dress Þórr as the bride. The thunder-god protests — until Loki answers that without the hammer the giants will soon hold Ásgarðr. Veiled, hung with Brísingamen and jingling keys, Þórr rides east with Loki as his maidservant (Þrymskviða). The comedy is exact: the 'bride' devours an ox and eight salmon and drains three casks of mead, while Loki explains to the startled groom that Freyja has eaten nothing and slept not at all for longing. Þrymr lifts the veil for a kiss and leaps the hall's length from the fire in her eyes. Then he calls for the hammer — to hallow the bride, laid on her knees by the hand of Vár — and Þórr's heart laughs in his breast. His hand closes on the haft; he kills Þrymr, then the giant's whole household. The joke has a hard core: the hammer laid in the bride's lap is not a stage prop but the consecration itself — and the mightiest of the Æsir must wear bridal linen to recover his own. Skáldskaparmál 17: Hrungnir and the Whetstone The hammer's most dangerous duel came against the giant Hrungnir, who boasted in Asgard itself that he would kill all the gods, carry Freyja and Sif off to Jötunheimr, and drain the Æsir's ale. The gods sent for Þórr, and at the ford of Grjótúnagarðar the giant waited behind his stone shield, hurling his whetstone weapon. Mjǫllnir and the whetstone met in mid-air: the hammer smashed the stone and drove on into Hrungnir's skull — but a shard of whetstone lodged in Þórr's own head . The god walked home with the fragment still in him, and the sorceress Gróa was summoned to sing it loose. Her spells worked; Þórr felt it stir, and in his joy told her that her long-lost husband was on his way home — Gróa forgot her charms mid-verse in her delight, and the whetstone stayed in Þórr's skull forever. Snorri adds the custom: whetstones are forbidden as grave-goods, for this reason. The myth means the hammer's victories are never clean — its greatest triumph left its bearer permanently scarred, and the one thing Mjǫllnir could not fix was the wound it won by. Gylfaginning: Hallowing Baldr's Pyre When Baldr lies dead, the gods build his pyre on the ship Hringhorni, and the giantess Hyrrokkin, riding a wolf with vipers for reins, must be fetched to launch it. Baldr's wife Nanna dies of grief and is laid beside him. Þórr steps forward and hallows the pyre with Mjǫllnir — the god of thunder blessing the burning of the best of the gods — and when a dwarf named Litr runs across his path, he kicks him into the flames (Gylfaginning). The same gesture revives his slaughtered goats after they have been eaten, hallows the bride at the wedding feast, and here blesses the grave. Hammer at the cradle, hammer at the marriage-bed, hammer at the pyre: Snorri's picture of Þórr is of a god whose weapon marks every threshold of life — destruction and consecration in one motion, never separated. The Viking-age custom of wearing the hammer at the throat simply hung that threshold-power around the neck. Syncretism: The hammer did not stay inside Iceland's manuscripts. On the continent its god appears as Donar, and when Adam of Bremen describes the temple at Uppsala he says that Thor 'with his mace looks like Jupiter' — the interpretatio romana equating thunder with thunder. Saxo Grammaticus gives Thor an oak club and, tellingly, preserves the short handle: in the Gesta Danorum the hero Høther disables the weapon by lopping off its shaft, an euhemerized echo of the fly at the bellows. Archaeology reaches further back: scholars have long connected the hammer pendants to the older club-of-Hercules amulets of the Roman frontier provinces, and Bronze Age rock carvings already show axe- and hammer-bearing figures in consecrating poses. Comparativists place Mjǫllnir in a wide Indo-European family of thunder-weapons — Indra's vajra , the club of the Dagda, the axe of Perun — and one proposed etymology would make the name itself a cousin of Slavic mólnija , 'lightning', though the derivation is contested. In later folklore the weapon survived transmuted: Neolithic axe-heads and belemnites were kept as 'thunder-stones' ( torshammare ), guards against lightning, and early-modern Icelandic grimoires went so far as to label the swastika 'Thor's hammer'. The twentieth century folded the hammer back into myth again through comics and film — a modern transmutation as thorough as any Saxo performed. Cultural legacy: Nineteenth-century art made the hammer visible: Mårten Eskil Winge's Thor's Fight with the Giants (1872) swings it over the goat-chariot, and the book illustrations of Lorenz Frølich and Elmer Boyd Smith fixed the bridal veil and the forge in the popular imagination. In Wagner's Ring it is Donner — the continental Þórr — who raises the hammer in Das Rheingold to summon the storm that clears the air for the rainbow bridge to Valhalla. Games have made the weapon interactive, from Smite and Valheim to God of War Ragnarök , where Mjölnir is an antagonist's instrument. Marvel's Mjolnir, introduced in 1962, added the 'worthiness' enchantment — whosoever holds this hammer — a modern invention with no Eddic basis, and arguably the single most successful addition to the mythology since Snorri. In modern Heathenry and Ásatrú the hammer is worn and wielded again in earnest: the hamarsigna , the sign of the hammer, blesses rites much as the sources describe, and since 2013 the Mjölnir emblem has been approved for the government headstones of American service members. Restoring Mjǫllnir in Unicode preserves the name's Old Norse specificity — the rounded ǫ and the geminate ll — against the flattening force of plain ASCII. Extended meditation: The hammer is the argument that the fiercest weapon is also the holiest instrument — that the force which breaks the giants is the same force that blesses the bride, the child, and the dead. Its haft is short because perfection was sabotaged and the flaw endured; gods and men alike made do with the tool they had, and it was enough. For a thousand years people wore this name against their skin as the storm made portable, protection you could carry. Unicode restoration returns that world to readable form. Original script note: The Old Norse form is Mjǫllnir , with o-ogonek for the short rounded vowel [ɔ] and a geminate ll; the medieval manuscripts wrote it in Latin letters, varying between miǫllnir , miöllnir , and kindred spellings. In the Viking age itself the word was carved, not written: the Younger Futhark, the sixteen-rune alphabet of the period, carries both of the hammer's surviving runic witnesses — the Købelev amulet's proud hamar × is ('this is a hammer') and the Kvinneby amulet's invocation of Þórr 'with his hammer'. The site's Unicode restoration Mjǫllnir keeps what ASCII cannot: the o-ogonek and the geminate ll of the dictionary form, registrable as the internationalized domain mjǫllnir.com (punycode xn--mjllnir-bnc.com ). The plain form mjolnir survives only as the anglicized shadow — the name as comics rendered it, with the old rounded vowel and the long lateral filed away.

title: Moon, Night, Time
text: Moon, Night, Time: The domain of Máni In the Norse tradition, Máni is the moon itself made personal — the shining body that crosses the night sky, imagined as a god who steers it. Where Sól, his sister, drives the sun, Máni governs the gentler light: Snorri says he 'steers the course of the moon and rules the new and the waning moons,' the phases by which men first learned to count their days. Every month that turns is his signature: mánaðr , 'month', is his own word, and Monday is his day. Mundilfari's Boast: A father's pride named his children Moon and Sun; the gods answered the boast by setting the pair to drive the lights of heaven. Hati's Pursuit: The wolf Hati Hróðvitnisson runs before the moon and will one day take it; at Ragnarǫk the Moon-Hound swallows the light and spatters the sky with blood. Bil and Hjúki: Two children with a pail on a pole, taken up from the well Byrgir; they follow Máni, Snorri says, 'as can be seen from earth' — the man in the moon. Measurer of Months: He rules the new and waning moons, the counting of time itself; mánaðr, 'month', is his word, and the calendar was his first temple. Symbols: Ný ok nið (new and waning moons) — The phases over which Máni rules, the divine charge by which the gods ordained the counting of years for men; Hati Hróðvitnisson — The wolf who runs before the moon and gives its crossing its haste, the promise that even the lights of heaven are hunted; Mánagarmr (Moon-Hound) — The mightiest of the Iron-Wood brood, who fattens on the lives of the dying and swallows the moon at the world's end; Sægr and Simul (pail and pole) — The burden Bil and Hjúki carried from the well Byrgir, still legible as the markings on the moon's face; The month-mark — Mánaðr, the month — the unit of time that bears his name in every Germanic calendar Máni's mythology is brief but exact: he has no hammer-duels and no disguises, only a course to keep and a hunter behind him. The Eddas give him four scenes — a father's fatal boast, the breeding of the wolf that hunts him, two children lifted from a well, and the swallowing that ends the sky — and together they explain both why the moon moves and why it keeps its human face. Vafþrúðnismál / Gylfaginning: Mundilfari's Boast In the Vafþrúðnismál , the giant Vafþrúðnir tells Óðinn that Mundilfari is the father of Máni and of Sól alike. Snorri, in Gylfaginning (ch. 11), gives the story its edge: Mundilfari's two children were so fair that he named his son Máni, 'Moon', and his daughter Sól, 'Sun', and married Sól to a man named Glenr. The gods were angered by this ofdramb — this overweening pride — and took the siblings and set them in the heavens. The punishment is an appointment. Sól is made to drive the horses of the sun, Árvakr and Alsviðr, while Máni is charged with steering the course of the moon and ruling its waxing and waning. What a father claimed in arrogance, the gods confirmed in office: the names became the duties, and the children became the sky. The myth is the Eddas' quiet essay on vanity — the one boast the gods could not leave unpunished was a claim of ownership over light. Gylfaginning / Grímnismál: The Iron-Wood Brood Why does the moon flee? Because something was bred to chase it. Snorri preserves the genealogy ( Gylfaginning , ch. 12): east of Midgard, in the forest called Járnviðr — Iron Wood — a giantess in troll-woman's shape bore a brood of giant sons in wolf forms, and from that pack come the wolves that hunt the lights. Two of them the Æsir caught and set to their courses: Skǫll runs after the sun, and Hati Hróðvitnisson runs before the moon, and he will catch it — so it must be. The Grímnismál names them in verse: Skǫll follows the shining god, while Hati, Hróðvitnir's son, runs before the bright bride of heaven (st. 39). And the brood is not finished: from the same Iron Wood, Snorri says, will come the mightiest of all, Mánagarmr, the Moon-Hound, who feeds on the lives of the dead; the Vǫluspá laments the coming tormentor in a troll's shape (st. 40). The myth makes the night sky a battlefield of kinship: the lights of heaven are pursued by the children of the giantess, and Máni's speed is the speed of survival. Grímnismál / Gylfaginning: The Wolf at the Moon's Heels The moon does not drift; it flees. Snorri explains the physics by the hunter: the wolves run with the lights of heaven, and Hati Hróðvitnisson is the one who runs before the moon and means to take it — and so it will come to pass ( Gylfaginning , ch. 12). From earth, men watching the moon hurry across a winter sky believed the wolf was near; the chase is the Eddic explanation of lunar speed, and of eclipses, when the hound closed its jaws for a moment and the world held its breath. The chase has an ending, and the Eddas do not flinch from it. At Ragnarǫk the Moon-Hound Mánagarmr — fed all his life on the blood of the dying — swallows the moon whole and spatters the sky and the air with blood, so that the sun itself loses its shining and the stars are shaken from the heavens. The image is exact and terrible: time, which Máni measures, is also time, which is eaten. Every month closes because the wolf behind it is a month closer. Gylfaginning: Bil and Hjúki at the Well Snorri records that Máni took two children up from the earth, Bil and Hjúki, as they walked from the well called Byrgir, carrying on their shoulders the pail Sægr — often read as a mead-tub — slung from the pole Simul. Their father is named Viðfinnr. 'These children follow Máni,' Snorri adds, 'as can be seen from earth': look at the moon and you will find them there. This is the Norse answer to the man in the moon — not a face but two small figures under a burden, fixed forever in mid-errand. The detail of the well, the pail, and the pole is too homely to be invented ornament; it reads as the residue of nursery-lore older than the manuscript, the kind of story told to children who had already been shown the markings in the moon. Scholars have sometimes linked the pair to the Jack and Jill of English rhyme, but that connection is modern speculation, not attestation. What the myth insists on is gentler: the moon-god's company is not warriors but errand-bearers, and the sky remembers two children on their way home from water. Syncretism: Máni belongs to the common Germanic inheritance in which the moon is grammatically and mythologically masculine — Old English Mōna , Old High German Māno , Gothic mēna — a striking counterweight to the feminine moons of the classical world, Greek Selēnē and Latin Luna . The word itself runs deeper: Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁nōt- / *mḗh₁n̥s meant both 'moon' and 'month', the double sense Máni still carries in mánaðr , so that his personification is the personification of time-reckoning itself. The pairing of a moon-god with a sun-goddess, brother and sister, is the Germanic reversal of the Greek Selene and Helios pattern, though the daily celestial chase — light pursued by devourer — has echoes from the wolves of Ragnarǫk back to the eclipse-monsters of other traditions. The liveliest survival is folkloric: the Norse reading of the moon's markings as two children with a pail stands at the head of the whole northern 'man in the moon' tradition that later fills English ballads and nursery rhymes, and the tempting equation of Hjúki and Bil with Jack and Jill has been argued since the nineteenth century — as speculation, never as proof. Cultural legacy: Máni's deepest legacy is calendrical: every month and every Monday in the Germanic-speaking world is his, for Mōnandæg and its Norse kin are simply the moon's day, and the words descend from his name. In literature his clearest heir is Tolkien's Tilion, the Maia who steers the vessel of the moon across the sky — the personified moon-driver of the Eddas translated into a new mythology. Notably, Wagner left him out: the Ring runs on gold, fire, and Wotan's will, and the moon-driver never steps onto that stage, a measure of how thin Máni's high-cultural afterlife is beside Þórr's or Óðinn's. The chase around him fares better: the pursuing wolves Skǫll and Hati stalk recent retellings, including God of War Ragnarök (2022), where the stolen moon and its hunters drive a whole arc of the story. And the oldest survival is still the most democratic — the face and figures people point out to children in the full moon, which Snorri already explained by Bil and Hjúki eight centuries ago. In modern heathenry Máni is honored quietly, at the turning of the months he still measures. Extended meditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Máni compresses the oldest technology there is: the counting of time by a light that reliably changes. Before calendars were written they were watched, and the watcher-god is the moon — not its conqueror, like Þórr riding out, but its keeper, driving a course he did not choose, with a wolf behind him and two lost children for company. His myth is the honest one about time: it moves because it is pursued, it is beautiful because it is borrowed, and it will one day be swallowed. Yet the word he leaves behind — mánaðr , the month — is how every farmer, sailor, and poet after him held the dark at bay. Unicode restoration returns that world to readable form: the acute on á is the long vowel the whole calendar leans on. Original script note: The Old Norse form is máni , the ordinary common noun 'moon' borne as a theonym, attested throughout the manuscript tradition of both Eddas. In the earlier epigraphic medium, the Younger Futhark , the name would be rendered approximately ᛘᛅᚾᛁ — the long á written with the ᛅ (óss) rune, the Younger Futhark's sign for the a-family vowels, nasalized and long alike; no runic inscription preserves the theonym itself. In the normalized Old Norse spelling the acute on á marks vowel length, [ɑː], the same long vowel heard in 'father'. The PUNICODEX registrable form Máni preserves that acute as a Tier-1 restoration — the single distinctive feature the ASCII form Mani loses — carrying the long vowel that links the god directly to mánaðr , the month he measures.

title: Victory, Dragon-Slaying, Heroism
text: Victory, Dragon-Slaying, Heroism: The domain of Sigurðr In the norse tradition, Sigurðr governed victory, dragon-slaying, heroism. The name encodes a sphere of power that shaped ritual, narrative, and social order. His is the northern form of the greatest heroic story the Germanic world ever told: the foster-son of a smith who reforged his father's shattered sword, the slayer of the dragon Fáfnir, the wooer of the valkyrie behind the flame, and the oath-brother destroyed by the very loyalty that made him great. What the Iliad is to Greece, the Vǫlsunga cycle is to the North. Gramr: The sword Óðinn thrust into the tree Barnstokkr and only Sigmundr could draw; shattered in his last battle, reforged by Reginn for the son who would avenge him. Fáfnir at Gnitaheiðr: The brother turned dragon by greed, slain by a hero lying in a trench; from his heart-blood Sigurðr learned the speech of birds. The Flame-Wall: Through the vafrlogi on Hindarfjall rode Grani's rider to wake Brynhildr, the valkyrie Óðinn had sunk in sleep — the oath sworn there could not survive the world of men. The Cursed Hoard: Andvari's gold, paid as weregild for Ótr and cursed at its surrender; every hand it passed through — Hreiðmarr, Fáfnir, Sigurðr, the Gjúkings — it brought to ruin. Symbols: Gramr — The reforged sword of Sigmundr, drawn from Barnstokkr and mended by Reginn; with it Sigurðr slew Fáfnir; Grani — The grey horse of Sleipnir's line who bore Sigurðr through the flame-wall and carried the dragon's gold from Gnitaheiðr; Andvaranautr and the hoard — The dwarf Andvari's ring and gold, taken as ransom and cursed at the taking — the engine of every death in the cycle; The dragon's heart-blood — Roasting Fáfnir's heart, Sigurðr tasted the blood and understood the birds — knowledge bought from the monster he killed; The vafrlogi flame-wall — The ring of fire around the sleeping Brynhildr, crossable only by the destined rider; crossed twice, once for love and once in betrayal Sigurðr is the dragonslayer of the Vǫlsunga cycle, the Norse original of the German Siegfried and the last great hero of the legendary North. Son of Sigmundr and Hjǫrdís, fostered by the smith Reginn, he reforged his father's sword, killed the dragon Fáfnir, and woke the valkyrie Brynhildr from her enchanted sleep — then lost her, and his life, to a draught of forgetfulness and the plotting of his sworn brothers. His story survives in the Poetic Edda, the Prose Edda, and Vǫlsunga saga, and through the Middle High German Nibelungenlied it became the backbone of Wagner's Ring. Where the gods of the Edda face a doom they know is coming, Sigurðr faces one he has forgotten — and that is the more human tragedy. Vǫlsunga saga: The Reforging of Gramr At the wedding feast of his sister Signý, a one-eyed stranger — Óðinn — thrust a sword to the hilt into the tree Barnstokkr that grew through the hall of Vǫlsungr, and only Sigmundr of all the company could draw it. Years later Sigmundr fell in battle, the sword shattering beneath him against the same god's spear, and his widow Hjǫrdís carried the shards away for her unborn son. That son, Sigurðr, was fostered by Reginn, a smith of the dwarf-kin, who urged him against the dragon Fáfnir and forged blade after blade that broke under the boy's testing — until Sigurðr demanded the shards of his father's sword be worked into the new steel. Reginn reforged them into Gramr , and the boy clove the smith's anvil to the stock and sheared a tuft of wool drifting on the current as though it were standing stone (Vǫlsunga saga 13–15; Reginsmál). The blade binds the hero to Óðinn from birth: the god who gave the sword also broke it, and the steel that passes from father to son is the visible thread of a destiny the boy never chose. In the North, inheritance is not property but appointment. Fáfnismál: The Slaying of Fáfnir Fáfnir was Reginn's brother, who had killed their father Hreiðmarr for the hoard paid as weregild for the slain Ótr, and crawled away to Gnitaheiðr, where greed long brooding over gold twisted him into a dragon. Guided by a one-eyed old man who would not give his name, Sigurðr dug a trench across the worm's path to the water and lay in it; when Fáfnir crawled overhead he thrust Gramr upward into the heart. The dying dragon warned him that the gold would be his death, and the hero answered with the northern creed: every man must die, and wealth must serve until that day (Fáfnismál; Vǫlsunga saga 18–20). Roasting the heart for Reginn, Sigurðr burned his finger, set it in his mouth, and the heart-blood opened the speech of birds to him: the nuthatches in the branches warned that the smith meant to kill him. He took Reginn's head, loaded the cursed gold onto Grani, and rode away the richest and most doomed man in the North. The birds that save him here will not be there at the end. The episode's point is exact: the monster's death transfers the monster's curse, and every new owner of the gold only inherits it. Sigrdrífumál: The Flame-Wall on Hindarfjall Before the dragon, on Hindarfjall, Sigurðr found the vafrlogi — a wall of flame no horse would cross — and within it a hall where a warrior slept in full armor, as if dead. The sleep-thorn in her corslet marked her as a valkyrie; he drew Gramr and cut the armor from her, and she woke as Brynhildr and taught him the runes and the lore of the worlds: the healing runes, the ale-runes, the speech of victory and the speech of weddings, and the caution that shapes the whole cycle — never to swear falsely (Sigrdrífumál; Vǫlsunga saga 21–22). They plighted their troth and parted, and she prophesied what he would forget. The flame-wall is the cycle's question about fate: it parts for the destined rider and for no one else, and the man it admits is not thereby saved from what comes after. Guðrúnarkviða: The Ale of Forgetfulness At the court of Gjúki's sons the queen Grímhildr brewed Sigurðr the ale of forgetfulness, and Brynhildr passed from his mind as if she had never been. He married Guðrún, swore oaths with her brothers Gunnarr and Hǫgni, and when Gunnarr wooed Brynhildr and could not cross the flames, Sigurðr exchanged shapes with him and rode the fire in his friend's likeness — wooing his own forgotten beloved for another man, with a drawn sword laid between them in the bridal bed (Vǫlsunga saga 28; Guðrúnarkviða I). The deception could not hold: from a ring and a quarrel at the washing-stones Brynhildr learned what had been done, and wounded in her pride she demanded the death of the man who had ridden the flames and then married another. The betrayal is the cycle's quiet engine: no one in it acts from malice until the ale is brewed — the draught of forgetfulness is the one weapon the curse of gold did not need to supply. Brot af Sigurðarkviðu: The Death of Sigurðr The brothers, bound to Sigurðr by oath, could not strike him; they incited the younger Guthormr, who had sworn nothing, and he stabbed Sigurðr as he slept. Some lays — Sigurðarkviða en skamma and Guðrún's own laments — have him slain out of doors, in the forest; Brot af Sigurðarkviðu , preserved only in a fragment around the Codex Regius lacuna, gives the death in bed and the last words. Dying, Sigurðr spoke gently to Guðrún, named the true traitors, and flung Gramr after the killers; the sword caught Guthormr in the doorway and took him too. Brynhildr laughed once at the bier, told the truth at last, and went onto the pyre to lie beside him (Sigurðarkviða en skamma; Vǫlsunga saga 31–32). The sources disagree on the place but not on the meaning: the hoard's curse reached the man who thought himself above it, through the only door he had left open — the trust of those he called his own. Syncretism: Sigurðr is the northern twin of a pan-Germanic hero. The continental tradition — preserved in the Middle High German Nibelungenlied (c. 1200), the Lied vom Hürnen Seyfrid , and the Old Norse Þiðreks saga , which repatriates German material — tells of the same dragon-fight, hoard, and betrayal under the name Siegfried, with the details reworked: the valkyrie becomes a Burgundian queen, the flame-wall drops away, and the murder moves to a forest spring. Scholars have long read the cycle's skeleton against history, seeing in Gunnarr and the fall of the Gjúkings the shadow of the Burgundian kingdom destroyed by the Huns in 437 — legend crystallized around remembered catastrophe. The dragon-slaying itself belongs to a still older inheritance: the Indo-European formula of the hero who kills the serpent, traced by Calvert Watkins through Indra and Vṛtra, Herakles and the Lernaean hydra, and Beowulf's fatal last fight. In later folklore the story lived on in the Faroese Sjúrðar kvæði ballads, still sung and danced in the islands centuries after the saga manuscripts were copied. Cultural legacy: No Norse figure has had a longer second life. William Morris retold the cycle in his epic The Story of Sigurd the Volsung and the Fall of the Niblungs (1876), which he called the great story of the North that should be to all his race what the tale of Troy was to the Greeks. Richard Wagner made it the armature of Der Ring des Nibelungen — Siegfried and Götterdämmerung follow the Norse sources where the Nibelungenlied had softened them, restoring the valkyrie Brünnhilde to the centre. Arthur Rackham's illustrations fixed the cycle's visual grammar for a century, and J. R. R. Tolkien, who read the Eddas closely, composed his own The Legend of Sigurd and Gudrún in Eddic metre. The dragonslayer persists in opera houses, novels, games, and film wherever a hero wins gold and is destroyed by it. In modern heathenry Sigurðr is honoured less as an object of cult than as the model of the heroic ethic — courage held fast inside a fate already written — and the runestones that depict him are among the tradition's most cited monuments. Restoring Sigurðr in Unicode keeps the eth and the nominative -r that the German Siegfried and the anglicized Sigurd alike have lost. Extended meditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Sigurðr carries within it a norse understanding of victory under guard: sigr , the thing won, held by a vǫrðr , a watcher — as if the North already knew that every victory needs defending, and that the guard can fail. The hero who bore the name guarded the hoard, the oath, and the bride, and lost all three to a single draught of ale; the name outlived the man by eight centuries and counting.
