Völuspá 27: The Hearing Under the Tree The strangest of all the Heimdallr stanzas is Völuspá 27: 'She knows Heimdallr's hearing is hidden under the bright-grown sacred tree; she sees it washed by a muddy torrent from the pledge of the Father of the Slain — do you understand yet, or what more?' The pledge of Óðinn is his eye, given to Mímir's well, and Snorri says the Gjallarhorn itself lies hidden in that same well. Whether the völva means the horn or the god's hearing itself — whether Heimdallr pawned an ear to the water as Óðinn pawned an eye — the stanza will not say, and the debate is more than a century old. What is certain is the pairing: the seeing god and the hearing god both paid a sense into the same well. Syncretism: Heimdallr resists the usual syncretic moves — no Roman writer ever matched him, and no continental charm securely names him — but the twentieth century built him a different kind of company. Georges Dumézil made Rígsþula a Scandinavian cornerstone of his trifunctional reading of Indo-European society: thrall, farmer, and noble begotten by one wandering god maps the pattern he traced from the Vedas to Rome. Within the Germanic record, the clearest pairing is the Saltfleetby spindle whorl from Lincolnshire, whose runic charm calls on Óðinn and Heimdallr and Þjálfi for help — the watchman invoked beside the Allfather in a working household. Scholars have also set his nine giantess-mothers beside Ægir's nine wave-daughters and his birth 'at the edge of the earth' beside other shore-born figures; none of the equations has won consensus, and the handbooks converge on the same honest word: enigmatic. Cultural legacy: Heimdallr's afterlife runs on the horn and the watch. The name never left the North — Norwegian Heimdal survives in place-names and as a given name, and Icelandic keeps Heimdallur — and in modern reception he has become the fixed image of the gatekeeper: the cinema's Heimdall, sighting across the Bifröst, is now the spelling most of the world meets first, and security software borrows the name when it wants to promise that nothing gets past. Modern Heathenry honors him as the father of mankind's orders and the god of vigilance, while the scholarship keeps him as its favorite unsolved problem — the white god whose dossier is large and whose meaning is still debated. Extended meditation: Heimdallr is the god of the unglamorous miracle: attention. No adventure of his survives whole — the great deeds are lost poems and kenning-fragments — but the corpus is unanimous about the senses. He hears grass grow. He sees through night. He needs less sleep than a bird. And the Edda builds the whole meaning of vigilance out of that patience: the watch is not the battle; the watch is what makes the battle survivable, and the horn is what makes the watch worth keeping. Rígsþula adds the stranger claim — that this same tireless attention once walked the green ways as Rígr and fathered every class of men, as if to say that society itself began as something watched over. His last act is not a victory: he blows the horn, and then he and Loki kill each other. The watch ends in the warning, not in the rescue. That is the whole of it, and it is enough: someone has to be awake when the rest of the world is not, and the Edda gave that someone a name. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Heimdallr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚼᛁᛘᛏᛅᛚᛦ (h-i-m-t-a-l-R, the ᛏ writing d, a single ᛚ standing for the geminate, and ᛦ the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: heimdallr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Death, Underworld, Souls
text: Death, Underworld, Souls: The Hidden One Who Keeps the Unheroic Dead Hel is the daughter of Loki and Angrboða whom Óðinn cast down into Niflheimr and set over the dead: half blue-black and half the colour of living flesh, she rules Éljúðnir, where those who die of sickness and old age — the vast, unburned majority of humankind — are sent to her keeping. Éljúðnir: Her hall, 'Sprayed with Snowstorms', behind high walls and great gates — the dwelling Snorri names as the terminus of every quiet death. Hungr and Sultr: Her dish is Hunger, her knife Famine: the furniture of her table names the slow wasting she presides over. Fallanda Forað: 'Plunging to Destruction' — the threshold of her bedchamber, one of the named fittings of the hall in Gylfaginning's grim inventory. The Half-Living Face: Half blue-black, half the colour of flesh — 'easily recognized', Snorri says, downcast and fierce: the visible seam between the quick and the dead. Symbols: The half-blue, half-flesh face — The two states of being worn on one head — life and corruption divided by a single line; Éljúðnir — The hall of the dead who were not burned in battle — architecture for the ordinary ending; Hungr the dish and Sultr the knife — Hunger and famine as table-service — the realm named out of what it takes away; Fallanda Forað and Kǫr — The plunging threshold and the sick-bed, hung with Blíkjanda Bǫl, 'Gleaming Bale' — the dead received as the sick received to bed; Ganglati and Ganglǫt — Her serving-man and serving-maid, both named for the slow walk — time in Hel moves at a dying pace Hel acts rarely and presides always. The corpus gives her one origin, one judgment, and a standing geography — and in exchange she receives nearly everyone. The myths agree that the gods could not kill her; they could only give her what they most wanted hidden, and make her keeper of it forever. Gylfaginning 34: The Casting Down Loki got three children on the giantess Angrboða in Jötunheimr: the wolf Fenrir, the serpent Jǫrmungandr, and Hel. When the gods learned that this brood was being raised, and read in the prophecies that great harm would come of them, Óðinn sent for the children and disposed of each: the serpent he threw into the deep sea that circles all lands, the wolf the Æsir kept to bind, and Hel he cast down into Niflheimr. There he gave her authority over nine worlds, that she should apportion all dwellings among those sent to her — and those are the sickness-dead and the age-dead. Snorri then gives the strangest inventory in the Edda. Her hall is called Éljúðnir; her dish Hungr, Hunger; her knife Sultr, Famine; her serving-man Ganglati and her serving-maid Ganglǫt, the slow-walking pair; the threshold she steps over is Fallanda Forað, Plunging to Destruction; her bed is Kǫr, the sick-bed, and its hangings Blíkjanda Bǫl, Gleaming Bale. And of Hel herself: she is half blue-black and half the colour of living flesh, and therefore easily recognized — rather downcast and fierce of countenance. The goddess of death is furnished out of the slow deaths she rules: her household is a ward, and she is its matron, wearing a corpse's half-face. Gylfaginning 49: The Weeping Condition When Baldr lay dead and Hermóðr the Bold had ridden nine nights down the dark road, he came to Helgrindr, the barred gate, spurred Sleipnir, and leapt it unopened. In the hall he found Baldr seated in the high seat — the most honoured of the dead already given Hel's highest place — and he stayed the night. In the morning he asked Hel to let Baldr ride home with him, and told her how great the weeping was among the Æsir. Hel's answer is her only speech in the corpus, and the whole ending of the world turns on it: she would test whether Baldr was as beloved as was said. If all things in the world, living and lifeless, weep for him, he shall go back to the Æsir — but he shall stay with Hel if anything speaks against it or refuses to weep. Everything wept: men and beasts, earth and stones, trees and metals. Only the giantess Þökk in her cave wept dry tears: 'Let Hel hold what she has.' The sentence is usually read as Loki's cruelty. It is also, word for word, Hel's own charter: she holds what she has. No one has ever gotten it back from her by force. Vafþrúðnismál 43 · Grímnismál 31: The Geography of the Hidden The Poetic Edda keeps her realm on the map rather than on the stage. When Óðinn, disguised, wagers his head against the giant Vafþrúðnir's wisdom, his proof that he has travelled farther than any god is this: 'Nine worlds I came through, down below Niflhel; thither men die out of Hel.' The line folds the dead downward through layers — there is a Hel, and there is something below Hel, a death beneath death for those already dead. Grímnismál plants the same region in the world-tree's architecture: three roots hold Yggdrasill, and Hel dwells beneath one of them, while men dwell beneath another and the frost-giants beneath the third. The dead are not elsewhere; they are under the same tree, at another root. The hidden one is hidden in the most literal way the Norse cosmos allows — covered by the world's own structure. Baldrs draumar: The Strewn Benches Before Baldr ever falls, Óðinn saddles Sleipnir and rides down the same road his son Hermóðr will ride after, to the grave of a völva east of Hel's gate. He raises her with spells and demands to know for whom the realm below is dressed. She answers unwilling: the benches are strewn with arm-rings, the dais fairly decked, the mead brewed, the shields overspread — for Baldr. The hope of the gods departs. The poem's glimpse inside the hall is the other side of Gylfaginning's inventory of hunger and slow walking: Hel's house is also a hall of honour, strewn and shining like Valhǫll for the guest it expects. The deadliest hospitality in the Edda is prepared in advance, and it is beautiful. Baldr will sit in that high seat within the year. Syncretism: The oldest syncretism is the one the sources perform on themselves: Saxo Grammaticus, writing Latin for a Danish court, cannot say 'Hel' and so writes Proserpina — in Gesta Danorum Book 1 the goddess appears to Balderus in a dream as Proserpina, promising the dead man her embraces, the interpretatio latina folded directly into the plot. The Greek comparison runs deeper than the name-swap suggests: like Hades, Hel is both a person and a place, and the Old Norse word does the same double duty — one goes til Heljar, to Hel, as one goes to Hades. Jacob Grimm projected the goddess backward onto the continent as *Halja, citing the Gothic and Old High German words; current scholarship (Simek, Lindow) is cooler, noting that the continental languages attest the realm but never the ruler, and that the goddess may be a Scandinavian personification of an older common noun — the hidden place given a face. The largest syncretism is the one history performed without asking: Christianity took the word itself and made it 'hell', the punitive fire of the damned, recoloring the goddess's quiet hall of the sick-dead into the most feared address in the language. Her name survived by being emptied of her. Cultural legacy: Hel's afterlife is the English language's own: every speaker of English, German, or the Scandinavian tongues still pronounces her name every time they say hell — the commonest relic any Norse deity has left behind, carried out of the temple and into the swear-word. The word's journey is her biography in reverse: the goddess faded, the place-name endured, and the place darkened from a hall of the age-dead into a prison of fire. Modern reception has restored the person, if not the theology: she returns in Wagnerian and Victorian mythography, in Neil Gaiman's retellings, and most visibly in Marvel's Hela, whose half-shadowed iconography reaches back past the comics to Snorri's two-coloured face. Modern Heathenry keeps her as the keeper of the ordinary ancestors — the goddess for everyone who will not die in battle, which is to say, for nearly everyone. Extended meditation: Hel is what the gods do with what they cannot destroy. Óðinn cannot kill Loki's daughter — the prophecies forbid the thought — so he hides her, and the hiding is so thorough that it becomes an office: the concealed one becomes the keeper of everyone else the world conceals. Her name says it plainly: the hidden one, from the verb for covering over. Every grave is a small act of heljan. And her charter is more honest than Valhǫll's: Óðinn's hall takes the spectacular few, the spear-marked and the chosen; Hel takes the rest — the sick, the old, the children, the farmers in their beds — which is to say she receives, in the end, almost the whole of humankind, and keeps it behind a gate no god has ever forced. 'Let Hel hold what she has' was meant as a curse. It is also simply the truth of things, and the Edda knew it: everything that dies quietly is already hers, and she has never once given it back. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Hel — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚼᛁᛚ (h-i-l, the ᛁ-rune covering e, as the Viking-Age row does not distinguish the front vowels). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: hel.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Wolf, Destruction, Binding
text: Wolf, Destruction, Binding: The Wolf Who Cannot Be Held Fenrir is the monstrous wolf of Norse myth — the son of Loki and the giantess Angrboða, reared in the gods' own stronghold because no one dared do otherwise. When the prophecies said he would be Óðinn's death, the Æsir bound him: two fetters of iron broke like string, and the third — Gleipnir, the ribbon made of six things that do not exist — held, at the price of Týr's right hand. Gagged with a sword and chained to a stone beneath the earth, he lies on the isle of Lyngvi until Ragnarök, when he breaks free, swallows the Father of the Slain, and is torn jaw from jaw by Víðarr, the silent avenger. Gleipnir: Smooth and soft as a silken ribbon, made of six impossibles — the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, a mountain's roots, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, a bird's spittle. Iron failed twice; impossibility held. The Pledge of the Hand: Týr alone laid his right hand in the wolf's jaws as surety that the fetter was no trap. When Gleipnir held, the wolf bit it off — the gods laughed, says Snorri, all but Týr. The Gagging Sword: Wedged in the raging jaws, hilt against the lower gum, point against the upper — and from the foam that runs from his mouth flows the river Ván, Expectation, until the world's end. The Torn Jaws: At Ragnarök the wolf swallows Óðinn; Víðarr sets his foot on the lower jaw, seizes the upper, and tears the beast apart — the son avenging the father, as the poems always said he would. Symbols: Gleipnir — The fetter of six things that do not exist — proof that what binds the unbindable is not strength but impossibility; Týr's hand — The pledge that made the trap honest — justice's price paid in the god of justice's own flesh; The gagging sword — The wolf silenced but never tamed: the gods could stop his bite, not his doom; The river Ván — 'Expectation' — the stream of the bound wolf's slaver, flowing from Lyngvi until Ragnarök; Gjǫll and Þviti — The slab and the boulder driven deep into the earth — the world itself recruited as an anchor for the chain Fenrir's mythology is a single arc told in two registers: Snorri's prose gives the binding in full narrative, while the poems — older, allusive, apocalyptic — carry the prophecy and the end. Together they make the most complete monster-story the North preserves: birth, fostering, fetters, pledge, gag, and the waiting that ends at Ragnarök. Hyndluljóð · Gylfaginning 34: The Brood of Angrboða Hyndluljóð says it in a line: Loki begot the wolf with Angrboða — the giantess 'herald of sorrow' who dwells in Járnviðr, the Ironwood. Snorri names all three children of that union: the wolf Fenrir, Jǫrmungandr the world-serpent, and Hel, who is half the colour of the living and half of the dead. Because all were of giant stock and Loki's, and because the gods had heard prophecies that great harm would come of them, Óðinn had the children fetched. He cast the serpent into the deep sea that lies around all lands, where it grew until it girdled the world; Hel he threw down into Niflheimr and gave her power over nine worlds. But the wolf the Æsir brought home with them and reared in their own stronghold — and only Týr had the courage to go to him and give him food. Gylfaginning 34: Lœðingr and Drómi The wolf grew at a pace the gods could watch, and the prophecies grew plainer: he was fated to harm them. So the Æsir made a strong fetter called Lœðingr and brought it to the wolf, challenging him to test his strength against it. The wolf judged himself equal to it, let them bind him, braced himself, kicked — and the fetter sprang apart; he was loose from Lœðingr. The gods made a second fetter, half again as strong, called Drómi, and told the wolf he would win great fame if he broke it — such a fetter, they said, would not hold even a beast of his power. The wolf reasoned that fame was worth the risk, let them bind him, dashed himself against the ground, kicked — and Drómi flew in pieces far away. It is from this, Snorri says, that the saying comes: to break loose from Lœðingr or to dash out of Drómi, when things are pushed to the utmost. Gylfaginning 34–35: Gleipnir and the Pledge of the Hand Then the Allfather sent Skírnir to the dwarfs of Svartálfaheimr, and they made the fetter Gleipnir from six things that do not exist: the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish, and the spittle of a bird. Stronger than either iron fetter the wolf had snapped. At the isle of Lyngvi the gods showed him the band; suspicious, the wolf refused to be bound unless one of them laid a hand in his mouth as surety. The Æsir looked at one another, and none would — until Týr set his right hand in the wolf's jaws. Fenrir struggled; the ribbon only tightened. Then all the gods laughed — all but Týr, who lost his hand. The cord was run through the slab Gjǫll and sunk in the earth, and a boulder, Þviti, driven deeper as a pin. The wolf gaped and snapped, so the gods thrust a sword into his mouth; from the foam that runs from his jaws flows the river Ván, 'Expectation.' Why not kill him, since the prophecies named him Óðinn's death? Because, says Snorri, the gods would not stain their sanctuaries with the wolf's blood. The binding is the myth's moral centre: order bought by a pledge honestly given and a price honestly paid — and a laughter that rings false in exactly one ear. Vafþrúðnismál · Vǫluspá: The Swallower Foretold The poems had the end written long before Snorri wrote the beginning. In Vafþrúðnismál, Óðinn, disguised, questions the wise giant about the world's end, and the answers keep returning to the wolf: a daughter the sun shall bear before Fenrir catches her — and at the last, when Óðinn asks what his own doom will be, the giant answers: the wolf will swallow the Father of Men, and Víðarr will avenge him; he will tear apart the cold jaws of the beast in battle. Vǫluspá's seeress sees the same scene: when Frigg's beloved goes to fight the wolf, her second grief comes to pass — Óðinn falls. Then comes the great son of the Father of Victory: Víðarr, to fight the beast of slaughter. With his hand he thrusts the sword into the heart of Hveðrungr's son — Loki's son — and so his father is avenged. Grímnismál gives the avenger his landscape: brushwood and high grass grow in Víðarr's land, where the son leaps from his horse's back, eager to avenge his father. Lokasenna · Gylfaginning 51: The Hand Remembered, the Jaws at the End The binding left one permanent scar in the pantheon, and Loki never let it heal. In Lokasenna, when Týr speaks for the gods, Loki flings the price of Gleipnir in his face: you could never deal straight between two — I must mention your right hand, the one Fenrir tore from you. The wolf, bound and gagged beneath the earth, had already cost the god of the thing his sword-hand. At Ragnarök the debt comes due. Snorri's vision of the last battle gives the wolf the sky itself: Fenrisúlfr goes with his mouth agape, the lower jaw against the earth, the upper against the heavens — he would gape wider if there were room — and fire burns from his eyes and nostrils. He swallows Óðinn, and at once Víðarr comes forward, sets one foot — shod in the shoe that has been gathering since the world began from every scrap of leather men cut from the toe and heel — upon the wolf's lower jaw, seizes the upper jaw with one hand, and tears the wolf's mouth apart. So dies the fen-dweller, and the world burns and sinks and rises green again without him. Syncretism: Fenrir's closest relative inside his own corpus is the hound Garmr, who breaks his chain before Gnipahellir at Ragnarök and fights Týr to mutual death: Vǫluspá's refrain 'now Garmr howls loud' announces the end, and scholars from Lindow onward have debated whether Garmr is a doublet of the bound wolf or a second beast of the same kennel. The chase-wolves of the sky — Skǫll, who pursues the sun, and Hati Hróðvitnisson, who will take the moon — belong to the same apocalyptic pack, and Vafþrúðnismál gives Fenrir himself the sun-swallowing role, a distribution of doom the sources never fully harmonize. Wider comparisons are made and immediately qualified: Cerberus is the obvious Mediterranean analogue for a chained hell-hound, and the Ironwood's brood of wolves in Vǫluspá has been set beside every Indo-European wolf-pack of the world's end — but Fenrir's story is structurally unique: a monster the gods themselves foster, bind by trickery, and preserve for the apocalypse, because killing him is the one thing their own holiness forbids. His kin in the lexicon are his family: [[loki|Loki]], [[angrboda|Angrboða]], [[jormungandr|Jǫrmungandr]], and [[hel|Hel]] — and [[tyr|Týr]], whose hand is the fetter's true price. Cultural legacy: Fenrir is the North's most famous monster, and his afterlife runs on two tracks. The scholarly track never stopped: the binding of the wolf was a set-piece of the Victorian Norse revival — the Kearys' Heroes of Asgard (1857) made the fetters and the pledge of Týr's hand a children's classic — and every handbook since has treated Gleipnir's six impossibles as the Edda's signature riddle-image. The popular track is enormous: Marvel's comics gave Thor a recurring Fenris Wolf; J. K. Rowling named her most savage werewolf Fenrir Greyback; the wolf fights through Final Fantasy (where Fenrir is a summoned beast), Smite, and Assassin's Creed Valhalla, and God of War: Ragnarök (2022) built part of its end-of-days on him. The idiom of the bound monster who must not be killed for fear of worse has become a standing political and moral metaphor — the fettered danger whose release is the prophecy. In modern Heathenry Fenrir is no object of cult but the corpus's fixed figure of doom: the destruction the gods themselves are keeping, chained, until the chain is the last thing left. Extended meditation: Fenrir is the story a tradition told itself about what to do with the doom it cannot prevent. The gods cannot kill the wolf — prophecy has already named him, and their sanctuaries forbid the blood — so they bind him, and the binding costs the bravest just hand in the pantheon. Nothing about the arrangement is unjust on the surface: the wolf consents to each fetter, and the pledge is honestly given. But the myth knows what a pledge is for. Týr's hand in the jaws is the whole story in one image: order holds only because someone has already paid for it in flesh, and the price is not refundable. Every civilization chains some version of the fen-dweller and calls the chain permanent; the Edda's honesty is to say the chain is a delay — a good delay, bought at the right price, and worth it. Ván, the river that flows from the gagged jaws, means Expectation. Even the wolf's slaver knows how the story ends. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Fenrir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚠᛁᚾᚱᛁᛦ (f-i-n-r-i-R: the ᛁ rune covers both e and i, and ᛦ writes the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: fenrir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The Exalted One
text: The Exalted One: Poetry, Smithcraft, Healing — and the Undying Flame of Kildare Brigit, daughter of the Dagda, is the triple hearth of the Irish gods: Cormac's Glossary gives her two sisters of the same name — Brigit the smith and Brigit the leech beside Brigit the poet — so that the one name covers the forge, the well, and the word. Her feast is Imbolc, the first of February, when the ewes come into milk; and at Kildare a fire burned for her, Giraldus says, that no man might approach and no night ever saw go out. The Sacred Flame: The perpetual fire of Kildare, tended by nineteen nuns in turn — on the twentieth night, Giraldus says, it was left to Brigid herself. The Anvil: Smithcraft, one of the three provinces Cormac assigns to the sisterhood of Brigits — the forge where Goibniu's art and mortal craft meet. The Poet's Harp: The first of her provinces in the Glossary — Brigit banfhiled, Brigit the woman-poet, patroness of the learned craft of filidecht. The Rush Cross: St Brigid's cross, woven of rushes on Imbolc eve — the small loom on which the goddess's feast was carried into the saint's day. Symbols: The flame of Kildare — The fire that neither dies nor accumulates ash — patronage that outlasts the night-watch of its keepers; The anvil and the forge — Smithcraft, the making province — skill that transforms raw metal the way poetry transforms raw speech; The holy well — Healing drawn from the ground — the countless wells of St Brigit where the leech-sister's province is still visited; Fea and Femen, the two oxen — The Dagda's daughter's beasts, who gave their names to plains of Ireland — wealth and the working land; Imbolc — The first of February, the milk returning to the ewes — the year's first hinge, kept as her day Irish tradition gives Brigit few long tales but a peculiar density of testimony: the great pseudohistory of the Lebor Gabála knows her genealogy, the battle-tale Cath Maige Tuired gives her the first keening heard in Ireland, and Cormac's Glossary preserves the triad that made her three goddesses in one name. Lebor Gabála Érenn: The Dagda's Daughter The Book of Invasions places Brigit firmly in the family of the Túatha Dé Danann: Brigit the poetess, daughter of the Dagda, the good god who owns the cauldron and the club. The same tradition marries her to Bres, the half-Fomorian king whose beautiful face and niggardly rule nearly undid the Túatha Dé Danann, and gives her three sons — Ruadán, Iuchar, and Iucharba — so that the exalted one stands, by marriage and blood, on both sides of the great conflict of Irish myth. The later tradition adopted her sons into another house entirely, making them the three sons of Tuireann for whose killing Lugh exacted a blood-price. The Lebor Gabála is pseudohistory, written by Christian scholars ordering the gods into an ancestry, but its genealogies are the tradition's own filing system: Brigit belongs to the Dagda's house, and her griefs run through both armies. Sanas Cormaic: Three Sisters, One Name Cormac mac Cuilennáin's glossary, compiled around 900 by the bishop-king of Cashel, preserves the tradition's clearest statement of her triple nature. Brigit, it says, is the poetess, daughter of the Dagda — and she had two sisters, Brigits also: Brigit the woman of smithcraft and Brigit the female physician, from whose names all the Irish used to call a goddess Brigit. Three crafts, three sisters, one name: from this single entry comes the familiar picture of the triple goddess of poetry, smithcraft, and healing. No saga ever dramatizes the three sisters — their entire biography is this glossary entry and the keening of the Second Battle — which is itself a kind of testimony: Brigit's worship was a matter of crafts and calendar, not of story. Whether the triad records three genuinely distinct figures or one goddess's three provinces arranged in the Irish love of threes, the Glossary is the witness every later account follows. Cath Maige Tuired: The First Keening in Ireland The Second Battle of Mag Tuired gives Brigit her one moment of action, and it is grief. Her son Ruadán, sent by his Fomorian kin to spy on the smith Goibniu — whose forge armed the Túatha Dé — hurled a spear at the smith; Goibniu drew it out of his own side and cast it back, and Ruadán went to his father's camp to die. Brigit came to the field and bewailed her son — and the text says she wept and shrieked over him, the first keening and the first whistling for grief that was heard in Ireland. The tradition sets her love against her blood: she was of the Túatha Dé, her son of the Fomorians, and the battle made her choose which grief to keep. The inventor of lamentation is a terrible dignity: the goddess of the word is the one who first taught Ireland what a mother says at a grave — and the saga sets poetry's darkest strain beside the forge it avenges. Giraldus Cambrensis, Topographia Hiberniae: The Fire at Kildare Writing about 1188, Gerald of Wales describes the wonder of Kildare with a traveller's precision: a fire hedged round with a circular fence of brushwood, which no male may cross — any man who tries, he says, does not escape Brigid's vengeance. Nineteen nuns tend the flame, one each night, each adding fuel; on the twentieth night the last nun lays the wood and says, 'Brigid, guard your fire, it is yours.' In the morning the fire is found still burning, and its ashes, Gerald marvels, never increase though the wood is always consumed. The nuns themselves, he adds, hold that once the fire is out it can never be rekindled — so it is never allowed to go out. Half a millennium earlier, Cogitosus's Life of St Brigit (c. 650) already described the same hearth tended at Kildare. Gerald records it as a marvel of the saint's church; scholarship has never doubted that the hedge, the number nineteen, and the unashing flame belong to a far older hearth. Sanas Cormaic · the quarter days: Imbolc, the Ewe's Milk Her feast stands at Imbolc, the first of February, one of the four great hinges of the Irish year beside Beltaine, Lugnasad, and Samain. Cormac's Glossary explains the word itself as oimelc, 'ewe's milk' — the season when the sheep come into milk and the year's hunger begins to turn. The old texts keep the day as Brigit's own; the keening, the forge, and the word all gather at the one date, when the light is just beginning to return and the flocks give their first milk. In the Scottish Highlands the eve was kept with the rhyme Carmichael recorded in the Carmina Gadelica: the serpent will come from its hole on Bride's morn, though it dreads the cold. It is the oldest continuously observed fact about her: whatever else changed, the first of February stayed hers. Syncretism: Brigit's syncretic life runs in two directions. Across the water, her name is one with the goddess Brigantia of Roman Britain, honoured in inscriptions from the Wall country and portrayed on the Birrens relief with Minerva's globe and spear — the interpretatio romana pairing the exalted one with the Roman goddess of craft and war-wisdom; the tribal Brigantes and the Gaulish Brigindu carry the same name-element, and the old comparison with Sanskrit bṛhatī, 'the high, exalted one', shows how deep the root runs. Within Ireland, the identification is Christian: Brigit of Kildare, the sixth-century saint whose feast falls on Imbolc, whose church kept a perpetual fire, and whose wonder-tales in Cogitosus's Life echo the goddess's provinces. Whether saint succeeded goddess, goddess was Christianized into saint, or two figures fused in one name, the sources do not let us decide — and Mac Cana and Koch both counsel holding the question open. What is certain is the continuity of the name: the Exalted One never left Ireland's calendar. Cultural legacy: No Celtic deity has a longer unbroken afterlife. Imbolc is still celebrated as St Brigid's Day — Lá Fhéile Bríde — and since 2023 it has been a public holiday in the Republic of Ireland, the first named for a woman. Rushes are still woven into Brigid's crosses on the eve of the feast and hung above doors; hundreds of holy wells bear the saint's name, and the clootie and cure customs at them preserve the leech-sister's province in folk practice. Modern paganism and Celtic Reconstructionism restored the goddess explicitly, keeping Imbolc as the feast of the returning light and of the three crafts; poets, smiths, and healers alike claim her patronage. And the name itself — Brigid, Bridget, Bríd — never ceased to be given to Irish daughters, carrying the Proto-Celtic word for exaltation into every generation since the Iron Age. Extended meditation: Brigit is the rare goddess whose three provinces are one act seen from three sides. The smith and the poet do the same thing: they take what is raw — ore, breath — and by heat and pressure give it a form that outlasts them. The healer does it too, coaxing the broken body back toward the shape it was made for. Cormac's three sisters are really a single lesson: that making is sacred wherever it happens, at the anvil, on the tongue, or at the sickbed. Her fire at Kildare, hedged and watched and never consumed, is the emblem of that lesson — a flame tended by nineteen keepers that still belongs, on the twentieth night, to the name itself. Craft, kept in common, does not go out. Original script note: The normalized Old Irish form is Brigit — already plain ASCII in its modern scholarly spelling, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover (hence Tier 2 by the mechanical rule). The medieval manuscripts wrote the name in Insular script, the Irish hand of the Latin alphabet; in the older Ogham alphabet it would have been notched ᚁᚏᚔᚌᚔᚈ (B-R-I-G-I-T), a normalized reconstruction only — no Ogham stone records the theonym. Because the name is pure ASCII, its .com was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: brigid.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The Good God of All Arts
text: The Good God of All Arts: The Club of Life and Death, the Cauldron of Plenty, the Harp of the Three Strains The Dagda — Eochu Ollathir, the All-Father — is the great father-figure of the Túatha Dé Danann: their king for eighty years, master of every art, and owner of three wonders no other Irish god can match — the club whose one end kills nine men at a blow while the other restores them, the cauldron from which no company ever went away unsatisfied, and the harp that leaps to his hand from the enemy's wall and plays the world to tears, to laughter, and to sleep. The Great Club: So heavy it had to be dragged on a wheel; one end kills nine men at a stroke, the other brings the slain back to life. The Cauldron: The fourth treasure, brought from the city of Murias — the pot of plenty from which no company ever went away unthankful. The Harp of the Three Strains: Daur Da Bláo, the Oak of Two Greens; Coir Cethar Chuir, the Four-Angled Music — it killed nine men coming to his hand, then played tears, laughter, and sleep. Eochu Ollathir: 'The All-Father' — father of Óengus, Midir, Bodb Derg, and Brigit; the Túatha Dé Danann's provision and, for eighty years, their king. Symbols: The great club — Life and death hung on opposite ends of one tool — power that answers for both; The cauldron of Murias — Plenty that no company can exhaust — abundance as a standing fact, not a lucky day; The harp and its three strains — Weeping, laughing, sleeping — the whole register of feeling under a master's hand; The porridge pit — The Fomorians' mock-feast swallowed whole — insult converted into endurance; Brú na Bóinne — The Brug on the Boyne, his Otherworld house — the mound his son Óengus won for a day and a night The Dagda's dossier is the largest of any Túatha Dé Danann god: he is king, laborer, glutton, lover, harper, and father, and Cath Maige Tuired gives him the war's two strangest set-pieces — the porridge pit before the battle and the harp on the enemy's wall after it. Lebor Gabála / The Four Treasures: The Cauldron from Murias When the Túatha Dé Danann came to Ireland, the tradition says, they came from four cities of the north of the world — Falias, Gorias, Finias, and Murias — and each city yielded a treasure. From Murias came the Dagda's cauldron, and the poem of the four jewels fixes its fame in one line: no company ever went away from it unthankful. Cormac's Glossary glosses the god's own name in the same spirit: dago-dēwo-s, 'good god' — the adjective of a craftsman, not a confessor. The Lebor Gabála Érenn, Ireland's medieval book of invasions, then gives him the longest reign of the divine kings: Eochu Ollathir, that is the Dagda, held the kingship for eighty years — and it records his death at the Brug, his mound on the Boyne, from the wound that Cethlenn, Balor's wife, had dealt him at Mag Tuired. Plenty and longevity: the two things a tribe asks of its father, fixed in one reign and one grave. Cath Maige Tuired: The Builder of Bres' Forts When the half-Fomorian Bres was made king and laid the Túatha Dé Danann under tribute, the greatest of them were put to work like serfs: Ogma carried the firewood, and the Dagda was set to building raths around Bres' stronghold, laboring every day at the forts of a usurper. There the satirist Cridenbél found him, and demanded the three best bits of the Dagda's ration every night — for a satirist's curse could raise blisters on a king's face, and no one dared refuse him. The Dagda's health failed under the tax until his son Óengus took a hand. On Óengus's counsel the Dagda asked Bres for the pick of the cattle of Ireland as his wages, and hid three gold coins in the porridge meant for Cridenbél's portion. The satirist swallowed greed and gold together and died of it; when Bres demanded the Dagda's death for the killing, Óengus's plea turned the case — the gold found in the dead man's belly was itself the proof of his greed. The episode is the tradition's slyest portrait of the god: a king enduring serfdom, rescued not by force but by a father's patience and a son's wit. Cath Maige Tuired: The Porridge Pit and the Tryst at the Ford On the eve of the second battle of Mag Tuired the Dagda went to the Fomorian camp to win a truce, and the Fomorians, who knew his love of food, prepared a mock-feast to kill him with: eighty measures of new milk and the same of meal and fat, with goats and sheep and swine boiled into it, all poured into a great pit in the ground. Eat it all, they told him, or die — for to him death was no worse than leaving the porridge. He took his ladle, big enough for a man and a woman to lie in the hollow of it, ate to the scraping of the pit, and walked away with his belly dragging on the ground — and the truce was won. That Samain night he met the Mórrígan at the ford of the Unius in Connacht, where she stood washing with one foot on either side of the water. They lay together at the ford — the place was afterward called the Bed of the Couple — and she pledged herself to the Túatha Dé Danann's cause: she told him where the Fomorians would land, and promised to bring him the hearts of their fighting-men and the blood of their king Indech. The glutton the Fomorians mocked came home from the truce with the war-goddess's promise in his hand. Cath Maige Tuired: The Harp on the Wall After the battle the Fomorians had carried off the Dagda's harper, Uaithne, and the harp itself hung on the wall of the hall where Bres feasted — the harp the Dagda called Daur Da Bláo, the Oak of Two Greens, and Coir Cethar Chuir, the Four-Angled Music, in which he had bound the melodies so that they would not sound until he summoned them. Lugh, the Dagda, and Ogma pursued the retreating host and came to that hall, and the Dagda called the harp to him. It sprang from the wall and came through the hall to his hand, killing nine men in its path. Then he played the three strains that Irish music ever after took as its whole art. First the goltraí, the weeping-strain, until their women wept; then the gentraí, the laughing-strain, until their youths and maidens laughed; last the suantraí, the sleeping-strain, until the whole host slept — and the three of them walked out of the hall through sleeping enemies. When the harpers of Ireland later divided their music into three kinds, they were naming the Dagda's set. Tochmarc Étaíne / De Gabáil in t-Sída: The Day and the Night The Dagda's most famous fatherhood begins with a deception of time itself. He desired Bóand, the wife of Elcmar of the Brug, and sent Elcmar away on a day's errand; and to hide what followed, the tales say, he held the sun fast in the sky for nine months, so that the child Óengus was conceived and born within a single day — whence the boy was called mac ind Óc, the son of the young. Years later, when the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of Ireland among the defeated Túatha Dé Danann, Óengus was away fostered with Midir and received nothing. He came home and asked his father for land, and the Dagda, having no mound left to give, granted him Brú na Bóinne for a day and a night. When the term was spent and the Dagda asked for his house back, Óengus answered that it is in days and nights that the whole world is spent — and kept the greatest mound in Ireland on a quibble. The All-Father lost the argument, and one suspects he meant to. Syncretism: The Dagda's clearest cross-border witness is not Welsh but Gaulish. The Mabinogion and the whole Welsh corpus know no counterpart of him — the Brythonic silence is total, and no scholar has repaired it convincingly. The comparison the handbooks prefer runs to Gaul: the god Sucellos , 'the Good Striker', shown on altars with his long-shafted mallet in one hand and a pot in the other, often beside his consort Nantosuelta. Sjoestedt and Mac Cana both set Sucellos beside the Dagda — the good god with the enormous club and the vessel of plenty — as two regional faces of one Celtic figure-type: the all-providing father whose tool serves both ends of life. The Christian scribes who preserved him euhemerized him in their own way, demoting the god to an ancient king mighty in magic and druidry; the medieval glossaries kept his name's meaning anyway, and Cormac's Glossary was already printing 'good god' around the year 900. Cultural legacy: The Dagda rode the Celtic revival better than almost any Irish god. Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried Cath Maige Tuired into English — porridge pit, ford, and harp complete — and made him the genial giant of a generation's reading, the counterweight to Yeats's more ethereal Sidhe. Twentieth-century scholarship gave him his modern standing: Mac Cana's Celtic Mythology made him the type-case of the Celtic all-skilled father, and the Sucellos comparison fixed him in the pan-Celtic frame. Modern Druidry and Celtic pagan practice honor him as god of plenty, craft, and fatherhood; and Brú na Bóinne — Newgrange, the most visited prehistoric monument in Ireland — keeps his mythic address, the Brug of the Dagda that his son won for a day and a night. In Irish itself the name never went anywhere: an Dagda has meant the same large, shrewd, inexhaustible father of the gods for twelve hundred years of the written language. Extended meditation: The Dagda is the god of competence, and his name says so: the 'good' of the Good God is the goodness of the craftsman, not the confessor — he is good at things, all the things, and the tradition loves him for it without ever making him solemn. He is the only great god in the Irish corpus whom the myths allow to be ridiculous: belly dragging, porridge-smeared, out-argued by his own son, set to digging forts by a usurper. And every one of those scenes ends the same way — the job finished, the pit scraped clean, the truce won, the satirist buried by his own greed. His three treasures are really one treasure in three keys. The club settles accounts at both ends of life; the cauldron makes sure the table never runs out; the harp keeps feeling itself in order — grief, joy, and rest, each in its strain. Provision, power, and harmony: the whole duty of a father, enlarged to divine scale. The Dagda asks the question every household answers daily — not whether you are good, but whether you are good for something, and whether there is enough. Original script note: The normalized Old Irish form is Dagda — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: dagda.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Wilderness, Animals, Fertility
text: Wilderness, Animals, Fertility: The Antlered Lord Between the Wild and the Otherworld Cernunnos is the horned god of Gaul: named once in stone at Paris, pictured across the Celtic world as the cross-legged, antlered lord who holds the torc of rank in one hand and the ram-horned serpent of the underworld in the other, with the beasts of the wild gathered at his back. The Antlers: The stag's crown the single inscription illustrates: the name means 'the horned one', and the Paris stone shows exactly that. The Torc: The gold neck-ring of rank — held in the god's hand on the Gundestrup plate, hung from the antlers on the Paris pillar. The Ram-Horned Serpent: The hybrid creature of Gaulish art — serpent's body, ram's horns — coiled in the god's left hand on the cauldron plate. The Cross-Legged Seat: The seated posture of the Gundestrup figure, echoed at Reims and Saintes: the stillness of the lord of animals. Symbols: The antlers — Sovereignty over the wild, written into the name itself — the horn made godhead; The torc — Rank and offering at once: the wealth the lord of beasts holds, wears, and dispenses; The ram-horned serpent — The underworld's animal, held bare-handed — the chthonic power no other Gaulish figure touches so calmly; The gathered beasts — Stag, boar, and the beasts of the deep wood: the retinue that answers to him and to no one else Cernunnos has no mythology in the literary sense — no tale, no genealogy, no surviving word of his deeds. Gaul wrote no epics down. What survives is a dossier of stone, silver, and bronze: one inscription that names him and a gallery of images that show him, and the whole tradition must be read from those. Pillar of the Boatmen: The Name on Stone Under the choir of Notre-Dame, in 1711, workmen uncovered the monument the boatmen's guild of the Parisii — the nautae Parisiaci — had raised to Jupiter in the reign of Tiberius, early in the first century CE. Among its carved gods, one block shows a balding, bearded head wearing antlers, with a torc hanging from each antler, and above the figure runs the inscription [C]ERNVNNOS. The first letter is lost and restored by convention, but the reading has held for three centuries of scholarship: this is the only text in the world that names the horned god. Everything else called Cernunnos is an identification argued from this single stone. The same monument shows the bull-god Tarvos Trigaranos and the woodcutter-god Esus: Cernunnos keeps company with a whole pantheon of Gaulish powers, all carved beneath a dedication to Jupiter — Rome's frame around native gods. Gundestrup Cauldron: The Cross-Legged Lord In 1891 a peat-cutter's spade struck silver in the Rævemosen bog at Gundestrup in Jutland: a great gilded vessel of thirteen plates, the masterpiece of Celtic metalwork, now in the National Museum of Denmark. On one interior plate sits the figure the whole world now pictures when it hears the name — cross-legged, antlered, a torc gripped in the right hand and a ram-horned serpent in the left, while a stag with matching antlers stands beside him and the animals of the wild close round: boar, bull, and a wolfish beast padding toward him. No inscription names him, and honest scholarship marks the identification as inference — but the face, the horns, the torc, and the serpent are the Paris pillar's figure seated in full. The vessel's other plates — the wheel-god, the antlered lord before a cauldron of warriors, elephants and griffins of exotic tribute — place the horned figure inside a complete cosmology of sacrifice and plenty. Gallo-Roman Iconography: The Antlered Lords of Gaul The figure recurs across the Roman Gaulish world without ever being named again. At Reims an altar shows an antlered, cross-legged god seated between Apollo and Mercury, emptying a sack of grain or coin over a bull and a stag — the horned one as the source of abundance. At Saintes a relief gives the cross-legged figure his serpents again. In the rock carvings of Val Camonica in northern Italy a standing antlered figure with torcs on his arms was cut perhaps four centuries before the Paris pillar — the oldest of all the horned images, and the proof that the type long predates the name's one surviving attestation. At every site the figure keeps his two attributes — horns and stillness — while everything Roman around him changes: the god outlasts his interpreters. Comparative Debate: Conall Cernach and the Insular Echo Insular Celtic literature preserves no Cernunnos — but it preserves a name that has tempted scholars since the nineteenth century. Conall Cernach, the Ulster Cycle hero who stands beside [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]] as the second champion of Ulster, bears the epithet cernach, and the possibility that his name continues the same horn-root as the Gaulish god has been argued from Vendryes to Mac Cana. The honest verdict is suspension: the philology permits the connection, the sources never confirm it, and Mac Cana himself counsels caution. The horned god of Gaul may have an Irish cousin in the hero-lists — or the resemblance may be the oldest false friend in Celtic studies. Either way the debate itself is instructive: it shows how much weight Celtic philology places on a single shared root, and how rarely the texts cooperate. Syncretism: Rome met the horned god the way Rome met every god: by pairing him with her own. The Reims altar seats the antlered figure between Apollo and Mercury — a Roman frame built round a native centre — and the Pillar of the Boatmen itself is dedicated to Jupiter, with the Gaulish gods carved in attendance. The deepest Roman comparison is inferential: Caesar reports (De Bello Gallico 6.18) that all the Gauls claim descent from Dis Pater, father of the underworld, and since the nineteenth century scholars have wondered whether the antlered lord with his serpent and his cross-legged stillness is the god Caesar's informants meant. The identification is suggestive, never provable, and the best handbooks — Mac Cana, Green, Koch — keep it filed under hypothesis. His closest kin inside the lexicon are the other lords of the Celtic otherworld: [[arawn|Arawn]] of [[annwn|Annwn]], who hunts with white red-eared hounds, and [[dagda|the Dagda]], the good god whose cauldron never empties. Cultural legacy: Cernunnos has the strangest afterlife in the lexicon: a god named once in antiquity who became, two millennia later, the most famous horned figure in modern religion. Margaret Murray's The God of the Witches (1931) made him the prime exhibit of her pan-European witch-cult — a thesis academic history has since dismantled (Ronald Hutton's The Triumph of the Moon is the standard autopsy) — but the image outlived the theory. Gerald Gardner placed the Horned God at the centre of modern Wicca, and 'Cernunnos' became his conventional name in contemporary pagan practice worldwide. The Gundestrup plate did the visual work: that cross-legged, antlered silhouette is now one of the most reproduced images of the ancient world, from album covers to fantasy games. A god with no surviving myth became the emblem of every wild thing that refuses to be tamed. Extended meditation: Cernunnos is the god built from evidence alone. No hymn, no saga, no genealogy — one word on a Paris stone, one silver plate from a Danish bog, and a scattered congregation of images that agree with each other across six hundred miles and four hundred years. He asks a different kind of attention than the storied gods: not 'what did he do?' but 'what did they see, that they carved him so carefully and wrote his name so rarely?' The answer the monuments give is always the same: the still one in the middle of the animals, holding rank in one hand and the underworld in the other, entirely at peace. Some gods are known by their stories. This one is known by his posture — and the posture has proved enough. Original script note: The name is attested exactly once, in Roman capitals on the Pillar of the Boatmen: [C]ERNVNNOS — the initial letter lost and restored by convention, the double NN and final -OS certain. Gaulish was also written in the Greek alphabet elsewhere in Gaul, but this name survives only in the Latin-letter epigraphic tradition; no native Celtic script attests it. The form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — which fixes the name in Tier 2. Because it is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: cernunnos.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: War, King of Tuatha
text: War, King of Tuatha: The Silver-Handed King of the Tuatha Dé Danann Nuada Airgetlám is the first king of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Ireland — the ruler who lost his arm at the First Battle of Mag Tuired, lost his throne to the law that a blemished man cannot be king, and won both back through the physicians' craft: first the silver arm that named him, then the living arm that restored him. His sword from Findias was one of the Four Treasures of his people, and he died at the Second Battle of Mag Tuired at the hands of Balor of the Evil Eye. The Silver Hand: Dian Cécht's silver arm, made with Credne the brazier, moved in every joint — and gave the king his name, Airgetlám. The Sword from Findias: One of the Four Treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann; once it was drawn from its sheath, no one escaped it. Mag Tuired: The plain of the two battles: against the Fir Bolg, where the arm was lost; against the Fomorians, where the king fell. The Unblemished Throne: Irish kingship law held that no man with a blemish could rule; Nuada's wound cost him Tara, and his healing restored him. Symbols: The silver arm — Wholeness made by craft when nature failed — the prosthesis that kept a king king in all but law; The sword of Nuada — The irresistible weapon from the city Findias, one of the Four Treasures brought to Ireland; Tara (Temair) — The seat of the kingship of Ireland, which a blemished man could not lawfully hold; The physician's craft — Dian Cécht's silver-work and Miach's flesh-work — healing as the instrument of sovereignty; Dog and fisherman (as Nodens) — The hound figurines and sea imagery of the Lydney Park temple, where his Gaulish cognate was worshipped Nuada's story is the Irish tradition's great parable of kingship and the body: a ruler can be unmade by a single wound and remade by healing, and the law watches both. The record runs from the Lebor Gabála Érenn through the two battles of Mag Tuired, and his Welsh and Gaulish cognates carry the same silver-handed name across the Celtic world. Lebor Gabála Érenn: The First Battle of Mag Tuired When the Tuatha Dé Danann came to Ireland, Nuada had been their king for seven years. They demanded the country from the Fir Bolg, and the two peoples met at Mag Tuired in Connacht. In the battle Nuada fought Sreng, champion of the Fir Bolg, and Sreng struck off his right arm at the shoulder — yet the Tuatha Dé Danann won the field, and the Fir Bolg king Eochaid mac Eirc was driven to his death. The victors then offered the defeated a quarter of Ireland, and the Fir Bolg chose Connacht, which their descendants held. The victory that made the Tuatha Dé Danann masters of Ireland thus cost their king the wholeness the kingship required: one champion's sword-stroke bought a kingdom and unmade its king in the same afternoon. Lebor Gabála Érenn: The Silver Hand and the Hand of Flesh Because a blemished man could not hold the kingship, Nuada yielded the throne to Bres. The physician Dian Cécht, with Credne the brazier, made him a full arm of silver that moved in every joint — whence his byname Airgetlám, Silver-hand. But Dian Cécht's own son Miach went further: he set the severed arm to the stump and healed it 'joint to joint and vein to vein' in thrice nine days. Jealous that the son had outdone the father, Dian Cécht struck Miach dead; from the young healer's grave grew three hundred and sixty-five herbs, which his sister Airmed sorted by their virtues — and which Dian Cécht scattered, so that their full knowledge died with him. Healing, in this cycle, is never free of the wound of envy. Lebor Gabála · Cath Maige Tuired: Bres, the Satire, and the Restoration Bres mac Elatha, half Fomorian by blood, ruled badly: the warriors of Ireland were set to menial labour, hospitality failed, and the poet Cairbre mac Étaíne composed against him what the tradition calls the first satire ever made in Ireland — and Bres's face broke out in blotches. Shamed and deposed, Bres fled to his Fomorian kin and came back at the head of the host that forced the Second Battle. The same law that had unseated Nuada now unseated Bres, for a blemished king could not stand; and with his arm made whole by Miach, Nuada took back the kingship and held it until the war came. The symmetry is exact: one king falls by the body's wound, the other by the wound of the word, and the same unforgiving law of wholeness judges them both. Cath Maige Tuired: The Second Battle and the King's Death At Tara, on the eve of the war, a stranger came to Nuada's hall claiming every skill at once — harpist, warrior, smith, poet, healer — and Nuada, testing Lugh and finding him unmatched, gave the young god his own seat, the champion's seat, to lead the counsel of war. The Second Battle of Mag Tuired was fought against the Fomorians, and there Nuada Airgetlám and Macha his wife fell together at the hands of Balor of the Evil Eye. Balor's own death followed within the hour, Lugh's sling-stone through the destroying eye, and with the two kings' deaths the war ended and the tribute was lifted forever. The first king of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Ireland died in the victory that secured his people's rule; the sword of Findias passed into memory as the measure of a weapon that cannot be withstood. Syncretism: Nuada belongs to one of the clearest pan-Celtic name families. In Welsh he is Nudd and, in full form, Lludd Llaw Eraint — 'Lludd of the Silver Hand' — the king of Britain in Lludd a Llefelys , whose byname renders Airgetlám word for word (llaw 'hand', eraint 'silver'). In Gaulish he is Nodens (also Nodons, Nudens), worshipped at the great temple at Lydney Park in Gloucestershire, where Roman dedicants equated him with Mars and where the imagery — hounds, fishermen, the sea — suggests a healer and hunter as much as a warrior. The Romano-British curse tablet of Silvianus, asking 'Lord Nodens' to deny health to the thief of his ring, shows the god working as an enforcer of justice. Scholars (Mac Cana, Koch) reconstruct a Common Celtic *Noudont- or *Noudo- behind all three, though the root's meaning — 'cloud-maker' or 'catcher, fisher' — remains genuinely debated. Cultural legacy: Nuada's afterlife runs through scholarship into fantasy. When R. E. M. and T. V. Wheeler published their excavation of the Nodens temple at Lydney Park in 1932, the young philologist J. R. R. Tolkien contributed the appendix 'The Name Nodens', tracing the god's name to a root of catching and acquiring — a fragment of Tolkien's scholarly life that fans of his fiction still chase. In modern Irish the name survives as Nuadha, and Maynooth University's old arms carried Nuada's sword. In popular culture the silver-handed king rides again as Prince Nuada Silverlance in Hellboy II: The Golden Army (2008), and the motif of the magical prosthetic hand — from A Song of Ice and Fire to Japanese fantasy — descends, knowingly or not, from Airgetlám. Modern Celtic pagans honour Nuada as a god of rightful rule, healing, and sovereignty restored. Extended meditation: Nuada is the king of the necessary surrender. The Irish law of the unblemished king looks cruel — a man maimed in his people's victory loses his throne — but the myth refuses both easy readings. It does not mock the law: Bres, who takes the throne, is judged by the same standard and falls to a blemish of the face raised by satire. And it does not abandon the wounded: the whole craft of the physician-gods bends itself to making Nuada whole, first in silver, then in flesh. What the cycle teaches is that sovereignty is not possession but fitness, and fitness can be lost and restored. The silver hand is the emblem of every function that has to be rebuilt after catastrophe: it moves in every joint, it does the work, and it is not the thing it replaces — until Miach's deeper healing shows that even that distinction can be overcome. The king who rules again is not the king who fell. He is the king who was remade. Original script note: The attested Old Irish form is Nuadu (later Nuada ), written by medieval Irish scribes in the Insular Latin bookhand of the great vellum codices; in the Ogham letter-row the name would have been notched ᚅᚒᚐᚇᚐ (N-U-A-D-A), though no Ogham stone yet found carries it. Because the name is already plain ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: nuada.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The Rider No Horse Can Catch
text: The Rider No Horse Can Catch: Horses, Sovereignty Rhiannon is the Great Queen of the Mabinogi: the lady of the Otherworld who rides past Gorsedd Arberth on a pale horse at a slow, even pace that the fastest mounts of Dyfed cannot close — the goddess who chooses her own king, bears a false charge with unbroken dignity, and endures the penance of the horse-collar without bending. Gorsedd Arberth: The mound above Narberth where wonders are seen: whoever sits there receives blows — or sees a marvel. Pwyll saw her ride past. The Uncatchable Pace: She rides a pale horse at a slow, steady walk, and the swiftest riders in Dyfed cannot close the distance — until she is asked to stop. The Birds of Rhiannon: Adar Rhiannon: three birds whose song, though heard far over the sea, is as clear as if they sang beside you — sweeter than any earthly song. The Horse-Block: The marble mounting-block at the gate of Arberth, where she sits out her penance and offers to carry every guest to court on her back. Symbols: The pale horse — Sovereignty arriving at its own pace — the mount no pursuit can overtake, because the rider alone decides when to stop; The three birds — Adar Rhiannon, whose song crosses the boundary between the living and the dead — the Otherworld made audible; The horse-block — Dignity under a false sentence: the queen who carries her guests rather than break under the charge she did not earn; The bottomless bag — The cleverness that out-plots a forced marriage — Gwawl's undoing, and the game of Badger in the Bag; The collars of asses — The enchantment endured in the Third Branch — humiliation worn without surrender, until the spell is undone Rhiannon is the strongest female figure in the Four Branches of the Mabinogi, and the tales give her a complete arc: the uncatchable rider who chooses her husband, the accused mother who bears her penance, the captive of the enchantment who comes home still a queen. Every word of her story is medieval Welsh prose, preserved in two great manuscripts. First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed: The Rider on the Pale Horse Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, goes up to Gorsedd Arberth, the mound where a man either suffers blows or sees a wonder, and there he sees a lady in shining gold brocade riding past on a great pale horse — at a slow, even pace. He sends his swiftest rider after her; the faster the pursuit, the farther she draws ahead. Day after day it happens, with Pwyll's own horse and Pwyll himself, until at last he calls out: 'Maiden, for the sake of the man you love best, wait for me.' She stops at once: 'I will wait gladly — and it would have been better for the horse had you asked me that long ago.' She is Rhiannon, daughter of Hefaidd Hên, and she has come of her own will: she is being given to a man she does not want, and she has chosen Pwyll instead. First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed: The Bag That Would Not Fill At the wedding feast, Pwyll grants a request before he hears it — and the petitioner is Gwawl fab Clud, the suitor Rhiannon refused, who claims her by the promise. Rhiannon is not dismayed; she devises the counter-plot. A year later Pwyll comes to Gwawl's feast disguised as a beggar, asking only that a certain small bag she has given him be filled with food. The bag cannot be filled: it will never be full, she has told him, unless a true lord treads the food down with his feet and declares that enough has been put in. Gwawl rises and treads it down — and Pwyll draws the bag shut over him, blows his horn, and his war-band falls on the hall. Each man strikes the bag and asks what is in it; 'a badger,' comes the answer, and from that night the Welsh played the game called Badger in the Bag. Gwawl buys his release with sureties and a renounced claim, and Rhiannon marries the man she chose. First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed: The May-Eve Vanishing and the Penance After three childless years the nobles of Dyfed press Pwyll to take another wife; he begs one year more, and Rhiannon bears a son. On the night of the birth the six women set to watch all fall asleep, and the child is gone. Terrified of the blame, the women kill the pups of a hound, smear the blood on Rhiannon's face, lay the bones beside her, and swear she has destroyed her own child. Pwyll will not put her away, but a penance is imposed: she is to sit beside the horse-block at the gate of Arberth, tell her story to every traveller who comes, and offer to carry guests and strangers to the court on her back. She accepts the sentence she did not earn, and she bears it without breaking. The child, meanwhile, has fallen into the strangest rescue in Welsh prose. Teyrnon Twrf Liant, a lord by the sea, loses a foal every May-eve; keeping watch over his mare, he sees a great clawed hand reach through the window to seize the newborn foal, and strikes it off with his sword. Outside the door he finds a baby wrapped in silk brocade. He and his wife rear the boy as Gwri Wallt Euryn, Gwri of the Golden Hair — who grows with uncanny speed and bears, year by year, the very likeness of Pwyll. When Teyrnon hears of Rhiannon's penance, he knows what he must do, and he and his wife bring the boy to Arberth. Rhiannon looks at him and says that if this is true, her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her. From that word the boy is named Pryderi, and the penance ends. Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr: The Enchantment of Dyfed and the Collars of Asses After Pwyll's death, Rhiannon is given in marriage to Manawydan fab Llŷr, and the four of them — Rhiannon and Manawydan, Pryderi and his wife Cigfa — return to Dyfed. There comes a peal of thunder and a fall of mist, and when it lifts, the land is emptied: not a person, not a dwelling, not a beast remains. For two years the four live by hunting; then they try their hand at saddlery, shield-making, and shoemaking in the towns of England, and each time the local craftsmen drive them out for making work too good to allow. Back in empty Dyfed, a shining white boar leads Pryderi and Manawydan to a fortress that was never there before; Pryderi goes in, lays hold of a golden bowl hanging by chains above a marble fountain, and is rooted to the spot, struck dumb. Rhiannon goes in after him, takes hold of the same bowl, and is trapped beside him — and fort, bowl, and both prisoners vanish. Manawydan undoes the spell by patience. Sowing wheat, he watches three ripe fields stripped bare by mice on successive nights, and on the third he catches one slow, heavy mouse and condemns it to hang as a thief. A clerk, a priest, and a bishop come one after another to beg it off, each offering more than the last, and Manawydan names his price: Pryderi and Rhiannon released, the enchantment lifted from Dyfed, and no vengeance taken. The mouse is the wife of Llwyd fab Cilcoed, transformed with all his household; Llwyd had laid the spell to avenge his friend Gwawl fab Clud. Pryderi comes home with the gate-hammer about his neck, and Rhiannon with the collars of asses about hers — the second humiliation she has worn like a queen, and the second she survives. Second Branch · Branwen ferch Llŷr: The Birds of Rhiannon Rhiannon never steps on stage in the Second Branch, but her birds do. When the seven survivors of the Irish war come back over the sea bearing the wounded head of Brân the Blessed, they feast at Harlech for seven years, and there come three birds — the Birds of Rhiannon, Adar Rhiannon — that begin to sing to them. Every other song seems unlovely beside it; and though the birds must be gazed at far out over the sea, their singing is as clear as if they sang in the hall. At Gwales in Penfro the company feasts on for eighty years with the uncorrupted head, in the presence of the birds' song, until the door toward Cornwall is opened and memory and sorrow return. Later Welsh tradition says of the Adar Rhiannon that their song wakes the dead and lulls the living to sleep — the music of a world that does not end. Syncretism: The great comparative debate pairs Rhiannon with Epona, the Gaulish horse-goddess whose dedications — more than two hundred inscriptions from Britain to the Balkans — make her the best-attested Celtic deity of the Roman west. A queenly rider whose whole story is bound to horses, whose name the handbooks reconstruct as 'Great Queen', looks very like an insular reflex of the mare-goddess; Mac Cana and others have argued the parallel, and Koch registers it as the standard comparison — but no inscription names Rhiannon or *Rīgantonā, and the identification remains typological, not epigraphic. The second frame is sovereignty: Mac Cana reads the First Branch against the Irish pattern in which the land's queen chooses and validates the king, so that Pwyll's marriage to Rhiannon is his investiture as much as his wedding. The third is Macha, the Irish sovereignty figure forced to race the king's horses: horse, humiliation, and queenship cluster around both women, and the handbooks have compared them for a century. None of these parallels is an identity; together they map the kind of goddess the Welsh prose is remembering. Cultural legacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Rhiannon out of the Welsh manuscripts and into the English-speaking world, and the Victorian Celtic revival made her one of the best-known figures of Welsh tradition. Evangeline Walton's twentieth-century retellings of the Four Branches kept her before modern readers, and in 1975 Fleetwood Mac's 'Rhiannon' — written by Stevie Nicks, who found the name in a novel and only afterwards learned it belonged to a Welsh goddess — made the name famous worldwide; the given name Rhiannon, already living in Wales, spread across the English-speaking world in the song's wake. In modern Druid and pagan practice she is honoured as a goddess of horses, sovereignty, and endurance under injustice, and scholars of the Mabinogi rank her among the most fully realized women in medieval European literature — a figure whose dignity the prose never once allows to slip. Extended meditation: Rhiannon cannot be caught because she has already decided where she is going. The fastest horses in Dyfed gallop themselves to exhaustion behind a rider who is barely trotting — and the moment she is asked, she stops, because stopping was always hers to give. That is the secret the First Branch teaches about power: the pace of a sovereign is not set by her pursuers. The rest of her story tests the lesson. Falsely accused, she does not rage or plead; she sits down by the horse-block and carries her guests, one by one, until the truth walks home on its own legs. Trapped in the enchantment, she endures the collars of asses and comes out still the Great Queen. Endurance, in her telling, is not passivity — it is the refusal to let an unjust sentence write your name. She waits, she carries, she outlasts; and the land is hers again. Original script note: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Rhiannon — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: rhiannon.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/rhiannon/ in the meantime.

title: Magic, Poetry, Trickery
text: Magic, Poetry, Trickery: Enchanter of Gwynedd — illusion, craft, and the fate of Lleu Llaw Gyffes In the Welsh tradition, Gwydion fab Dôn is the foremost magician of the Mabinogi: master of illusion, disguise, and the hidden name, whose tricks win a war — and whose craft finally puts a broken world back together. The Enchanted Swine: Disguised as a poet, Gwydion conjured illusory stallions, hounds, and shields to trade for Pryderi's otherworld pigs — the first swine in Wales — and started a war with a vanishing herd. Math's Wand: The wand that transformed Gwydion and Gilfaethwy into deer, boars, and wolves for three years — and that later struck Lleu from eagle back into man. The Flower-Maiden: With Math, Gwydion fashioned Blodeuwedd from the flowers of oak, broom, and meadowsweet — a wife made by craft for the man no earthly wife was allowed. The Eagle on the Oak: When Lleu was struck into eagle-shape, Gwydion followed a sow to the oak, sang three englynion to bring him down, and turned vengeance into restoration. Symbols: The magic wand — Math's wand of transformation — punishment, testing, and restoration carried in a single rod; Oak, broom, and meadowsweet — The three flowers from which Blodeuwedd was made by enchantment; The illusory horses and hounds — Gwydion's conjured wealth, real for a day and gone by morning — craft as currency; The eagle on the oak — Lleu wounded into bird-shape, rotting flesh feeding a sow beneath the tree; The sow — The beast Gwydion followed through the valley to find his foster-son; The shoemaker's disguise — The craft under which Gwydion tricked Arianrhod into naming her own son Gwydion fab Dôn is the enchanter of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, 'Math fab Mathonwy': nephew of Math the king of Gwynedd, brother of Gilfaethwy, and the foremost magician of medieval Welsh literature. He is poet, trickster, foster-father, and avenger in one figure — the man who makes illusions that pass for wealth, who pays for his crimes in animal skins, and who ends the tale as the careful hand that puts a broken world back into shape. Math fab Mathonwy: The War for the Swine King Math of Gwynedd could live only with his feet in the lap of a virgin, except in time of war, and the maiden Goewin held that office. When Gilfaethwy desired her, Gwydion devised the remedy: war. He went to Pryderi of Dyfed in the guise of a poet and asked for the swine — the hobeu, the first pigs ever brought to Wales, a gift from Arawn of Annwfn. Refused, he conjured twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars, and twelve golden shields, and traded the apparitions for the herd. By the time Pryderi's glamour faded, Gwydion was gone, and Pryderi came north with an army. While Math marched to meet him, Gwydion and Gilfaethwy forced Goewin. At the peace-talks Pryderi demanded single combat, 'for it was because of me that the hosts came'; at Maenor Penard, the tale says, Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour and by magic and enchantment', and Dyfed went home under tribute. The victory is real and so is its cost: Gwydion's finest trick is also his crime, and the Fourth Branch never lets the two be separated. Math fab Mathonwy: The Punishment of the Brothers Math's justice is the strangest in the Mabinogi. He struck Gwydion and Gilfaethwy with his magic wand and turned them into a stag and a hind, and sent them into the wild for a year; when they returned with a fawn, he made them a boar and a sow for the second year, and a wolf and a she-wolf for the third. Each year their offspring — Hyddwn, Hychddwn Hir, and Bleiddwn — were sent to the court, baptized, and raised. After the third year Math struck them back into their own shapes: 'You have had punishment enough, and you have been greatly shamed.' The punishment is exact and even-handed — the brothers suffer in the flesh what they did, and when the debt is paid the king takes them back into honour. It is the Fourth Branch's doctrine of justice in miniature: transformation as sentence, restoration as mercy. And it matters that the wand passes finally into Gwydion's own hand: the man punished by shape-shaping becomes the master of it, and the tale watches to see what he does with the power that once unmade him. Math fab Mathonwy: The Naming and Arming of Lleu When Gwydion proposed his sister Arianrhod as Math's new footholder, she stepped over the wand for the virginity test and dropped a yellow-haired boy — Dylan, who made for the sea — and 'something small' that Gwydion hid in a chest at the foot of his bed. From the chest came the boy who would be Lleu. Gwydion fostered him, and Arianrhod, shamed, laid three tynghedau upon him: he should have no name until she named him, no arms until she armed him, and no wife of any race then on earth. Gwydion undid the destinies by craft. Disguised as a shoemaker with the boy at his side, he came beneath Caer Arianrhod, and when Lleu flung a stone and struck a wren's leg askew, Arianrhod cried that the fair one had struck it with a skilful hand — and so named him Lleu Llaw Gyffes.
