Even her name works this way — Fullness is not a thing she does but a thing she keeps. The tradition gives her no adventure because her office is the adventure's opposite: Gná rides out with the queen's words; Fulla stays, and what is entrusted to her stays with her. Nanna's ring from Hel is the tradition's own verdict on that office — when the dead send gifts home, they send one to the keeper. In a mythology that ends in fire and betrayal, Fulla is the quiet counterweight: the proof that some things, once entrusted, are simply kept. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Fulla — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚠᚢᛚᛅ (f-u-l-a, the sixteen-rune row writing the geminate ll with a single ᛚ). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: fulla.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The Hound of Gnipahellir
text: The Hound of Gnipahellir: Guardian, Underworld Hound Garmr is the blood-bayed watchdog of Helheim: the hound bound before the cave of Gnipahellir whose howling, sounded three times in Vǫluspá, opens the world's last age. Grímnismál calls him simply the best of hounds; at Ragnarök he breaks his fetter and meets one-handed Týr, and each is the other's death. Gnipahellir: The Gnipa-cave — the overhanging rock at the border of Hel before which the hound is bound until the world's unbinding. The Breaking Fetter: Vǫluspá's refrain: the fetter will snap and the wolf run free — the chain that holds only until the end. The Bloody Breast: The hound Óðinn met on the Hel-road in Baldrs draumar, bloodied about the breast and baying long — the poem's own portrait of the watcher. Týr's Last Sword: At Ragnarök Garmr fights the one-handed god who once fed the wolf, and each is the other's death. Symbols: Gnipahellir — The overhanging cave at Hel's border — the fixed post of the watcher until the end of the world; The fetter — The binding that is only a postponement — every chain in the Edda is a clock; The thrice-sounded bay — The howl that punctuates Vǫluspá's collapse — the sound by which the seeress counts down the world's ending; The bloodied breast — The mark of the hound that comes out of Hel — death's evidence carried on the watcher's own body; The mutual death — Garmr and Týr killing each other — the Edda's justice, in which even Ragnarök's victories are paid for in kind Garmr has no adventures and no childhood; he exists in the sources the way a bell exists — to sound at the appointed hour. Three poems and one prose chapter hold the whole dossier: the best-of-hounds catalogue, the thrice-sounded bay of Vǫluspá, the bloodied watcher on the Hel-road, and the last fight with Týr. Grímnismál 44: The Best of Hounds Grímnismál closes its catalogue of the world's first things with a litany every Norse listener could recite: Yggdrasill is the best of trees, Skíðblaðnir of ships, Óðinn of the Æsir, Sleipnir of steeds, Bifrǫst of bridges, Bragi of skalds, Hábrók of hawks — and Garmr of hounds. The hound of Hel takes his place in the superlative order of the cosmos without explanation and without rival: whatever else the poets disagreed about, the office of watchdog at the world's border had one incumbent. Vǫluspá 44, 49, 58: The Thrice-Sounded Bay Vǫluspá counts down the end of the world by the hound's voice. Three times, as the vision darkens — when the bonds of the world loosen, when the giants and the dead come to the field, and at the last, before the earth sinks into the sea — the seeress breaks off with the same refrain: 'Garmr bays loudly before Gnipahellir; the fetter will snap, and the wolf run free.' The poem never names the wolf that runs: freki, 'the ravenous one', is the word the kennings use for Fenrir, and Snorri reads the freed beast as the Fenris-wolf — but the refrain hangs the moment on Garmr himself, the watcher whose post is the first to fall. Three stanzas, three howls: the Edda's own clock of doom. Baldrs draumar 2–3: The Bloodied Watcher on the Hel-Road When Baldr dreams baleful dreams, Óðinn saddles Sleipnir and rides down the road to Niflhel — and the first living thing the poem sets on that road is the hound. 'He met a hound come out of Hel: it was bloody about the breast in front, and it bayed long at the Father of Spells. Óðinn rode on — the earth resounded — until he came to the high hall of Hel.' The poem never names the hound, but the tradition has never hesitated: the watcher bloodied at Hel's gate is Garmr, doing in Baldrs draumar exactly what Gnipahellir's bound hound does in Vǫluspá — announcing that something living has crossed, and that the dead know it. Gylfaginning 51: The Death of Týr Snorri's Ragnarök gives Garmr his single act and his single line of description. When the sons of Muspell ride over Bifrǫst and the gods arm at Vígríðr, 'then Garmr, who is bound before Gnipahellir, breaks loose; he is the most terrible of monsters — mesta forað. He fights with Týr, and each becomes the other's death.' The pairing is the Edda's quiet arithmetic: Týr is the god who gave his hand to bind one wolf, and at the end he is spent killing another. Fenrir takes Óðinn; Garmr takes the one-handed god; the wolves of the North divide the gods' courage between them. The Kennings' Parallel: Fenrir's Double The tradition itself seems to have kept two ledgers for one hound. Týr's kennings in Skáldskaparmál call him 'feeder of the wolf' and 'the one-handed god' — titles earned in the binding of Fenrir — yet it is Garmr who kills him at Ragnarök. Vǫluspá's refrain makes the same ambiguity work the other way: it is Garmr who bays, and 'the wolf' who runs free. Scholars from the handbooks onward have read the two figures as a doublet — Simek notes that Garmr is probably best understood as a double of the Fenris-wolf, the bound monster of the end seen from the side of Hel rather than from the side of the gods. Whether kinsman, understudy, or echo, Garmr holds the watcher's half of the story Fenrir holds the devourer's half of. Syncretism: Garmr belongs to one of the oldest comparative dossiers in Indo-European studies: the hellhound. Greece keeps Kerberos, the many-headed hound of Hades whom Hesiod names among the monstrous brood of Echidna; the Ṛgveda gives Yama, the first of the dead, two four-eyed brindled hounds — the Sárameyas — who guard the path and watch over men; and Wales keeps the Cŵn Annwn, the white, red-eared hounds of Arawn's otherworld pack in the First Branch of the Mabinogion. Linguists since the nineteenth century have connected Kerberos with Sanskrit śarvara-, the epithet of Yama's hounds, and Bruce Lincoln's classic study 'The Hellhound' traces the full complex — the watcher at death's border, the barred return, the dog that must be fed or fought by the crossing hero. The North's witness fits the pattern with one northern difference: where Kerberos guards the gate of a permanent kingdom, Garmr guards a gate that will not hold. He is the hellhound of a mythology whose underworld itself has an expiry date. Cultural legacy: Garmr's afterlife runs on the two rails his sources laid down: the watchdog and the countdown. Victorian and modern retellings of Ragnarök keep the Vǫluspá refrain as the moment the end becomes audible — the howl before the fire. Tolkien gave the name, half in jest, to the talking dog Garm of Farmer Giles of Ham, a watchdog who cannot keep watch; and the modern games industry has restored the full terror, with God of War Ragnarök (2022) casting Garm as the giant unkillable wolf whose unbinding threatens the realms. In Iceland the name never left the kennels: Garmur remains an ordinary dog's name, which is perhaps the truest survival of all — the hound of Hel, brought home and given a bowl. Extended meditation: Garmr is the guardian of a gate that is fated to open. Every element of his myth is a postponement: the fetter holds until Ragnarök, the cave holds the hound until the refrain is sounded, the border holds the dead until the last age. He does his duty perfectly and it changes nothing — the Edda's whole theology of duty in one animal. What the North saw in him is what it saw everywhere: that watching is not winning, that the fiercest fidelity serves a world already sentenced, and that the howl at Gnipahellir is not a warning anyone can act on. It is simply the sound the world makes when it keeps its appointments. Garmr bays because that is what the watch is for; the fetter breaks because that is what time is for. The guardian and the doom are the same fact, heard from two sides of the gate. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Garmr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚴᛅᚱᛘᛦ (g-a-r-m-R, ᛦ writing the final nominative -r), a normalized reconstruction only, as no runic attestation of the name is known. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: garmr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The Courteous Knight
text: The Courteous Knight: The Hawk of May, the Quest Completed, and the Girdle of the Green Chapel Gawain — Welsh Gwalchmai, Arthur's nephew — is the courteous knight of the Welsh and continental cycles: the one who never came home without the quest he went to seek, the measure against whom Chrétien ranks every other knight of the Round Table, and the man the Green Knight chose to test, at the turning of a year, for the one virtue the pentangle guards — truth. The Hawk of May: Gwalch + Mai: the name itself is a raptor and a season — the spring hawk of the Welsh court. The Pentangle: The five-pointed star Solomon set on Gawain's shield in the Green Knight poem — five fives, and truth at the center of them all. The Green Girdle: The lace of silk and gold kept back from the exchange — worn home as the 'token of untruth' the court turned into a badge of honor. Gringolet: Gawain's horse from Chrétien onward — the mount that carries him, in the Green Knight poem, through the winter forest to the Green Chapel. Symbols: The hawk — The name made image: gwalch, the raptor of the Welsh genealogies — swift sight, swift return; The pentangle — The endless knot of five fives: senses, fingers, wounds, joys, and the five knightly virtues bound by truth; The green girdle — The kept-back token: one small failure of truth worn openly, until shame becomes the court's badge; The waxing strength — The romancers give him a power that rises with the sun to noon and fails after — the trace the scholars read as a faded solar hero; The nick in the neck — The single cut of the third stroke: the wound that is also a judgment, and a verdict he refuses to forget Gawain's dossier runs from a Welsh triad to a fourteenth-century masterpiece: in every century someone is testing him, and the test is always the same — not whether he can fight, but whether he will keep faith. He passes every quest and fails one truth; the tradition has been debating which matters more for seven hundred years. Culhwch ac Olwen: The Knight Who Finished the Quest The oldest Arthurian tale in Welsh names him in its great muster at Arthur's court: Gwalchmei mab Gwyar — Gwalchmai son of Gwyar — 'because he never returned home without achieving the quest he had gone to seek; he was the best of walkers and the best of riders; he was nephew to Arthur, the son of his sister, and his first cousin.' In a catalogue of hundreds of warriors, giants, and wonders, that is the whole of his entry, and it is the whole of his character: the Welsh tradition remembers him not for a single exploit but for completion itself — the errand that always comes home. Centuries later, when Chrétien and the Gawain-poet needed a knight whose courtesy could carry an entire narrative, they were still writing in the shadow of that one sentence. Trioedd Ynys Prydein: One of the Three Well-Endowed Men The Welsh Triads — the medieval memory-system that files the Island of Britain's heroes in threes — name Gwalchmai son of Gwyar among the Three Well-Endowed Men of the Island of Britain, beside Llacheu son of Arthur and Rhiwallawn Broom-Hair (Triad 4). Rachel Bromwich's edition of the Triads is also the standard witness for his name: Gwalchmai, gwalch 'hawk' + Mai 'May', the 'hawk of May' — a name that stands in Welsh, glossed and explained, generations before any French romance ever sang of Gauvain. Bromwich notes that the second element has also been compared to the British god Maponos, the 'Divine Son' of the spring, so the name may carry a youth-and-season resonance older than the month itself. To be filed in a triad is to be fixed in memory: the Welsh gave him no long tale, but they gave him a slot no one else could fill. Historia Regum Britanniae: The Nephew of the King Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia (c. 1136) made him Latin and sent him across Europe: Walganus, son of Loth of Lodonesia and Arthur's sister Anna, given as a boy to the service of Pope Sulpicius in Rome, recalled to Britain to be knighted, and made the steel edge of Arthur's Roman campaign — the knight who cuts through the emperor's host and slays the nephew of Lucius. When Mordred's treason calls the army home, Walganus falls at the landing, in the first fighting on the shore, and is buried as the chronicle says. A generation earlier, William of Malmesbury had already written him down as Walwen — and reported his tomb, found at Rhos in Pembrokeshire, fourteen feet long. Geoffrey's Walganus is grave, dutiful, and doomed: already the nephew whose loyalty is his tragedy, three centuries before Malory would make that loyalty the hinge of the whole downfall. Chrétien de Troyes: The Measure of Courtesy In the romances of Chrétien (c. 1160–1190), Gauvain is not the hero of any single quest but the standard against which all the heroes are measured: Erec et Enide ranks him first of the knights of the Round Table, and through Cligés, Lancelot, Yvain, and the Conte du Graal he moves as the court's fixed point — courteous without effort, brave without boasting, the knight whose speech is as ready as his sword. Chrétien lets Perceval's innocence test him and the world test them both; the Continuators of the Perceval give him stranger gifts — a strength that doubles as the sun climbs to noon and fails as it falls — the trace that later scholarship would read as the memory of a solar hero. Where other knights must learn courtesy, Gauvain simply is it; that is precisely why he is so hard to write a story about. Sir Gawain and the Green Knight: The Bargain of the Green Chapel At Camelot's New Year feast a giant all in green rides into the hall and offers a Christmas game: any knight may take one stroke at his neck with the great axe, on condition of receiving one in return, a year and a day hence, at the Green Chapel. Gawain takes the challenge, strikes the head clean off, and the Green Knight rides out holding it, reminding him of the tryst. The year turns, and Gawain rides north to keep his bargain. At Hautdesert, Lord Bertilak proposes an exchange of winnings: each evening they will swap whatever the day has gained. Three days the lord hunts; three days his lady tests Gawain in his chamber; and each evening Gawain faithfully renders the kisses he has received — but on the third day he keeps back the green girdle the lady swears will save his life. At the Green Chapel the axe falls three times: twice withheld, and once, for the kept-back lace, a nick in the neck. The Green Knight is Bertilak, sent by Morgan le Fay; the girdle was the whole point. Gawain wears it home as his 'token of untruth' — and Camelot laughs, and binds green laces on every shoulder. The poem's subject is not whether a knight can fight but what truth costs, and whether one small love of life can be forgiven . Le Morte Darthur: The Last Letter Malory's Sir Gawaine is the courteous knight grown tragic: head of the Orkney clan, Arthur's dearest nephew, whose feud with Lancelot — after Gareth and Gaheris are slain in the fire of Guenevere's rescue — drags the fellowship to ruin. Wounded at Dover by Lancelot in the last single combat, he dies of the reopened wound, writing with his own hand the letter that calls Lancelot 'flower of all noble knights' and begs him to come see his tomb. And on the eve of Salisbury Plain he returns in Arthur's dream with a troop of ladies, warning the king not to fight Mordred on the morrow — the nephew still trying, from beyond death, to bring his uncle's last errand home. It is the pattern's final turn: the knight who always finished the quest dies writing an errand he will not live to see delivered, and begs the one man he fought to come anyway. Syncretism: Gawain's deepest comparative file is Irish. The beheading game itself has its classic Celtic witness in Fled Bricrenn, Bricriu's Feast, where the giant Uath — 'Horror' — offers the Ulster heroes exactly the Green Knight's bargain: strike off my head today, and I strike yours tomorrow. Only Cúchulainn takes the axe twice and kneels for the return stroke; the giant brings the blade down blunt, and the champion's portion is judged his. Kittredge's Study of Gawain and the Green Knight (1916) made the Irish episode the standing source-analogue of the English poem, and the comparison has been refined, never abandoned. The loathly-lady strand of Gawain's story — Dame Ragnelle, whose riddle is answered with sovereignty — has its own Irish kin in the sovereignty-goddess tales, where a hag by a well becomes a queen when a king will kiss her. Within the pantheon his standing kin are [[kai|Cei]] and [[bedwyr|Bedwyr]], the two companions Culhwch pairs beside him, and [[cuchulainn|Cúchulainn]], the only other hero in Celtic story who knelt under the return stroke. The Welsh tradition itself never made him a god; it made him something rarer — the knight every other knight is measured against. Cultural legacy: Gawain is the Arthurian figure with the longest continuous critical life. Chrétien made him the definition of cortoisie; the Gawain-poet made him the test-case of truth; Malory made him the tragedy of loyalty. Tennyson split him in two, taking his courtesy for the early idylls and his Orkney darkness for the last; the twentieth century gave him back to the scholars — Weston and Loomis argued his solar and Celtic pedigrees, and the Tolkien–Gordon edition of 1925 made Sir Gawain and the Green Knight a fixed star of the English canon. Harrison Birtwistle's opera Gawain (1991) set the Green Chapel to music, and the twenty-first century has filmed the poem twice. Through it all the Welsh name never went anywhere: Gwalchmai still stands in the Triads, the hawk of May, waiting at Arthur's court for the quest to be finished. Extended meditation: Gawain is the patron of the errand that must be finished and the word that must be kept — and the Green Knight poem's genius is to show that these are not the same virtue. He finishes everything: the quest, the journey north, the appointment no one would blame him for missing. And still he fails, once, by the width of a green lace — not from cowardice, says the poem, but from love of his own life. The court's answer is the tradition's answer: the failure is not hidden but worn, and what one man wears as his shame the fellowship takes up as its badge. The pentangle on his shield has truth at its center because truth is the one knot that cannot be slipped; everything else — courage, courtesy, purity, fellowship, pity — hangs from it. Gawain asks the question every promise asks: not whether you are brave enough to keep it, but whether you are honest enough to say what it cost. Original script note: The name is transmitted in the Latin alphabet throughout: Middle Welsh writes Gwalchmei in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, Geoffrey of Monmouth writes Walganus , and the Cotton Nero manuscript writes Gawayn . The name's single epigraphic witness is the carved label GALVAGIN(VS) on the Modena Archivolt (c. 1120–1140) — the earliest Arthurian image in art. There is no non-Latin original script to restore, and the canonical English form Gawain is plain ASCII: because the name needs no diacritic, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way — gawain.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release . No form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The Ploughing Goddess
text: The Ploughing Goddess: The Four Oxen, the Wager of King Gylfi, and the Making of Zealand Gefjun is the giver who made an island: the Æsir-born goddess who accepted King Gylfi's jest of a plough-land — as much as four oxen could turn in a day and a night — and answered it by begetting four sons on a giant, yoking them as oxen, and dragging the whole of Zealand out of Sweden into the sea. The Four Oxen: Her sons by a giant of Jötunheimr, shape-changed into draught-beasts — Bragi counts them: eight eyes and four heads. The Plough: Driven so deep and hard that it tore the bedrock: the instrument by which a piece of Sweden became an island. Zealand (Selund): The land she set in the sound and named — drawn west, Ynglinga saga says, until it lay opposite Odense. Lake Mälaren: The mould the island was cast from: water filled the wound, and the lake's bays answer Zealand's headlands. Symbols: The plough — Creation by furrow: land made by turning earth — the oldest technology of order doing the work of a god; The four oxen — Giant strength yoked to a goddess's purpose: brute force given direction; The plough-land — The wager's unit — a day and a night's ploughing, stretched within its own terms until it holds an island; The answering coasts — Zealand's headlands and Mälaren's bays: the two halves of one tear, the myth's own map Gefjun has one of the few land-creation myths in the whole Norse corpus, and it opens the Prose Edda itself: the ploughing of Zealand. Around that single great deed the sources add a catalogue entry, a dynastic marriage, and one sharp exchange in verse. Gylfaginning 1: The Plough-Land of King Gylfi When Snorri opens Gylfaginning, before Gylfi ever reaches Ásgarðr, he tells how the king was first tricked out of a piece of his kingdom. Gylfi gave a wandering beggar-woman, as reward for the entertainment she gave him, one plough-land in his realm — as much as four oxen could plough up in a day and a night. But the woman was of the family of the Æsir, and her name was Gefjun. She took four oxen out of Jötunheimr — her own sons, begotten on a certain giant — and set them before the plough. The share went so deep and hard that it tore the land loose, and the oxen drew it out into the sea and westward until it stopped in a sound. There Gefjun set the land and named it Selund, Zealand. And where the land had been taken from, the water filled in: that is now the lake called Lögrinn, Mälaren, and the bays of the lake, Snorri says, correspond to the headlands of Zealand. The myth lets its hearers read their own map as the scar of a wager — geography kept as evidence of a goddess out-negotiated by no one. Ynglinga saga 5: The Völva and the Founding of Lejre Heimskringla tells the same making as dynastic history. Gefjun, the saga says, was a spákona, a seeress, and Óðinn sent her north across the sound to look for land. King Gylfi met her and gave her one plough-land. She went to Jötunheimr, bore four sons to a giant there, changed them into the likeness of oxen, yoked them, and drew the land out into the sea westward, opposite Óðinsvé — Odense. Then the saga adds what the Edda leaves out: Gefjun settled on the land she had made and married Skjöldr, a son of Óðinn, and their seat was Hleiðra — Lejre, beside Roskilde, the royal seat of Denmark. The goddess who made the island also stood at the root of its kings: Skjöldr is the eponym of the Skjöldungar, the Scyldings whose line Beowulf opens by praising. Bragi inn gamli: Eight Eyes and Four Heads Both Snorri and the saga close the account with the same four lines, attributed to Bragi inn gamli Boddason, the ninth-century skald — the oldest datable witness to the story. In the verse's kennings, Gefjun gladly drew from Gylfi 'the wave-trove's free-hold' until smoke rose from the running sweat-beasts, and the oxen bore 'eight forehead-moons and four heads' as they carried off Denmark's increase. Eight eyes and four heads: the poet counts the team for us. The making of Zealand was already a fixed story, with fixed imagery, centuries before Snorri wrote it down. The verse matters beyond its antiquity: it fixes the story’s legal core in skaldic memory — a land transacted as a wager, celebrated by the court poets as the founding bargain of the Danish realm, and remembered in fixed kennings long after the kings who told it were dust. When a ninth-century poet counts a goddess’s oxen by their eyes, the myth is already scripture: quoted, not invented, by everyone who came after. Gylfaginning 35: Fourth Among the Ásynjur In Gylfaginning's catalogue of the ásynjur, Gefjun stands fourth, after Frigg, Sága, and Eir, and Snorri gives her a single, startling office: 'she is a maiden, and those who die maidens serve her.' The sentence sits unresolved beside the Zealand story — the maiden of the catalogue is the giant's consort of the myth — and the tradition never reconciled the two. Skáldskaparmál keeps her in the þulur, the metrical name-lists of the ásynjur, where her name is licensed as a base-word in kennings for women: a skald praising a woman could reach for Gefjun as readily as for any goddess. The unresolved contradiction is the point: the catalogue’s maiden and the myth’s consort stand side by side, and the tradition declines to choose between them. Lokasenna 19–21: The Necklace and the Fair Lad Gefjun speaks once in the Poetic Edda, and it costs her. In Lokasenna, as Loki works his way down the bench of goddesses at Ægir's feast, Gefjun intervenes: why, she asks, do you Æsir bandy bitter words here in the hall? Óðinn's rebuke is immediate — she is mad, he says, to rouse Loki, for Loki knows the fates of all as well as Óðinn himself. Then Loki turns on her with the only scandal the corpus attaches to her name: a fair youth once gave her a bright necklace, a sigli, and she wound her legs about him. The taunt echoes the necklace-stories of the other goddesses, and the poem moves on; nothing in the corpus answers it, and nothing repeats it. Syncretism: Gefjun's nearest relative lives inside the pantheon itself. Gylfaginning names Gefn — 'the giver' — among Freyja's bynames, and both names stand on the same root, gefa; Simek treats the two as possibly once-connected figures, distinct in the surviving sources. Beyond the North, scholars have long set her story among the land-measure foundation legends of the ancient world — the type of tale in which a people explains how its territory was won by stretching a definition, Dido's ox-hide at Carthage being the classical case — with the difference that Gefjun stretches not a hide but a day's ploughing, and the unit she stretches is agricultural. Her other life is dynastic: through Skjöldr she belongs to the origin-complex of the Danish kings, the same stratum that produced Beowulf's Scyld Scefing and Saxo's Skioldus. The handbooks read the marriage as the point where myth and royal genealogy were deliberately joined — a plough-goddess at the root of a farming aristocracy's line. Cultural legacy: Gefjun's afterlife is monumental and national. The Gefion Fountain on Copenhagen's harbourfront — Anders Bundgaard's great bronze group, unveiled in 1908 as the Carlsberg Foundation's gift to the city — shows her exactly where the myth leaves her: driving the four oxen as they strain toward the sea. It is among the largest monuments in Copenhagen and the standard image of the goddess worldwide, and the story itself remains Denmark's foundation tale, the way Danish children learn why Zealand lies apart in the sea. Her name has even left the planet: the main-belt asteroid 1272 Gefion, discovered in 1931, gives its name to the Gefion family of asteroids. The name never became a common given name in the North, but in Denmark it needs no introduction. Extended meditation: Gefjun is the patron of the answer that exceeds the wager. Gylfi sets the terms — four oxen, a day and a night — and keeps his word; she keeps it too, and ruins him within the terms. The myth is about measure outwitted by measure: the smallest unit of farmland, a plough-land, stretched until it holds an island and a royal house. What she gives is not only the land but the lesson the name already carries: the giver decides the scale of the gift. Every telling of her is a reminder that the terms you set will be met — by someone cleverer at keeping them. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Gefjun — already plain Latin letters, with no diacritic and no distinctive character for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved roughly ᚴᛁᚠᛁᚢᚾ (k-i-f-i-u-n: the k-rune writes g, and the single i-rune covers both the vowel e and the glide j). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: gefjun.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Primordial Void
text: Primordial Void: The Yawning Gap Where Rime Met Flame Before the World Began Ginnungagap is the emptiness that was there first: the vast, mild, windless chasm between Niflheimr's rime and fog in the north and Muspellsheimr's fire and sparks in the south, in whose middle the two extremes met, melted, and quickened into Ymir — the condensation from which the whole made world, and the Æsir themselves, descend. Niflheimr: The world of fog and rime in the north, made long before the earth — its spring Hvergelmir feeds the rivers called the Élivágar. Muspellsheimr: The burning world in the south, bright and impassable to any not native to it, where Surtr stands at the frontier with a flaming sword. The Meeting: Where the sparks and embers flying from the south touched the rime drifting from the north, the gap thawed, dripped — and the drops took on life. Ymir: The first shape the void made: the frost-ogre who quickened in the meltwater, called Aurgelmir by the rime-giants who descend from him. Symbols: The gap itself — Emptiness as precondition — the room in which opposites can meet and anything at all can begin; Rime and spark — The two extremes the void holds apart and joins — ice from Niflheimr, embers from Muspellsheimr; The quickening drops — Life condensing out of the meltwater where the two worlds' weather collided; The windless mildness — Snorri's strange detail that Ginnungagap was as mild as a windless sky — the void is neutral, not hostile Ginnungagap has no adventures, because it is not a character but a place — or rather the condition of there being places at all. Its mythology is the first chapter of everything: the Norse creation, told in Völuspá's three terse lines and unpacked by Snorri into the finest cosmogony the Germanic world preserved. Völuspá 3: The Gap of Ginnungs The seeress of the Völuspá reaches back before memory, and her third stanza is the northern world’s first sentence: ‘It was at the beginning of time, when Ymir had settled — there was no sand nor sea nor cool waves; earth existed nowhere, nor sky above; a gap of ginnungs was there, but grass nowhere.’ That is the entire notice the oldest poem gives — two words, gap ginnunga , in the reversed order the later prose preferred — and everything Snorri builds hangs on them. Nothing acts in the verse; no god speaks. The poem simply registers an emptiness where the world will later be, with the first giant already housed at its edge and no grass yet anywhere. The compound itself is a puzzle the stanza declines to solve: whether ginnunga means ‘magic-charged powers’ or is kin to ginna , ‘to deceive, bewitch’, the lexica still argue. The void enters literature already wearing its oldest trick: a name no one could agree on, and a silence no one could fill. Gylfaginning 4–5: Fog in the North, Fire in the South Asked what was before the earth, Hár tells Gylfi that Niflheimr was made many ages before the world: a dark world of mist with the spring Hvergelmir at its heart, from which run the rivers called the Élivágar — Svǫl, Gunnþrá, Fjǫrm, Fimbulþul, Slíðr and Hríð, Sylgr and Ylgr, Víð, Leiptr, and Gjǫll, which flows nearest the gate of Hel. Far from that spring the rivers hardened like the slag that runs from a forge, turned to ice, and spread rime and freezing fog northward. But the southern part of Ginnungagap faced Muspellsheimr, the bright, burning world no foreigner can enter, where Surtr stands guard at the border with a flaming sword — and the sparks and glowing embers that flew out of Muspellsheimr lightened the gap from below. Gylfaginning 5–6: The Mild Void and the Quickening Between the two, Snorri says, Ginnungagap was as mild as a windless sky. Where the warm air from the south met the rime from the north, the ice thawed and dripped — and by the power of the one who sent the heat, the running drops quickened and took the likeness of a man. He is named Ymir, though the rime-giants call him Aurgelmir, and from him their whole race descends; asked whether Ymir was a god, Hár answers flatly that he and all his kin were evil. From the same rime-drops came the cow Auðhumla, whose four rivers of milk fed the giant, and who licked the salty rime-stones until, over three days, a man emerged whole from the ice: Búri, the grandfather of the gods. Gylfaginning 7–8: The Flood and the Fashioning Búri's son Borr married Bestla, daughter of the giant Bǫlþorn, and their sons were Óðinn, Vili, and Vé — and the first act of the new gods in the old void was a killing. They slew Ymir, and so much blood ran from his wounds that the whole race of rime-giants drowned, save one: Bergelmir, who climbed with his wife onto his lúðr — a word that may mean a boat or a chest — and from whom the giants of the frost descend anew. The brothers dragged Ymir's body into the middle of Ginnungagap and made the world of it: the earth from his flesh, the sea and lakes from his blood, the mountains from his bones and teeth, the sky from his skull, held up at the four corners by the dwarfs Norðri, Suðri, Austri, and Vestri, and the clouds from his brains. The sparks that flew out of Muspellsheimr they set in the sky as stars. Thus the gap was not filled so much as furnished: everything that exists is a giant's body arranged inside the old emptiness. Vafþrúðnismál 21 · Grímnismál 40–41: The Poets' Version The Poetic Edda confirms Snorri’s outline from its own witnesses. Vafþrúðnir the giant, questioned by Óðinn about the first origin of giant-kind, answers that out of the Élivágar sprang venom-drops, eitr , which grew and hardened until a giant quickened from them (Vafþrúðnismál 21). And Grímnismál gives the fashioning in verse: ‘From Ymir’s flesh the earth was shaped, the mountains from his bones, the sky from the skull of the frost-cold giant, and from his blood the sea’ — adding that the gracious powers made Miðgarðr for the sons of men from his eyebrows, and the hard-mooded clouds from his brains (Grímnismál 40–41). The poems do not name the gap as often as Snorri does, but they supply its inventory: ice-rivers, venom, melt, and a world assembled from a corpse. Between verse and prose the account is told twice from independent witnesses — a redundancy rare enough in Norse myth to count as corroboration, and the reason this cosmogony is among the best-attested in the medieval North. Syncretism: The obvious cross-border twin is Hesiod's Chaos: 'first of all came Chaos' opens the Greek theogony, and the Greek word itself derives from a root meaning 'to yawn, gape' — chaos and gap are the same image in two languages, the world beginning as an open mouth. The parallel is real but easy to overdraw: Hesiod's Chaos is a begetter, parent of Erebos and Night, while Ginnungagap begets nothing by itself — it is the neutral stage on which rime and fire do the begetting, and the North reserves the making for the gods who arrive later. Scholars such as Lindow have set the Norse account among the broader Indo-European creation patterns — the primordial being dismembered into the world has cousins from Vedic Puruṣa onward — but the void itself, cold at one end and burning at the other, is the corpus's own signature. Cultural legacy: Ginnungagap is the rare cosmological term that never had to be revived, because it was never allowed to die: Modern Icelandic keeps ginnungagap as its word for the primordial void, and Icelandic science writing reaches for it when describing the nothing before the Big Bang. The nineteenth-century Norse revival made the scene a set-piece — the Kearys' The Heroes of Asgard (1857) opens its cosmology in 'the great gulf' between ice and fire — and every handbook since, from Simek to Orchard, has treated the word as the North's answer to chaos. Modern Heathenry honours the creation narrative as its cosmogony, and popular culture borrows the name wherever a story needs a primal abyss, from Marvel's Thor comics to fantasy games. Its deepest legacy is conceptual: the idea, natural to the North, that the precondition of creation is not a maker's word but an empty space where opposites can meet. Extended meditation: Every cosmogony must answer the same rude question: what was there before anything was? The North's answer is the strangest and, in its way, the most honest — room. Not a god, not a word, not even darkness with a personality: a gap, mild as a windless sky, with ice weather at one end and fire weather at the other. Creation, in this telling, is not commanded; it condenses. Two climates that could never touch are given somewhere to meet, and the world is what drips out of the meeting. Ginnungagap asks a quieter question than most voids: not what made you, but what made room for you — and it suggests that every beginning, cosmological or personal, starts the same way: with an emptiness patient enough to hold the opposites apart until they are ready to collide. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Ginnungagap — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the compound would have been carved ᚴᛁᚾᚢᚾᚴᛅᚴᛅᛒ (k-i-n-u-n-k-a-k-a-p, the k-rune writing g, the b-rune writing final p, and the doubled n written once, as runic orthography economizes geminates). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: ginnungagap.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Valkyrie of War
text: Valkyrie of War: Battle Made Divine — the Rider Who Chooses the Slain Gunnr is the valkyrie whose name is the whole battlefield: Old Norse gunnr is simply the word for war, and the þulur and the Völuspá seeress set her riding among Óðinn's choosers of the slain. Snorri gives her the purest job-description in the corpus: Gunnr and Rota and the youngest norn, Skuld, always ride to choose the slain and decide battles. The Chosen Slain: The einherjar — the warriors she marks on the field and carries to Valhǫll, the harvest a valkyrie exists to gather. Skuld's Shield: Völuspá's image: Skuld held a shield and Skögul rode with her, and Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and Geirskögul rode behind — the armed company of the god-folk. The War-Spear: The valkyrie's weapon and the battle's own emblem: Snorri says Gunnr, Rota and Skuld ride to every fight to award the victory. The Val-Knot of Choice: The act her office names: val-kjósa, to choose the slain — the divine prerogative of saying who falls and who is taken. Symbols: The spear — The weapon of the chooser — the stroke that both kills and elects; The shield of the company — Völuspá's riding detail: the valkyries go armed and ranked, not as omens but as soldiers; The choice of the slain (valr) — The office itself — war's harvest selected by name, the power the name gunnr carries into personhood; The name that is a noun — Gunnr the valkyrie and gunnr the battle are one word — war personified walking its own field Gunnr has no adventure of her own; her mythology is her office, told in lists that are anything but dry. Four witnesses fix her in the corpus: the Völuspá seeress sees her ride, Snorri states her function in a single sentence, the þulur keep her name in the valkyrie roll, and the skaldic poems describe the choosing she personifies — the tradition's way of saying that battle, in the North, had a chooser, and the chooser had a name. Völuspá 30: The Riders the Seeress Saw Deep in the völva's prophecy, between the world's making and its burning, the seeress turns her eyes to a road in the sky: 'She saw valkyries come from far and wide, ready to ride to the gods' people; Skuld held a shield, and Skögul was with her; Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and Geirskögul — now are counted Herjan's ladies, the valkyries ready to ride over the earth' (Völuspá 30, trans. Larrington). Herjan, 'lord of hosts', is Óðinn, and the company is his household cavalry, mustered with shield and spear like a war-band rather than a flock of omens. The detail that fixes Gunnr here is sequence: she is named fourth in the most famous roll-call of the Poetic Edda, riding behind a norn carrying a shield, among spear-women ranked and armed. The seeress tells no story about her because the tradition needs none — battle with a chooser is as fixed a feature of the Norse cosmos as the norms and the doom they enforce. In this poem her whole biography is one line of a list, and the list is the point: war has personnel. Gylfaginning 36: The Choosers of the Slain Snorri, explaining Óðinn's household to his skeptical king, gives the valkyries their job-description and Gunnr her one great sentence: Óðinn sends the valkyries to every battle, 'to allot death to men and to award victory'. Then the roll-call: 'Gunnr and Rota and the youngest norn, who is called Skuld, always ride to choose the slain and to decide the fighting' (Gylfaginning 36, trans. Faulkes). The grouping is precise and chilling — two choosers of the slain and one weaver of fate riding together, because in Norse thought the choice of the fallen and the doom of the fallen are one act seen from two sides. The same chapter fills Valhǫll with valkyries waiting, drinking-horns in hand, and Grímnismál's catalogue (st. 36) arms the mead-bearers with names like Hrist and Mist — 'shaker' and 'mist'. Snorri's Gunnr needs no adventure, because her function is the adventure of everyone else: she is what war looks like when a warrior culture refuses to call its harvest random. Skáldskaparmál þulur: Kept in the Roll The þulur — the metrical name-lists a skald learned as working vocabulary — file Gunnr among the heiti of the valkyries, and the same tradition hands her name back to the battlefield as a common noun: gunnr, 'war, battle', a word a poet could set inside a kenning. Cleasby–Vigfusson's dictionary gives both entries side by side, the woman and the war, without apology, because Old Norse poetry refuses to separate them. When a skald sang that 'Gunnr's snow' drifted on the field, his hearers were meant to catch the double exposure — snowfall and battle, the white thing that covers the slain. De Vries registers the same double filing in his etymological dictionary, and the þulur's matter-of-factness is itself the evidence: no gloss was needed, because everyone knew. The lists are usually called dry; here they are a theology in shorthand. To put battle in the feminine, give it a horse, and enter it in the god's roster of women is to personify without allegory — the word itself walks, armed, and the name it walks under is Gunnr. The Office: What the Choosing Looked Like No Eddic poem gives Gunnr a scene of her own, so the corpus describes her office instead — and the office is among the best-attested in Norse verse, though the honest record must say that none of these poems names her. Hákonarmál (Eyvindr skáldaspillir) sends Göndul and Skögul to weigh two kings in the balance and choose which falls; Geirskögul 'shook her spear' over Hákon's host, and the chosen king is greeted on the field by valkyries with wine. The anonymous Eiríksmál wakes the dead heroes Sigmundr and Sinfjötli because a king is coming whom the valkyries must receive in Valhǫll. Grímnismál's mead-bearers and the dying warrior's welcome — a horn from a woman's hand — are the consolation carved and cast across the Viking world, from the gilt-silver valkyrie of Hårby on Funen to the picture stones of Gotland. All of it is the meaning of gunnr when the word rides: war's harvest gathered by named women, and the fallen comforted at the moment of election. The tradition's reticence about Gunnr herself is the meaning — battle's chooser needs no biography, only a name. Syncretism: Gunnr's nearest kin are not borrowings but reflections. Within the Norse corpus she belongs to the tight triad Snorri names — herself, Rota, and the norn Skuld — where the valkyrie's battlefield choice and the norn's weaving of fate are one operation; Skuld carries the same office into the world of time itself. Across the sea, the Old English cognate gūþ never grew a person: Beowulf sings of gūþ as plain war, and the personification stayed Norse. Scholars comparing traditions point to the Irish Morrígan and Badb — battle-goddesses who also decide fights and choose their dead — as the closest functional parallel in the neighbouring mythology, though no historical link is provable and none need be claimed. Gunnr needs no foreign template: she is what happens when a warrior culture declines its own word for war in the feminine and gives it a horse. Cultural legacy: Gunnr's afterlife flows through two channels. The first is the word itself: gunnr lived on as the battle-element of Scandinavian naming — Gunnarr ('warrior of battle'), Gunnhildr ('battle-fight'), and the living Icelandic and Faroese women's name Gunnur — so that the valkyrie's name is still spoken daily in the North, worn by ordinary people. The second is the image she helped fix: the armed maiden riding to the field to choose the dead, the seed from which the whole later figure of the valkyrie grew — the Valkyries of Wagner's Walküre, the shieldmaidens of modern fiction and games, and the revived valkyrie devotion of contemporary Heathenry. In scholarship she stands as the standing example of the Norse habit of personifying abstractions: not an allegory imposed on war, but war itself, named and riding. Extended meditation: Gunnr is the most honest figure in the valkyrie roll because she pretends to be nothing but what she is. Other choosers of the slain carry names of tumult, of rulership, of the spear; hers is the field itself. To say that Gunnr chooses the slain is to say that battle chooses its own — that once the spears cross, the outcome belongs to something no combatant commands. The Norse did not soften that thought; they dignified it. They gave the blind lottery of combat a rider, a rank among Óðinn's women, and a place in the seeress's vision, as if to say: what you cannot control, you can at least name. Every soldier who ever marched out knowing the choice was not his own has stood, without knowing it, in Gunnr's shadow. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Gunnr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚴᚢᚾᛦ (k-u-n-R, the k-rune writing g and ᛦ the final nominative -r, the doubled n written with a single rune by runic convention). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: the plain-ASCII gunnr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The Moon-Chaser
text: The Moon-Chaser: The Hater, the Fame-Wolf's Son, and the Darkening of Heaven Hati Hróðvitnisson is the wolf who runs before the sun and after the moon: son of the fame-wolf Fenrir, bred in the Ironwood, and fated to seize Máni out of the sky — the chase on which the Edda hangs its explanation of the darkened moon and one of the certainties of Ragnarǫk. The Chase: Grímnismál's picture: Hati runs before the bright bride of heaven — ahead of the sun, at the heels of the moon that flees before her. Hróðvitnir's Son: The patronymic names his father: Hróðvitnir, 'fame-wolf', a heiti of Fenrir himself — the apocalyptic kennel's own lineage. Járnviðr, the Ironwood: Völuspá's forest east of the world, where the old giantess breeds Fenrir's brood — and from them all comes the one who takes the moon. The Seized Moon: The catch Snorri says must come: the moon swallowed, the sky spattered with blood, and the light of the world going out at Ragnarǫk. Symbols: The running wolf — Pursuit without rest: the sky itself read as a hunt that has never once paused; The fleeing moon — Máni's course as flight — the measured path of the heavens reinterpreted as terror; Járnviðr, the Ironwood — The eastern forest where the wolf-brood is bred: chaos with an address, growing older by the year; The darkened sky — Völuspá's 'the sunshine turns black' — the eclipse and the world's ending written in one image Hati's mythology is a single image carried by a handful of verses: a wolf, a moon, and a chase that ends only with the world. The Poetic Edda names him once, Snorri gives him his quarry and his ending, and Völuspá's seeress supplies the brood he springs from. Grímnismál 39: The Pair Before Heaven The name's one poetic attestation comes in Óðinn's great catalogue of the cosmos in Grímnismál, where the disguised god enumerates the heavens for the torture-bound Geirrøðr: 'Skǫll is the name of the wolf who follows the bright-faced god to the sheltering wood; but the other is Hati, Hróðvitnir's son, who runs before the bright bride of heaven.' The bright bride of heaven is the sun; the wolf who runs before her is on the heels of the moon, which travels ahead of her. In four lines the Edda converts the machinery of the sky into a hunt: what astronomy calls a course, the poem calls a chase. Gylfaginning 12: Skǫll After the Sun, Hati After the Moon Snorri systematizes the verse. When Gangleri asks why the sun hurries so — 'she speeds as if she were afraid' — High One answers that she has good cause: 'the one who seeks her is right behind her, and she has no other way out than to run.' Two wolves do the work of the heavens: Skǫll chases the sun and will catch her, and 'the other wolf is called Hati Hróðvitnisson; he runs in front of her and wants to catch the moon — and that is what will happen.' Snorri's gloss fixes the reading the poem left compressed, and with it the moon's doom is put on the schedule of things foretold. Gylfaginning 12: Mánagarmr, the Moon-Hound In the same chapter Snorri names the mightiest of the wolf-brood: Mánagarmr, 'moon-hound' — 'he will be filled with the flesh of all who die, and he will swallow the moon and spatter the sky and all the air with blood; from this the sun will lose its brightness.' Whether Mánagarmr is Hati under a second name or a third wolf beside the pair, the manuscripts and the handbooks leave open; Simek and Lindow record the identification as probable but unprovable. What is certain is the image: the moon taken, and the blood of the swallowed light staining heaven. Völuspá 39-40: The Brood of the Ironwood Völuspá's seeress supplies the kennel. 'In the east sat the old one in the Ironwood and bred there Fenrir's brood; from all of them comes one in particular, a snatcher of the moon in a troll's skin. He gorges on the life of doomed men, reddens the gods' dwellings with red blood; the sunshine turns black in the summers after, and all weathers run hostile.' The poem names no name — but the tungls tjúgari, the 'snatcher of the moon', is the role Grímnismál and Snorri assign to Hati, and the handbooks read the figures together: the Ironwood breeds the chase, and the chase ends the world. Gylfaginning 51 · Völuspá: The Catch at Ragnarǫk The ending is shared by every witness. When Ragnarǫk comes, the wolves' running stops: Skǫll takes the sun, Hati takes the moon, Fenrir himself swallows Óðinn, and 'the sun turns black, earth sinks into the sea, the bright stars vanish from the sky.' The Edda's cosmology is built so that the nightly order of the heavens is only an interval — the long meanwhile between the start of the chase and its foreknown end. Hati never fails of his quarry; he simply has not caught it yet. Syncretism: Hati has no cult, no continental cognate, and no existence outside the Eddic record: he belongs to the North's own eschatological machinery. Scholars since the nineteenth century have noted that the doubling of the apocalyptic wolf — one chasing the sun, one the moon — is probably a secondary systematization of the older single figure, the bound Fenrir who breaks loose at the world's end; Simek and Lindow treat Skǫll and Hati as elaborations within the Fenrir-complex rather than independent tradition. What the pair does uniquely well is etiology: the chase gives the sky a reason for its haste, and the wolf drawing near gives the North its explanation of the eclipse — when the pursuer closes, the moon darkens. The devouring-monster account of eclipses is a comparative commonplace across cultures; the Norse version is distinctive for giving its monsters names, a pedigree, and a date. Cultural legacy: Hati's afterlife is the eclipse-wolf's: wherever the Ragnarǫk story is retold, the pair Skǫll and Hati run in the sky above it. Victorian and later handbooks of Norse myth made the chase a set-piece of cosmological explanation — the sky's motions as a hunt, the eclipse as the moment the wolf gains — and modern retellings, novels, and games keep the two wolves as Ragnarǫk's outriders. In scholarship the name is the standing example of the Edda's transparent theonymy: a god-figure called, without ornament, 'the Hater'. The name never entered the living name-pool as Baldr's did; it survives where it was born, in the poetry, doing the one job it was given. Extended meditation: Hati is the Edda's most economical idea: take the verb 'to hate', give it legs, and set it running after the light. There is no malice-scene, no dialogue, no character beyond the name — only pursuit. And that is the point. The Norse imagination looked at the most orderly thing in the world, the clockwork of sun and moon, and read it as flight: the lights hurry because something hates them and is coming. Time itself becomes the distance still left between the wolf and the moon — every night the moon escapes is a night the world continues. Hati asks the uncomfortable question the whole Ragnarǫk cycle asks: how do you keep the light moving, knowing exactly what follows it? The Edda's answer is the one it gives everywhere. You keep running. The chase is the world. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Hati — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚼᛅᛏᛁ (h-a-t-i, four runes with no ambiguity). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: hati.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Giant, Duel with Thor
text: Giant, Duel with Thor: The Stone Heart, the Golden Mane, and the Wager of a Head Hrungnir is the strongest of the jötnar — the stone-hearted giant who rode his gold-maned stallion Gullfaxi into Ásgarðr on a wager of heads, drank Thor's liquor from the god's own horns, boasted he would carry off Valhǫll, and met Mjǫllnir at Grjótúnagarðar with nothing in his hand but a whetstone. His duel is the most fully narrated single combat between god and giant in the Old Norse corpus. Gullfaxi: 'Golden mane' — the stallion Óðinn envied aloud, whose speed Hrungnir wagered his head against Sleipnir to disprove. The Whetstone: His weapon of stone — hurled against Mjǫllnir, it shattered in mid-air; one shard fathered every whetstone rock on earth, one lodged in Thor's skull. The Stone Heart: Three-cornered, sharp-edged, and hard — the Edda says his heart, head, and shield were all of stone, a giant made of his own weapon's material. Grjótúnagarðar: The 'stone-fence-yard' at the edge of heaven and giantland, where the single combat was appointed — the oldest named duelling-ground in the myths. Symbols: The whetstone — The honing-stone hurled against the hammer — stone against iron, and the shard still buried in Thor's head; Gullfaxi — The gold-maned stallion whose speed was worth a giant's head — and ended in the hands of three-night-old Magni; The three-cornered stone heart — Courage of the wrong material: resolve that is hard, sharp, and entirely without flexibility; Mǫkkurkálfi — The nine-league clay giant with a mare's heart — the giants' engineered champion, terror to look at and nothing within; The fallen foot — Hrungnir's leg across Thor's neck, which all the Æsir together could not lift — the weight of the foe after the foe is dead Hrungnir has essentially one story, and it is the greatest fight in the Edda: the wager, the drunken boasting in the hall of the gods, the appointed duel at Grjótúnagarðar, the shattered whetstone, and the fall that left even victorious Thor pinned beneath his enemy's leg. Snorri tells it in Skáldskaparmál, and the skald Þjóðólfr of Hvin had carved it into verse three centuries earlier. Skáldskaparmál 17: The Wager of Heads It begins with a boast Óðinn could not keep to himself. Riding Sleipnir through Jötunheimr, he met the giant Hrungnir, who asked who this man was with the golden helmet, riding so well over sea and air, and praised the horse. Óðinn answered with the stake that decides everything after: he wagered his head that no horse in Jötunheimr was Sleipnir's equal. Hrungnir sprang to his own stallion Gullfaxi, the gold-maned, and gave chase in a fury. The race ran to the very gates of Ásgarðr — and Hrungnir, carried past his own turning, galloped through them and in among the gods. Skáldskaparmál 17: Drunk in the Hall of the Gods The Æsir received him with the hospitality due an uninvited guest: they set before him the great horns Thor himself drank from, and Hrungnir emptied them one after another. Drunk, he let the boasts out — he would take Valhǫll up and carry it off to Jötunheimr, he would sink Ásgarðr, he would kill all the gods, save only Freyja and Sif, whom he would carry home; and the mead, he said, he would drink up all by himself. The Æsir, tired of the noise, named Thor; and Thor came in swinging his hammer, demanding who had given jötnar leave to drink in Valhǫll. Hrungnir, looking at him with anything but friendly eyes, answered that Óðinn had invited him and he stood under Óðinn's protection — then claimed his rights: Thor would gain little honour from killing him unarmed. It would be a greater trial of courage, he said, if Thor dared meet him in single combat at the frontier, at Grjótúnagarðar. And Thor, Snorri says, would by no means refuse a challenge to single combat. Skáldskaparmál 17–19: Grjótúnagarðar: The Whetstone and the Hammer The giants made much of the appointment, for Hrungnir was the strongest of them and they expected one outcome or the other to be decisive. For his second they built a champion of clay: Mǫkkurkálfi, nine leagues tall and three leagues broad across the chest, with no heart big enough for the frame — so they gave him a mare's heart, and it quaked within him when Thor came. Hrungnir stood with his heart of stone, three-cornered and sharp-edged, his head of stone, and his broad shield of stone, holding his hone — the whetstone — before him. Þjálfi ran ahead and called out that Thor was coming from below, and Hrungnir, fearing a strike through the earth, set the shield beneath his feet and stood on it. Then Thor came in an ásmegin-fury, lightning running before him, and hurled Mjǫllnir from afar. Hrungnir threw the hone with both hands, and the weapons met in the air. The hone burst in two: one half fell to earth, and from it come all the whetstone rocks in the world; the other half drove into Thor's head, and he fell forward. But Mjǫllnir did not stop — it struck Hrungnir's head and crushed the skull to small pieces, and the giant fell forward across Thor, his foot lying on Thor's neck. Þjálfi went at Mǫkkurkálfi, and the clay giant fell with little glory. Skáldskaparmál 19: The Foot No God Could Lift Then the strangest aftermath in the corpus: Thor lay pinned, and neither he nor Þjálfi could shift the giant's foot from his neck. All the Æsir came, when they learned, and together they could not lift it. At last came Magni, son of Thor and the giantess Járnsaxa — three nights old — and threw Hrungnir's foot off his father, saying it was a pity he had come so late: he thought he would have struck the giant dead with his fist. Thor gave him Gullfaxi for the deed, and Óðinn objected that he had given the fine horse to a giantess's son rather than to his own father. The hone stayed in Thor's head. The völva Gróa, wife of Aurvandill the Bold, came to sing it loose with her spells, and the stone was already working free — until Thor, to please her, told how he had carried Aurvandill in a basket out of Jötunheimr, and how the man's frozen toe, broken off and thrown into the sky, became the star called Aurvandill's Toe. Gróa rejoiced so greatly at the news that she forgot her spells; the hone stirs in Thor's head to this day. Therefore, Snorri warns, whetstones must never be thrown across the floor. Haustlöng: The Skaldic Witness Snorri quotes his sources, and for this myth the source is Þjóðólfr of Hvin's Haustlöng — a shield-poem composed in the early tenth century, among the oldest mythological verse we have. Þjóðólfr tells the whole combat in dense dróttkvætt: the 'defier of the gods' who rode to the fight, the earth shaking beneath the giant's host, the whetstone bitten from the hard stone of the heart, the hammer answering. That a skald within living memory of the Viking Age's pagan courts could assume his hearers knew the whetstone, the clay giant, and the fall proves the story was not Snorri's construction: it was already old, already fixed, already the standard account of the hardest fight Thor ever fought. Syncretism: Hrungnir resists the usual syncretic moves. Attempts to read him as a reflex of an Indo-European dragon-slaying have been made — a stone-bodied chaos-being struck down by the thunderer's missile does resemble the Vedic Vṛtra pattern — but the fit is partial, since Hrungnir steals nothing, hoards nothing, and threatens no waters; scholars treat the combat as a native Norse contest-epic rather than an inherited myth. His truer company is within the corpus itself: he is one of the named great fights of Þórr, standing between Geirrøðr, killed by a thrown glowing iron, and Hymir, fished with and nearly killed by the sea. The whetstone lodged in Thor's head has been compared with the embedded weapons of other mythologies — the fragment that will not come out — but no source identifies a borrowing, and the handbooks register Hrungnir as a distinctively Norse invention, a giant built of the very landscape the North knew: stone, clay, and weather. Cultural legacy: Hrungnir's afterlife runs through the skalds before it runs through anyone else: Haustlöng made his fall one of the foundation-texts of Norse poetics, and Snorri cites the poem as the authority for the myth, so that every handbook of Old Norse literature meets him early. The Victorians took up the clay giant — Mǫkkurkálfi recurs in retellings as the archetype of the hollow colossus, all size and mare's heart — and the detail that whetstones must not be thrown across the floor survived in folklore collections as a curiosity of thunder-lore. In modern reception he is the template for every stone-hearted boss the genre has built since: fantasy games and novels cast his duel whenever a hero must fight a mountain that can throw back. His name never entered living use the way Baldr's or Thor's did; it remains exactly what the Edda made it — the name of the strongest thing the hammer ever had to kill. Extended meditation: Hrungnir is the Edda's essay on confidence without flexibility. Every part of him is the hardest available material — heart of stone, head of stone, shield of stone — and the myth's arithmetic is that hardness is not the same as strength. The whetstone is the perfect weapon for him: a stone whose entire purpose is to sharpen other things, hurled once, shattering on the first iron it meets. Against him the Edda sets two counter-images. Mǫkkurkálfi, the engineered champion, enormous and empty, a mare's heart quaking in nine leagues of clay — the warning about size without courage. And Magni, three nights old, lifting what all the gods together could not — the warning about measuring strength by age, rank, or expectation. Hrungnir wagered his head on a horse race and lost it in a duel. The name survives, etymology unknown, as the corpus's permanent reminder that being the strongest thing in the room is a wager too — and someone always holds the hammer. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Hrungnir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚼᚱᚢᚴᚾᛁᛦ (h-r-u-k-n-i-R, the ᚴ-rune writing g and ᛦ the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: hrungnir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Giant, Owner of Cauldron
text: Giant, Owner of Cauldron: The Host at Heaven's End, the Ox-Head Bait, and the Cup Broken on a Giant's Skull Hymir is the sea-giant of Hymiskviða: the fierce host at the eastern edge of heaven whose herd feeds his hall, whose fishing-ground is the cold reach of the Élivágar, and whose treasure is the one thing the gods lack — the mile-deep cauldron in which Ægir could brew ale for all the Æsir at once. The Mile-Deep Cauldron: The roomy, hard-forged kettle Týr says his fierce father owns — a mile deep, the only vessel large enough to brew for all the gods. The Ox-Head Bait: The head of the black bull Himinbrjótr, torn off by Þórr for bait — the offering that drew the Miðgarðsormr up from the sea-floor. The Crystal Cup: Hymir's unbreakable drinking-cup, which no pillar could crack — smashed at last on the one thing harder: the giant's own skull. The Hall of Cattle: The giant's byre at heaven's end, where Þórr devoured two of the three oxen at supper and beheaded the finest for the fishing. Symbols: The mile-deep cauldron — The vessel of plenty the giants keep and the gods must win — hospitality's measure in the Eddic world; The ox-head bait — The price of the catch: the herd's finest head traded for the serpent that girdles the world; The cup broken on the skull — The giant's own hardness turned against his treasure — strength answering strength; The nine-hundred-headed grandmother — The monstrous ancestry of the giant-house, set against the golden-browed mother who hides the guests Hymir lives in one great poem and its prose retelling: Hymiskviða, the comic and terrible lay of the cauldron-quest, and Gylfaginning 48, where Snorri tells the fishing-trip for the Miðgarðsormr with all its sea-cold detail. It is Þórr's most famous adventure, and the giant is its immovable setting. Hymiskviða 1–13: The Demand for the Cauldron The Æsir had hunted and taken auguries from the blood, and saw that Ægir — called also Gymir — had brew-stuff in plenty. Þórr ordered the sea-giant to brew ale for the gods, and Ægir, to be rid of the demand, set an impossible price: first let them bring a cauldron a mile wide. Týr knew where one stood: east of the Élivágar lives the shrewd Hymir at heaven's end, and "my fierce father owns the roomy kettle, a mile deep." So Þórr and Týr drove to the giant's hall. There they met Týr's grandmother, loathsome, with nine hundred heads — and another woman, golden-browed, Týr's mother, who hid the guests under the great cauldron, for her husband was often cruel to visitors. Hymiskviða 13–16 · Gylfaginning 48: The Host Comes Home Hymir came in from the hunting with the ice rattling in his beard. The pillar he looked toward burst apart; eight cauldrons crashed from the broken beam, and one hard-forged kettle came down whole. The guests came out, and the hall fed them: three oxen were slaughtered, and Þórr alone ate two before he slept. In the morning the giant eyed his thinned herd and told his guest they must fish for the next day's meal — Þórr might row out with him, if the little fellow dared the cold and the long pull to his fishing-ground. Hymiskviða 17–27 · Gylfaginning 48: The Fishing for the Miðgarðsormr Asked for bait, Þórr went to the herd and wrenched the head from the black bull Himinbrjótr — Snorri calls him Himinhrjóðr. Hymir rowed hard, then harder, and still Þórr matched him, past the giant's own grounds into water he said was unsafe, where the serpent lies. Hymir pulled up two whales at once on his hooks; Þórr cast the ox-head overboard. The Miðgarðsormr gaped on the bait, the hook caught, and Þórr braced his feet through the bottom of the boat and hauled the serpent's head to the gunwale — the two glaring, the sea foaming, the boat nearly swamped — until the hammer struck and the serpent sank back into the sea. Hymir rowed home in gloomy silence. Hymiskviða 28–39 · Gylfaginning 48: The Cup, the Skull, and the Carrying-Off Back on land Hymir demanded proof of strength, and set his crystal cup: break that, and be counted mighty. Twice Þórr hurled it through the stone pillars, and twice it came back to the giant's hand unbroken — until the fair counsellor whispered to strike it on Hymir's own skull, harder than any cup. The cup shattered. Hymir mourned it with the formula of loss: he could no longer say over it "ale is brewed." Then, sullen, he yielded the wager — take the cauldron, if you can carry it out. Týr heaved twice and could not shift it; Þórr hoisted it over his head and strode off with the rim ringing at his heels. They had not gone far before he looked back and saw Hymir coming east from the caves with a troop of many-headed giants; he set down the cauldron, raised Mjöllnir, and slew the whole host. One of Þórr's goats went lame on the road — Loki's doing, the poem says — but the cauldron came to Ægir, who brews ale in it for the Æsir ever after. Syncretism: Hymir's poem has drawn comparatists for a century because the cauldron-quest is one of the old travelling stories of the North Atlantic: a vessel of plenty, kept by a grudging power beyond the sea, won for the feast of the gods. Scholars since Dumézil have set Hymiskviða beside the Celtic cauldron-quests — the Welsh Preiddeu Annwfn, where Arthur sails for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn, and the Irish cauldrons that no company leaves unsatisfied — and beside Vedic parallels for the winning of the gods' drink. The fishing scene has its own comparative trail: the thunder-god's combat with the sea-serpent belongs with the wide Indo-European dragon-fight. Inside the Norse corpus the neater tension is genealogical: Hymiskviða makes the giant Týr's father, while Snorri elsewhere counts Týr among Óðinn's sons — two filiations the tradition never reconciled. Cultural legacy: Hymir's afterlife is carried almost entirely by the fishing-trip, which became the most retold of all Þórr's adventures: Victorian mythographies made it a set-piece, modern handbooks open their Þórr chapters with it, and every popular retelling keeps the ox-head, the glaring serpent, and the giant rowing home in silence. In scholarship the poem holds a double distinction — it is both the fullest portrait of a giant household in the Edda and the standing exhibit in the debate over the cauldron-quest's Celtic kin. The name itself stayed where the þulur put it: a giant-name, rarely borrowed, carried into modern fantasy and games chiefly as the surly host of the world's most famous fishing story. Extended meditation: Hymir is the Edda's portrait of hospitality under strain: the host who feeds his guests two oxen and counts the cost, who rows farther than he means to because pride will not let him ship his oar first, who wagers his treasures on contests he frames himself — and loses both. The poem never makes him a monster; it makes him a householder with a monstrous ancestry and a mile-deep kettle, and lets the comedy and the cold do the work. What the story measures is not his failure but the difference between keeping plenty and sharing it: the cauldron that brews for all the gods spent its best years in a hall where even a guest's supper was tallied. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Hymir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚼᚢᛘᛁᛦ (h-u-m-i-R, the ᚢ rune covering the rounded y and ᛦ writing the final nominative -r). title: The Steward of Arthur's Hall
text: The Steward of Arthur's Hall: The Nine Days' Breath, the Fire in His Hands, and the Sword No Physician Can Heal Cei son of Cynyr is the first companion Arthur assigns to Culhwch: the tall man of the Mabinogion's oldest Arthurian tale, who could hold his breath nine nights and nine days under water, go nine nights and nine days without sleep, deal a wound no physician could heal, grow as tall as the tallest tree in the forest, and carry so much heat in his body that rain dried a handbreadth above and below his hand and his companions lit their fires from him in the cold. Centuries of romance would remember him as the steward of the court — the seneschal Kay. The Nine Days' Breath: Nine nights and nine days under water; nine nights and nine days without sleep — the Mabinogion's measure of the tall man's endurance. The Fire in His Hands: His heat kept his hand dry a handbreadth in the hardest rain; in the bitterest cold he was fuel for his companions' fire. The Unhealable Sword: A wound from Cei's sword no physician could heal — and the sword of Wrnach the giant came into Arthur's hand by Cei's trickery. The Seneschal's Office: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Caius dapifer — steward of Arthur's household, given Anjou, buried at Chinon: the office the later romances never let him leave. Symbols: The nine days' breath — Endurance past the human limit — the hero who outlasts water and sleep alike; The fire in his hands — Heat as provision: the companion who keeps the whole company warm, dry, and fed with fire; The unhealable sword — A stroke beyond remedy — the oldest stratum's mark of the warrior, before romances made him a steward; The beard of Dillus — The quest accomplished by cunning — and Arthur's mocking englyn that ended the fellowship; Cei Hir, 'the Tall' — Tall as the tallest tree in the forest when it pleased him — stature as the visible sign of the older, larger hero Kai's mythology lives in the oldest stratum of Welsh Arthurian tradition: Culhwch ac Olwen gives him the tale's largest dossier after Arthur himself, and the fragmentary dialogue poem Pa Gur remembers exploits the prose never told. The later Latin and French traditions kept the man and quietly spent the magic. Culhwch ac Olwen: The First Companion When Culhwch comes to Arthur's court to win Olwen daughter of Ysbaddaden Chief Giant, Arthur grants him help, and the first companion named is Cei son of Cynyr. The warrior-list fixes his peculiarities in one breath: nine nights and nine days he could be under water; nine nights and nine days he could go without sleep; a wound from Cei's sword no physician could heal. Cei the Tall — when it pleased him he could make himself as tall as the tallest tree in the forest. And the list adds the attribute the whole fellowship depended on: when the rain was heaviest, whatever he carried in his hand stayed dry for a handbreadth above and below, so great was his heat; and when the cold was hardest on his companions, he was fuel to them to light their fire. The list also preserves his mother's prophecy that his heart would be cold — the oldest trace of the coldness the later romances turned to mockery. Culhwch ac Olwen: The Salmon and the Sword Two of the hardest anoethau — the 'things hard to get' that Ysbaddaden sets as the bride-price — fall to Cei. To free Mabon son of Modron from his prison at Caer Loyw, the company follows the oldest animals to the Salmon of Llyn Llyw, and Cei and Bedwyr ride up the Severn on the salmon's shoulders; while Arthur's men assault the fort from the front, Cei carries Mabon away on the salmon's back. And when Arthur's band comes to the hall of Wrnach the giant, whose sword is needed to hunt the boar Twrch Trwyth — no guest had ever left that hall alive — Cei claims to be a master polisher of swords. Admitted, he burnishes the giant's blade, asks to hold it to test the work, and strikes Wrnach's head off with his own sword; the company destroys the fortress. The wonder-hero's greatest feats in the tale are won with a craftsman's hands, not a charge of horse — a hint of how the tradition will later make him the man who keeps the tools, not the one who swings them. Culhwch ac Olwen: The Beard of Dillus and the Englyn The beard of Dillus the Bearded was wanted to make a leash for the whelp Drudwyn, and Cei and Bedwyr found the giant alone. Cei dug a pit, tricked Dillus into it, plucked his beard out with wooden tweezers, and killed him afterward — and Arthur, watching, sang an englyn mocking Cei for making a leash from a living beard he could never have taken from a healthy man. Cei answered nothing, but the tale records the consequence in a line: because of that englyn there was enmity between Cei and Arthur ever after. The tale gives him no further feat of note; the fellowship's first companion becomes its first estrangement. The closing tally keeps the ending: Gwyddog son of Menestyr slew Cei, and Arthur slew Gwyddog and his brothers to avenge him — the rift repaired only in vengeance, and too late for either of them to enjoy it. It is the oldest Arthurian story about how a court breaks: not by siege, but by a joke aimed at the wrong man's pride. Pa Gur / The Welsh Triads: Nine Witches and the Cat of Anglesey The fragmentary dialogue poem Pa Gur yv y Porthaur?, preserved in the Black Book of Carmarthen, shows Arthur and the gatekeeper Glewlwyd Mighty-grasp trading boasts, and the boasts are Cei's: Cei pierced nine witches, and Cei the Fair went to Anglesey to destroy the monster the Welsh called Cath Palug — the gigantic cat that the triads say was born of the sow Henwen and raised by the sons of Palug as one of the island's plagues.
