Around that spine stands the fosterage: the lord of Brí Léith reared [[aengus|Óengus]]. The Bride-Price: The Sloe and the Bride-Price Midir of Brí Léith was the foster-father of Óengus, and he came to Brú na Bóinne to visit his fosterling. While the boys of the Brug were at their hurling, a sloe-thorn sprang from the play and put out Midir's eye; he stayed a year in the mound while Dían Cécht, the physician of the Túatha Dé Danann, made him whole. For his reward and his heart's desire he named Étaín Echraide, daughter of Ailill, the fairest woman in Ireland — and it was Óengus who went to win her. Her father Ailill mac Máta, king of the Ulaid, set a bride-price no mortal could pay: twelve plains cleared of their stones and wood, and twelve rivers led out of the land to the sea. Óengus performed the labors with the Dagda's strength behind him, and Midir brought Étaín home to Brí Léith as his wife. The tale's arithmetic is exact: the god's first possession of Étaín was bought by service, the price of a wounded eye — and it was the one part of the story that ended peaceably. The Fly: The Fly in the Crystal Bower Midir already had a wife: Fuamnach, foster-daughter of Bresal the druid, and versed in her foster-father's arts. When Étaín came home to Brí Léith, Fuamnach's jealousy found its instrument — a rod of scarlet quicken-tree — and one stroke made her rival a pool of water, then a worm, then a purple fly of wondrous size and sweetness. For seven years the fly that was Étaín went with Midir wherever he went, and he knew her in her shape; but Fuamnach's malice outlasted his keeping. The fly came at last to Brú na Bóinne, where Óengus knew her and built her a grianán, a crystal sun-bower filled with healing herbs — until Fuamnach raised a magic wind that swept her across Ireland for seven years more, to fall into the cup of the wife of Étar, an Ulster warrior, at the Bay of Cíú. She was drunk, conceived, and born again a thousand and twelve years after her first birth: Étaín, daughter of Étar. Midir's house is the still center of the storm — the husband whose hall became the battlefield of two women's powers, and who waited out the centuries the tale demanded of him. The Game: The Long Game at Tara In her second life Étaín married Eochaid Airem, high king of Ireland at Tara, and Midir came for her as the tale had promised. First he came in the shape of Ailill Anglonnach, the king's brother, who was wasting with love of her — three nights he lay beside her in that likeness and did not touch her, and so saved both her honor and Ailill's life. Then he revealed himself and asked her to come away with him; she answered that she would not go without her husband's leave. So Midir took the leave the hard way. He came to Tara and challenged Eochaid to fidchell, and game after game Midir lost, paying the stakes without stint — horses and treasures in such plenty that the king's greed was schooled by the god's purse. Then the board was set once more, and the stake named was an embrace and a kiss from Étaín; Midir won. Eochaid deferred the payment for a month, and when the month was out Tara stood ringed with warriors. Midir appeared all the same in the midst of the hall, sang to Étaín the invitation to the wondrous land, took her in his arms, and the two rose through the smoke-hole as two swans linked by a silver chain, and the host of Ireland could do nothing. The Choice: The Fifty Women in One Likeness Eochaid's answer was the spade: he set the men of Ireland to digging up the síd-mounds one by one, a war of delving against the hollow hills, until the host stood over Brí Léith itself. Then Midir came to the parley, and the bargain struck was surrender of a kind: on the morrow fifty women came out of the mound, every one of them in Étaín's exact likeness, and the king was told to choose his wife. He chose — and chose his own daughter, born to Étaín in the síd and hidden in the likeness of her mother. By that unwitting union a daughter was conceived who was exposed and spared, reared as Mess Búachalla, the cowherd's fosterling, and through her the line ran down to Conaire Mór, the doomed king of the Bruiden Da Derga. When Midir revealed the deception he gave back the true Étaín as well; the tale lets the god keep the last word and the king keep his shame. It is the Otherworld's coldest jest: the wager was never about the game, and the digging was never going to win. The Fosterage: The Foster-Father of the Young God Behind the wooing stands the fosterage. When the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of Ireland among the Túatha Dé Danann, his son Óengus was away with Midir of Brí Léith, being fostered, and received nothing — the absence that led to the famous quibble of the day and the night, and to Brú na Bóinne passing to the son. The tradition thus ties the two mounds together from the beginning: the young god reared at Brí Léith, the proud god's eye healed at the Brug. The foster-bond runs both ways through the dossier. It was for Midir that Óengus won Étaín Echraide and performed her father's labors; it was in Óengus's bower that Étaín the purple fly found her one refuge. Irish fosterage was no light tie — it stood beside blood, and the tales honor it. Midir's proudest title is not lord of Brí Léith but the one the stories keep proving: the man who raised the son of the young. Syncretism: Midir has no cross-border witness of his own, and the honest comparison is typological rather than genetic. No Gaulish altar names him and no scholar has proposed one; where the Dagda can be set beside Sucellos on the strength of club and cauldron, Midir's dossier — the wager, the hunted bride, the mound that is a court — belongs to the Otherworld-king figure-type that Mac Cana and Sjoestedt trace through the Celtic materials without anchoring it to any single epigraphic god. Within Ireland his structural kin are the síd-lords of the neighboring tales: Bodb Derg of the Munster síde, who answers the Dagda's search in the Aislinge, and [[manannan|Manannán]], the sea-going master of the Otherworld's glamour. The Welsh corpus offers only a functional parallel — [[arawn|Arawn]], the lord of Annwn who likewise binds a mortal king by a bargain with a hidden edge — and the parallel is a pattern, not a pedigree. The comparisons instruct; none of them identifies him. Cultural legacy: Midir's afterlife is the afterlife of Tochmarc Étaíne itself, the tale that never let him go. P. W. Joyce carried 'The Wooing of Etain' into modern English in Old Celtic Romances (1879), and Lady Gregory made the fidchell game and the swans part of the Celtic revival's furniture in Gods and Fighting Men (1904). James Stephens gave the story its strangest modern retelling in In the Land of Youth (1924), where Midir's arrival at Tara is staged as high comedy turning to awe. Bergin and Best's edition in Ériu (1938) fixed the text for scholarship, and Jeffrey Gantz's Penguin translation (1981) put the whole dossier on the general reader's shelf, where it has stayed: the fidchell game is now the standard citation whenever Irish literature wants to prove that its gods play a longer game than its kings. The name itself took no second path — no Angus, no Brigit: Midir never became a given name, a place, or a pub, and remains what the manuscripts made him, a proper noun with a single bearer. Extended meditation: Midir is the god of the long game, and the tradition tells you so in his name before it tells you in his story: the handbooks gloss it, cautiously, as judge — and a judge is exactly what a wager needs. Watch how he plays Eochaid. He loses, and loses, and pays without stint, because the losses are the lesson: the king is being taught that the man across the board can afford anything, that the stakes are a language, and that the only sentence being written is the last one. When the final stake is named — an embrace, a kiss — the game has already been won for a month. The fidchell board is a court, and the house always already holds the verdict. That patience is the Otherworld's whole tempo. A mortal wooing is measured in seasons; Midir's spans a thousand and twelve years, two births of the same woman, and a war of spades against his own roof — and he never hurries, because time is the one currency his kind does not spend. His foster-son [[aengus|Óengus]] parses time into a loophole and holds a mound on a day without a term; the foster-father plays time into a stake and holds a woman across two lifetimes. Between them the síd of Ireland teaches the same doctrine: the hollow hills do not take what they want. They wait until the wanting itself concedes. Original script note: The name is preserved in medieval Irish manuscripts in the Insular Latin script as Midir — the spelling Bergin and Best print from Lebor na hUidre; many modern editors add the fada and write Mídir to mark the long vowel, an editorial convention rather than the manuscript norm. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the restored form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: midir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The Wild Prophet of the Forest
text: The Wild Prophet of the Forest: Seer, Wild Man Myrddin is the original Welsh form of the name the world knows as Merlin: the prophet who went mad at the battle of Arfderydd in 573, fled into the Caledonian forest, and lived there as a wild man — lamenting his dead lord Gwenddolau, sheltering beneath an apple tree, and uttering the prophecies that made him the canonical voice of Welsh vaticination before Geoffrey of Monmouth made him the wizard of the Arthurian world. The Apple Tree: The sweet apple tree that shelters Myrddin in the Afallennau — his only house in the forest of Celyddon, addressed like a friend. Arfderydd: The northern battle of 573 where his lord Gwenddolau son of Ceidio fell; grief and slaughter drove Myrddin mad, says the Welsh Triad. The Threefold Death: The death Myrddin prophesies in the Vita Merlini — from a rock, in a tree, and in the water — fulfilled to the letter; the wild prophet's own end in the northern tale. The Brud: The prophetic poems gathered under his name — the Black Book's Afallennau and Oianau, and Geoffrey's Prophetiae Merlini, the most copied political prophecy of the Middle Ages. Symbols: The apple tree — The wild man's shelter and confidant — prophecy spoken from hiding, sweet and bitter at once; The forest of Celyddon — The Caledonian wood — madness, exile, and second sight in one landscape; The stag — The wild mount he rides to court in the Vita Merlini, driving the forest's herds before him; Rock, tree, and water — The three elements of the foretold death — prophecy that cannot miss, however it is guarded against; Gwenddydd's questions — The sister's dialogue — prophecy as the speech left between the mad and those who loved them Myrddin's dossier divides in two, and the tradition itself knew it: the northern prophet who went mad at Arfderydd and fled to Coed Celyddon, preserved in the Welsh Triads, the Annales Cambriae, and the Black Book poems; and Geoffrey of Monmouth's Merlinus, who carried the wild man into Latin and grafted him onto the Arthurian world. Gerald of Wales already separated them in the twelfth century: Merlinus Ambrosius, the boy prophet of Vortigern's tower, and Merlinus Celidonius — Sylvester — the wild man of the Caledonian forest. Annales Cambriae / Trioedd Ynys Prydein: The Battle of Arfderydd The Annales Cambriae enter under the year 573 the battle of Arfderydd, fought in the north between the sons of Eliffer and Gwenddolau son of Ceidio — a historical-seeming conflict of the British Old North. The Welsh Triads count it among the futile battles of the Island of Britain, brought about, in the triad's famous understatement, for a lark's nest; and the triad records the consequence that matters here: Gwenddolau fell, and Myrddin became mad. From that seed the whole legend grows. Myrddin son of Morfryn, his lord dead and his side defeated, flees the world of the mead-hall into Coed Celyddon, the Caledonian forest, and becomes Myrddin Wyllt — the Wild — living from the forest's gifts and speaking only in verse and prophecy. Black Book of Carmarthen: The Apple Trees and the Oianau The earliest Welsh manuscript, the Black Book of Carmarthen (c. 1250), preserves the poems that give the wild man his own voice. In Yr Afallennau, 'The Apple Trees', Myrddin addresses the sweet apple tree that shelters him: he laments Gwenddolau, slain in the bloodshed of Arfderydd; he grieves that he endures want while once he rode at the head of warriors; he hides from Rhydderch's men; and the refrain returns to the tree, his one companion and hiding-place. The companion poem, Yr Oianau, keeps the same voice — the outcast prophet calling his mournful 'oian' through the forest, mourning his dead, marked out by madness as the gods' or fate's chosen sufferer. These are not narrative poems but laments with prophecy threaded through them; together they made Myrddin the patron and mouthpiece of the whole Welsh prophetic genre. Red Book of Hergest: The Conversation of Myrddin and Gwenddydd The Cyfoesi Myrddin a Gwenddydd ei chwaer — 'The Conversation of Myrddin and His Sister Gwenddydd' — is the tradition's most human document. Gwenddydd, wife of Rhydderch and sister of the wild prophet, questions her brother across the gulf his madness has opened: she mourns the warrior he was, the mead-feasts he no longer honours, the lord they both have lost. Myrddin answers her with prophecy — the fate of Wales, the coming of its deliverers — but the prophecy keeps breaking against grief. The dialogue fixes what the poems imply: the wild man is not forsaken but watched from the world he left. Gwenddydd survives in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin as Ganieda — Rhydderch's queen, Myrddin's sister, and, at the end of the Vita Merlini, his successor in prophecy itself. Vita Merlini: The Threefold Death and the Life of the Forest Geoffrey of Monmouth's Vita Merlini (c. 1150) is the wild man's fullest biography. Merlinus — poet, prophet, and king in Geoffrey's telling — loses his reason at a battle among the northern princes and flees to the Caledonian wood, where he lives as a silvester homo, a man of the forest, feeding on roots and fruit, snow on his shoulders, unknown to his own court. Rhydderch's men find him and drag him back; at court he laughs at things no one understands, and his laughter is always a prophecy. To a boy he foretells a threefold death: from a rock, in a tree, and in the water — and the boy, falling from a cliff, is caught by a tree with his head in the stream, dying all three deaths at once, as no human prudence could have guarded against. The poem lets him go home to the forest at last. He appears riding a stag, driving the woodland herds before him like a shepherd of the wild; [[taliesin|Taliesin]] — Telgesinus in the Latin — comes to him, and the two seers discourse at length on the winds, the waters, the fishes, and the making of the world. In the end Merlin gives his observatory to his sister Ganieda, who takes up the prophetic gift, and retires to the forest for good — the mad king become the wise wild man, the only sovereignty he can still keep. Historia Regum Britanniae / Historia Brittonum: The Boy at Vortigern's Tower Geoffrey's other Merlin came from another book. The ninth-century Historia Brittonum of Nennius tells of the boy Ambrosius — a child without a father — brought to King Vortigern to be sacrificed so that his collapsing tower at Dinas Emrys might stand; the boy instead reveals the pool beneath the foundations and the two dragons, red and white, whose battle is the prophecy of Britain: the red dragon of the Britons, the white of the Saxons. Geoffrey took Nennius's boy and gave him Myrddin's name: Merlinus Ambrosius. The graft made one figure of two traditions — the royal prophet of the tower and the mad prophet of the forest — and Gerald of Wales, a generation later, was already insisting they were two. The composite Merlin who results is the one the world inherited: prophet to Vortigern, architect of kings, and, in the romances that followed, counsellor of Arthur himself. Syncretism: Myrddin's comparisons run north, not east. The twelfth-century Life of St Kentigern by Jocelyn of Furness knows a mad prophet at the court of Rhydderch Hael named Lailoken, who foretold his own threefold death; a fragmentary Latin life of 'Merlin the Wild' preserved in the Cotton collection tells the same penitence, conversion by Kentigern, and triple end — stoned, fallen on a stake, drowned in the Tweed. Nikolai Tolstoy's Quest for Merlin argued that Lailoken and Myrddin Wyllt are two records of one north-British wild-man figure, and the modern handbooks treat the kinship as real, its exact shape unproven. The Irish tradition offers no namesake — the wild men of the Irish tales, Suibhne Geilt above all, share the type rather than the name: the king driven mad by battle who lives in trees, speaks in verse, and is watched by the court he left. Within the Welsh corpus his truest kin is [[taliesin|Taliesin]], the other great prophetic poet, with whom the Vita Merlini pairs him in discourse; and his own tradition split him in two, as Gerald of Wales records — Merlinus Ambrosius of Dinas Emrys and Merlinus Celidonius of the Caledonian forest, the tower-boy and the wild man the romances later fused. Cultural legacy: No Celtic figure has had a stranger second life. Geoffrey's Prophetiae Merlini — the seventh book of the Historia — circulated separately for centuries and became the most copied political prophecy of the Latin Middle Ages, mined for omens by kings and rebels alike; the romances then turned the prophet into the enchanter, and by the thirteenth-century Vulgate cycle Merlin is Arthur's maker: arranger of Uther's night at Tintagel, keeper of the Round Table's founding, and prisoner of the Lady of the Lake. Lady Charlotte Guest's Mabinogion (1838–49) and the nineteenth-century Arthurian revival carried the Welsh roots back into English view, and modern scholarship — Jarman above all — rebuilt the northern prophet behind the wizard. In Welsh memory the original never disappeared: Caerfyrddin, 'Myrddin's fortress', still bears the folk etymology Geoffrey loved, and the Myrddin of the Black Book remains the patron of Welsh prophecy — the figure every later brud quietly pretended to be. The name now means the wizard worldwide; the temple's task is to hand the name back to the wild man it began with. Extended meditation: Myrddin is the figure who paid for knowledge with the ordinary world. Every version of him loses something before he sees: a lord, a battle, his reason, his hall. The tradition is strikingly honest about the transaction — the prophecy is real, and so is the madness, and the same event, the slaughter at Arfderydd, gives him both. He is the answer Celtic literature gives to the question of what a seer is: not a priest with a technique but a survivor whom grief has put outside the human settlement, close enough to the trees that the future can get a word in. His sister comes to the edge of the forest to ask what will happen; he tells her, and stays. That is the shape of the gift — the future, at the price of the present. And his name tells the same story in miniature. It is not a theonym but a place-name: Caerfyrddin, the sea-fort, Moridunum, given to a man. The wild prophet carries a fortress in his name — the ordered world he was driven out of, remembered every time anyone calls him. Original script note: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Myrddin — attested in the Black Book of Carmarthen (NLW Peniarth MS 1, c. 1250, the earliest Welsh manuscript) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), and in the Welsh Triads. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive atomic letter for the restoration to recover — the digraph dd for the soft 'th' is orthography, not a lost character — which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: myrddin.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Joy, Wife of Baldr
text: Joy, Wife of Baldr: The Wife Who Followed into the Fire Nanna, daughter of Nepr, is the wife of Baldr the Good and the mother of Forseti — and the only figure in the Norse corpus who dies of a broken heart. When she saw her husband laid on his pyre aboard Hringhorni, her heart burst with grief, and the Æsir laid her on the fire beside him. In Hel she keeps her place at his side, and when Hermóðr comes to ransom the dead god, it is Nanna who sends gifts back up the road: a linen robe for Frigg, a gold ring for Fulla — love's tokens out of the land of the dead. The Linen for Frigg: The robe of linen Nanna sent from Hel to her mother-in-law — a household gift carried up the nine-night road by Hermóðr, proof the dead still keep their obligations of love. The Ring for Fulla: The gold finger-ring for Frigg's maid Fulla, Baldr's sister-in-law by the goddess's own household — the small exact kindness of a woman who remembers her friendships even in death. The Burst Heart: The one death in the Edda that needs no weapon: seeing Baldr on the pyre, Nanna's heart burst with grief, and she was laid on the fire beside him. Glitnir: The hall of gold and silver in heaven where her son Forseti dwells, stilling all strife — the living continuation of the house Nanna and Baldr began. Symbols: The linen robe — The gift sent from Hel to Frigg — domestic love that death does not cancel; The gold finger-ring — Fulla's keepsake from the dead — friendship remembered across the boundary; The pyre of Hringhorni — The fire she entered unslain and unbidden — grief as its own cause of death; Glitnir — The gold-and-silver hall of her son Forseti — the household's survival in the world above; The high seat in Hel — Her place beside Baldr in the hall of the dead — marriage persisting past the grave Nanna's dossier is among the shortest in the Edda and among the most devastating: she is named, married, widowed, dead of grief, and found again in Hel — in scarcely more lines than that. Snorri gives her the two moments the tradition never forgot, and Saxo gives her a second life as a wooed princess; between them stands a figure made almost entirely of devotion. Gylfaginning 32: The Wife of Baldr Snorri names her in the catalogue of the Æsir's houses with genealogical economy: Baldr's wife is Nanna, daughter of Nepr, and their son is Forseti. Of Nepr nothing else is told — the father exists only to place the daughter. The son, by contrast, inherits a hall and an office: Forseti dwells in Glitnir, the hall whose pillars are red gold and whose roof is silver, and there he stills all strife, the great reconciler of gods and men. Grímnismál keeps the same hall in its numbered survey of heaven's dwellings. The ásynja þulur preserved with Skáldskaparmál hold Nanna in the catalogue of the goddesses by name, beside Hlín and Sól. Beyond these notations the corpus gives her no adventure, no quarrel, no single act in life: the tradition saves everything for her death, and for what she does after it. Gylfaginning 49: The Heart That Burst When Baldr fell to the mistletoe and the Æsir could neither weep nor take vengeance in the sanctuary, they bore him to the sea and brought out Hringhorni, his ship, the greatest of all ships. The giantess Hyrrokkin launched it with one shove, and the gods built the pyre on board. Then comes the sentence that defines Nanna for all time: when she saw her husband's body carried to the ship, her heart burst with grief, and she died. She was laid on the pyre beside him, and the fire was kindled. Óðinn laid the ring Draupnir on the flames; Þórr hallowed the pyre with Mjölnir; Baldr's horse was led to the fire with all its gear. No weapon touches her; no enemy wills her death. In a corpus full of spear-thrusts and poisoned cups, hers is the one death by love alone — the Norse tradition's starkest statement that grief itself can kill, and that the gods are not exempt. Gylfaginning 49: The Gifts from Hel Hermóðr the Bold rides nine nights through dark valleys to ransom Baldr, and in Hel's hall he finds his brother in the high seat — and Nanna is there, keeping her place beside him in death as in life. Hel sets the famous condition: all things in the world, living and lifeless, must weep Baldr out. When Hermóðr turns for home, the dead send tokens with him. Baldr sends the ring Draupnir back to Óðinn — and Nanna sends a robe of linen to Frigg, her husband's mother, with other gifts, and a gold finger-ring to Fulla, Frigg's trusted maid. The detail is small and it is the whole of her: in the land where nothing returns, she answers the errand with household gifts — a robe for the mother, a ring for the friend. The ransom fails at Þökk's dry tears, and Nanna and Baldr remain in Hel together. Even Völuspá's promised return after Ragnarǫk names Baldr and Höðr reconciled, and does not name her; the poem leaves her where Snorri left her, at her husband's side. Saxo, Gesta Danorum III: Nanna and Høtherus Saxo Grammaticus gives Nanna the fuller life the Icelanders withheld — and a different husband. His Nanna is the daughter of Gevarus, king of Norway, and Høtherus, Gevarus's foster-son, loves her. When Høtherus sues for her hand, she answers with one of Saxo's set speeches: mortal and demigod are ill-matched, she warns, and unions across that boundary end in sorrow — the maid argues theology against her own marriage. But Balderus, son of Odin, has seen her and burns for her too, and the rivalry becomes war. Høtherus, armed with the sword Mimming won from the satyr Mimingus, defeats the gods' fleet at sea — even Thor's club is cleft — and wins Nanna's hand. Only later, in the renewed feud, does Høtherus wound the invulnerable Balderus with the one blade that can harm him. Where Snorri's Nanna is the wife who dies on her husband's pyre, Saxo's is the bride two rivals bleed for — the same woman read as devotion in Iceland and as desire's prize in Denmark. The two portraits never meet, and together they prove the Baldr cycle was told up and down the North in irreconcilable keys. Syncretism: Nanna's closest kin are inside the corpus itself: she is the divine pattern of which Brynhildr is the heroic echo — the woman who mounts her dead beloved's pyre, as Brynhildr has herself burned beside Sigurðr in the Völsung cycle. Lindow notes the motif as the Norse 'faithful unto the pyre' type, and the parallel is structural, not borrowed. Cross-culturally, nineteenth-century scholars reached for the widows of Greek and Sanskrit tradition — Alcestis dying in her husband's place, the debated Indo-European comparisons around the suttee — but current handbooks are cooler: Simek and Orchard treat Nanna as a figure of the Baldr complex whose attestation is too thin for cult reconstruction, and her etymology too disputed for safe comparison. What can be said cleanly is that no other northern goddess is defined so entirely by a single act of grief, and none answers from the grave with so domestic a grace as a robe and a ring. Cultural legacy: Nanna's afterlife runs quietly through the Baldr story's long reception: every retelling of the death of the shining god, from the Kearys' Victorian 'Heroes of Asgard' onward, keeps her two scenes — the burst heart on the shore and the gifts entrusted to Hermóðr. Nineteenth-century romanticism made much of the wife on the pyre; twentieth-century scholarship made her the test case for how little the Edda needs to say. Her sturdiest legacy is the name itself: Nanna never died out in the North and remains a living given name in Denmark and Iceland, borne today by women who inherit the most grief-stricken and most faithful name in the Edda. Modern Heathenry remembers her in Baldr rites as the goddess of devotion measured past death's door. Extended meditation: Nanna is the Edda's proof that grief is not a lesser fate than battle. Every other death in the Baldr cycle is negotiated — prophesied, sworn against, tricked, ransomed, avenged. Hers alone simply happens, at the sight of the pyre, and the narrative grants it without comment, as if the gods understood this was a death no oath could have prevented. And then the tradition does something finer still: it lets her act after death. From Hel, where nothing returns, she sends a robe and a ring — not pleas, not prophecy, but the remembered kindnesses of a daughter-in-law and a friend. The ransom fails; the gifts arrive. In a mythology hurtling toward Ragnarǫk, Nanna is the small, exact consolation: that love keeps its accounts even in the land of the dead, and pays them in linen and gold. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Nanna — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚾᛅᚾᛅ (n-a-n-a). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: nanna.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The Mist-World Before the World
text: The Mist-World Before the World: Hvergelmir, the Élivágar, and the Northern Pole of Ginnungagap Niflheimr is the oldest address in the Norse cosmos: the world of fog and rime that existed, Snorri says, many ages before the earth was made — the cold northern pole of the yawning gap, from whose roaring well every river in creation flows and from whose poisoned ice the first living thing quickened. Hvergelmir: The roaring kettle: the well in Niflheimr's middle, whence Grímnismál says all waters have their course. The Élivágar: The ice-waves: eleven rivers older than the earth — Svöl, Gunnþrá, Fjörm, Fimbulþul, Slíðr, Hríð, Sylgr, Ylgr, Víð, Leiptr, and Gjöll, which runs nearest the gate of Hel. The Rime and the Venom: Frost fog layered across the gap and the yeasty eitr that hardened like dross from a fire — creation's raw material, and its warning. Níðhöggr: The malice-striker: the serpent that gnaws Yggdrasill's third root from below, where it stands over Niflheimr above the well. Symbols: Hvergelmir, the roaring kettle — The source beneath all sources: every river in the world is one of its children; The Élivágar — The ice-waves older than the earth — water carrying the venom that froze into the first flesh; The rime fog — Cold as a substance, not an absence: the raw material the warm south breathed on until it lived Niflheimr's mythology is the mythology of before: it stars in no adventure and houses no hero, because its story is over before the gods' stories begin — and yet every river, every frost giant, and every corpse that sinks past Hel is still paying its tribute to the mist-world. Gylfaginning 4: The World That Came First Snorri's chronology begins not with a god but with a climate. 'It was many ages before the earth was made,' he says, 'that Niflheimr was made' — and in its middle stands the well Hvergelmir, 'the roaring kettle,' from which flow the rivers named one by one in Gylfaginning 4 and already in the verse lists of Grímnismál 27–29: Svöl the cool, Gunnþrá the battle-defiant, Fjörm the swift, Fimbulþul the loud-babbling, Slíðr the fearsome and Hríð the storming, Sylgr and Ylgr, Víð the broad, and Leiptr the flashing — and Gjöll, the resounding, which runs nearest the gate of Hel. Snorri is careful to say the mist-realm was not found but made: the first work of whatever order preceded the gods. Before there was a world to water, the mist-world already had its watershed — the Norse cosmos keeps, at its bottom, a memory that geography came first and inhabitants came after. Gylfaginning 5–7 · Vafþrúðnismál 21: The Yeasty Venom and the Quickening The Élivágar ran so far from their source that the yeasty venom in them hardened, like dross running out of a fire, and turned to ice; rime and fog rose layer upon layer across Ginnungagap's northern half, while sparks and molten flecks flew out of Muspellsheimr in the south. Where the warm breath met the rime, the ice thawed and dripped — and the dripping drops quickened into the likeness of a man, named Ymir by the gods and Aurgelmir, the mud-yeller, by the rime-giants who descend from him. The Poetic Edda keeps the same recipe in three lines: out of Élivágar spurted venom-drops, Vafþrúðnismál says, and grew until a giant was made. The first life in the North was brewed from poisoned ice thawed by a fire it could not see. Gylfaginning 15–16 · Grímnismál 26: The Root Over the Well When the world was finally built, Niflheimr kept the oldest seat in it. Yggdrasill's third root, Snorri says, extends over Niflheimr, and beneath that root is Hvergelmir, and the serpent Níðhöggr gnaws the root from below — the ash is always being eaten at its oldest corner. Grímnismál completes the water-cycle: the hart Eikþyrnir stands on Valhöll's roof cropping the leaves, and from his horns it drips into Hvergelmir, whence all waters have their course. The rivers of gods and giants alike — the Fjörm and the Slíðr, the Gjöll and the Leiptr — are one well's outflow, and the well sits in the mist. Vafþrúðnismál 43 · Baldrs draumar 2 · Gylfaginning 3: Niflhel, Down in the Ninth World In the poems the mist-world darkens into something lower. Óðinn, proving his wisdom to the giant Vafþrúðnir, says he journeyed through nine worlds below Niflhel; in Baldrs draumar he saddles Sleipnir and rides down to Niflhel to wake a dead seeress and wring the prophecy of Baldr's death from her. Snorri states the grim geography plainly: evil men go to Hel, and thence down to Niflhel — that is down in the ninth world. The world that was first becomes the world that is lowest: creation's old north pole, demoted to the cellar of the dead. Syncretism: Niflheimr needs no borrowing to be explained: its first element is one of the most securely inherited words in the Germanic vocabulary, the same mist that Greek keeps in nephélē, Latin in nebula, and Sanskrit in nábhas — three daughter languages and the North all descended from the same cloud. The genuine scholarly argument is internal. Niflheimr is a prose word: the poems overwhelmingly know niflhel, mist-Hel, and several handbooks treat Snorri's fully mapped Niflheimr — with its well, its eleven rivers, and its place opposite Muspellsheimr — as a thirteenth-century systematization raised on genuinely older material, since Hvergelmir and the Élivágar are Eddic and attested in Grímnismál and Vafþrúðnismál centuries before the Prose Edda. The comparative pattern is common enough: a pole of cold set against a pole of fire at the beginning of things — but the Norse version is unusual in making the cold not merely older than the gods but older than the earth itself. Cultural legacy: The mist-world's afterlife runs through every retelling that needs a bottom floor for the cosmos. Wagner rebuilt it as Nibelheim, the smoke-filled subterranean forge-realm of Alberich in Das Rheingold — a conflation of Niflheimr with the Nibelung dwarf-lore that no saga ever made, and one of the most consequential mistranslations in myth reception. Modern fantasy keeps the map: Marvel's comics and films count 'Niffleheim' among their Nine Realms, and games from the God of War series to a dozen smaller titles send players trudging through its fog as the endgame of cold. In Iceland the word never needed reviving — Niflheimur is simply the old word, still in service. What survives beneath every adaptation is the Edda's strangest idea: that the first thing was not light but fog, and that everything warm is a late arrival. Extended meditation: Niflheimr is the patron of what was here first. Before the gods, before the giants, before the earth itself, there was a world of mist with a well in the middle of it, and rivers already running. The Norse imagination refused to let creation begin with a decree; it began with weather — with frost accumulating in a silence no one had yet named, thawed, at last, by a warmth it never asked for. Every river still runs from that well, which is the myth's way of saying that every living thing is downstream of the cold it rose from. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Niflheimr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the compound would have been carved ᚾᛁᚠᛚᚼᛁᛘᛦ (n-i-f-l-h-i-m-R, the i-rune writing both e and i, the ᛦ carrying the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: niflheimr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Peace, Brother of Efnysien
text: Peace, Brother of Efnysien: The Gentle Twin of the Second Branch Nisien is one half of the strangest doublet in the Mabinogi: twin brothers, sons of Euroswydd, whom the Second Branch introduces with a single matched sentence — Nisien, the good man who would make peace between two armies when they were most furious; Efnysien, who would set two loving brothers fighting to the death. The tale then gives the whole war to the cruel twin and keeps the gentle one as its standing might-have-been: peace personified, present at the court that marches to Ireland, and never once allowed to prevail. The Peace Between Hosts: The tale's whole dossier in one clause: he would bring two armies to peace at the very height of their rage. The Twin: Son of Euroswydd and Penarddun, twin of Efnysien — the gentle half of a pair the tradition built as peace and strife in one cradle. Euroswydd's Line: Half-brother to Brân the Blessed, Branwen, and Manawydan — kin to the children of Llŷr by his mother's side. The Road Not Taken: Wherever the Second Branch's counsel is weighed, Nisien is the standing alternative: the peace that was in the house and was not chosen. Symbols: The paired sentence — The Second Branch's balanced character note — peace and strife defined as twin brothers, one clause each; The twin's shadow — Efnysien's cruelty measured against Nisien's gentleness — each brother the other's definition; The house of Euroswydd — The second father-line of Penarddun's children — the gentler inheritance beside the children of Llŷr; The mutilated horses — His brother's unprovoked outrage against Matholwch's team — the act of strife that no peace in the tale can undo; The silent presence — The peace-maker carried with the host to Ireland and given no scene — the might-have-been that haunts the branch Nisien has the smallest dossier in the Mabinogi and the clearest definition: he exists as one half of an antithesis. The Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr, names him exactly once as a character and then spends its whole length on the war his brother kindles. What survives of him is a sentence, a lineage, and a presence — and the Welsh tradition built an entire moral pole out of that spareness. Branwen ferch Llŷr: The Two Sons of Euroswydd The Second Branch introduces the twins in a single balanced construction, the most quoted sentence either brother ever gets. Nisien, the tale says, was a good man: he would bring about peace between two armies when they were at the height of their fury. Efnysien would bring about a quarrel between two brothers when they loved each other most. They are twins, sons of Euroswydd by Penarddun — and so half-brothers to Brân the Blessed, Branwen, and Manawydan, Penarddun's children by Llŷr. The construction is the whole point: Welsh prose has no other pair like it. The tradition does not describe two temperaments; it defines two forces — peace and strife — as brothers born in one hour, and then sets them loose in the same household. Every reader of the branch knows, before the horses are harmed, exactly which twin will act and which will stand by. Branwen ferch Llŷr: The Horses at Aberffraw When Brân consents to give Branwen in marriage to Matholwch, king of Ireland, and the wedding is held at Aberffraw, it is Efnysien — insulted that the match was made without his leave — who takes revenge on the groom's horses: he cuts off their lips to the teeth, their ears to their heads, their tails to their backs, and the eyelids to the bone. The outrage becomes the war's first cause, patched over with reparation and the gift of the Cauldron of Rebirth, and reopened in Ireland when Branwen is made a scullion and struck daily in the kitchen. Nisien's place in all this is the tale's deliberate emptiness: the peace-maker is there, kin to all parties, gifted by his own description with the one power the crisis needs — and the text never once shows him using it. The mutilation stands unappeased from its author; no embassy of Nisien's is ever recorded. The Second Branch's tragedy is written so that the reader supplies the missing twin. Branwen ferch Llŷr: The War Over the Sea Brân wades the sea at the head of the hosts of Britain, for no ship can carry him, and the war that follows destroys both kingdoms. The Irish revive their slain in the Cauldron of Rebirth, so that they rise to fight again, and the balance breaks only when Efnysien — feigning death among the corpses, flung living into the cauldron — stretches himself out and bursts it, dying in the act: the strife-twin consuming himself to undo the one weapon his own first outrage helped set in motion. Of the men of Britain only seven come home; Branwen dies of a broken heart on the shore of the Alaw. Nisien's name is not among the dead, the seven, or the counsellors: the tale simply stops mentioning him. Scholars have long read the silence as the branch's own verdict — Mac Cana and MacKillop alike treat the twins as a personified antithesis, peace and discord hypostatized as brothers, and on that reading Nisien's function is complete the moment the paired sentence is spoken. He is not a character the tale forgot; he is the peace the tale declined. Scholarly Reading: The Antithesis Made Flesh The modern handbooks are unusually agreed about what the twins are. Mac Cana reads the pair as the Mabinogi's clearest case of abstract forces embodied as kin: the redactor names Nisien and Efnysien in one breath because they are one idea in two bodies. MacKillop's dictionary keeps both entries short for the same reason — there is no cycle, no second tale, no folklore of Nisien to collect; the dossier is the Second Branch and nothing else. Koch's encyclopedia files both under Branwen ferch Llŷr. The names themselves resist resolution. The traditional glosses — 'peaceful one' for Nisien, 'double enemy' for Efnysien — are older scholarly convention rather than settled etymology, and the Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru and the handbooks record the derivations as uncertain. What is certain is the structure: two names, two clauses, one cradle. The Welsh tradition made its peace-maker the way myth usually makes its gods — by naming the opposite and letting the pair do the work. Syncretism: Nisien has no counterpart anywhere, and the honesty of that fact is part of his record. No Irish figure bears his name or his office: the Irish cycles know war-goddesses and peace-breaking satirists in abundance, but no personified peace-twin, and Sims-Williams's survey of Irish influence on Welsh literature — which finds deep Irish strata in the Second Branch itself, from the giant king who wades the sea to the cauldron of revival — supplies no Irish original for the sons of Euroswydd. The twins look like the Welsh redactor's own construction. The nearest comparisons are structural, drawn from inside the lexicon: his brother [[efnysien|Efnysien]], the necessary other half of the antithesis; [[manawydan|Manawydan]], his half-brother, whose own branch turns on patience and forbearance rather than force; and [[matholwch|Matholwch]], the wronged king whose horses his brother maimed. Beyond the Mabinogi the antithesis device has famous analogues — the paired forces of other traditions — but the Welsh pair needs no borrowing to explain: peace and strife as twin brothers is the sort of idea a mature prose tradition can invent in a single sentence, and the Second Branch is exactly that tradition. Cultural legacy: Nisien's afterlife is as quiet as his dossier. Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried the twins into English, and every retelling of Branwen since has kept the paired sentence — it is the one line of the Second Branch that anthologies quote whole. The scholarly tradition made the antithesis canonical: Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi and MacKillop's dictionary fixed the reading of the twins as personified peace and strife, and the pair now serves Celtic studies as the standard example of the Welsh redactor's art of definition-by-contrast. Nisien himself never became a cult figure, a comic-book antihero, or a given name in the way louder Mabinogi figures did — Efnysien, the interesting twin, took all of that. The gentle brother's legacy is the sentence itself: in a tale about a war no one could stop, Welsh literature wrote its peace-maker in one clause and let the silence around him say the rest. Extended meditation: Nisien is the proof that a figure can be made of almost nothing and still be one of the most exact things in his tradition. One sentence, one lineage, no deeds — and from that the Second Branch draws a whole theology of peace: that it exists, that it lives in the same house as strife, that it can be kin to the war-makers and married into every court, and that a host can carry it over the sea and never once take it out. The tragedy of Branwen is often told as Efnysien's story, but it is just as much Nisien's: the war happens in the presence of the one man whose nature is to end it, and the text makes sure we notice by telling us his nature first and his absence always. There is a further quietness the restoration makes visible. The name is plain ASCII — no accent to rescue, no letter to put back — because Middle Welsh wrote Nissyen and modern Welsh writes Nisien, and the keyboard never lost anything. Tier 2 says only that. The tradition said the rest nine centuries ago: the gentle twin, defined once, standing at the shoulder of the war for its whole length, the road the house of Llŷr did not take. Every court has a Nisien. The Mabinogi's question is why he is so seldom asked. Original script note: The normalized Middle Welsh form is Nisien (manuscript Nissyen ) — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Middle Welsh was written in the Latin alphabet in the medieval Welsh bookhand; the earlier epigraphic scripts of Britain, the Latin and ogham memorial stones, name no figure of the Mabinogi. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: nisien.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The Honey-Tongued Champion
text: The Honey-Tongued Champion: Eloquence, Writing Ogma is the champion — in trenfer, the strong man — of the Túatha Dé Danann, and the Irish tradition made his strength and his speech one gift: the Auraicept na n-Éces calls him a man well skilled in speech and in poetry, and credits him with the invention of the ogham itself. His Gaulish cognate Ogmios, the old-man Herakles of Lucian's account, drags a willing crowd by golden chains fastened to his tongue: in the Celtic world, eloquence is what the strongest god is for. The Ogham: The notched alphabet of early Ireland, carved along the edge of standing stones — of which the Scholars' Primer says: the father of the ogham is Ogma, the mother of the ogham is the hand or knife of Ogma. Orna, the Speaking Sword: The sword of Tethra, king of the Fomorians, found by Ogma after Mag Tuired — which recounted every deed that had been done with it, as swords did in those days. The Flagstone of Tara: The great stone Ogma hurled to test the stranger at the gate — which Lugh threw back through the rath to its own place, proving the stronger champion had arrived. The Firewood: The champion's portion under the tyranny of Bres: hauling fuel for a usurper's fires, so weakened by hunger that the sea washed over him as he carried it. Symbols: The ogham fews — The notched letters along the stemline — writing itself, fathered by the champion's hand; Orna, Tethra's sword — The weapon that tells its own deeds — even the champion's steel answers to speech; The flagstone of Tara — Strength as the doorkeeper's test — the stone only the worthiest arm can move; The firewood bundle — The strong man reduced to serf-labor — endurance under the usurper, repaid at Mag Tuired; The golden chains of Ogmios — Lucian's Gaulish image of eloquence: men led willingly, ear fastened to tongue Ogma's dossier is compact and exact: the Lebor Gabála gives his lineage, Cath Maige Tuired gives his deeds — the serf-labor under Bres, the flagstone test at Lugh's coming, the killing of the Fomorian king's son, and the talking sword — and the learned tradition gives him his strangest honor, the invention of the ogham. Lebor Gabála Érenn: The Son of Elatha The Lebor Gabála Érenn, Ireland's medieval book of invasions, writes Ogma into the divine genealogy: Ogma son of Elatha, of the line of Delbaeth, and so the brother of the Dagda himself. The surname carries a sting the saga does not hide — the same Elatha, the beautiful Fomorian prince who came as an arbiter to the Túatha Dé, is father of Bres by a Fomorian woman, which makes the champion of the gods the half-brother of the usurper who will set him hauling firewood. When the Túatha Dé Danann came to Ireland out of the four northern cities, Ogma came with them as the champion of the race — in trenfer, the strong man, the standing title the texts give him. His place in the pantheon is therefore double from the first mention: the arm of the Túatha Dé Danann, and the brother of their all-father, with the enemy's blood already in his own house. Cath Maige Tuired: The Firewood of the Serf-Years When the half-Fomorian Bres was made king and laid the Túatha Dé Danann under tribute, the greatest of them were put to work like serfs — deliberately, for the tribute was calculated to break the mighty. The Dagda was set to building raths, and Ogma — the champion of the whole divine race — was set to hauling firewood for the fortress. The tale does not spare him: so weakened was he by hunger that the sea washed over him as he carried the fuel. The servitude did not blunt him; when the war came he killed the Fomorian king's son with his bare champion's art, and the firewood years became the measure of what was repaid. But the image stands as the tradition's sharpest statement of what Bres' kingship cost: the strong man of the gods, bent double under a usurper's faggots, with the tide at his knees. Cath Maige Tuired: The Flagstone Test When Lugh came to Tara before the battle, asking admission by his arts, it fell to Ogma to test the stranger's strength — the doorkeeper's office, and the champion's. Ogma hurled the great flagstone of the rath, a stone beyond the lifting of ordinary men, and Lugh answered by hurling it back through the rath to its own place. Ogma then challenged the newcomer to single combat, and Lugh declined: his arts, he said, would be tested soon enough against the Fomorians. The episode is the tradition's own changing of the guard, and it is conducted with a courtesy the Túatha Dé rarely manage elsewhere — a test, a verdict, and no feud. The old champion made way, stone by stone, for the many-skilled king who would lead the war, and the championship of Ireland passed hands without a blow struck in anger. Cath Maige Tuired: Indech Slain, and the Sword That Spoke At the second battle of Mag Tuired the champion earned his title back. In the press of the fighting Ogma killed Indech, son of Dé Domnann, a king of the Fomorians — the same Indech whose blood the Mórrígan had promised the Dagda at the ford. And after the battle came the strangest prize in the Irish corpus: among the spoils Ogma found Orna, the sword of Tethra, king of the Fomorians. He unsheathed it and cleaned it, and the sword recounted all the deeds that had been done with it — for it was the custom of swords in those days, when drawn, to tell what they had done. The champion of the gods carried the only weapon in the world that could bear witness to itself: in Ogma's hand even the enemy's steel testified, because testimony is what this champion is for. Cath Maige Tuired: The Recovery of the Harp After the rout, the Fomorians had carried off the Dagda's harper, Uaithne, and the harp itself hung on the wall of the hall where Bres feasted. Three of the Túatha Dé Danann went in pursuit: Lugh, the Dagda, and Ogma — the king, the all-father, and the champion. The Dagda called the harp by its names, Daur Da Bláo and Coir Cethar Chuir, and it sprang from the wall to his hand, killing nine men in its path, and played the three strains of weeping, laughter, and sleep until the whole enemy host slept. Ogma walked out of that hall beside his brother and his king, through sleeping foes — the serf of the firewood years restored to the company of the gods' great deeds. Auraicept na n-Éces: The Father of the Ogham The Scholars' Primer — the Auraicept na n-Éces, the medieval Irish grammar of the poets — closes Ogma's dossier with the honor no other Irish god receives. Ogma, a man well skilled in speech and in poetry, invented the ogham for the speaking of Gaelic; and the tract fixes the paternity in a formula: the father of the ogham is Ogma, and the mother of the ogham is the hand or the knife of Ogma. Cormac's Glossary, compiled a generation before the Primer, already glosses the god's name from ogum, the ogham itself — in the Irish learned tradition, the alphabet and its father were one word. The glossarial tradition adds the epithet Grianainech, the Sun-faced. The champion who hauled firewood under a usurper is the same figure the learned tradition made the author of the alphabet itself — strength and letters, in Ireland, kept in one hand. Syncretism: Ogma has the strongest cross-border witness of any Irish god, and it is a classical author's eyewitness account. Lucian of Samosata, writing in the second century CE, describes a picture the Gauls showed him of their Herakles: not the young Greek athlete but a very old man, bald and wrinkled and sun-dark, drawing after him a great crowd of men — each one fastened by the ears to the god's tongue with slender chains of gold and amber, and following willingly, none struggling. The Gauls, Lucian's guide explains, do not give eloquence to Hermes as the Greeks do; they give it to Herakles, because he is the more powerful, and because the hero achieves everything by persuasion — his arrows are words. In the Gaulish tongue, the guide adds, Herakles is called Ogmios . The equation Ogmios = Ogma is the standard comparison of the handbooks — Vendryes' LEIA derives the Irish name from Proto-Celtic *Ogmios, and Mac Cana and Koch print the Lucian passage as the god's continental portrait. It remains comparison rather than identification: the Irish texts never call Ogma old or bald, and the ogham invention is Ireland's own learned myth. The Welsh corpus, meanwhile, is silent — the Mabinogi knows no counterpart, and no scholar has convincingly supplied one. Cultural legacy: Ogma's afterlife runs on the two rails his name already laid down: strength and letters. Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried Cath Maige Tuired into English and made the champion of the firewood years part of the revival's reading; the later romantic cycle, in Oidheadh Chloinne Tuireann, made him the father of Tuireann and so grandfather of the three sons whose blood-price Lugh exacted. His larger legacy is the script itself. The four hundred ogham stones of Ireland and Wales became the national patrimony of early Ireland, and with them Ogma's paternity: the medieval claim that the champion fathered the alphabet is quoted wherever the stones are studied. In the twentieth century Robert Graves's The White Goddess (1948) built a whole modern mythology on the ogham letters — a construction of Graves's own, not a medieval doctrine — and carried the script, and with it Ogma's fame, into modern esoteric and Druid practice, where he is honored as the god of eloquence, writing, and the poet's craft. The scholars, meanwhile, kept the older wonder alive: Lucian's chained crowd remains the most-quoted image of Celtic eloquence in the literature. Extended meditation: Ogma is the Celtic answer to a question every culture asks: what is strength for? The Irish texts could have left him a strong man — the champion who carries the wood, hurls the stone, and kills the Fomorian king's son, and nothing more. Instead the learned tradition took the same hand that dragged the firewood and made it the mother of the alphabet, and the Gauls, three centuries before the Irish manuscripts, had already painted the answer: the strongest god is the one whose victories need no chains, because men follow his tongue willingly. Even Ogma's weapon obeys the rule — Orna, the sword of the enemy king, becomes precious not for what it cut but for what it tells. The champion's whole dossier argues one proposition: the word is the deed that survives the doing. The stones of Ireland still stand along their stemlines, notched with the letters Ireland assigned to Ogma's paternity — the strongest kind of monument, because it is made of speech. Original script note: The normalized Old Irish form is Ogma — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script of the great codices; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham — the very script the medieval tradition credits Ogma with inventing — survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: ogma.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The Lord Who Spans the Four Branches
text: The Lord Who Spans the Four Branches: Son of Pwyll, King Pryderi is the hinge of the whole Mabinogi: the only figure who walks through all Four Branches — stolen on the night of his birth and found outside a stable door, named from his mother's lifted anxiety, emptied out of Dyfed by an enchanter's mist, and killed at last in single combat by Gwydion's craft. Son of Pwyll and Rhiannon, lord of Dyfed, he is the king the tales keep taking things from — and the name he carries is the Welsh word for care. The Stable Door: Outside Teyrnon's stable, where a great clawed hand had come for the newborn foal, lay an infant wrapped in silk brocade — the stolen heir of Dyfed. The Naming: Rhiannon looks at the boy and says her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her; from that word the child is named Pryderi. The Golden Bowl: Hanging by chains above a marble fountain in a fortress that was never there before: when Pryderi grasps it, his hands stick, his feet root to the slab, and his voice dies. The First Swine: The hobeu, first pigs ever brought to Wales — Arawn of Annwn's gift to the house of Pwyll — which Gwydion wins with illusory gold and pays for with Pryderi's life. Symbols: The silk brocade wrapping — Royal blood declaring itself at a stable door — the foundling child whose swaddling says what no witness can; The clawed hand — The Otherworld reaching through the window on May-eve — the unseen power that takes foals and princes alike; The golden bowl on its chains — Bait that looks like treasure — the trap at the heart of the enchanted fortress, and the cost of touching what is not yours; The gate-hammer about his neck — What he wore out of the enchantment — the humiliation of the Third Branch, borne home and buried in silence; The swine of Annwn — Otherworld wealth with a geis upon it — not to be sold or given until the herd had doubled — and the war a broken promise bought; The grave at Maen Tywynog — The mound above Y Felenrhyd where the slain lord was buried — the one fixed point of a life lived under enchantment Pryderi's mythology is unique in Welsh prose: he is the only character who appears in all Four Branches of the Mabinogi, and his life is the thread the whole cycle is strung on. The First Branch gives his birth, theft, and naming; the Second carries him through the Irish war as one of the seven survivors; the Third empties his kingdom and takes him captive; the Fourth kills him. Every word of it is medieval Welsh prose, preserved in two great manuscripts. First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed: The May-Eve Vanishing Pryderi is born to Pwyll and Rhiannon after the nobles of Dyfed have pressed for an heir, and on the night of his birth the six women set to watch all fall asleep — and the child is gone. Terrified of the blame, the women kill the pups of a hound, smear the blood on Rhiannon's face, lay the bones beside her, and swear she has destroyed her own son; her penance at the horse-block begins, and it will last until the boy comes home. The child, meanwhile, has fallen into the strangest rescue in Welsh prose. Teyrnon Twrf Liant, a lord of Gwent Is Coed by the sea, loses a foal every May-eve; keeping watch over his mare, he sees a great clawed hand reach through the window to seize the newborn foal, and strikes it off with his sword. Outside the door he finds a baby boy wrapped in silk brocade. He and his wife rear the child as their own and call him Gwri Wallt Euryn — Gwri of the Golden Hair. First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed: The Naming at Arberth Gwri grows with uncanny speed — at the end of his first year sturdier than a child of three, at two like a boy of six — and year by year he bears the very likeness of Pwyll. When Teyrnon hears of Rhiannon's penance, he knows what he must do, and he and his wife bring the boy to Arberth. The court sees the likeness at once, and Rhiannon says that if this is true, her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her. Pwyll declares that the boy should take his name from the word his mother spoke when the news was brought to her, and so the child is named Pryderi. The penance ends; Teyrnon will take no reward beyond the boy's friendship; and Pryderi is fostered with Pendaran Dyfed until he is of age, when Pwyll gives him the realm. Second Branch · Branwen ferch Llŷr: One of the Seven When Bendigeidfran — Brân the Blessed — leads the host of Britain into Ireland to answer the wrong done to Branwen, the war ends in near-total ruin: the Irish are destroyed, and of the host of the Island of the Mighty only seven men come back alive, bearing Brân's wounded head. The tale names them, and the first two it names are Pryderi and Manawydan, with Glifieu, Taliesin, Ynawg, Gruddieu, and Heilyn. With the others Pryderi feasts seven years at Harlech, where the Birds of Rhiannon sing, and eighty years at Gwales in Penfro in the Assembly of the Wondrous Head — a man who has sailed out of his own branch into the middle of someone else's tragedy, and who carries its grief home into the Third. Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr: The Enchantment of Dyfed After Pwyll's death, Pryderi rules Dyfed and gives his mother Rhiannon in marriage to Manawydan fab Llŷr; with his wife Cigfa, the four come home to Arberth. There comes a peal of thunder and a fall of mist, and when it lifts, Dyfed is emptied — not a soul, not a dwelling, not a beast remains. After years of hand-craft that English market towns punished for making work too good to allow, a shining white boar leads Pryderi and Manawydan to a fortress that was never there before. Against Manawydan's counsel Pryderi goes in, lays hold of a golden bowl hanging by chains above a marble fountain — and his hands stick to the bowl, his feet to the slab, and speech leaves him. Rhiannon goes in after him, takes hold of the same bowl, and is caught beside him; fort, bowl, and both prisoners vanish. Manawydan undoes the spell by patience: he catches the one slow mouse stripping his third ripe field of wheat, condemns it to hang as a thief, and names his price to the bishop sent to beg it off — Pryderi and Rhiannon released, the enchantment lifted, no vengeance taken. The mouse is the wife of Llwyd fab Cilcoed, who had laid the spell to avenge his friend Gwawl, the suitor Rhiannon refused. Pryderi comes home with a gate-hammer about his neck, Rhiannon with the collars of asses about hers; the land wakes, and the Third Branch ends with the four feasting as they began. The myth is the cycle's thesis in parable: what enchantment took, only patience could restore. Fourth Branch · Math fab Mathonwy: The Swine and the Fatal Combat Among Pryderi's treasures are the hobeu, the first swine ever brought to Wales — a gift to his house from Arawn of Annwn, which Pryderi had sworn neither to sell nor to give until the herd had bred twice its number. Gwydion fab Dôn comes to his court in the guise of a poet, is refused the pigs, and conjures twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars and leashes, and twelve golden shields — apparitions good for a day and gone by morning — and trades them for the herd. When the glamour fades, Pryderi musters Dyfed and comes north, and the war that follows forces the crime Gwydion and Gilfaethwy commit against Goewin. At the peace-talks Pryderi demands single combat, for it was because of him the hosts had come; at Y Felenrhyd, the tale says, Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour, and by magic and enchantment'. They buried Pryderi there, at Maen Tywynog above Y Felenrhyd — and his grave, the Fourth Branch says, is there. Syncretism: Pryderi's great comparative frame is the Celtic divine son. The handbooks set him beside Mabon ap Modron — 'Son son of Mother' — the youth of Culhwch ac Olwen who was taken from his mother Modron when he was three nights old and found again after a search that outlasts every living memory, and behind Mabon the Gaulish Maponos, the 'Divine Son' whom Romano-Celtic dedications pair with Apollo. A child of an Otherworld mother, stolen at birth and restored, whose name carries his story: the figure-type is one, and Mac Cana and Koch both register the comparison — but the names are not cognate, and no scholar claims identity. The second frame is sovereignty-by-loss: like the stricken kings of Irish tradition, Pryderi holds a kingdom that enchantment can empty in a night, and his rescue comes not by his own strength but by Manawydan's patience — the Third Branch's quiet thesis about where a king's real safety lies. Within the corpus his closest kin are his parents [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] and Pwyll Pen Annwn, his stepfather and rescuer [[manawydan|Manawydan]], his benefactor [[arawn|Arawn]] of [[annwn|Annwn]], and his slayer [[gwydion|Gwydion]] — the enchanter whose conjured wealth bought the pigs and, with them, the war. Cultural legacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Pryderi out of the Welsh manuscripts and into English, and the Victorian Celtic revival made the vanished child of the First Branch one of its set-pieces. Twentieth-century scholarship gave him his modern standing: Ifor Williams's edition fixed the standard Welsh text, W. J. Gruffydd's Rhiannon (1953) built its whole argument about the First and Third Branches around the Pryderi complex, and Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi made the boy who spans all four branches the structural key to the cycle. Evangeline Walton's Mabinogion tetralogy retold his theft and naming for modern readers, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain — five novels built openly on the Mabinogi's world — carried the matter of Pryderi's branches to a vast young readership, though the boy himself never appears under his own name. In modern Druid and pagan practice he is honoured as the lost-and-found divine son and the lord who endured the emptied land, and the name survives in scholarship as the standing example of the Mabinogi's own method: a person named, deliberately and explicitly, out of a single spoken word of grief relieved. Extended meditation: Pryderi is named out of relief. His mother has carried a false charge for years — sitting by the horse-block, offering her back to strangers — and when the lost boy is set before her she does not say vengeance, or justice, or even joy: she says her care is lifted, and the court builds the child's name out of that word. Anxiety, made into a name and then, astonishingly, into a king. The rest of his story keeps faith with the naming. His is the kingdom a mist can empty between one hour and the next; his is the hand that sticks to the golden bowl; his is the herd of otherworld pigs that a poet's illusion can buy; his is the grave above Y Felenrhyd. Nothing in the Four Branches is safe, and Pryderi is the figure through whom the Mabinogi says so — the lord who loses everything except the thread of the tale, and who walks through all four branches carrying it. Care, the Welsh word means; and also what care is for: the watch kept, the debt counted, the mother who waited at the gate. Original script note: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Pryderi — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: pryderi.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/pryderi/ in the meantime.

title: Squirrel of Yggdrasil
text: Squirrel of Yggdrasil: The Drill-Tooth, the Malicious Messages, and the Trunk of the World-Ash Ratatoskr is the squirrel of the world-ash Yggdrasill: the small tireless runner of Grímnismál who bears the eagle's words down from the crown and carries Níðhǫggr's answers back up from the roots — and whom Snorri names as the courier of öfundarorð, malicious messages, between the two great enemies of the tree. Yggdrasill's Ash: The world-tree itself, 'the greatest and best of all trees': Ratatoskr's whole road, from the eagle's crown to the roots over Hvergelmir. The Unnamed Eagle: The great eagle perched in the ash's limbs, wise in many things — with the hawk Veðrfölnir sitting between its eyes. Níðhǫggr: The Malice-Striker: the serpent at the root in Niflheimr who gnaws the ash and sucks the corpses of the dead — the eagle's eternal correspondent. Veðrfölnir: The hawk between the eagle's eyes — the watcher in the crown, witness to every word the squirrel carries down. Symbols: The world-ash — The vertical axis of the cosmos — and the only road Ratatoskr ever runs, crown to root and back; The malicious message (öfundarorð) — Snorri's word for the squirrel's cargo: slander carried between powers too proud to speak to each other; The drill-tooth — The name itself — rati, the boring auger, and toskr, the tusk: a tooth that drills, a tongue that bores; The hawk between the eyes — Veðrfölnir, set in the eagle's brow — the unblinking audit above the squirrel's errands Ratatoskr's dossier is two passages long and perfectly cut: one stanza of Grímnismál and one chapter of Gylfaginning. Between them they give him a road, a cargo, and a character — and nothing else in the corpus adds a word. Grímnismál 32: The Squirrel's Stanza In Grímnismál, Óðinn — masked and bound between the fires of King Geirrøðr — recites the inhabitants of the world-ash, and the squirrel gets his stanza: Ratatoskr is the íkorni who must run on Yggdrasill's ash; the eagle's words he must carry from above and tell to Níðhǫggr below. The verb is skal — 'shall, must': the running is not a habit but an office, written into the tree's economy as fixedly as the dew that falls from its branches. In a single stanza the Edda gives the smallest creature in the cosmos a route that spans it, from the eagle's wisdom in the crown to the dragon's malice at the root. Nothing else is said of him in the poem — no origin, no exploit, no epithet — because the route is the whole figure: Ratatoskr is the road between the highest thing and the lowest, wearing the shape of the animal that knows every branch. Grímnismál 33-35: The Suffering Ash The stanzas around the squirrel build the tree's full menagerie: four harts — Dáinn and Dvalinn, Duneyrr and Duraþrór — bite the new shoots; more serpents lie beneath the ash than any unwise ape would think, Góinn and Móinn, Grábakr and Grafvölluðr, Ófnir and Sváfnir, and they gnaw the roots forever; and the poem closes the survey with its most famous sentence: the ash of Yggdrasill suffers agony, more than men know — the hart bites from above, the trunk rots at the side, and Níðhǫggr gnaws from below. The squirrel does not appear in this list of devourers, which is precisely the point: Ratatoskr runs his messages through a tree that is being eaten alive at every level, adding no tooth of his own. The Edda divides the cosmos's parasites by appetite — those who bite and the one who carries — and gives the carrier a name and an office. Gylfaginning 16: Malice Up and Down the Trunk Snorri's prose fills out the stanza into a portrait. An eagle sits in the limbs of the ash, and it has knowledge of many things, and between its eyes sits a hawk called Veðrfölnir. A squirrel called Ratatoskr springs up and down the ash and bears öfundarorð — words of malice, slander-tidings — between the eagle and Níðhǫggr. Where Grímnismál described a messenger, Snorri describes an agent provocateur: the squirrel does not merely deliver the correspondence of the crown and the root, he keeps the feud alive, carrying each insult to the ear best placed to feel it. The four harts and the wells of Urðr and Mímir complete the chapter — but the squirrel is its only animal with an errand, and its only named speaker of any creature in the crown. Snorri's single word, öfundarorð, is the oldest surviving description of what a rumor-monger actually does. Gylfaginning 15 · Völuspá 66: The Dragon at the Root The lower terminus of Ratatoskr's road is the worst address in the cosmos. Snorri sets the third root of the ash over Niflheimr and the spring Hvergelmir, and there Níðhǫggr gnaws the root from below while countless serpents coil with him. Völuspá gives the Malice-Striker his other aspect: in Nástrǫnd, the corpse-shore, he sucks the bodies of the dead, and the wolf tears men — and at the poem's end the dark dragon comes flying up from Niðafjǫll, bearing corpses on his wings, in the last light before the world sinks. Every word Ratatoskr carries down lands in that ear; every word he carries up rises from it. The squirrel's whole mythology is the maintenance of that terrible conversation — the axis of the world kept humming, crown to root, with the one subject on which eagle and dragon never disagree: how much they hate each other. Syncretism: Ratatoskr belongs to a pattern far older and wider than Iceland: the tree that holds the worlds, the eagle in its crown, the serpent at its root. The famous ancient parallel is the Mesopotamian Etana myth, where the eagle and the serpent dwell in the same great tree and their broken pact drives the story — a resemblance scholars have noted for over a century without being able to trace a line of borrowing; Lindow and Simek treat the configuration as a widely distributed world-tree motif rather than a loan. Within the North, the squirrel has no counterpart at all: he is the Edda's own invention, the one member of the tree's menagerie defined by speech rather than appetite. His nearest functional kin are Óðinn's ravens, who likewise range the world and return with words — but the ravens gather news, and Ratatoskr manufactures a feud. Comparativists have also pointed to the squirrel as the classic trickster go-between: small, deniable, and indispensable to enemies who must not be seen to speak. Cultural legacy: Ratatoskr's afterlife grew with the tree he runs. Padraic Colum's The Children of Odin (1920) carried the squirrel into English-language retellings for children, and every popular handbook since has kept him running. Modern readings have made him the patron of the poisonous go-between — the forwarder of insults, the courier of feuds — a role that has only sharpened in the age of the message-board and the screenshot. He has become a minor star of games and pop culture: a playable god in Smite (2015), and the scene-stealing squirrel of God of War Ragnarök (2022), where the ancient slander-courier is played, faithfully to Snorri, as the most insulting creature in the Nine Realms. In Iceland the name lives on as Ratatoskur, and modern Heathen and Ásatrú retellings keep him as the comic-dark emblem of how small tongues keep great hatreds fed. Extended meditation: Ratatoskr is the Edda's smallest cosmological fact and one of its sharpest. The universe is held in a tree; the tree is being eaten from crown to root; and through the middle of the disaster runs a squirrel, up and down, carrying the worst things the top and the bottom can think of to say to each other. Snorri's word for the cargo is exact: öfundarorð — not news, not warnings, but malice. The myth knows something the etiquette books miss, that feuds do not survive on hatred alone but on delivery — that between every great enmity runs some small, quick, indispensable creature who keeps the words fresh. Ratatoskr never appears in a saga, never wins a fight, never speaks a line the sources record. He only carries. And the Edda gives him eternity for it: while the ash stands, the squirrel runs, and the eagle and the dragon never lack for ammunition. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Ratatoskr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚱᛅᛏᛅᛏᚢᛋᚴᛦ (r-a-t-a-t-u-s-k-R, the ᚢ rune writing o and ᛦ the final nominative -r), though no runic attestation survives and the manuscript spelling remains the primary witness. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: ratatoskr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Dwarf Smith, Fafnir's Brother
text: Dwarf Smith, Fafnir's Brother: The Smith Who Forged a Dragon-Slayer Reginn, son of Hreiðmarr and brother of Fáfnir and Ótr, is the master smith of the Völsung cycle — 'a dwarf in stature', the eddic prose says, 'wise, grim, and skilled in magic'.
