He formed the hills and rivers, planted the trees, and made the animals. Then he made the first people and gave them their languages, their countries, and the laws by which they should live — the earliest ethnographers of the Euahlayi, above all K. Langloh Parker in The Euahlayi Tribe (1905), record the Baayami of creation as the maker whose work is the country itself. Every mountain, waterhole, and plain became a reminder of his creative act, and every clan received the responsibility to care for the part of country made for it (Parker 1905; Berndt and Berndt 1964). Creation here is not a finished product handed over but a continuing arrangement: the world is a country made by an ancestor and entrusted to his descendants, and the deed of trust is the story itself. Sky: The Retreat to the Sky When the work of creation was finished, Baiame rose into the sky and made his camp there. From that distant place he watches over the world he made — remote, but not absent, his presence announced by the dark lanes of the Milky Way, which are said to be his camp or the tracks of the emu he placed there, and by the stars themselves, the campfires of the ancestors who went before. The early recorders of the southeast (Parker; Elkin 1938) heard the same withdrawal in many nations: the Sky Father who made the world does not govern it day by day, because the law he gave does that work for him. The withdrawal is the gift: a maker who stayed would be a ruler, but a maker who leaves behind law becomes an ancestor. Distance is how the Sky Father turns creation into inheritance. Law: The Son Daramulum Baiame's son Daramulum moves between earth and sky as a messenger and teacher. Often associated with the rainbow and with thunder, Daramulum taught the people the secrets of initiation and the songs that must be sung at each stage of life; it is his voice that the bullroarer carries at the bora ground, and his figure that the initiated recognize in the images kept from the uninitiated. Through him, Baiame's law is passed on without the Sky Father needing to descend himself (Parker 1905; Elkin 1938). The arrangement is precise: the father's law, the son's voice. A law that can only be delivered by the lawgiver in person would die with him; a law carried by a messenger becomes a tradition. Sky: The Emu in the Sky The dark shape of the emu stretches across the Milky Way — the great bird read not from stars but from the dust lanes between them, its head in the Coalsack, its body along the galactic plane. It is both a constellation and a story: the emu in the sky tells the people when to collect emu eggs, when to hold ceremonies, and how to read the seasons, and Aboriginal astronomers and their collaborators have shown the reading is practical — the constellation's turning marks the breeding season of the emu on the ground. Baiame placed it there as a calendar and a memory, so that the connection between sky and country would never be lost (cf. Fuller, Harney and Norris on Aboriginal astronomy). The bird above and the bird below are one fact in two places: the sky is not a separate world but the same country seen at night, and the calendar is written in darkness rather than light. Syncretism: Early colonial observers sometimes compared Baiame to the Christian God, and some recorded traditions show signs of post-contact reinterpretation. Modern scholarship, led by Berndt and Berndt and by AIATSIS, treats Baiame as a specifically Aboriginal Sky Father whose identity is tied to country, kinship, and initiation rather than to any universal deity. He is not interchangeable with the biblical creator, and each nation retains its own protocols for how his name and stories may be used. Cultural legacy: Baiame remains a powerful symbol of Aboriginal sovereignty over country and culture. His name appears in place names, in rock art and stencil sites, and in contemporary Aboriginal art and literature. The Emu in the Sky is now widely recognised as one of the best-known Aboriginal astronomical traditions. At the same time, Aboriginal custodians have rightly insisted that Baiame's sacred aspects — especially those connected with men's law and initiation — are not open-source material for casual adaptation. PuniCodex presents only the publicly documented, scholarly record and directs readers to AIATSIS and to the relevant Aboriginal communities for authoritative teachings. Extended meditation: Baiame asks the modern reader to think about creation as responsibility. The world is not a finished product handed to humanity; it is a country made by an ancestor and entrusted to his descendants. To speak the name Baiame is therefore to remember a covenant: the land, the water, the animals, and the sky are kin, and the law that governs them is older than any statute. That is why the restoration matters. The plain ASCII form flattens the name into a string of letters with no memory of the languages that carried it. The Unicode restoration Baiame does not add diacritics, because the original sources were oral, but it does reclaim the capitalized, scholarly citation form by which the figure is named in museums, universities, and Aboriginal-studies curricula. The name is Tier 2 not because it is less important, but because the DNS-friendly ASCII form already encodes the same phonemic sequence. The work of preservation here is cultural and historical, not diacritical. Original script note: Baiame belongs to an oral tradition that had no pre-contact writing system. The name first enters the written record in nineteenth-century ethnographies. PuniCodex therefore restores it as Baiame , the conventional capitalized romanization, rather than as an 'original script' in the strict sense. The ASCII form baiame is a practical DNS compromise; the restored form is the scholarly citation form used in Australian Indigenous studies.

title: Creator Eaglehawk
text: Creator Eaglehawk: Sky Ancestor, Law-Giver, and Moiety Founder Bunjil is the wedge-tailed eaglehawk made ancestor of the Kulin nations of central Victoria. In the Dreaming he shaped the mountains, rivers, plants, animals, and the laws by which people should live. He is one of two moiety ancestors, paired with Waang the crow, and after his work on earth he was lifted into the sky, where he remains as the star Altair. Creator of Country: He shaped the land, water, flora, and fauna of south-eastern Australia, and established the order of the living world. Sky Ancestor: After creation he ascended to the sky and became the star Altair; his two wives became the black swans beside him. Law-Giver: He gave the Kulin peoples their social and ecological laws, including the obligation to care for Country and each other. Moiety Founder: As the eaglehawk ancestor he heads one of the Kulin moieties, balanced by Waang the crow on the other side. Symbols: Wedge-tailed eagle — The living form of Bunjil and the largest bird of prey in Australia; a sign of creative power and watchful authority; Spear — The instrument with which Bunjil commanded the rising sea to stop, and a mark of law-giving authority; Black swan — Bunjil's two wives, who became the stars flanking Altair after his ascent; Rainbow — His son Binbeal, the rainbow spirit, who continues the creative lineage in the sky Bunjil's stories belong to the Dreaming of the Kulin nations — the Woiwurrung, Boonwurrung, Wathaurong, and their neighbors — recorded by A. W. Howitt, Aldo Massola, and the communities themselves. They explain how Country was made, how law was given, and how the creator withdrew into the sky so that he might continue to watch over the world. Creation: Shaping the Land and the Law In the Dreaming, Bunjil travelled across what is now central Victoria and shaped Country into its living form: he raised the mountains, traced the courses of the rivers, named the plants and animals, and taught each where it belonged. Then he did what a mere landscape-maker would not: he gave law. The Kulin peoples remember him establishing the rules of kinship and marriage, the obligations between clans, and the duties each people owes to its Country — seasonal burning, careful taking, respect for the places where spirit beings remain. His two wives, the black swans, and his son Binbeal the rainbow accompanied the work. Crucially, the stories insist that Country and law were made together : the mountains are not scenery but scripture, and the river's bends are not geography but instruction. (Howitt 1904; Massola 1968) The tradition encodes a complete environmental philosophy — creation, tenure, and responsibility in a single narrative. Deluge: The Sea That Would Not Stop Rising In the telling recorded from Boonwurrung elder Carolyn Briggs, the Kulin nations fell into conflict and began to neglect family and Country, and the sea rose in anger and would not stop. The people gathered and asked Bunjil to intervene. He agreed — but on a condition: they must change their ways and return to the law. He walked to the water's edge, raised his spear, and commanded the sea to stop, and the sea stopped. (Briggs, 'Boon Wurrung Story', Yarra Healing 2000) The story is told as a moral charter, but it carries what may be a far older memory: at the end of the last Ice Age, rising seas flooded the Bassian Plain and cut Tasmania from the mainland — an inundation the ancestors of the Kulin peoples witnessed over generations, and which Australia's oral traditions are now famous for preserving with geological accuracy. The myth's force lies in its bargain: the sea keeps its bounds only while the people keep their obligations — a covenant, not a one-time miracle. Ascent: Lifted into the Sky When his work was finished, Bunjil called his family together and asked Waang, the crow, to release the winds — which Waang kept tied in skin bags — so that they might all be carried to the sky. Waang opened the whirlwind, and the wind lifted Bunjil and his wives and son upward. Bunjil became the bright star Altair ; his two wives, the black swans, became the stars on either side; and some tellings say he departed from the island of Deen Maar, off the coast of what is now south-western Victoria, which remains a sacred place of the Gunditjmara and Eastern Maar peoples. (Howitt 1904; Mudrooroo 1994; NIAA, Deen Maar Indigenous Protected Area) The departure is not an abandonment: the eaglehawk still circles above Country, and the star still marks the season. The creator withdrew so that the creation could belong to the people — and he stayed close enough to watch what they do with it. Sacred site: Bunjil's Shelter In Gariwerd — the country now known as the Grampians — Bunjil took shelter in a cave in the Black Range, and there, in red ochre, his image was painted: the creator figure flanked by two dingoes, gazing out over the valley. The site known as Bunjil's Shelter is one of the most important Aboriginal rock-art places in Victoria, protected under the Aboriginal Heritage Act 2006 and visited only under the protocols its Traditional Owners set. It is not treated as a relic of a finished religion. For the Jardwadjali and Djab Wurrung peoples, and for the wider Kulin community, the shelter is a place where the ancestor's presence is understood to remain — a working site of memory, education, and obligation, cared for rather than merely conserved. (Parks Victoria 2009) The painting turns myth into address : whoever stands before it is standing where the creator once stood, being looked at by the one who is supposed to be watched for. Syncretism: Bunjil is not a solitary deity but one half of a Kulin social and cosmological pair. The eaglehawk moiety, headed by Bunjil, is balanced by the crow moiety, headed by Waang — a pairing that structures kinship, marriage, and ritual obligation across the Kulin nations, so that every person belongs to one ancestor's side and marries into the other. Different clans preserve different episodes: the Woiwurrung stress the sky ascent and Altair, the Boonwurrung remember the rising sea, and the peoples of Gariweld keep the place-based accounts tied to Bunjil's Shelter. In the colonial period the name was recorded under many spellings — Winjeel, Wingeel, Pundjel, Bunjel — reflecting dialect variation and the difficulty of rendering Kulin phonology in English orthography; several survive in Victorian place names. Cultural legacy: Bunjil remains a powerful and public symbol of Aboriginal Victoria. Bunjil's Shelter in the Black Range Scenic Reserve is a protected cultural site and a focus of education and careful tourism. Melbourne's skyline carries his name and form: Bruce Armstrong's monumental eagle sculpture Bunjil (2002) rises from Wurundjeri Way in the Docklands, and Bunjil Place in Narre Warren carries the name into the suburbs. For the Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung, Boonwurrung, and other Kulin communities, Bunjil is not only an ancestral figure but a living authority in Welcome to Country ceremonies, land-care work, language revival, and the ongoing negotiation of recognition and reconciliation — the creator whose law still describes how Country should be held. Extended meditation: Bunjil teaches that creation is not a single event but a continuing responsibility. He did not make the land and depart; he shaped it, gave it law, and then withdrew into the sky so that he could go on watching. The eaglehawk's eye is still understood to be turned toward Country. For non-Indigenous visitors, Bunjil is an invitation to understand 'Country' not as real estate but as a living inheritance — a place that includes people, animals, plants, water, sky, and story, all held together by obligations that precede the colony by tens of thousands of years. The name Bunjil, even in its simple Latin transcription, carries that whole relationship. To restore the capital is a small act; to remember what it names is the larger one — and the first of the obligations it describes. Original script note: The Kulin languages were traditionally oral, and Bunjil has no original alphabetic script. The name survives in Latin transcription made by early settlers and anthropologists. PuniCodex therefore treats Bunjil as the scholarly citation form and bunjil as the DNS compromise. The restoration adds only the capital initial; the absence of diacritics or special letters places the name in Tier 2, not because the figure is less significant, but because the ASCII form already carries the conventional spelling.

title: Sky Hero of the Bora
text: Sky Hero of the Bora: Initiation, Law, and the Emu in the Sky Daramulum is the one-legged son of Baiame, sky father and creator of the Aboriginal nations of south-eastern Australia. He presides over the bora , the initiation ground where boys become men and the Law is handed down, and he lives on in the sky — his emu-shaped body traced in the dark dust-lanes of the Milky Way as a seasonal clock for ceremony and hunt. Sky Hero: Son of Baiame and a power of the upper world; his camp is said to lie in the sky, especially among the stars of the Milky Way. Keeper of the Bora: Guardian of the bora ring and the initiation ceremonies through which Law, identity, and adult responsibility are transmitted. Emu in the Sky: His one-legged form is identified with the dark emu traced in the Milky Way, a seasonal clock and sacred map. Son of Baiame: The principal male descendant of the creator-sky father, acting as his agent in teaching, judging, and protecting the Law. Symbols: Boomerang — Emblem of initiation and the lawful exchange between earth and sky; also a weapon associated with Daramulum's authority over the bora ground.; Emu — His one-legged or emu-footed form; the dark emu in the Milky Way is read as his celestial body or his watching sign.; Bora ring — The sacred earthwork where initiation is performed and where Daramulum's presence is invoked through the bullroarer's roar.; Bullroarer — The whirled board whose drone is heard as Daramulum's voice — the sound of the Law approaching the novices.; Centre of the Milky Way — The camp or turning-place of Daramulum and Baiame in the sky; a focus of southeastern Aboriginal astronomy. Daramulum's mythology is preserved in the ceremonial life and oral traditions of the Dharug, Eora, Euahlayi, and neighbouring nations of New South Wales. He is not a remote deity but an active guardian of social order: he descends for initiations, his voice sounds in the bullroarer, and he lives in the sky as a permanent sign of the Law. Origin: The One-Legged Son of Baiame In the traditions recorded around Sydney and the Blue Mountains, Daramulum is the son of Baiame — maker, sky father, the great being who shaped country, animals, and Law before withdrawing to his camp in the heavens. He serves as his father's principal agent on earth: he descends to the bora ground when boys are made men, he watches that initiates keep the secrets, and he punishes those who mock the ceremonies. K. Langloh Parker, writing from Euahlayi country in The Euahlayi Tribe (1905), describes him as a being of fearsome power, while A. W. Howitt's surveys of south-eastern Australia ( The Native Tribes of South-East Australia , 1904) record the same sky-hero under variant spellings in the rites of many nations. His most striking feature is his body: several accounts make him one-legged, or emu-footed — a form that marks him as other-than-human and ties him to the great bird of the plains. The tradition does not explain the missing limb so much as let it speak: the enforcer of the Law moves like the emu, guardian bird and sky-sign at once. Ceremony: The Bora and the Voice of the Bullroarer The bora — from the Kamilaroi word for the initiation ground — is the hinge of a boy's life in south-eastern Australia, and Daramulum is its patron and its terror. When the season comes, the novices are taken from the camp to a cleared ring of earth, often ringed with stones and marked by carved trees; the women and the uninitiated remain behind a screen of branches and are told that the great spirit himself has come down. From the bush beyond the ground comes a deep roaring: men are swinging bullroarers — flat boards whirled on a cord — and the sound is Daramulum's voice, or Baiame's voice speaking through his son. Parker records that the novices were warned he would kill them if they revealed the secrets, and A. P. Elkin's Aboriginal Men of High Degree shows how the same sound-structure guarded the deepest teachings of the doctors. The bullroarer's roar does the theological work of a sermon: it tells the boys that the Law is older, larger, and more dangerous than any man, and that they are now answerable to it. Astronomy: The Emu in the Sky Aboriginal astronomy of the south-east reads the dark dust-lanes of the Milky Way, not its stars, as its principal constellations, and chief among them is the Emu. The head is the Coalsack beside the Southern Cross; the long neck and body run through Centaurus and Scorpius; the legs reach toward Sagittarius. Robert Fuller and colleagues have documented, in the Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage (2014), how the sky-emu serves as a seasonal clock: when she stands tall in the evening sky it is time to gather her eggs on earth, and when she sits — legs folded, low on the winter horizon — ceremony and story-time begin. In several south-eastern traditions the celestial emu is read as Daramulum's body or his sign, and his recorded one-legged, emu-footed form strengthens the identification — though the ethnographic sources preserve this link only partially, and the honest reader must hold it lightly. What is certain is that both figures do the same work: the emu in the sky is a map on which hunting, law, and season are written together, and Daramulum is that map's keeper. Cosmology: The Sky Camp When his work below is done, Daramulum withdraws to the sky, where Baiame keeps camp in the Milky Way — the river, road, and camping-ground of the ancestral powers. Initiates at the bora were taught that the dead journey toward this sky-country, and that the spirits of great doctors might rise to join the company there; Howitt recorded the belief across a dozen south-eastern tribes, and the rock engravings of Baiame Cave near Singleton, New South Wales, fix the same sky-father imagery in stone. Daramulum's place in that camp is the place of the enforcer: he is the one who comes down when the Law is transgressed and goes back up when order is restored. The cosmology gives a small human community a vast civil service — the sky is not heaven in the Christian sense but government: camps, paths, sentries, and a son of the highest authority permanently on call. The Milky Way turns overhead like a patrol route, and Daramulum is its most diligent officer. Syncretism: Daramulum entered the written record through colonial ethnography, and his reception is entangled with it: nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century recorders like Parker, Howitt, and Mathews set his traditions down in English even as the bora ceremonies they described were being suppressed, and missionaries read Baiame through the lens of the Christian sky-father — a comparison the recorders themselves sometimes encouraged. The twentieth century brought correction: A. P. Elkin and Ronald and Catherine Berndt treated the bora and its beings as a complete theology of initiation rather than a pagan shadow of Genesis. Since the 1970s, Aboriginal astronomy has returned the Emu in the Sky to active cultural use, with community elders teaching the dark constellations in schools, planetariums, and Welcome to Country ceremonies. The Christian frame passed over him; the living tradition keeps the older one — Law, season, and sky read as a single text. Cultural legacy: Daramulum's legacy survives in three registers. Ceremonially, the bora tradition that was his theatre continued in modified form into the twentieth century and is now being revived on country, with bora rings — the stone and earth circles that once centred initiation — protected as heritage sites across New South Wales and Queensland. Astronomically, the Emu in the Sky has become one of the most widely taught Indigenous knowledge systems in Australia, carried by Euahlayi knowledge-keepers such as Ghillar Michael Anderson and by the astronomy programs of national observatories and science agencies. Philologically, his name lives in the scholarly literature of Aboriginal religion as the south-east's clearest case of a personified enforcer of sacred law. He belongs to no church and has no festival date; his calendar is the emu in the dust-lanes, still rising on time, still telling when to teach. Extended meditation: Daramulum is the Law made audible. Where Baiame creates, his son enforces: the bora is terrifying on purpose, because a covenant that costs nothing is not yet a covenant. The bullroarer's roar is the sound of a society agreeing to be afraid of the right thing — to hand its boys over, for one long season, to something older and larger than any family. To study him is to be shown, uncomfortably, how much of any moral order runs on voice: on the rumour of a watcher in the dark. He is one-legged, and the tradition leaves the reason unspoken, which is itself a lesson — sacred things do not owe us symmetry. And in the sky he is a dark shape read against the stars, visible only by the light he blocks: the Law as negative space, present exactly where brightness fails. A temple to Daramulum is therefore an honest oddity. His house is a ring of earth, his hymn is a whirled plank of wood, and his image is the absence of stars.

title: Mother Snake of the First Time
text: Mother Snake of the First Time: Creation, Water, Fertility, and the Law of Country Eingana is the great Mother Snake of the Aboriginal Australian cosmology recorded in the western Arnhem Land region. She is not merely a serpent but the living body from which the land, water, plants, animals, and human beings emerged. In the Creation Time — the epoch Aboriginal English calls the Dreaming — she moved beneath the surface of the world, raised hills and watercourses, and gave birth to all life. Where she rests, water collects; where she travels, the country remembers her shape in rivers, rocks, and springs. World Birth: She is the primordial mother: from her body come the first people, animals, and the very contours of the land. Water and Wet Season: Her presence fills billabongs and brings the rains; she governs the renewal that follows the dry. Sacred Law: The stories, songs, and designs that belong to her country encode moral and ecological law for those who hold them. Fertility and Kinship: She is mother of peoples and species alike; her mythology binds human lineage to the land that gave it form. Symbols: Rainbow serpent / water snake — Her body is the river, the rainbow, and the serpent-shape seen in rock art and sacred design.; Waterhole and billabong — Places where she rests are sources of life, healing, and danger; they demand respect and correct behaviour.; Stone spear points and ochre — Sacred objects linked to her ceremonies and to the authority of those who keep her law.; The wet-season storm — Her power is felt in the thunder and rain that transform the Arnhem Land landscape each year. Eingana's mythology belongs to the oral traditions of the stone country and adjacent regions of western Arnhem Land. It is not a single fixed narrative but a corpus of songs, dances, and designs held by senior custodians. The common threads are her primordial motherhood, her shaping of the country, and the enduring obligation of human beings to care for the land she made. Creation: The Mother Who Made the World The fullest published accounts of Eingana come from twentieth-century ethnographers working in western Arnhem Land — Mountford's Arnhem Land expedition records, the Berndts' studies, Elkin's syntheses — and from custodians of the stone country who have spoken for their country in more recent decades. The shared core is immense and simple: in the Creation Time, Eingana lay beneath the surface of the world, huge and pregnant with all life. She moved through the darkness, and where she pushed upward the land rose into ranges and escarpments; where she rested, water pooled into billabongs and rivers. She gave birth to the animals, the plants, and the first people, each carrying a portion of her law, and then — in most tellings — withdrew into the deep waterholes to sleep. The country is therefore her descendant and her body: every rock and spring a memory of her movement, every songline a tracing of her track. Details belong to particular custodians and are properly withheld from publication; what can be said publicly is the architecture — a creation that is not an event of the past but the permanent structure of the present land. Birth and Danger: The Snake Who Swallows and Regenerates Eingana's power is life-giving but not safe, and the tradition is honest about both halves. Stories recorded in the Arnhem Land literature tell of her swallowing the dead, or those who transgress her law, and of her power to restore or transform what she has taken. This double nature — mother and devourer — is characteristic of the Rainbow Serpent family across Australia, from the Murngin's Yurlunggur to the Noongar's Wagyl: the same being who creates the world punishes those who forget their obligations to it. The danger is not malice; it is law. A waterhole where she rests must not be fouled; a site of her story must not be spoken of by the wrong people; resources must be taken with the proper observances and in season. Those who keep the law receive her abundance; those who break it meet her body. Modern commentators sometimes soften the swallowing into symbolism, but the older accounts present it plainly — the mother who made every life remains sovereign over each, and sovereignty includes the taking back. Seasonal Cycle: The Wet and the Dry Eingana is read in the annual transformation of Arnhem Land itself. Through the long dry she sleeps in the deep waterholes, her presence contracting to those few surviving pools where life clusters; when the first storms of the wet break, she stirs — and the thunder is her voice, the flooding rivers her movement, the green explosion of the country her waking body. The monsoon's violence is not a disruption of creation but its renewal: the land dies back each year and is born again when the great snake moves. Ceremonies at the turning of the seasons re-enact this cycle and re-commit the human community to its part — proper burning of the country, care of the waterplaces, observance of the right songs. Stanner named the underlying ontology the Dreaming: a time that is not past but continuous, in which the ancestors' acts remain available to the present. Eingana's breathing — dry sleep, wet waking — is the Dreaming's clearest annual signature, written across a third of the continent each year in fire, smoke, rain, and green. Custodianship: The Law of Country The stories of Eingana are not entertainment and not antiquarian record; they are the charter under which her country is looked after. Specific clans, families, and individuals hold the right to speak for particular sites, songs, and designs — a system anthropologists have described as a marriage of land tenure, intellectual property, and liturgy. To sing her name without authority, to damage her waterholes, to take resources out of season or without observance is to break a living relationship, and the tradition is explicit that the consequences are real: the water fails, the law's keepers sicken, the country itself suffers. Because the most sacred dimensions are restricted to initiated custodians, the public record — books, museums, even this entry — holds only the outer layer of a much deeper corpus; the centre is deliberately not published. The mythology therefore encodes land management, kinship, and ethics in a single narrative field, and its modern force has been proven: Aboriginal land-rights claims across Australia have succeeded precisely by demonstrating this continuous custodianship, with the old songs and sites as evidence that the relationship with country never lapsed. Syncretism: Eingana belongs to the Rainbow Serpent family of beings that stretches across Aboriginal Australia, from the Wagyl of Noongar country in the southwest to Yurlunggur and Barramundi in Arnhem Land. Each figure is distinct, named in its own language, and tied to specific country, but all share the grammar of a creative water-being who shapes the land and punishes transgression. Scholars such as A. P. Elkin and later anthropologists traced this distribution while warning against collapsing local differences into a single pan-Australian 'Rainbow Serpent.' In non-Indigenous reception, Eingana has sometimes been flattened into a generic 'mother goddess,' a reading that obscures the specific kinship, site-based, and ceremonial dimensions of her Jawoyn and Arnhem Land context. Cultural legacy: Eingana is part of the living heritage of the Aboriginal peoples of western Arnhem Land. Her image appears in rock art galleries of the region — among the oldest continuous artistic traditions on Earth — and her stories continue to be performed in ceremony under the authority of traditional custodians. Outside those communities, her name has entered anthropological literature, environmental writing, and popular accounts of Aboriginal spirituality as an emblem of the creative, serpentine powers of the Australian landscape. The challenge for contemporary use is to cite her respectfully: not as a brand or a decorative motif, but as a named figure within a specific system of country, law, and custodianship. Extended meditation: Eingana asks the modern imagination to think about creation not as a single event but as a continuous relationship. The land is not a backdrop for her story; it is her body, still present, still requiring care. In Aboriginal Australian thought, the ancestors did their creative work in the Dreaming and then withdrew into the landscape, but they did not cease to be active. Every waterhole, every seasonal flood, every ceremony is a renewed encounter with the power that made the world. To meditate on Eingana is therefore to meditate on dependence. Human beings are not lords of the land but late-born children of it. The law she left is not a set of abstract rules but a practical ecology: know your country, take only what is needed, perform the ceremonies that keep the relationship in good repair, and pass the knowledge on only to those who are entitled to receive it. This is a much older model of sustainability than the one environmental movements have recently invented, and it is held in song and story rather than in policy documents. The name Eingana, even in its Latin transcription, carries a reminder that creation can be serpentine: not straight, not simple, moving underground and surfacing where it is needed. She is mother and danger, water and law, the deep past and the next wet season. To speak her name is to be drawn into the obligation of country. Original script note: There is no indigenous written script for Eingana. Aboriginal Australian traditions are primarily oral and visual, transmitted through song, dance, rock art, body painting, and sacred objects. The name appears in English-language sources as 'Eingana,' a phonetic transcription of the oral form. PuniCodex therefore labels the form honestly as a scholarly transliteration : the Latin letters are a modern tool for citation, not the original vehicle of the name. The restoration capitalises the initial letter as is conventional for proper names in English scholarly prose.

title: The Sun Woman
text: The Sun Woman: Light, Search, and Maternal Devotion Gnowee is the sun of the Wurundjeri people. In the Kulin telling she was once a woman who went up into the sky carrying a bark torch, searching for the child she had lost in the eternal darkness below. Her daily journey across the heavens is that search still in progress: when her torch burns bright, the world is day; when it dims and gutters, evening comes; when she stops to rekindle it, night falls. She is therefore light-giver, wanderer, and bereaved mother at once. Solar Light: Her torch is the sun itself; she illuminates the land so that life can continue and the search can go on. Maternal Search: The sun's daily movement is interpreted as a mother still looking for her lost son beneath the dark earth. Day and Night: Dawn, noon, dusk, and darkness are read as the changing state of her bark torch rather than as separate powers. Wurundjeri Cosmos: Her story anchors a specifically Woiwurrung understanding of sky, country, and the moral obligations carried by fire. Symbols: Bark torch — The sun itself; a domestic fire carried into the sky and kept alight across the day; Yam stick / digging stick — The tool that drew her away from her camp and set the search in motion; The southern sky path — Her track across the heavens, observed as the sun's daily arc; Darkness below — The earth that once swallowed her child and that she now lights from above The Gnowee story belongs to the Wurundjeri-willam clan of the Woiwurrung language group. It explains the origin of the sun and the reason for its daily movement: the sun is not an indifferent orb but a woman still looking for her child. The myth is ecological as well as cosmological — it binds fire, food gathering, maternal care, and the rotation of day and night into a single narrative. Wurundjeri tradition: The Woman Who Became the Sun In the time before the sun, the world lay under an unbroken darkness. Gnowee, a woman of the Wurundjeri-willam clan country, camped with her small son, and each day went out to dig for yams with her digging stick. One day she wandered farther than she meant to, gathering food in the dark, and when she turned for home she could not find her camp — the country had closed over it like water. She searched until she was exhausted, calling for her boy, and the darkness gave nothing back. In her grief she gathered armfuls of stringybark, twisted the bark into a great torch, set it alight, and climbed with it into the sky, so that its light might fall on every part of the country at once and reveal where her child lay. That torch is the sun. The version best known beyond the community was retold by A. W. Reed from the nineteenth-century records of the Melbourne district; Wurundjeri tellers of today keep the story as their own. Cosmology: Why the Sun Moves Gnowee does not rest in one place, because her search is not finished. Across the day she carries the torch from one side of the sky to the other, and the light slides over the land as she goes: where the torch hangs highest, the light stands straight at noon; where it tilts, evening leans in. When the bark at last burns low and the light goes ragged, she stops — and that stillness is night, the long pause while she gathers fresh stringybark and coaxes a new flame from the old embers. Then the first grey kindling before dawn is her new torch catching, and the search resumes. The story reads the sun's whole daily round as a narrative, not a mechanism: day is the burning of the torch, dusk its guttering, night the gathering, dawn the re-lighting. Sky events that other traditions count and calculate, the Kulin telling explains with a mother's errand — light as labor, repeated without complaint, for as long as the loss lasts. Social teaching: Fire and Responsibility The story is also a teaching about fire and care. In the versions recorded in the Melbourne district, fire is not stolen from a deity or given by culture-heroes: it is carried, gathered, and tended by a woman, and its keeping is bound to women's work and women's knowledge. The digging stick that drew Gnowee away from camp is the same tool that feeds a family; the son left sleeping beneath the tree is the caution at the story's heart — a child unwatched is a child the dark can take. And there is grief, and the tradition does not soften it: the sky's most powerful light is explained as a bereavement still in progress, which dignifies every searching mother in the community. To tell the story is to teach several obligations at once — tend the fire, watch the children, respect the dark, and remember that those who carry light for others may be carrying loss. Recorded retellings: The Story in the Records Versions of the Gnowee narrative reached print through the records made by the nineteenth-century Protectors of Aborigines around Melbourne — men such as William Thomas, whose field notes preserved fragments of Woiwurrung language and story — and through later collectors who worked the same material into popular anthologies, most fully A. W. Reed's Aboriginal Myths, Legends and Fables (1982). That provenance needs to be stated plainly: the printed versions passed through colonial notebooks, and their spellings, details, and even their morals carry the marks of the recorder's hand. The authoritative telling today belongs to the Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung Cultural Heritage Aboriginal Corporation, which presents the story on country as a teaching about sky, fire, and care. The contrast between the two afterlives — a museum-piece in an old anthology, a living lesson on the Yarra — is itself part of the story's meaning. Syncretism: Gnowee is a specifically Wurundjeri figure and is not equated with the sun deities of other Aboriginal nations, each of which owns its own solar narratives. She has sometimes been grouped with 'Mother Sun' figures in comparative anthologies, but such comparisons must respect the local ownership of the story. In contemporary Victoria she appears in educational and reconciliation materials as a Woiwurrung cultural teaching, not as a generic Aboriginal sun goddess. Cultural legacy: The Gnowee story is one of the best-known narratives of the Wurundjeri people. It is told in Victorian schools, on Wurundjeri-led country walks, and in materials produced by the Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung Cultural Heritage Aboriginal Corporation. The figure has also inspired Australian children's literature, public art, and environmental education, where the sun-as-torch remains a potent image of renewable light and searching care. Extended meditation: Gnowee invites meditation on the inseparability of love and loss. The sun rises not because it is a machine but because a mother is still looking. That reading transforms the sky from a clock into a story: every dawn is the relighting of a torch, every noon the height of a search, every dusk the guttering of a flame that will be renewed. There is also a lesson about fire. In the myth, fire is not stolen or given; it is carried. It must be gathered, tended, and passed on. The sun is therefore the largest campfire, and the obligations that govern a small fire on country scale up to the cosmos itself. To remember Gnowee is to remember that light is labor and that care can outlast even the longest night. Original script note: The Woiwurrung language was not written before colonization. The name survives in Latin transcription, most commonly spelled Gnowee . The PuniCodex restoration capitalizes the initial letter as a proper name. No additional diacritics or special letters are used, because the surviving scholarly sources do not record distinctive phonemic length or stress marks for this name.

title: The Lightning Man
text: The Lightning Man: Thunder, Storm, and the Power of the Wet Season Mamaragan is the Lightning Ancestor of western Arnhem Land, a sky being whose body is the storm and whose weapons are the lightning. In the wet season, when thunder rolls across the stone country and the sky splits with light, his presence is felt across the land. He is not merely a weather spirit; he is a living ancestor whose actions renew the country, fill the waterholes, and remind human beings of the power that moves behind the visible world. Lightning: His signature power: the bright flash that strikes from cloud to earth, carrying both danger and renewal. Thunder: The sound of his stone axes striking together, or of his voice rolling across the wet-season sky. Wet-Season Renewal: The storms he brings break the dry season, fill billabongs, and regenerate the plants and animals of the stone country. Sky Ancestor: A being of the upper realms, connected to the stars, clouds, and the winds that announce the monsoon. Symbols: Zigzag lightning — The visible trace of his power; in rock art it may issue from his head, limbs, or body; Stone axe — The weapon or tool that makes thunder when struck; a common motif in Arnhem Land lightning imagery; Dilly bag — The container that holds his lightning stones or axes in some accounts; Rain cloud — The body of the storm in which he travels; the wet-season cloud mass brings both life and danger; The wet-season sky — The whole build-up and monsoon arc — humidity, first storms, knock-'em-down squalls — read as one ancestral passage Mamaragan belongs to the Aboriginal sacred geography of western Arnhem Land. His mythology is preserved not in a single written narrative but in rock art, song cycles, dance, and the seasonal knowledge carried by senior custodians. The published accounts are necessarily general, and some layers of meaning are restricted; what can be told publicly, the stories emphasize relationship: the lightning does not simply happen — it is the action of an ancestor who must be respected. Seasonal myth: The Return of the Storms In the build-up to the wet season, the humidity gathers, the cloud masses stack over the sea, and the first storms roll in across the escarpment. The lightning ancestor is said to travel with these storms, his presence announced by thunder and the flash that splits the stone country (the seasonal cycle behind these stories was documented by the 1948 Arnhem Land Expedition: Mountford, Art, Myth and Symbolism , 1956). The rains transform the country: dry creek beds run, billabongs fill, the spear grass greens, and the animals breed. His arrival is both welcomed and feared — the same storm that brings life can burn a tree or strike the careless. In this tradition weather is not background to the ancestors' stories; it is their presence. The build-up months are read from beginning to end as a passage: the sky darkens, the ancestor walks, and the land answers. Rock-art tradition: The Lightning Figure Across western Arnhem Land, rock shelters preserve images of lightning beings: human-like figures with zigzag lines radiating from the head, arms, or torso, some shown with the axes or dilly bags that carry their power (Mountford 1956; Chaloupka, Journey in Time , 1993). These images are not portraits in the Western sense; they are manifestations of ancestral power tied to specific places, and to the right of particular clan groups to paint, sing, and recount them. Regional names differ — Namarrkon is the best-known Kunwinjku Lightning Spirit — and Mamaragan belongs to the same complex of beings: a name recorded for the lightning ancestor of the Liverpool River and surrounding country. The pictures are the ancestors' signatures in the stone: to see the zigzag issuing from a painted head is to be shown, without words, whose country you are standing in. Moral teaching: Respect for the Sky The stories teach that the lightning is not random. It follows the paths of the ancestors and answers the moral order of the country (the framework was set out by Berndt & Berndt, The World of the First Australians , 1964). To be out in the open in a severe storm, to mock the thunder, or to ignore the signs of the season is to risk the ancestor's anger. The teaching is practical as much as spiritual: it encodes when to travel and when to shelter, where the creeks will run, and how to read the sky of the stone country. An oral tradition keeps this knowledge alive by making it personal — the storm is not an 'it' but a 'who', and one behaves differently toward a who. Respect for the sky, in this teaching, is a technology of survival dressed as reverence. Seasonal myth: The Knock-'Em-Down Storms The Kunwinjku seasonal calendar of western Arnhem Land divides the year into six seasons, and the storm ancestor's year has a second, louder movement. After the main monsoon months (Gudjewg) come the great late storms of Banggerreng — 'knock 'em down' — when violent squalls flatten the tall spear grass across the floodplains and the lightning returns in its last great passages (the seasonal round is documented in the published Kunwinjku calendars of the region). The turn of Banggerreng is a hinge of the year: the grass goes down, the air begins to cool, and the country readies itself for the dry. To the communities who read it, the flattening storm is the ancestor's final word of the wet season — a clearing of the ground, a loud punctuation, and a signal stored in story: the season is turning, and the country is about to change its face. The calendar is astronomy, meteorology, and theology in a single sky. Syncretism: Mamaragan is best understood within the regional lightning-being tradition of western Arnhem Land rather than as a figure with wide intercultural syncretism. Nearby and related traditions speak of Namarrkon, a powerful lightning spirit whose stone axes are said to be visible in certain rocks and whose image is common in rock art. The relationship between Mamaragan and Namarrkon varies by clan and by song cycle; some accounts treat them as overlapping names or aspects of a single ancestral power, while others keep them distinct. Non-Indigenous writers have regularly conflated regional lightning beings into a generic 'Lightning Man' — a simplification the living tradition does not make. Contemporary Aboriginal artists and custodians continue to paint and sing these figures, negotiating the boundary between restricted sacred knowledge and publicly shared cultural expression. Cultural legacy: Mamaragan and the wider lightning-ancestor tradition remain part of the living culture of western Arnhem Land. Aboriginal artists from Kunwinjku and surrounding communities continue to depict lightning beings in bark paintings, prints, and rock-art-inspired works, often for public audiences while withholding the most restricted layers of meaning (Taylor, Seeing the Inside , 1996). The figure entered Australian popular consciousness through books such as Ainslie Roberts and Charles Mountford's The Dreamtime Book , where Arnhem Land lightning beings were introduced to non-Indigenous readers. In environmental discourse, the wet-season storms that Mamaragan embodies are recognized as essential to the ecology of northern Australia, linking ancestral knowledge with modern climate and land-management science. Extended meditation: Mamaragan asks us to think of weather as relationship. A lightning storm is not a meteorological event that happens to a landscape; in the Aboriginal understanding of western Arnhem Land, it is the action of an ancestor moving through country he knows intimately. The flash that splits a tree, the thunder that rolls off the escarpment, the rain that fills the billabongs — all of these are signs of a being who is present, purposeful, and powerful. For the modern observer, Mamaragan is a reminder that scientific and ancestral ways of knowing can describe the same phenomena without replacing one another. The barometer measures the pressure drop; the ancestor stories measure the moral and relational significance of the storm. Both are true. Both are needed. To restore the name Mamaragan is to remember that the lightning has a name, a home, and a people who have been listening to it for millennia. Original script note: The languages of western Arnhem Land were traditionally oral; there is no pre-contact written form of the name Mamaragan. The name has been recorded by non-Indigenous ethnographers, artists, and linguists using Latin transcription. PuniCodex therefore labels the form as a scholarly transliteration rather than an 'Original Script' in the strict sense. The restoration capitalizes the first letter as a proper name; otherwise the spelling follows the most widely attested romanization.

title: The Rainbow Serpent
text: The Rainbow Serpent: Water, Law, Monsoon, and the Dreaming Ngalyod is the great Rainbow Serpent of the Kunwinjku-speaking peoples of western Arnhem Land. In the wet season she — or he, for gender shifts with country and ceremony — arcs across the sky as the rainbow; in the dry she sleeps beneath the earth in waterholes, springs, and rocky escarpments. She is not merely a weather spirit: she is a creator being who carved out the rivers, stocked them with fish and waterlilies, and laid down the law that still governs the relationship between people, country, and kin. The Rainbow: Ngalyod is the rainbow itself, the visible sign of the serpent moving between waterholes and bringing the rains that renew the land. Waterhole Guardian: In the dry season Ngalyod rests in permanent waterholes; to disturb or pollute those places is to risk the serpent's anger. Law Giver: The Rainbow Serpent established moiety, marriage rules, and the ceremonial obligations that bind clans to country. Creator of Abundance: Ngalyod created the fish, waterlilies, and other foods of the wetlands; her body shaped the country people still live from. Symbols: Rainbow — The serpent's visible body arching across the sky after rain; Waterhole — The resting place and dwelling of Ngalyod in the dry season; Stone spear-points — Sacred objects sometimes identified as the serpent's teeth or gifts; Lightning — The flash that accompanies the serpent's movement and the breaking of wet-season storms Ngalyod's stories are told in rock art galleries, song cycles, and ceremonial narratives across western Arnhem Land. The serpent is not a single fixed character but a continuum of powers : creator, law-giver, healer, and avenger. The myths explain why certain waterholes never dry, why the wet season returns, and why human beings must respect the boundaries between clans and countries. Creation: Carving the Country In the Dreaming, Ngalyod travelled across a flat and featureless land. Where she raised her body, ridges and escarpments rose; where she lay down, waterholes and rivers formed. Her tracks are the deep channels that still carry floodwater in the wet; her resting places are the spring-fed waterholes that never run dry, and every one of them is remembered as a place where the serpent paused. Each such waterhole is owned and cared for by the clan whose ancestors witnessed her passage, and the right to paint the serpent's story or sing its country belongs to that clan alone. The creation is thus also a map of title: the landscape is the deed, and the myth is the conveyance. To tell where Ngalyod travelled is to say, precisely, who owns which water. Law: The Two Moieties Ngalyod divided the people into the two great moieties — Dhuwa and Yirritja in the regional terminology — the two halves of society whose rules of marriage, ceremony, and land ownership still structure Kunwinjku social life. Every person, place, species, and ancestral being belongs to one moiety or the other; a Dhuwa person marries a Yirritja person, and the serpent's body itself is apportioned between them in the stories. The serpent's law is not written down; it is sung, painted, and enacted in ceremony, and the moiety system it founded is less a rule-book than a grammar — a way of knowing, from any single thing, what it may be joined to. To break it is to disturb the balance of country and to invite illness, accident, or the withdrawal of the waters. Season: The Wet's Return When the first storms build over the Arnhem Land plateau, elders say that Ngalyod is moving from one waterhole to another. The rainbow is her body seen between earth and sky; the thunder is her voice; and the first floodwaters running down the escarpment are the proof that she has taken up residence in the pools for another year. The arrival of the wet season is therefore not only a meteorological event but a ceremonial one, requiring the songs and restrictions that announce the serpent's presence — and the dry season's shrinking billabongs are read the same way, as the serpent settling down. The myth is a complete weather lore: it predicts, explains, and prescribes the behaviour owed to the sky's most beautiful and most dangerous visitor. Moral: The Boy who Laughed A widely recorded story tells of a boy who mocked or wounded Ngalyod — laughing at the rainbow arched over a forbidden waterhole, in some versions spearing into the pool where the serpent lay. In retaliation the serpent rose from the water, swallowed him, and carried him underground through the water system itself, through channels no living person has walked, releasing him far from his own country — or, in the versions told around particular landmarks, transforming him into a rock or stone country that marks the boundary of the serpent's domain. The details shift from teller to teller and from country to country, as they should: the story is attached to real waterholes, and each clan tells it of its own place. What does not shift is the teaching. Elders cite the tale when instructing children at the pools: approach with restraint, take only what you need, never mock what you do not understand. The serpent's anger is not arbitrary temper; it is the boundary of the sacred, patrolled. Syncretism: The Rainbow Serpent is one of the most widely distributed figures in Aboriginal Australia, yet it is not a single deity under many names . Each language group knows a distinct serpent with its own country, kinship, and ceremonies: Yurlungur in Yolŋu country, Wagyl in Noongar country, Julunggul among some north-eastern groups, and Ngalyod among the Kunwinjku. Anthropologists and art historians have long debated whether these figures share a common origin or whether the rainbow-serpent concept is a convergence of regional powers onto a similar natural sign. What is clear is that Ngalyod must be understood on Kunwinjku terms first, before any wider comparison is attempted. Cultural legacy: Ngalyod survives most visibly in the x-ray rock art of western Arnhem Land, where the serpent is painted with internal organs, ribs, and backbone showing — a visual convention that identifies the figure as both animal and ancestor. These galleries, some thousands of years old, are now part of a living heritage managed by traditional owners in partnership with archaeologists and park authorities. In contemporary Australia the Rainbow Serpent has also become a national symbol of Indigenous ecological knowledge, appearing in public art, children's books, and environmental education. That wider fame brings a risk: the specific clan-owned meanings of Ngalyod can be flattened into a generic 'Aboriginal' icon. The restoration of the Kunwinjku name is a small act of precision against that flattening. Extended meditation: Ngalyod is not a god in the sense of a being who stands outside the world and rules it. She is country itself in serpent form : the water that does not forget, the law that does not sleep, the rainbow that returns after every drought. To speak her name is to acknowledge that the land is not inert backdrop but a living body with memory. The name also asks something of the people who use it. In a colonial country where many Aboriginal languages were suppressed, to restore Ngalyod rather than settle for the generic English 'Rainbow Serpent' is to recognise a specific intellectual tradition. The ASCII form *ngalyod* keeps the letters but loses the capital that marks a proper name; more importantly, it loses the social fact that the name belongs to a language and a people. Unicode cannot carry the whole of that inheritance, but it can at least make the name visible as a name. Original script note: The Kunwinjku languages were traditionally oral; no Indigenous writing system was used before European contact. The form Ngalyod is therefore a modern scholarly transliteration designed to represent the spoken name in the Latin alphabet. The initial capital marks it as a proper noun, and the digraph ng represents the single velar nasal phoneme /ŋ/. Because the name is not Greek, Devanagari, or CJK, the project labels it 'Scholarly Transliteration' rather than 'Original Script'.

title: Ancestor of the Peoples
text: Ancestor of the Peoples: Bat, Rainbow Serpent, and Ancestral Law Tjinimin is an ancestral being in the mythology of the Murrinh-Patha peoples of the Daly River region, Northern Territory. He is remembered as an ancestor of the Australian peoples, closely associated with the bat or flying fox and with Kunmanggur , the great Rainbow Serpent. His story turns on a quarrel, a vow, and the origin of the bat's short nose — a narrative that encodes law, social restraint, and the place of humans within the Dreaming. Ancestry: Tjinimin is identified in Murrinh-Patha tradition as an ancestor of the Australian peoples, a foundational figure in the genealogical memory of the Daly River communities. Bat and Flying Fox: The figure is associated with the bat; a key myth explains the bat's short nose as the result of Tjinimin's vow and transformation. Rainbow Serpent: Tjinimin's narrative is bound to Kunmanggur, the Rainbow Serpent, whose consorts and authority set the moral stakes of the story. Trickster and Law: His attempt to transgress social boundaries, his defeat, and his lasting vow form a cautionary tale about desire, consequence, and the establishment of ancestral law. Symbols: Bat or flying fox — The animal form and kinship emblem linked to Tjinimin; the myth of the short nose explains the bat's distinctive face.; Rainbow Serpent (Kunmanggur) — The great water-spirit and law-giver whose authority Tjinimin challenges; the serpent marks the boundary between acceptable and forbidden desire.; The upside-down tree — The place where Tjinimin hung after his defeat, looking at the stars and making his vow of abstinence.; Stars — The night sky that Tjinimin contemplated while suspended; a symbol of reflection, withdrawal, and transformation. The principal Murrinh-Patha narrative of Tjinimin, recorded by W. E. H. Stanner from the Daly River country, is a compact myth of boundary-crossing and transformation. It explains kinship, animal form, and the moral order through a single ancestral episode — and its fuller ritual meanings remain with the custodians who still keep it. Murrinh-Patha Dreaming: The Quarrel with Kunmanggur In the beginning-time, when the ancestral beings walked in their first forms, Tjinimin set his desire against Kunmanggur, the great Rainbow Serpent, the water-being whose body made the rivers and whose authority ordered the relations between all the ancestral peoples. He coveted Kunmanggur's consorts, the Green Parrot-Girls, and pressed his claim in the quarrel that the old men still tell. Stanner recorded the narrative in the mid-twentieth century from Murrinh-Patha speakers at Port Keats (Wadeye), and it must be said that the published account is the publicly speakable layer of the story: senior custodians hold fuller versions that ethnography does not print. What the published telling makes plain is the myth's charge — desire aimed at what is not one's own, aimed, moreover, at the possessions of the most powerful law-giver in the country. The quarrel defines the boundary of the permissible by showing what it costs to cross it. Murrinh-Patha Dreaming: The Vow beneath the Stars Defeated in the quarrel, Tjinimin withdrew from the world in the most literal way the country allows: he hung himself upside down in a tree, head toward the earth, feet toward the sky, and there he gazed at the stars. In that suspension, between the ground of the living and the camp of the dead, he made a vow that the Murrinh-Patha tell as absolute: he would never lie with a woman again. No council imposed this sentence and no serpent demanded it — the old men emphasize that Tjinimin pronounced it himself, and that such a vow, once spoken beneath the stars, binds the speaker past recall. He hung there through the nights, looking down at the world he had forfeited and up at the order he could no longer join. The myth makes law interesting: its deepest form is not punishment from above but sentence passed on oneself, self-exile from the ordinary human sentence of desire and consequence. Murrinh-Patha Dreaming: The Short Nose of the Bat Soon after the vow, the story says, Tjinimin's nose fell off. The detail is the myth's signature: it is the reason, the old men explain, that the bats of the Daly country have short noses — the ancestral being's bodily transformation became the permanent anatomy of the animal with which he is thereafter identified. In Murrinh-Patha understanding this is not merely an etiological curiosity. The bat, the flying fox that camps in the river trees, is kin: its face is the visible record of an ancestral choice, read every evening as the colonies rise at dusk. Tjinimin's punishment and his animal form are the same event — to be changed into the bat is both the consequence of the transgression and its memorial. The myth means that ancestral law is not written anywhere but on the bodies of the country: in the short nose of the bat, in the course of the river, any child can read what happens to those who reach for what the law withholds. Transmission: The Keeping of the Story The final episode of the Tjinimin narrative is its modern history. W. E. H. Stanner, the Australian anthropologist, worked among the Murrinh-Patha of the Daly River from the 1930s and set down the Tjinimin cycle in his studies of Aboriginal religion (published in the 1950s–60s), moved by what he famously called the 'metaphysical pity' of a tradition that endures against enormous pressure. The story continues to be kept the older way as well: senior men teach it in initiation, holding the restricted meanings close, and recordings sit with AIATSIS in Canberra as the people's own archive. The sources are therefore honest about their limits — what is printed is what may be printed — and the myth's custodians, not its ethnographers, remain its authors. This afterlife completes the story's meaning: a tale about the cost of taking what is not yours is itself handled under a law of custodianship, passed hand to hand, never simply taken. Syncretism: Tjinimin belongs specifically to Murrinh-Patha tradition rather than to the wider cross-cultural networks of the Kimberley Wandjina or Arnhem Land Rainbow Serpent complexes. Within Murrinh-Patha cosmology he is grouped with the ancestor-figures whose stories encode law, kinship, and the origins of animal species. Comparative scholarship sometimes links him to the broader Australian theme of the Moon-Man or to nocturnal transformation myths, but these connections remain speculative; the primary attested context is the Daly River region, and responsible scholarship says no more than the record allows. Cultural legacy: Tjinimin survives in Murrinh-Patha oral tradition, initiation teaching, and the ethnographic record compiled by W. E. H. Stanner and later scholars. The story is used in initiation contexts to instruct young men in ancestral law, social restraint, and the consequences of transgression, and the bat of the Daly country remains its daily reminder. Unlike the widely commercialised Wandjina imagery of the Kimberley, Murrinh-Patha sacred narratives such as that of Tjinimin are generally restricted to initiated custodians and are not reproduced as open visual art — a form of protection that has kept the story intact but also largely invisible to the wider world. For Murrinh-Patha communities themselves, Tjinimin is family: an ancestor whose face rises with the flying foxes every dusk. Extended meditation: Tjinimin is a difficult ancestor because his story turns on failure rather than triumph. He desires what is not his, loses, withdraws, and is transformed. The myth does not celebrate his ambition; it records the cost of transgression and the permanent mark it leaves on the body. In this he is close to the trickster type, but he is also a cautionary figure: the ancestor whose own choice limits him. For contemporary readers, Tjinimin raises questions about the relationship between desire and law. What does it mean to make a vow that cannot be undone? How does a community remember the one who overreached and was changed? The bat's short nose is not merely an etiological detail; it is a material reminder that ancestral actions continue to shape the living world. Original script note: No indigenous writing system is securely attested for Murrinh-Patha proper names in the pre-contact period. The name Tjinimin appears in scholarly transcription using the Latin alphabet, with tj representing a palato-alveolar affricate. The PuniCodex restoration capitalises the initial letter; the ASCII form tjinimin is otherwise identical. Because no diacritic, stress mark, or original-script character is recoverable, the name is classified as Tier 2.

title: Spirits of the Storm
text: Spirits of the Storm: Cloud, Rain, Lightning, and the Law of Country Wandjina are the cloud-and-rain beings of the Kimberley region of Western Australia. Painted on rock shelter walls with large eyes, no mouth, and radiating halos, they are not merely art but living ancestral powers who control the monsoon, punish wrongdoers, and keep the moral and ecological order of country. Rain Bringer: The Wandjina bring the wet-season storms that replenish waterholes, rivers, and the coastal plains; without their consent, the country dries. Lightning Law: Their eyes are said to be the source of lightning; their displeasure is expressed in thunder and destructive storm. Guardian of Country: They are the owners and managers of specific tracts of land, water, and species; their authority is tied to clan estates and sacred geography. Restricted Knowledge: The right to paint, name, and speak for Wandjina belongs to senior initiated custodians; the images carry protocols that protect both culture and country. Symbols: Large eyes — The source of lightning and the all-seeing gaze of the ancestors; Absence of mouth — A sign of sacred reticence; the Wandjina do not speak casually, and their power is enacted rather than narrated; Radiating halo — Clouds, storm light, and the luminescence of the wet-season sky; Rock shelter — The gallery walls where the Wandjina retreated after bestowing law, leaving their images as witnesses; Rainbow serpent — A related power of water and transformation, sometimes associated with the same sacred geography Wandjina cosmology is not a single narrative but a body of law carried by clan estates, initiation sequences, and painted galleries. The common thread is that the Wandjina came from the sea and the sky, shaped the country, gave law to the people, and then returned to the rock walls, where their images remain as living presences. Creation: The Wandjina Shaped the Kimberley In the ancestral past, the Wandjina travelled across the Kimberley, creating the hills, rivers, waterholes, and species that define the country. Each clan holds the part of the journey that passes through its estate; the full map of their travels is known only through the combined authority of many custodians. When their work was complete, they lay down on the rock-shelter walls and left their images behind, yet they remain present in cloud and rain. Law: The Giving of Custom The Wandjina did not only make the land; they gave the Law ( bugarrigarra or comparable terms) that governs kinship, marriage, food restrictions, fire management, and the treatment of sacred sites. This Law is not static scripture but a living obligation transmitted through initiation, story, and country. Season: The Return of the Wet As the build-up gives way to the monsoon, the Wandjina are understood to be active in the thunderheads and lightning that cross the coast. Their anger can bring destructive cyclones; their blessing brings the rain that fills the waterholes and revives the country after the long dry. Protocol: Images That Must Be Renewed Wandjina paintings are periodically refreshed by those authorised to do so. A faded image is not abandoned; it is a spirit in need of care. The act of repainting is a renewal of the relationship between the custodians, the ancestors, and the country. Reproduction or commercial use of these designs by outsiders is widely regarded as a serious breach of cultural protocol. Syncretism: Wandjina belief has never been a unified 'religion' in the colonial sense; it is a regional complex shared across linguistically distinct peoples of the Kimberley, including the Worrora, Ngarinyin, and Wunambal. Each group holds its own portion of the total tradition, and knowledge is stratified by age, gender, and initiation status. In the late twentieth century, artists such as David Mowaljarlai and other Kimberley elders began to explain Wandjina significance to wider Australian and international audiences, not as a syncretic new movement but as a deliberate act of cultural translation on their own terms. The Wandjina have also entered Australian popular culture, sometimes without permission, prompting ongoing debates about copyright, cultural heritage, and the right of traditional owners to control sacred imagery. Cultural legacy: The Wandjina are among the most recognisable and culturally significant rock-art traditions in Australia. Their galleries in the Kimberley, including sites on the Mitchell Plateau and along the Gibb River Road, are visited under strict protocols and are sometimes closed to the public. The images have shaped Australian understandings of Indigenous art, cosmology, and land tenure, and they continue to be a focus of heritage management, repatriation discussions, and Aboriginal self-determination. Contemporary Kimberley artists work within and against this legacy, producing new art that honours ancestral authority while addressing modern audiences. Extended meditation: The Wandjina ask us to think about power differently. They are not remote gods in a heaven separate from earth; they are in the clouds, the lightning, the rock shelters, and the Law. Their images do not 'represent' them the way a portrait represents a person; the image is a site of presence, a place where the ancestral power continues to act. This is why the question of who may paint, photograph, or reproduce a Wandjina is not merely a matter of copyright. It is a question of who holds the relationship. In a world that treats images as endlessly reproducible content, the Wandjina stand as a reminder that some images are obligations, not assets. To speak their name respectfully is to acknowledge the country, the custodians, and the living Law they protect. Original script note: The Aboriginal languages of the Kimberley were not written in a European sense before colonisation. The name is known orally in Worrorra, Ngarinyin, and Wunambal forms and was first rendered in Latin script by anthropologists and linguists in the twentieth century. The spelling 'Wandjina' follows the conventional scholarly romanisation used by AIATSIS and by researchers such as Ian Crawford. Because the distinctive sounds and semantic fields of the original languages cannot be conveyed by basic Latin letters alone, and because the restoration does not add diacritics or special letters, the name is classified as Tier 2. The Unicode form remains the scholarly citation form; the ASCII form is a DNS compromise.

title: The Two Sisters
text: The Two Sisters: Creators, Law-Givers, and the Monsoon Wawalag are the two ancestral sisters of north-eastern Arnhem Land. In Yolŋu and related traditions they are at once travellers, mothers, law-givers, and the agents through whom the Rainbow Serpent reshapes the country. Their journey establishes clan territories, marriage classes, and the rituals that still renew the monsoon. They are not domesticated heroines: they carry sacred power in their bodies, and the land responds to that power with flood, fire, and transformation. Ancestral Sisters: Two women travelling with a child, their camp sites and actions founding the ritual geography of Arnhem Land. Rainbow Serpent: Yurlunggur rises from the waterhole when the sisters' blood enters the water, swallowing and later releasing them to create the clans. Monsoon and Water: Their myth encodes the coming of the wet season: flood, renewal, and the waterholes that hold life through the dry. Sacred Law: The sisters' story underpins initiation, kinship rules, and the obligations between clans and country. Symbols: Waterhole — The sacred well where the sisters' blood awakens Yurlunggur and where the rainbow serpent dwells; Rainbow Serpent (Yurlunggur / Ngalyod) — The transformer who swallows the sisters and, in releasing them, establishes clan order and the monsoon; Blood and menstruation — The sisters' blood is not impure; it is a potent sacred substance that moves the ancestral power of the land; Camp sites and journey tracks — Each stopping place on the sisters' walk becomes a named site tied to clan identity and ritual responsibility; The child — The infant born on the journey links the sisters to future generations and to the transmission of law The Wawalag sisters travel across Arnhem Land with their mother and a newborn child, and everything they do — every camp, every name spoken, every birth — becomes law, geography, and weather. The cycle is not a single fixed text but a song performed in ceremony, whose episodes encode land tenure, marriage class, and the coming of the wet season; the spellings Wawalag, Wauwalak, and Wawilak record different transcribers and different estates. Travelling song cycle: The Journey and the Birth In the Arnhem Land song cycle, the two Wawalag sisters travel from the interior toward the coast, their mother with them and the younger sister heavy with child. Every camp is a future sacred site: they name the waterholes, gather yams and shellfish, dig for honey — and each ordinary act, performed at that place by those women, becomes the charter for a clan's ownership and a ceremony's script. The younger sister gives birth at a camp near the great python's waterhole, and the blood of childbirth, flowing with the storm-rain into the pool, is the event the whole country has been waiting for. W. Lloyd Warner recorded this cycle among the Yolŋu in the 1920s (A Black Civilization, 1937) under the spelling Wulareg; Ronald and Catherine Berndt later recorded Wawilak and Wauwalak versions (The Speaking Land, 1989). The journey's meaning is tenure: to walk the sisters' track and name their camps is to read the land's title deeds aloud, and to know which clan is responsible for which waterhole. Rainbow Serpent: Yurlunggur Swallows the Sisters The blood reaches the waterhole, and Yurlunggur — the great Rainbow Serpent, in Warner's rendering of the python's name — rises. Attraction and anger are one movement: the serpent swallows the sisters, the child, and their mother. Inside the serpent, however, the story does not end; the sisters keep singing, and their songs within the belly become part of the sacred repertoire that men will later receive in initiation. The episode is not framed as punishment for impurity — the blood is powerful, not dirty; it is ancestral substance answering ancestral substance, and the serpent acts because the law of the land demands a response to the power in women's bodies. The myth carries a theology without sin: violation and response, swallowing and singing, are parts of one exchange between people and country. What swallows you also carries you, and what carries you transforms the world outside. Creation: Regurgitation and the Clans Yurlunggur cannot keep what he has swallowed: he releases the sisters, and from that act of being taken in and given back comes the architecture of society — the moieties (in Warner's Murngin terminology, Dua and Yiritja), the marriage classes, and the rights and duties of each clan to its named places. The sisters' bodies mark the geography: this waterhole where he rose, that camp where she bore the child. The myth thereby solves, in narrative, the problem every human society must solve: how to divide the land without war. The division is a bodily memory — the country itself, taken in and given back, is the deed of title, and every ceremony that re-tells the swallowing re-issues it. Berndt and Berndt emphasized that versions differ by estate and that the deepest layers belong to initiated custodians; what is public is exactly this: the clans came out of the serpent, together. Season: The Coming of the Wet The python's rising is the monsoon. The storm that breaks when the blood enters the waterhole is the wet season itself, and the flood that follows fills the swamps, breeds the geese and the fish, and greens the woodlands — the annual renewal on which everything in Arnhem Land life depends. To sing the Wawalag cycle, then, is meteorology as liturgy: the performers do not merely remember the first flood but summon the next one, timing the ceremony to the build-up of the season. Warner recorded how the song cycles move with the year's ecological rhythm, and the Berndts noted that the same narrative anchors rain-making rites. The myth's final meaning is ecological: the country is not scenery behind the story; it is the story's body. When the sisters bleed and the serpent rises, the rains come — because the law has been spoken, and the land always answers. Syncretism: The Wawalag sisters are specific to the Aboriginal traditions of Arnhem Land, especially the Yolŋu peoples, and are not simply interchangeable with other creator figures.
