Hangul ‘소신’; no single canonical Hanja is fixed for this shamanic figure. The ASCII form sosin is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Sosin is the scholarly citation form.

title: Stribog
text: Stribog: Winds Stribog is the wind-god of the Kyiv pantheon, sixth of the six idols cast into the Dnieper in 988. His name's second element is the word for 'god'; its first is opaque — but the epic tradition calls the winds his grandsons, and that one formula is the whole of his surviving theology. The Winds: His domain by every ancient inference: the moving air that brings thaw, storm, and war-weather. Grandfather of Winds: The Slovo o polku Igoreve calls the winds 'grandsons of Stribog' — a complete genealogy in one phrase. Sixth of the Six: Listed among the idols of Kyiv in the Primary Chronicle: Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, Mokosh. The Opaque Name: No other god's name so resists analysis; its first element is an open problem of Slavic philology. Symbols: Wind and weather — The element itself, which the epic makes his family: the winds do what grandsons do; Storm cloud and squall — The war-weather of the Slovo — the black sky under which Igor's campaign marched; The steppe horizon — Kyiv's winds came off the open steppe; his one vivid scene is a steppe wind rising from the sea; The moving air of thaw — The spring winds that break the river ice — function inferred from his wind-kin, not attested The sources for Stribog are two lines long: a place in the chronicle's list of drowned idols, and a genealogy in the nation's greatest poem. Everything else — his character, his rites, his season — is inference, and this entry says so wherever inference is doing the work. Kyiv, 988: The Idols in the Dnieper When Vladimir's baptism swept the old pantheon into the Dnieper in 988, the Primary Chronicle preserved the full list of the drowned: Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh. No anecdote attaches to Stribog — no oath, no sorcerer, no gloss, no weeping crowd. Of the six he is the most silent: not first like Perun, not glossed like Dažbog, not folk-remembered like Mokosh. Yet the chronicler's list is itself a kind of myth — the orderly procession of gods into the river, each name checked off as it sinks, is the Christian founding story of Rus', and Stribog's place in that procession is the entire record of his worship. A god can be a major power and still leave no story; the river took his narrative along with his statue, and the list is the wake. Slovo o polku Igoreve: The Grandsons of Stribog The single vivid sentence about Stribog stands in the Slovo o polku Igoreve (c. 1185), the greatest work of Old Rus' literature. As Igor's doomed army rides out against the Polovtsians, the poet summons the omens, and the winds rise on cue: 'Then the winds, Stribog's grandsons, blew from the sea' — a squall driving the dust and the portents before it. The phrase is a fossil of theology. Where a monk would write 'God sent a storm,' the epic poet instinctively reaches for kinship: the winds are not Stribog's subjects or his weapons but his grandsons , doing what grandsons do — arriving uninvited, raising a racket, unmistakably of the family. Two centuries after the idols sank, the grammar of the old pantheon still blew through the language like weather that knows its own name. Philology: The Name That Won't Decode Everything else about Stribog is a problem on a philologist's desk. The second half of the name is *bogъ, 'god' — the same element that gives us Dažbog, 'giving god' — but the first half, *strib-, has no agreed root. Comparisons with words for 'arrow' and for 'spreading' or 'scattering' have circulated in the literature for a century; none carries the field, and even the vowel of the name wavers in the manuscript tradition. Some scholars have wondered whether the first element is not Slavic at all — a loan like the Iranian Simurgh behind Simargl — though no convincing donor language has stepped forward. The handbooks (Gieysztor; Brückner) state the honest position plainly: we hold the god's name, a wind-function inferred from one epic line, and nothing else. A whole deity, reduced to one sentence and an unsolved etymology. Honest Silence: What the Sources Do Not Say It is worth stating plainly what the tradition does not contain, because Stribog is the clearest case of a god known by structure rather than by story. No chronicle puts a curse in his mouth; no treaty swears by him; no saint inherits his day; no festival, icon, or temple is recorded; and no folk song or charm preserves his name past the Middle Ages. His rank — sixth of the six gods of the capital — implies a cult of real standing; his total silence implies that the sources which would have given him a biography either never existed or did not survive. Modern Slavic Native Faith has had to invent his feast-day, his attributes, and his character outright — a revealing anachronism, since Stribog today is exactly what a wind-god would be if reconstructed from the bare name alone. The scholarship knows the limits, and says so; the temple should too. Syncretism: Stribog attracted no Christian successor — no saint took the winds from him the way Elijah took Perun's storm — and Byzantine writers had no classical slot for a wind-god, so no interpretatio rescued him either. His afterlife is purely literary and comparative. Comparative mythology seats him beside the Vedic Vāyu, master of the winds, and beside the Greek winds as a brood rather than a person — Aeolus managing his bag of quarrelsome grandchildren. In the twentieth century Rodnover calendars promoted him as a god of winds and weather, roles extrapolated from the Slovo formula; fantasy fiction and games drift him as a stock 'old Slavic' name. The most honest syncretism is the one the poet performed unwittingly: naming the winds a family. That is how a polytheist sky is actually experienced — every gust somebody's relative, every storm a household arriving. Cultural legacy: Stribog's legacy is almost entirely onomastic and literary. The Slovo's phrase 'Stribog's grandsons' entered every anthology of Old Rus' literature and every schoolroom, so that his name survives more widely read than those of gods with far richer cults. Modern paganism adopted him enthusiastically but thinly: he appears in Rodnover calendars and in fantasy fiction, games, and brand names, usually as a generic wind or storm patron — attributes supplied by authors, not sources. For linguists he remains a standing exhibit in seminars on Slavic theonymy, a name whose opaque first element defeats each new generation of etymologists. If Perun is the god who would not die and Veles the god who would not stay hidden, Stribog is the god who never quite existed in the record — a place kept for the wind in the pantheon's seating plan, honored now mostly by being quoted correctly. Extended meditation: Stribog is the god of what passes through. Wind cannot be sworn by, cannot be fed, cannot even be consistently blamed — and so the tradition left him almost nothing to hold. What the epic gives him instead is better than a cult: a family. The winds are his grandsons — not his subjects, not his weapons, his grandsons, the way weather actually behaves, arriving uninvited, full of intentions, unmistakably related. The phrase is a miniature of how polytheism worked before it learned to be systematic: the world is not governed, it is inhabited, by beings with kin. Stribog matters to the modern imagination precisely because he is so nearly empty — a vessel into which every age pours its theory of the wind, from philology's unsolved root to fantasy's storm lord. Perhaps a god who is only a name and a family of winds is the truest wind-god of all: felt everywhere, pinned down nowhere, and quoted — 'the winds, Stribog's grandsons' — whenever the air itself needs a lineage.

title: Supay
text: Supay: Underworld Supay is the lord of uku pacha , the inner world beneath the Andes — the domain of the dead, of cave-dwelling spirits, and of the mineral wealth the earth conceals. No temple bore his name; he was propitiated, not praised. Under Spanish rule the name was reforged: supay became the Quechua word for 'devil', and the lord of the inner world survives today as the miners' Tío . Lord of Uku Pacha: Master of the inner world beneath the earth where the dead dwell and the ore veins run (Polo de Ondegardo 1571; Cobo, Historia 13.10). Master of the Supaykuna: The dangerous spirits — the supaykuna — who send illness and haunt caves and crossroads; offerings kept them from taking the living. The Caves of Tambillos: Caverns near Huarochirí where the people said the supay dwelt; the Huarochirí manuscript records the rites paid there. The Miners' Tío: In the colonial mines, above all Potosí, miners fed the underground lord coca, alcohol, and cigarettes under the alias El Tío. Symbols: Cave mouth or mine shaft — The visible entrance to uku pacha; every shaft sunk into the earth is a doorway into Supay's jurisdiction; Coca and chicha — The standard offerings that made the underground lord generous toward the living who disturbed his realm; Funerary goods — Food, tools, and treasure interred with the dead as provision for the journey down to Supay's household; The horned devil figure — The post-conquest iconography in which the extirpation campaigns re-imagined Supay as the Christian Devil No Inca myth cycle of Supay survives on its own terms. Everything we know comes through colonial chroniclers, Quechua-language manuscripts, and the living memory of Andean communities — the record of a lord of the inner world who was propitiated, feared, demonized, and finally renamed, yet never quite dethroned. The Inner World: Lord of Uku Pacha The earliest European witness is the corregidor Polo de Ondegardo, whose 1571 report De los errores y supersticiones de los indios explains Inca cosmology as three stacked worlds: hanaq pacha , the upper world; kay pacha , this present world; and uku pacha , the inner world within the earth. The dead descended to uku pacha, Polo reports, and there remained in the power of the being they called Supay . Bernabé Cobo repeats the scheme a century later ( Historia del Nuevo Mundo 13.10), adding that the dead were furnished with food, tools, and treasure for the journey down. Nowhere in these accounts is Supay a god of a temple or a priesthood: he is the one who holds the dead, and the offerings made at funerals are essentially payments that keep him from reaching further into the world of the living. The Inca underworld was not a place of punishment but of retention , and Supay was its jailer as much as its king. The belief encodes a sober arithmetic: every death adds to his household, so the living must forever feed the boundary between the worlds. Huarochirí: The Caves of Tambillos The Quechua-language Huarochirí manuscript , recorded by the extirpator Francisco de Ávila in the first years of the seventeenth century (trans. Salomon & Urioste, 1991), treats supay not as a single lord but as a class of dangerous beings — the supaykuna — who dwell in caves, springs, hills, and crossroads and send illness to those who offend them. The most famous haunt is the cavern of Tambillos , near San Pedro de Huarochirí, where the people made offerings of coca and maize beer so that the spirits of the rock would not take their children. Scholars have long debated whether the chroniclers' single 'Supay, lord of the inner world' is a Spanish simplification of this older, plural spirit-world, or whether the supaykuna were always understood as the lord's subjects. The manuscript itself does not resolve the question; it simply shows communities negotiating, offering, and appeasing. Whatever the hierarchy, the logic is constant: the earth's interior is populated, and it must be paid . Supay's power was never worshipped from a temple — it was managed at the cave mouth, one offering at a time. Conquest: Supay Becomes the Devil The most consequential chapter of Supay's history was written not by his believers but by his enemies. To convert the Andes, the missionaries needed Satan to have a local name, and they chose Supay's. González Holguín's Quechua Vocabulario (1608) glosses supay plainly as 'devil', and Pablo José de Arriaga's manual for destroying idolatry, the Extirpación de la idolatría (1621), names Supay as the demon who still receives the offerings poured at the Indian shrines. The campaign worked as language policy: within a generation Quechua speakers used supay for the Christian devil, and the pre-conquest meaning — 'spirit' — survived only in scholarly memory. Every colonial confession, sermon, and catechism pressed the word deeper into its new meaning. The transformation is a case study in conversion by redefinition : the church did not first destroy the lord of the inner world; it renamed him, and let the new name do the slow work of displacement. That the word, not the being, was conquered is proven by the mines, where the lord returned under another alias. The Mines: El Tío of Potosí In the silver mines of the colonial Andes, above all at Potosí , miners developed the cult of El Tío , 'the Uncle': an effigy seated at the deepest level of each mine, fed coca leaves, cane alcohol, and cigarettes on Tuesdays and Fridays, and honored with the ch'alla libation. Michael Taussig's The Devil and Commodity Fetishism in South America (1980) connected the Tío to the older Supay of uku pacha — the lord of the inner world now ruling a new and terrible wealth. The miners said it plainly: the metal belongs to the one below, and he will trade safety for tribute; fatal accidents were read as unpaid debts. Unlike the church's Supay, this underground lord was negotiated with , not merely feared — a business partner who could be generous and could be cheated, at one's peril. The tradition continues today at Cerro Rico and in the Diablada dances of Oruro. Supay's late history shows a power outliving its own demonization: renamed the Devil by the conquerors, he remained — under a new alias — the actual master of the underworld the miners worked in. Syncretism: Supay's entire afterlife is a history of forced translations. The conquering church mapped him onto Satan, and the mapping was so successful that modern Quechua and Aymara use supay as the ordinary word for devil. Yet the older figure survived the translation in the mines, where El Tío — the Uncle — continues the uku pacha lord's contract with those who take wealth from below. Scholars such as Taussig (1980) and Tristan Platt have read this double life as the emblem of colonial capitalism: the indigenous underworld lord re-employed as the owner of the silver that fed Europe. The Diablada dance traditions of Oruro and the miner rites at Potosí keep both identities visible at once — Christian devil masks performing unmistakably pre-Christian obligations. Cultural legacy: Supay remains embedded in Andean language itself: to this day supay means devil in Quechua and Aymara, a living fossil of the extirpation campaigns. In the mining regions of Bolivia the Tío effigies are still fed and still feared, and the Diablada festivals stage his masked dance before crowds of thousands. For scholarship, Supay is a key witness to how colonialism rewrote indigenous cosmology — studied by Taussig, Platt, and Duviols as the paradigmatic case of a deity demonized, renamed, and secretly retained. The name also circulates in global culture: Andean diaspora communities, museum exhibitions on Inca religion, and contemporary indigenous revival movements all return to the older, pre-Christian meaning of the word — spirit, not devil — as part of recovering what the extirpations tried to erase. Extended meditation: Supay is the lord of the underground who was renamed but never dethroned. Colonial priests thought that calling him 'devil' would finish him; instead the name became a mask, and behind the mask the old contract continued in the dark of the mines. There is a lesson in the economics of belief here: a power that controls what you need — passage for your dead, safety for your labor, metal for your markets — cannot be argued away. It can only be paid. The restoration of Supay is therefore more than philological courtesy. It returns to the figure his own name, before the extirpators rewrote it, and it asks the reader to hold both histories at once: the lord of uku pacha and the colonial devil, the cave offerings and the Tuesday cigarettes at Cerro Rico. The earth, this name insists, keeps its own accounts, and its oldest creditor is still collecting.

title: Taaroa
text: Taaroa: Creator In the old religion of Tahiti, Taaroa is not one god among many but the ground of all divinity — the self-existent one who dwelt alone in the primal darkness, burst the shell of his own being to make sky and earth, and fathered or simply is every other god. The first missionary scholars recorded his cosmogony with respect verging on awe. The Unbegotten: Ta'aroa has no father and no mother: the accounts insist he was never made, because before him there was nothing that could make him. Maker of Sky and Earth: He broke his world-shell: the upper half became the sky, the lower half the earth, and the space between them the living world. Father of the Gods: In the fuller tellings he fashioned the other great gods — Tane, Rono, Tū, 'Oro — and set each over a domain of the world. The Distant One: When creation was finished he withdrew to the highest heaven; every prayer began and ended with his name. Symbols: The world-shell — The egg-like shell in which Ta'aroa crouched alone in the darkness; when he broke it, sky rose from the upper half and earth spread from the lower (Henry, Ancient Tahiti).; The spiral — The ʻōro spiral of growth by which creation proceeds outward from a point — the geometry the priests saw in the unfolding world and in the sacred hair of the gods.; The primal darkness (Te Pō) — The night in which Ta'aroa existed alone before anything else; creation is not the defeat of darkness but its self-opening.; The opening invocation — Every Tahitian prayer and chant began with Ta'aroa's name and closed with it — the priests named him 'the god of gods' before any other name was spoken (Henry, Ancient Tahiti).; The raised stones of the marae — The open-air temple platforms of Tahiti with their carved god-houses (ʻōroʻō); his cult was administered by the highest priesthood of the islands. Taaroa's mythology is a cosmogony in the strict sense — an account of how anything at all came to be. The Tahitian priests told it to the first missionaries, and it survives in two nineteenth-century witnesses: the narrative taken down by the missionary John Davies and the longer version preserved by Teuira Henry from the scholars of Papeari. The Self-Existent: Before There Was Anything The old scholars of Tahiti told the missionary John Davies — and Teuira Henry heard it again two generations later — that before there was sky, sea, land, light, or any other being, Taaroa was . He had no father and no mother, for nothing existed before him that could beget him; his cult name Ta'aroa-'onohi-'ote-na'i-'atu means 'Ta'aroa, the self-existing, the origin of all things.' He dwelt in the primal darkness called Te Pō, wrapped in his own shell like a chick in the egg, calling into the void — and no one answered , because there was no one else to answer. The whole of the world-to-come lay folded inside him, as the tree lies folded in its seed, and the first act of the cosmos was that loneliness outgrew its shell. (Davies' account, preserved in Ellis, Polynesian Researches I; Henry, Ancient Tahiti 336–338.) The myth makes the first moment of existence a soliloquy: creation begins as a being who has no one else to speak to, speaking himself into company. The Shell: Sky from the Upper Half, Earth from the Lower Weary of confinement, Ta'aroa broke his shell open . The upper half of it he raised high above him and made the sky; the lower half he spread out beneath him and made the earth. From himself he brought forth the sea, the springs, the rocks and sands, the trees and plants, the fish and birds, and the land animals — the whole inventory of the world drawn, item by item, out of his own being, nothing borrowed and nothing left over. In Henry's version he then turned to its government, which is where the third myth begins. (Henry, Ancient Tahiti 336–349; Ellis, Polynesian Researches I.) The image is precise and strange: the cosmos is not built from outside materials but hatched — the world as the broken shell of a god who could no longer bear to be alone. Progenitor: The Maker of Gods and of Men In the fuller tellings, Ta'aroa did not keep the world to himself. He fashioned the other great gods — Tane of the forests and birds, Rono of peace and cultivated food, Tū of war and of humankind, Ta'ata , and the young warrior god 'Oro who would inherit the great national marae — and set each over his portion of creation. He then made men and women to people the earth he had spread. The sources are early and do not always agree on the details — Davies' version, gathered in 1818, is sober where Henry's, drawn from priestly families of Papeari, is expansive — but all agree on the order: gods first, then people, and Ta'aroa before and above both . (Davies in Ellis, Polynesian Researches I; Henry, Ancient Tahiti.) The theology is remarkably austere: a single unbegotten power delegates everything, and rules by having made the rulers. The Withdrawal: The Distant One Ascends When the work of creation was complete, Ta'aroa did not remain to govern the world day by day. He withdrew to the highest heaven , above the dwelling of Tane and all the other gods, and from that remove he was invoked as 'the god of gods.' Every prayer and every sacrifice on the marae began with his name and ended with his name, whatever lesser deity was being petitioned in between; the priests addressed him as the root from which the other divinities grew, the trunk of which they were branches. It is this withdrawal that his name's traditional gloss — 'the distant one' — is usually taken to mean. (Henry, Ancient Tahiti.) The pattern is the deus otiosus , the resting god familiar from many traditions: having made the world, the creator leaves it running and becomes a direction — the vertical axis toward which all prayer climbs. Syncretism: When the London Missionary Society reached Tahiti in 1797, the first catechists did not find a clutter of squabbling idols — they found a supreme god whose creation narrative sounded uncomfortably like Genesis, and they said so in their journals. Tahitian scholars who worked with them, the deacons of the mission schools, readily compared Ta'aroa to Jehovah, a comparison that eased conversion and ultimately doomed the cult: the great marae were abandoned within a generation, the god-houses burned or left to rot. Ta'aroa survived in the cult of his son 'Oro, whose war-god religion absorbed the national priesthood. In the western islands his own name lived on as Tangaloa , creator of Tonga and Samoa; in Aotearoa it had already become Tangaroa , lord of the sea; in Hawai'i, Kanaloa , god of the deep. One god, three more names, many biographies — the comparative method's favorite case. Cultural legacy: Taaroa's direct cult ended in the early nineteenth century, but his name never left Tahiti. It lives in the great marae the Polynesian nations are rebuilding: Taputapuātea on Ra'iatea, dedicated to his son 'Oro, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2017 and re-consecrated by delegations from across the triangle. The cosmogony recorded by Henry remains a foundational text of Polynesian studies, taught wherever the old religion is taken seriously as theology rather than curiosity. Contemporary Tahitian dancers and orators invoke Ta'aroa as the name of origins in the renaissance of ʻōrero and ori Tahiti. And because the creation chant opens every traditional ceremony with his name, 'Ta'aroa' has become the shorthand Polynesians reach for when they want to say: this is where we begin. Extended meditation: Most creation stories start with a problem: chaos to be fought, a dragon to be split, a rival to be overthrown. Taaroa's story starts with something rarer — sufficiency . Before there was anything, there was a being who needed nothing: no parents, no materials, no opponent. The world is not a conquest but an overflow, the cracking of a shell that had become too small for the being inside it. And there is a loneliness in this that the myth does not hide: the first thing the god does in the darkness is call out, and no one answers. Creation, on this reading, is not an act of power but of company — the universe as the solution to solitude. When the work is done, Ta'aroa withdraws to the highest heaven and leaves the world to his children. Power that creates and then steps back is the most difficult kind to imagine, and the Tahitians imagined it — a supreme being whose supremacy consists in having delegated everything and in being, still, the direction of every prayer. That is a theology of confidence: the maker does not need to manage, because the making was perfect. The name Ta'aroa, with its gentle glottal catch like a held breath, is the sound of that confidence.

title: Tagaloa
text: Tagaloa: Creator Tagaloa is the supreme creator god of the Samoan islands, lord of the layered heavens who looked down on the empty sea and made the land. He is the maker of islands, the father of gods and chiefs, and the dweller in the highest sky — the figure around whom Samoan cosmology turns. Creator of the Isles: He threw down the vine and stone from which the Samoan islands were formed, founding the world itself. Lord of the Heavens: He dwells in Lani-uli, the highest of the layered heavens, above wind, rain, and the soaring birds. Father of Sina: His daughter Sina, mother of chiefs, anchors the island's greatest cycle of stories. Ocean's Lord: Across Polynesia his name is the sea's: Tangaroa in Aotearoa, Ta'aroa in Tahiti, Kanaloa in Hawai'i. Symbols: The Vine of the Isles — The heavenly vine Tagaloa let down into the sea, whose parts became the islands of Samoa; The Layered Heavens — Lani-uli and the descending storeys of the sky, his dwelling above all clouds; The Coconut Palm — Born from the body of the eel Tuna in the Sina cycle that belongs to Tagaloa's household; The Star-Path — In the wayfinding revival, the ocean road by which his dispersed namesakes are rejoined Tagaloa's mythology is cosmogony in the strict sense — stories of how land, people, and rank came to be . It survives not in epic but in creation chants recorded by nineteenth-century missionaries and ethnographers, whose accounts disagree in detail but agree that the world began when the Lord of the Heavens acted upon the sea. The Making of the Isles: The Vine Let Down into the Sea In the beginning Tagaloa dwelt alone in Lani-uli , the highest heaven, and beneath him lay only the boundless sea. He let down into the waters a vine from the sky; where its parts touched the surface, the islands of Samoa rose. On the largest he set the first settlement, and from the sky he watched over it. The fullest form of this creation account was recorded by the missionary J. B. Stair in Old Samoa (1897) and compared with related versions by Augustin Krämer in The Samoa Islands (1902); George Turner had published a shorter form in Nineteen Years in Polynesia (1861). Manu'a, the island group of the myth's first landing, is still styled the 'beginning of Samoa' in formal oratory, and the creation chant remained the deep charter for its paramount titles. The story is the charter of Samoan identity:The story is the charter of Samoan identity: the homeland is not discovered but made — thrown down from heaven and rooted in the sea . The Daughter of Heaven: Sina and the Eel Tagaloa's daughter Sina came down to the pool of Mata o le Alelo to bathe, where a great eel, Tuna, confessed its love. When the eel was killed at Sina's command, she buried its head, and from it grew the first coconut palm — its two eyes, mouth, and body still showing on the nut. The tale was recorded across Polynesia (Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific , 1876; Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology , 1970, §§ on the coconut cycle) and became the most retold of all Samoan stories. In Samoa the cycle carries a chiefly resonance as well: Sina's name became a byword for beauty in proverb, and her bathing pool, Mata o le Alelo, was pointed out to visitors into the twentieth century. The myth answers a child's questionThe myth answers a child's question — why does the coconut look like a face? — and binds the staple tree of island life to the death of an impossible love . The Heavens Above: The Storeys of the Sky Samoan cosmology stacks the sky into storeys — Lani-uli, Lani-ʻula, and the heavens beneath them — and places Tagaloa at the summit, above the winds that carry rain. Krämer ( The Samoa Islands , 1902) recorded prayers addressing the ascending heavens by name, each storey ruled or traversed on the way to the Lord's seat. No text gives a complete, consistent map; the ethnographers themselves note that districts preserved different orders of the heavens. Below the storeys of the sky the same cosmology placed the underworld and the remote ends of the earth, and prayers were imagined to rise through the layers like visitors announced at the thresholds of a great chief's house. Yet the structure is constant:Yet the structure is constant: the sacred is vertical, and the higher the heaven, the nearer the Lord . Cosmology here is not speculation but orientation — the same layering a navigator reads in cloud and star. The Polynesian Dispersal: Tangaroa Driven to the Sea In the Māori version of the same divine name, Tangaroa is a child of Ranginui and Papatūānuku, the sky-father and earth-mother crushed in their parents' tight embrace. When Tāne thrust his parents apart to let in the light, Tangaroa fled to the ocean, and his enmity with Tāne — whose forests silt the sea — endures in myth (Grey, Polynesian Mythology , 1855; Orbell, A Concise Encyclopedia of Māori Myth and Legend , 1998). The Hawaiian Kanaloa and Tahitian Ta'aroa preserve further branches of the same god. Linguists reconstruct the shared ancestral form and read the god's names as a map of settlement itself — each island's dialect keeping its own office for the one Lord. Read across the ocean, the dispersalRead across the ocean, the dispersal of Tagaloa's name is itself the story: wherever Polynesians voyaged, the Lord went with them, changing office — creator in Samoa, sea-god in Aotearoa — but never name . Syncretism: Christian missionaries arriving in Samoa in the 1830s found Tagaloa the principal rival of their God and absorbed rather than destroyed him: his title 'Atua' became the generic word for the Christian deity , and his mythology was pushed into folklore, where it survived. The pan-Polynesian evidence suggests an older unity: Tangaroa of Aotearoa, Ta'aroa of Tahiti, and Kanaloa of Hawai'i are cognate names with divergent portfolios, a pattern linguists explain by the settlement of the Pacific out of the Samoa–Tonga region (Tregear's comparative dictionary; Craig 1989). In Hawai'i, Kanaloa survives as the twin and companion of Kāne, the two wandering the islands together as culture-bringers — a pairing that arguably preserves Tagaloa's original creative role. In the twentieth century the Polynesian Voyaging Society's revival of long-distance navigation deliberately re-enshrined these sea-gods: Hōkūleʻa's ocean road was, in the crews' own framing, Tangaroa's and Kanaloa's road again . Cultural legacy: Tagaloa's most durable legacy is genealogical. Samoan orators trace chiefly lines ( gafa ) to divine ancestors of his household, and the sacred honorifics of chiefly oratory still invoke the sky's lordship. His daughter Sina gave her name to one of the most widespread of all Polynesian story-cycles — found from Samoa to Mangaia to Hawaii — and the proverbial Sina remains a figure of beauty and longing in Samoan speech. The god's name lives quietly in the landscape: villages, titles, and the old name Savai'i -region traditions. Since the 1970s the Pacific-wide voyaging renaissance has restored Tagaloa–Tangaroa–Kanaloa to active cultural memory: the canoe is again read as the sea-god's vehicle, and the navigator's art, once missionized into silence, is once more taught as his inheritance . Extended meditation: What Tagaloa teaches is that creation can be an act of looking down . His world begins not with a battle or a body but with a lord in the highest heaven and an empty sea — and then a decision: to let something down. Polynesian cosmology is famously oceanic, yet its supreme god is a sky-dweller; the islands are the rope and bridge between the two. This is a theology suited to navigators: the world is made of layers — sky, sea, land, underworld — and authority flows along the vertical axis, from above downward, from the god to the chief to the people. Tagaloa is therefore less a 'god of' any one thing than the source of rank itself: where he acts, land appears; where his daughter descends, chiefs are born. To study him is to see how a non-literate society stored its constitution in cosmology, safe from conquest, until ethnographers wrote it down.

title: Tangaroa
text: Tangaroa: Ocean Tangaroa is the sea given will: lord of ocean, fish, and all that swims , son of the Sky Father and Earth Mother, and the brother who fled to the deep when his parents were torn apart. Every fish is his child, every canoe his guest, and every storm over the water is family business. Lord of Ocean: He took the sea for his domain when his parents were separated, vowing in the recitations never to return to the land. Father of Fishes: With Hine-moana, the ocean woman, he is ancestor of every finned and swimming creature the nets take. The Exiled Brother: Tāwhirimātea's war drove him from the coast; his grandchildren scattered to sea and shore, splitting into fish and lizard. One Name, Many Islands: Ta'aroa in Tahiti, Tangaloa in Tonga and Samoa, Kanaloa in Hawai'i — one ocean god under four island names. Symbols: The fish-hook (matau) — The carved hook with which his descendants take his children from the sea — every catch a petition, every offering a repayment.; The whale and the shark — His largest and most feared children; the whale (tohorā) and the shark (mangō) carry his mana in bulk.; The canoe (waka) — The vessel that crosses his domain; canoes were tapu and addressed as kin, because the sea is a relative who must be asked.; The tide — Tangaroa-whakamau-tai, 'Tangaroa who fixes the tides' — one of his names, and the rhythm by which fishermen read him.; The lizard (ngarara) — His grandchildren who hid ashore: the lizards, fish that chose the land — kin, yet forever on the wrong side of the beach. Tangaroa's stories are the Māori ocean chapter of the great separation cycle — and then the cycle widens: the same name, in other dialects, becomes the supreme creator of the whole Polynesian triangle. The Māori knew what the comparison would later prove. Genealogy: Born Between the Embrace Tangaroa was born into the darkness that lay between Ranginui, the Sky, and Papatūānuku, the Earth, whose embrace left no room and no light for their children. With his brothers Tāne, Tāwhirimātea, Tūmatauenga, Rongo, and Haumia-tiketike he grew to manhood in that cramped twilight, and with them he debated how to escape: Tūmatauenga counseled killing the parents outright, Tāne proposed forcing them apart. When Tāne at last pushed Ranginui into the sky and light flooded the world, Tangaroa looked at the dry land his brother had won and chose the other half of creation: he went down into the ocean, and took it for his own . (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1; Smith, The Lore of the Whare-wānanga.) The myth reads the coastline as a family wound: the sea is not the land's opposite but its brother, still angry. The Storm War: The Children Who Split in Two Not all the brothers accepted the separation. Tāwhirimātea, the wind, remained with his father in the sky and made war on the others, and Tangaroa's domain was his first battlefield: the sea boiled under the storm. In the rout, Tangaroa's grandchildren — the children of his son Punga — split forever . Ikatere, father of the fish, fled into the deep and cried 'swim, my children'; Tū-te-wehiwehi, father of the reptiles, scrambled ashore into Tāne's forests and cried 'hide, my children.' Hence the hostility the myth sees everywhere along the tideline: fish devour the lizards cast into the sea, and the sea never forgives the land. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1.) What looks like natural enmity is re-read as a family separated under fire — every fish a refugee, every lizard a deserter's child. The Ocean Wife: Hine-moana, Mother of All That Swim In the traditions recorded by Elsdon Best, Tangaroa's wife is Hine-moana , 'ocean woman' — not a separate power but the sea itself, personified as the mother of the fish tribes. Every species is their child, which is why the fisherman addresses the sea as kin, and why the first fish of a catch was laid back into the water: a family does not eat its greeting. The canoes that crossed Hine-moana to reach Aotearoa were themselves spoken of as her children, and the rituals of launching, fishing, and beaching observed her tapu; even the nets and lines were named and placated. (Best, Māori Religion and Mythology; Best, The Māori as He Was.) The theology is ecological before the word existed: the ocean is not a resource but a marriage, and the catch is a relative arriving for dinner. Pan-Polynesian: The Same God in Other Islands Travel west and Tangaroa grows greater. In Tahiti the name becomes Ta'aroa , the self-existent creator from whose body the world was hatched (Henry, Ancient Tahiti). In Tonga and Samoa it is Tangaloa , the supreme god whose messenger, the plover Tuli, dove to the sea-bottom and brought up the sand of the first islands (Craig, Dictionary of Polynesian Mythology). In Hawai'i it is Kanaloa , companion of Kāne in the company of gods who made the first man, and lord of the ocean's dark deep (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology). The Māori sea-god is thus the eastern branch of the oldest divine name in Polynesia — which is why the nineteenth-century comparatists made him their first case study. One proto-god, four biographies: the triangle itself emerges as a single story told in dialects. Syncretism: Tangaroa's syncretic career runs in two directions. Westward, in Tonga and Samoa, his name — Tangaloa — remained the supreme creator's, and Samoan Christians long prayed to a God they still sometimes called Tangaloa, a continuity the missionaries alternately welcomed and fought. Eastward, the Māori had already demoted him: from creator of the cosmos to lord of one domain, a brother among brothers, because the separation cycle re-hierarchized the gods around the family drama. In modern Aotearoa the name rides the cultural renaissance: Tangaroa appears in carving, kapa haka, and marine policy as the person of the moana, the sea that feeds and must be fed. The Treaty of Waitangi fisheries settlements of the 1980s and 90s, and the doctrine of kaitiakitanga over the marine estate, gave him a legal afterlife: his name is now cited wherever the sea is spoken of as an ancestor rather than a commodity. Cultural legacy: Tangaroa remains the most-seen of the Māori gods — in every coastal marae's imagery, in the school-taught separation cycle, and in the everyday word moana for the sea. Fishermen still speak of him half-jokingly and not entirely jokingly; the Māori fisheries claim and its settlement wrote his descendants' relationship with the sea into law. In Hawai'i, where his form is Kanaloa, the modern voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sails by the same star-compass the old navigators read — the sea-god's ancient craft, relaunched. Across the Pacific the name survives in hundreds of personal names, in ships, in the naming of research vessels, and in the quiet conviction of island peoples that the ocean is not empty water but occupied country. Extended meditation: Tangaroa is the sea as a relative — the most radical idea in the Māori cosmos. A god who is a brother, a domain that is a marriage, a catch that is a visit: the whole grammar of the ocean is familial, and the modern world's grammar of the ocean is exactly the opposite. When Māori negotiators in the 1980s and 90s said the sea is an ancestor, they were not inventing an environmentalism of convenience; they were quoting him. The name Tangaroa carries a complete theory of the deep: that the largest thing on the planet is a person with children, a temper, and a claim on our manners. There is tragedy folded into the name as well. He is the brother who lost — who left rather than accept the new world, and whose children still flee one another at the water's edge. The tide that has run between brothers for all these generations is the one argument nobody has won: the land says the fish are food, the sea says the fish are family, and every meal from the ocean is a negotiation between the two.

title: Themis
text: Themis: Divine Law Thémis is divine order — the rightness that exists before anyone legislates it. A Titaness daughter of Ouranos and Gaia, she keeps oracles, mothers the Seasons and the Fates, and counsels Zeus himself. Where her daughters administer what is fated, Thémis personifies what is fitting. Divine Right: Thémis is what is ordained — custom and right older than any written decree; the noun θέμις meant 'established order' before it was a name. The Delphi Succession: Before Apollo, Thémis kept the oracle at Delphi, inheriting it from Gaia and passing it on to Phoebe (Aeschylus, Eumenides 1–8). Mother of the Horae: By Zeus she bore the Seasons — Eunomía (Order), Díkē (Justice), Eirḗnē (Peace) — and the Moirai, the Fates (Hesiod, Theogony 901–906). Counselor of Kings: She warned Zeus against wedding Thetis, foreseeing a son mightier than his father (Pindar, Isthmian 8.26–47). Symbols: The scales — The balance of what is ordained; in later Greco-Roman art her figure merges with Justitia's, scales in hand.; The tripod — Her office at Delphi before Apollo took the oracle — the seat she held between Gaia and Phoebe.; The Horae — Her three daughters as her emblem: Order, Justice, and Peace — the visible seasons of a rightly governed life.; The Moirai — The Fates, her daughters by Zeus — spinners of the destiny even gods must accept; even Zeus 'gave them the greatest honor'.; The seat of assembly — Gods and mortals alike gather 'by Thémis' when they convene lawfully — her name is the Greek word for the lawful convocation itself. Thémis's myths are myths of legitimacy — who may hold an oracle, who may marry whom, and what order survives a flood. A Titaness of the first generation, she appears wherever the question is not 'what is powerful?' but 'what is right?' Homer swears by her; Aeschylus seats her at Delphi; Pindar makes her save the cosmos with a single prophecy. Genealogy: The Titaness Who Married Order to Power Hesiod enrolls Thémis among the twelve Titans — a daughter of Ouranos and Gaia born at the very beginning of the ordered cosmos ( Theogony 132–136) — and then gives her the most consequential marriage of the succession. Zeus 'lay with Themis, who bore him the Horae : Good Order (Eunomía), Justice (Díkē), and flourishing Peace (Eirḗnē), who watch over the works of mortal men; and the Moirai , to whom wise Zeus gave the greatest honor' ( Theogony 901–906). The pairing is the poem's thesis in miniature: the new Olympian king weds not a war prize but Order itself , and their children are the very forces that make civilized life possible. Even the Fates — sternest of powers — are born of this union, as if destiny itself were part of the design. Through Thémis, Zeus's reign is legitimized: he does not merely conquer the cosmos; he marries its law. Delphi: The Keeper of the Oracle The Pythia opens Aeschylus' Eumenides with a genealogy of her own altar: 'first, in this prayer, I honor Earth, the eldest of the gods, who brought me forth; then Themis , for she, they say, was the next to hold this seat, her daughter as she was; and third, with Themis' good will and none by force, another Titan, Phoebe... gave it as a birthday gift to Phoebus' (1–8). The scene is astonishing in what it omits: no Apollo seizes Delphi — the oracle passes by inheritance and gift , from mother to daughter to sister, until it reaches the god. Athens' most sacred institution is thus traced not to violence but to succession law, and Thémis stands at its center as the first rightful keeper. The trilogy that invents the jury-trial opens, fittingly, with a chain of legitimate title — the oldest property record in Europe is an oracle, and its second owner is Thémis . Prophecy: The Warning about Thetis All mortal life owed its safety to a piece of advice Thémis once gave Zeus. The sea-goddess Thetis was so beautiful that both Zeus and Poseidon desired her — until, Pindar says ( Isthmian 8.26–47), Themis revealed the secret : whoever wed Thetis would father a son stronger than his father. The gods instantly withdrew; Thetis was married off to the mortal Peleus, and her child was Achilles — destined to be 'a warrior son, mightier than his father', as the scholiasts spell out what Pindar leaves implied. Aeschylus assigns the same warning to Themis and Gaia ( Prometheus Bound 873–900), Apollodorus (3.13.5) to Themis alone — the sources agree on the prophecy, not on its prophet. Either way, the myth's logic is pure Thémis: the law of succession is the oldest law of all , and even Zeus governs by foresight, not force. The Titaness saves the universe with a single well-timed disclosure. After the Flood: Deucalion at Her Oracle When Zeus flooded the world and only Deucalion and Pyrrha survived, the couple drifted to Parnassus and climbed to the oracle of Thémis — in Apollodorus' version (1.7.2) they pray to her by name — and ask how the human race might be restored. The goddess answers in a riddle: leave the temple, veil your heads, loosen your robes, and cast 'the bones of your great mother' behind you. Pyrrha blanches at the impiety — until Deucalion decodes it: the Great Mother is Earth, and her bones are stones . They throw the stones; the hard ones become men, the softer ones women. Ovid ( Metamorphoses 1.381–415) retells the scene with Thémis presiding — and adds that the new humanity, born of stone, is a tougher breed than the first. The myth gives law an origin story of its own: after the flood, the first thing humanity rebuilds is not fire or shelter but an oracle — the place where right answers come from . Syncretism: Rome made no translation of Thémis — her name crossed into Latin unchanged, a rarity among the Titans, which tells us how abstractly the Romans took her: not a foreign goddess to be matched but a concept to be quoted. Cicero treats her as personified divine law, and late antique, medieval, and Renaissance art gradually fused her with Justitia , the Roman Justice whose scales and sword became the standard attributes of Lady Justice from the sixteenth century onward. The courthouse allegory of modernity — the robed figure with balanced scales — descends from this merger rather than from any classical cult image of Themis alone. In the Latin West her second life was thus juridical: she became the face the law chose for itself. Cultural legacy: Every courthouse statue of a robed woman with scales descends from Thémis — filtered through Justitia and the Renaissance, but unmistakably the Titaness who made order divine. Her name passed directly into modern institutions: asteroid 24 Themis (1853), NASA's THEMIS mission (2007), and countless law reviews and legal institutes. In the Greek world her name lived on as a word for lawful right — Homer has mortals and gods act 'by thémis' — and in the modern imagination she stands for the principle that law is not invented but recognized: what is right is discovered, not made . Restoring Thémis restores the name of the oldest idea in law. Extended meditation: Thémis is the most important figure in this lexicon that almost no one remembers. She has no epic adventures, no metamorphoses, no loves. She is simply what is established — the way things are rightly done, before anyone wrote it down. The Greeks could see that custom preceded law, that the unwritten order held where decrees failed, and they gave that order a mother: a Titaness, born before Zeus, honored after him. There is something quietly radical in making order a goddess rather than a king. Kings die; Thémis remains. When Aeschylus traces the Delphi oracle through her hands, he is tracing legitimacy itself — the idea that authority is valid only when held rightly. In an age that writes new constitutions every decade, Thémis asks a harder question: what do you already know is right, before you vote on it?

title: Urcaguary
text: Urcaguary: Underworld Jewels Urcaguary is the Inca guardian of what lies beneath the mountains: gold, silver, emeralds and the other precious things sealed in the earth. The figure is known only through the colonial chronicle tradition and later folklore, and the sources are late, brief and partly modern — but they agree on the core: the underground hoard has a watcher, and it is not a vault, it is a god. Guardian of the Hoard: Beneath the mountains Urcaguary keeps the metals and gems of the inner earth; the traditional description hangs gold chains and precious stones from the serpent's tail. The Serpent with a Deer's Head: The figure takes the body of a serpent and the head of a taruka, the Andean deer — wealth that watches and thinks like a mountain animal. He of the Underground: The name reads from Quechua urqu, ‘within the earth’, and quri, ‘gold’: the title is the domain, and the domain is the treasury. The Treasure That Judges: The hoard belongs to the guardian, not the miner: in the moral economy of the Andean mine, gold is taken only as tribute, never as theft. Symbols: Gold chains — Hung from the serpent's tail in the chroniclers' descriptions — wealth worn as the guardian's own ornament; Emeralds and precious stones — The green gems of the Andes stored in the subterranean house the serpent keeps; The taruka (Andean deer) head — The alert head he wears: the deer of the high puna, watchful and unreachable; The serpent body — The winding form that coils through the veins of ore inside the mountains; The mountain vault — Every sealed vein and hidden pocket of ore is a door of his treasury Urcaguary has no surviving epic. The sources are late, brief and partly modern, and honesty requires saying so plainly. What the tradition preserves is a portrait rather than a cycle: a serpent-bodied watcher below the mountains, a theology of treasure, and a mining etiquette that is still practiced in the Andes. The Chronicles: A God Seen Through Colonial Eyes Everything securely known about Urcaguary descends from the chroniclers writing after the conquest — above all Martín de Murúa, whose Historia general del Piru (1616) catalogues the gods of the Andes, and Bernabé Cobo, whose Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653) preserves the most orderly account of the Inca huacas. In their pages Urcaguary appears as the deity of metals, jewels and the other precious things hidden underground — a figure who presided over ore-rich mountains and mining shrines, but whose cult left no standing temple and whose myths were never written down in Quechua. The colonial writers worked decades after the religion they described had been outlawed, from informants under missionary pressure, so their catalogues are triage documents as much as testimonies. Read that way, Urcaguary is half-known by necessity: a god glimpsed through the gap between destroyed shrines and Spanish notebooks. The temple built here is therefore a temple over an archive, not over a ruin. The Watcher: The Serpent in the Veins of Gold Later tradition gives the figure a body. Urcaguary is pictured as a great serpent with the head of a taruka, the Andean deer, gold chains and precious stones linked along the tail, dwelling beneath the mountains in the uku pacha, the world within the earth. The deer's head is explained as a mark of the guardian's way of thinking — alert, swift, impossible to catch — and in the same layer of folklore the guardian serpent of the depths, Hurkaway, is identified with Urcaguary: the snake that coils through the ore veins is the treasure's own watchman made visible. The image is exact theology in zoological form. A vault guards wealth with walls; a serpent guards it with intention. The Andes buried their treasure in the most guarded shape the animal world offers. The Miners: Offering Before the Blast The etiquette the colonial writers describe at mining shrines still survives in the Andes, where ethnographers from the twentieth century to the present record miners pouring chicha, laying coca leaves and burning cigarettes for the powers of the mine before a single charge is set — the same ritual courtesy, the ch'alla, that crews in Potosí and the central Andes pay to the lord of the mountain and to the Tío, the old one of the deep workings. Urcaguary stands behind this courtesy as its theological ground: the underground metals belong first to the guardian, and gifts earn a share. Mining, in this ethics, is not extraction but tribute. The rite turns an act of violence into a negotiation, and that is the whole lesson of the god: the earth parts for those who ask and swallows those who only take. The Lesson: The Gold That Cannot Be Stolen The tradition's moral edge is aimed at thieves: Urcaguary protects the hoard from evil people who dare to steal it. After the conquest, when the ransom of Atahualpa filled a room with gold and the furnaces of Cuzco and Cajamarca melted down the sun god's garden and the huancas of the shrines, Andean storytellers had every reason to sharpen the point — the metal pried from the temples was only surface; the deep treasure has a serpent on watch, and it does not travel. Whether the tale circulated in exactly this form in the sixteenth century cannot now be shown, but the sentiment is old and Andean: gold is not owned, it is kept. It is the theology of every robbed sanctuary, and it is also simply true: the empire's gold crossed the ocean; the guardian's never left the mountain. Syncretism: Urcaguary's afterlife is a history of translations. Colonial missionaries folded the spirits of the uku pacha into Christian demonology — Supay, lord of the inner world, became the very word for devil in Quechua — while the miners kept the old courtesies under new names. The serpent body invited comparison with the amaru , the sacred Andean serpent of water, earth and the underworld, and in regional folklore the two guardians of the deep merge and separate: sometimes the amaru carries the treasure, sometimes Urcaguary carries the amaru's shape. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century compilations detached the figure from cult context entirely, presenting it as a ‘god of treasure’ in the European fairy-hoard sense, and modern summaries go further still, calling the gender ambiguous — a flattening the chronicles, which say little either way, cannot support. Read through all three layers, Urcaguary is best understood as the Inca theology of subterranean wealth caught mid-translation into European categories. Cultural legacy: The etiquette Urcaguary presides over is alive: Andean miners still offer coca, alcohol and smoke to the mountain and to the Tío of the workings before blasting, a rite documented ethnographically from Potosí across Bolivia and Peru for over a century. In folklore collections the name circulates as the guardian of hidden treasure — the tesoros ocultos whose gold turns to leaves in the hands of the unworthy, a pan-Andean motif his serpent keeps. In the museums of Cuzco and Lima the legacy is an absence: the gold and silver he hypothetically guarded, described at length by Cobo and Murúa, was melted into ingots within decades of the conquest, and his treasury survives only as chronicle. For Quechua language revival the name's elements remain living words — urqu , the mountain, and quri , gold — so the god's title is still pronounceable as a sentence of modern Quechua. Extended meditation: What does it mean that a civilization gave its wealth a god? The Greeks gave Hermes to commerce and the Romans gave Juno Moneta to the mint; the Inca gave Urcaguary to gold that was still in the earth. That choice contains a complete economics. Gold's natural place, the figure says, is inside the mountain, where it is sacred; extraction is not sin but negotiation, and the negotiation never ends, because ownership never begins. The serpent with the deer's head is posted at a boundary the modern world refuses to see — the line between the surface we live on and the interior we dig into. Every blast re-asks his question in dynamite grammar: did you ask, or did you only take? A civilization that must give its minerals a guardian has admitted something the ledger never records.

title: Vasubandhu
text: Vasubandhu: Abhidharma Vasubandhu is the great systematizer of Buddhist philosophy : author of the Abhidharmakośa, the encyclopedia of Abhidharma that every later school had to answer, and, with his half-brother Asaṅga, co-founder of the Yogācāra, the 'Mind-Only' school that reshaped Mahāyāna thought from India to Japan. The Kośa Verse: Six hundred verses of Abhidharmakośa kārikā summarizing the entire Sarvāstivāda analysis of mind, matter, and liberation. Abhidharma: His auto-commentary made the Kośa the standard curriculum: studied in Nālandā, debated in Tibet, translated in China by Xuanzang. Yogācāra: The Twenty and Thirty Verses argue the world is 'mind-only' — the doctrine his Kośa-era Sautrāntika readers found hardest to accept. The Conversion: Legend says his brother Asaṅga sent him a begging letter: compassion, not argument, turned the Kośa's author toward the Mahāyāna. Symbols: The Kośa stanza — A verse (kārikā) whose eight-syllable lines hold whole Abhidharma treatises — scholarship compressed into memorable sound; The begging bowl — The monk's only equipment; Vasubandhu remained a bhikṣu all his life even while moving courts and schools; The letter from Asaṅga — In the Tibetan biographies, the note that converted him — affection and mortality doing what doctrine could not; Treasury (kośa) — The storehouse metaphor of the Abhidharmakośa: every dharma catalogued like treasure in a vault, each with its own nature Vasubandhu was a historical philosopher, not a mythological figure — a monk of Puruṣapura (Peshawar) who, the early Tibetan biographies say, wrote the Abhidharmakośa as a Sarvāstivādin critic and then embraced the Yogācāra Mahāyāna of his half-brother Asaṅga. His 'myths' are the legends his tradition grew around a real life. The Kośa: Three Years in Seclusion The Tibetan biographies recount that Vasubandhu withdrew into seclusion to master the Abhidharma of the Kashmir Sarvāstivādins, and emerged with the Abhidharmakośa — six hundred verses (kārikā) of flawless eight-syllable metre that summarized the entire system. When the Kashmir masters admired the verses but missed their own subtlety, he added an auto-commentary (bhāṣya) of his own in which, tradition says, he quietly refuted them. The Kośa became what it remains: the one Abhidharma text every later school — Theravāda, Mahāyāna, and the Tibetan lineages — had to study, debate, or answer, translated in its entirety into Chinese by Xuanzang and memorized in fragments by generations of monks from Kashmir to Kyoto. Its author's own allegiance was already drifting as he wrote: the commentary, tradition says, shows the Sautrāntika reservations that would later make his conversion credible. To condense a library into verse, and the verse into a single lifetime, is the legend's whole point: scholarship can be a kind of asceticism. Conversion: The Begging Letter of Asaṅga Vasubandhu had mocked the Mahāyāna as a corruption of the Buddha's teaching, calling its scriptures fabrications. His elder half-brother Asaṅga, already a great Yogācāra teacher, sent him no rebuttal — only a note reporting that he was dying, and begging Vasubandhu to recite the Mahāyāna sūtras for him. Struck by the affection of the request, Vasubandhu read them, found them profound, and entered the Mahāyāna himself. The story is hagiography — no Indian source records it independently — yet it encodes the tradition's own account of its greatest conversion: Vasubandhu did not abandon analysis for devotion. He turned the same razor-sharp mind to the 'mind-only' philosophy, composing the Twenty Verses (Viṁśikā) and the Thirty Verses (Triṁśikā) that define the Yogācāra, and the two halves of his career became one continuous argument about how carefully the world must be taken apart before it can be seen whole. The Debate: The Victory over Vasurāta The biographies carry Vasubandhu to the courts of northern India, where the grammarian-philosopher Vasurāta, champion of an opposing school, had humiliated all comers. Vasubandhu entered the contest — the tradition describes a great assembly of rival teachers and lay patrons gathered to watch — and his opponent was worsted. After the debate he was offered a great patron's gold — and the legends insist that, as a monk, he spent the wealth on works of benefit to the saṅgha and on gifts to the poor. The story matters less as history than as the template it sets: the philosopher's victory is measured not in refutation but in what the victor refuses to keep. Every medieval debate culture of the Buddhist world — Nālandā's, Tibet's, Japan's — repeated this scene with Vasubandhu's name in it, and his reputation as the undefeated champion of two successive orthodoxies made the later conversion legend necessary: only love, the tradition decided, could have beaten him. The Problem: One Vasubandhu or Two? Modern scholarship has had to ask whether one man could have written both the Kośa's analytical Abhidharma and the Yogācāra's visionary metaphysics. Erich Frauwallner (1951) argued the dates fit a single long life; others have proposed two Vasubandhus — the Yogācāra co-founder and a later Kośa author — and the question is still argued in the journals. The tradition itself never doubted: one Vasubandhu, brother of Asaṅga, whose conversion joined the two oeuvres into a single career — and the hagiographies even extend that life into legend, saying he ended it in the Pure Land of Amitābha, or in Nepal, depending on which strand one follows. The modern debate is itself a tribute: few ancient authors are so prolific and so consistent in brilliance that posterity must ask whether they were two people. Syncretism: Vasubandhu's legacy is the creation of a pan-Asian scholastic commons. In China, Xuanzang's pilgrimage was undertaken substantially to resolve disputes over the Kośa, and his massive translation of 649–660 CE made Vasubandhu the doctrinal backbone of the Faxiang (Consciousness-Only) school. In Japan the Hossō school of Nara claimed him as its patriarch, while the Kyoto lineages of the future would read his Viṁśikā as the foundation of 'mind-only' meditations. In Tibet every monastery curriculum begins with the Kośa. Modern comparative philosophy — from Thich Nhat Hanh's engaged Buddhism to analytic treatments of idealism — still frames its questions in his vocabulary. He is perhaps the only ancient philosopher whose works are simultaneously a living liturgy, a graduate textbook, and a modern research programme. Cultural legacy: The Abhidharmakośa never went out of use: it has been memorized, commented, and debated continuously for some fifteen centuries, from Nālandā to the great Tibetan commentarial traditions (Prajñākaramati's and Yaśomitra's subcommentaries in Sanskrit; Sthiramati's in the mind-only line). Its author is honored as a patriarch in China and Japan, and Tibetan debate courtyards still open with his verses. In the modern academy Vasubandhu anchors the study of Buddhist philosophy — his Viṁśikā is a standard text in courses on philosophy of mind, cited in debates about idealism and representation. A brahmin-born monk of Gandhāra thus became one of the most-read authors in human history, his name a byword for the possibility that analysis itself can be a path to compassion. Extended meditation: Vasubandhu is the scholar as religious figure — proof that in the Buddhist world, thinking carefully was itself a sacred practice. His two careers look like a contradiction: the great classifier of the mind's parts, then the teacher who said the parts and the world they compose are 'mind-only'. Read together, they form one argument: you must take the world apart completely before you can see what holds it together. His legend conversion turns not on a vision but on a letter from a dying brother — intellect bending at last to love. Modern philosophy of mind still returns to his Viṁśikā, where a dream, a reflection, and the waking world are made to trade places in a few pages. Few ancient authors remain so contemporary: the question of what the world is made of, and whether mind is on the list, is still his question.

title: Veles
text: Veles: Cattle Veles — Volos to the East Slavs — is the god of cattle and wealth, of the underworld's moist depths, and, in the great reconstruction of Ivanov and Toporov, of poetry and magic. Where Perun strikes from above, Veles moves below: through herds, graves, bargains, and song. Lord of Cattle: The chronicles gloss him explicitly: Volos, 'the cattle god' — herders swore their oaths by him alone. The Underworld River: He rules the wet, root-filled depths beneath the world-tree: the realm of the dead and of hidden treasure. God of Poetry: In the reconstructed mythology he is patron of singers and sorcerers; the wandering volkhvy acted in his name. Adversary of Perun: The eternal enemy in the myth-cycle: thief of cattle, storm of wealth, struck down each spring by the thunderer's bolt. Symbols: Cattle horns — The herds that were his treasure and the sign under which herders and merchants swore; The serpent — His disguise in the myth-cycle: low, wet, and close to the earth — the eternal adversary of the eagle; The bear — His chthonic animal in the alternating lore of the Slavic year — master of the wilderness beyond the fence; Gusli (harp) — The instrument of the singer he protects; in folklore the magic fiddle makes even the forest dance; Wet earth and roots — The moist underworld into which he withdraws and from which wealth returns Veles has no surviving epic. His dossier is a chronicle oath here, a famine there, and — towering over the fragments — the modern reconstruction by Ivanov and Toporov of the myth-cycle in which he is the thunderer's eternal adversary. Read together, the fragments describe a god of everything that grows, burrows, and accrues out of sight. Oath-text: Sworn by Volos The Rus'-Byzantine treaty of 944, copied into the Primary Chronicle, has left the only verbatim ritual text of pre-Christian Rus'. For the clauses of war the envoys swear by Perun; for everything touching livestock — sale, theft, compensation — they swear by Volos alone, and the curse on the perjurer is total: 'may we be cursed by the god in whom we believe, by Perun and Volos, the furred one... may we not be protected by our shields, may we be slain by our own swords, may we be shot by our own arrows.' A later copyist glossed the unfamiliar name for his readers: 'Volos — that is, the cattle god.' The division of labor is the myth in miniature: the sky-god witnesses between warriors, while the god of herds and wealth underwrites the peasant's entire fortune, animal by animal. Where your property lives, there your god is invoked. The Famine: The Angry God of Suzdal In the terrible famine year of 1024, the Primary Chronicle (s.a. 6532) tells how wandering sorcerers came to Suzdal' and announced the cause of the people's misery: 'It is the god Veles who is angry.' The volkhvy demanded the sacrifice of a youth — a red-haired one, they specified, from a particular kin — and when the killing was done, they ate the body. The bishop of Rostov rode in, arrested the sorcerers, and drowned them in the Volga. The tale is told by Christian enemies, and its details are horrific precisely in order to damn the old religion; yet its center is precious evidence. A generation after the baptism, when the official gods were Perun's rivals long drowned, it was still Veles whose name a prophet reached for when the earth would not feed her children. The underworld god was the one who explained hunger. Reconstruction: The Theft of the Cattle In the reconstruction of Ivanov and Toporov, Slavic mythology's central cycle runs like this: Veles, dwelling in the underworld beneath the world-tree, commits a crime against the sky — he steals Perun's cattle, his treasure, sometimes his bride. Perun descends in pursuit, hurling his bolts; Veles transforms and wriggles — serpent, catfish, black eel — and each spring the thunderer strikes him down, and the rain returns to the herds. No East Slavic manuscript tells this story; it survives in the pairing of the gods in the treaty oaths, in wedding laments where the bride weeps for a brother struck or drowned, in South Slavic spring songs, and in the universal Indo-European pattern of the storm-god and the serpent. The scholars who built it were explicit that they were reconstructing — and the pieces fit with a stubbornness no rival hypothesis has matched. Cult Memory: Volos's Street Novgorod kept Veles in its very street plan. Birchbark letters of the eleventh and twelfth centuries — mundane shopping lists and debt notes scratched by ordinary citizens — give addresses on Volosova ulica , 'Volos's street', the commercial quarter by the market. No chronicle mentions it; the god's presence in the townscape was simply assumed, a neighborhood named for him the way others were named for craftsmen. When we read a debtor promise to pay on Volos's street, we watch the cult outliving the conversion in the least sacred of registers: commerce. Perun got treaties, curses, and weeping crowds; Veles got the marketplace — which may be the more honest monument, since people swore by the thunderer but they lived by the herder. A street, unlike a statue, has to be used to survive — and Volosova ulica was used every market day for a hundred years after the gods went under. Syncretism: Veles's Christian afterlife ran through the saints of the herd. In the Balkans he survives in Sveti Vlaho — Saint Blaise — the Dalmatian patron of cattle whose feast ends with animals blessed in his name; in Russia the same role fell to Saint Vlasiy, whose name is simply Veles re-clothed. The divine adversary was absorbed too: the serpent of the myth-cycle slithered into dragon-slayer legends, and Perun's spring victory was reassigned to Saint George and Elijah. Byzantine-educated writers performed interpretatio on the pantheon as a whole, while comparative scholarship drew bolder lines — Toporov's Veles–Varuna, the Norse Óðinn of poetry and the dead, Hermes as god of herds and boundary-crossings — each a hypothesis about what sort of god this was: sovereign of everything the sky does not see. Demonized in the languages (Czech veles gave way to čert for 'devil'), he remained the underworld's landlord in folklore down to the modern era. Cultural legacy: Veles endures most durably in words: toponyms like Volosovo across the Russian north, the Dalmatian cult of Sveti Vlaho, the devil-haunted velnias of Lithuanian folklore, and the root itself in Slavic speech. Folklore kept his portfolio — treasure guarded by a chthonic serpent, the magic fiddle of the singer who bargains below, oaths sworn over a herd at market. The nineteenth and twentieth centuries were less kind: the so-called Book of Veles , publicized in the 1950s, purports to be a pre-Christian epic of his people and is now universally judged a modern forgery — a tribute, of a crooked kind, to how badly moderns wanted the lost god back. Rodnover communities today honor Veles as lord of wisdom, wealth, and the written word, and his serpent still guards vaults in banks' logos and fantasy novels alike. Extended meditation: Veles is the god of the other economy. Perun owns everything visible — the strike, the oath, the battle won — but Veles owns what accumulates quietly: calves, coins, verses, graves. He is the patron of everyone who works below the threshold of glory: the herder, the merchant, the poet, the sorcerer, the dead. His mythology, reconstructed stitch by stitch by modern scholars, tells of a being who is defeated every spring and never finally destroyed — which is exactly the biography of wealth, and of life itself returning from underground. There is something subversive in his survival. The chronicles drown his sorcerers in the Volga, demonize his name, and reassign his cattle to Saint Blaise; and meanwhile ordinary Novgorodians keep doing business on his street, in writing, for centuries. Veles teaches that the underworld is not the opposite of prosperity but its storehouse: everything valuable is buried for a season, and the god of the deep is the one who remembers where.

title: Wiraqucha
text: Wiraqucha: Creator Wiraqucha is the maker of the Inca cosmos: sky father, creator of sun and moon, and the weeping wanderer who once walked the length of the Andes and was never seen again. The chroniclers knew him as the invisible god who made the world and then withdrew from it — and his name still survives in the politest word an Andean elder can offer a stranger: wiraqucha , sir, gentleman, lord. Sacred Name: The name compounds Quechua wira, 'fat, foam,' and qucha, 'lake, sea'; the chroniclers glossed it 'lake of fat,' more evocatively 'foam of the sea.' Creator: Maker of the sun, moon, and stars and of every nation; to the Andes he is Pachayachachic, 'creator of the world.' Living Tradition: Honored at Titicaca, Tiwanaku, and Cusco; his cult outlived the empire and endures in solstice pilgrimage, shrine, and everyday address. Unicode Restoration: Preserved as a flagship temple; the scholarly restoration Wiraqucha replaces the colonial spelling Viracocha with modern Quechua orthography. Symbols: Sea foam of the lake — The etymon wira-qucha, 'foam (or fat) of the lake' — the foam from which the name, and the god, emerged; The staff and traveler's bundle — He crossed the Andes as a staff-carrying beggar, weeping at springs and prophesying — the god as itinerant stranger; The reed float — The totora-reed float that bore the two survivors of the flood — the seed of the remade world; The stone models of Tiwanaku — The sculpted prototypes of every nation, from which Wiraqucha shaped humankind at his workshop; The golden image of Cusco — The solid-gold statue in the Coricancha, described by Cobo and Murúa and melted down within years of the conquest Wiraqucha's mythology reaches us only through the reports of conquered lords to Spanish chroniclers — Betanzos, Cobo, Sarmiento — yet it holds together a coherent cosmic biography: the making of the world, the flood that erased its first people, the shaping of the nations at Tiwanaku, and a final journey westward that ended in disappearance. Betanzos ch. 1: The Flood of Unu Pachakuti Juan de Betanzos, whose Suma y Narración de los Incas (1551) is the fullest early account, tells that Wiraqucha made the first people at Tiwanaku and gave them the world to keep; but they grew proud and lived without worship, so he resolved to undo them. He sent a great flood — unu pachakuti , a watery overturning of the world — that drowned the first race, the wari, while he himself rose into the sky above Titicaca. Yet he spared two, a man and a woman, calling them from the waters onto a float of totora reeds near the island, and commissioning them as the ancestors of a new humanity. The myth fixes the shape of Andean time: catastrophe and renewal in cycles, a world unmade and remade, with the creator always watching from above. It is also a charter for the lake itself — Titicaca is not scenery but the hinge where the first world ended and the second began. Cobo 13.3: The Making of Nations at Tiwanaku Father Bernabé Cobo's Historia del Nuevo Mundo (Book 13) preserves the imperial version: after the flood, Wiraqucha set to work at Tiwanaku, where he sculpted the forms of all the nations to come — each with its own face, dress, language, songs, and seeds — and brought them to life. When the work was done he dispatched them, calling them out of caves, springs, and rivers to find their homelands: one nation he sent by way of a cave, another along a river's course, and to the Inca ancestors he gave the special charge that would lead them at last to Cusco. Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa's Historia Indica (ch. 6–7) gives the same program and adds the full titulature: Ticci Uiracocha Pachayachachic, 'ancient foundation, creator of the world.' The myth is a map of the Andes read backward — every people is the deliberate work of the same hand, and the Inca are simply the nation that remembered best who made them. Sarmiento ch. 7: The Sun, Moon, and Stars The same accounts make Wiraqucha the maker of the sky. On the island of Titicaca in the great lake he fashioned the Sun — Inti — and the Moon, and set the stars in their courses, appointing the Sun the most honored of all, 'like a rich ornament' among the rest (Sarmiento de Gamboa, ch. 7; Cobo 13.3). In imperial theology Inti then became the visible ancestor of the Inca dynasties, while Wiraqucha remained the invisible maker behind the visible god — a two-tier heaven in which the sun was, as it were, the son, and the emperor the sun's line. The pairing let Cusco worship a present, national god without ever forgetting the older, unbounded one above and behind him. It is one of the few world mythologies in which the supreme creator deliberately steps back from the machinery of daily rule, delegating the visible sky to his own workmanship and reserving for himself only the authorship of everything. Betanzos ch. 2: The Weeping Stranger Betanzos closes the biography with Wiraqucha's departure. The maker walked the length of the Andes in the dress of a poor traveler, staff in hand, teaching as he went and weeping at springs; in the province of the Canchis he wept, foretelling that men dressed exactly as he was — bearded strangers from across the sea — would one day come and overturn the land. He came as far as the region of Manta on the coast and then, Betanzos says, passed into the sea and was gone. The detail is breathtaking in hindsight: a colonial-era text, written within twenty years of Pizarro, preserving a native prophecy that fits the conquest like a glove — and whatever its origin, the story made Wiraqucha the god who knew the strangers before they arrived. A maker who weeps over the future of his own work is a rare figure in any pantheon; the Andes kept him. Syncretism: Spanish missionaries moved quickly to identify Wiraqucha with the Christian God: Father Bernabé Cobo reports Andean lords hearing the gospel and concluding that this Dios must be their own Pachayachachic, finally named.
