His children, not he, are painted on vases; his wife, not he, is invoked when the gods swear their mightiest oath. He is the infrastructure of myth: present everywhere, visible nowhere. To meditate on Pállas is to ask what in our own world works the same way — the disciplines and crafts on which everything depends and whose names nobody knows. The spear is brandished; the brandisher is forgotten. Perhaps that is the truest thing the Titans teach: the old order does not always die fighting. Sometimes it is quietly outlived, married into the new one, and remembered only in its children's names. Original script note: The name is attested in Greek as Πάλλας . The acute accent falls on the first alpha. PUNICODEX restores this as Pállas ; the ASCII form 'pallas' flattens the pitch accent that ancient Greek speakers would have heard.

title: Original script provenance: Zeús
text: Original script for Zeús: Ζεύς Script: Greek Transliteration: Zeús Steps: The Greek form Ζεύς is attested from Mycenaean di-we / Diwos and Homeric Greek. The initial Ζ- in Attic represents the voiced affricate [zd], preserving the PIE cluster *dy- from *dyēws 'sky, god of the sky'. The diphthong ευ is long for accentual purposes and carries the acute accent, producing the single pitch peak Zeús. The final -ς is the nominative singular ending of the archaic stem *dyēu-s. title: Original script provenance: Rꜥ
text: Original script for Rꜥ: 𓂋𓂝𓇳 Script: Hieroglyphs Transliteration: Rꜥ Steps: The name is written rꜥ (𓂋𓂝) with the sun-disk (𓇳) as a determinative/rebus for 'sun'. The consonantal skeleton r-ꜥ is vocalised as Ra in Egyptological convention; the original vocalisation is unknown. Coptic ⲣⲏ provides a late phonetic reflex. From the New Kingdom onward Ra is frequently combined with Amun as Amun-Ra. Sources: [object Object], [object Object], [object Object]

title: Original script provenance: Śiva
text: Original script for Śiva: शिव Script: Devanagari Transliteration: Śiva Steps: Sanskrit Śiva is written शिव in Devanagari. The aksaras are शि (śi) and व (va); the inherent /a/ of व is phonetically reduced in connected speech. The name means 'the auspicious one', an epithet that rises from Vedic Rudra to become one of the supreme deities of Hinduism. IAST Ś retains the haček convention; Devanagari श is a palatal sibilant. Sources: [object Object], [object Object], [object Object]

title: Original script provenance: Lóng
text: Original script for Lóng: 龍 Script: Chinese characters Transliteration: Lóng Steps: The Chinese character 龍 (simplified 龙) represents the dragon, a central cosmological creature in Chinese religion and imperial symbolism. Modern Mandarin reading is lóng (second tone), written in Pinyin with an acute accent. Old Chinese reconstructions include *C-rjoŋ or *mə-roŋ (Baxter-Sagart); the initial consonant cluster is debated. The Unicode restoration Lóng preserves the Mandarin tone mark; the ASCII form loses tone and therefore meaning-distinctive information. Sources: [object Object], [object Object], [object Object]

title: Original script provenance: Nikkō
text: Original script for Nikkō: 日光 Script: Japanese characters Transliteration: Nikkō Steps: 日光 is a Sino-Japanese compound: 日 'sun' + 光 'light', hence 'sunlight'. The standard Hepburn romanisation is Nikkō, with a macron over the final o marking a long vowel. The geminate consonant -kk- reflects the sequential voicing assimilation of 日 (nichi) + 光 (kō) → Nikkō. The place name Nikkō is famous for the Tōshō-gū shrine, dedicated to Tokugawa Ieyasu. Sources: [object Object], [object Object], [object Object]

title: Original script provenance: Dāwîḏ
text: Original script for Dāwîḏ: דָּוִד Script: Hebrew Transliteration: Dāwîḏ Steps: The Masoretic spelling דָּוִד (Dāwîḏ) is preserved in the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia. The first dalet carries a dagesh (דּ) because it follows a silent shewa at the beginning of the word, marking the stop /d/. The vav (ו) with qāmeṣ and ḥīreq points indicates the diphthongal sequence /awī/. The name is traditionally explained as from the root d-w-d 'beloved', though some scholars connect it to a Northwest Semitic theophoric element. title: Original script provenance: Ahriman
text: Original script for Ahriman: 𐬀𐬢𐬭𐬀 𐬨𐬀𐬌𐬥𐬌𐬌𐬎 Script: Avestan Transliteration: aŋra mainiiu Steps: Written aŋra mainiiu in the Avesta (Gathic nom. aŋrō mainiiuš, Yasna 45.2; Younger form at Vendidad 19.1) The Younger spelling writes the ending with two i-letters (…mainiiu) 'Ahriman' is the Middle Persian (Pahlavi) development of the same name Sources: Yasna 45.2, Vendidad 19.1

title: Original script provenance: Ašavahišta
text: Original script for Ašavahišta: 𐬀𐬴𐬀 𐬬𐬀𐬵𐬌𐬱𐬙𐬀 Script: Avestan Transliteration: aṣ̌a vahišta Steps: Written aṣ̌a vahišta in the Avesta; the Aṣ̌əm Vohū prayer gives the oblique forms aṣ̌əm… vahištəm ṣ̌ is written 𐬴 (SSHE) and š 𐬱 (SHE) Sources: The Gathas (Amesha Spenta tradition), Aṣ̌əm Vohū prayer

title: Original script provenance: Serapis
text: Original script for Serapis: 𓊨𓁹𓀭𓎛𓐑𓊪𓃒 Script: Egyptian hieroglyphs Transliteration: wsjr-ḥp Steps: Serapis is written wsjr-ḥp, 'Osiris-Apis', at the Memphite Serapeum The bull determinative (E1) marks the Apis; Demotic wsjr-ḥp becomes Coptic ⲟⲩⲥⲉⲣϩⲁⲡⲓ, whence Greek Σάραπις Sources: Serapeum inscriptions (Late Period/Ptolemaic)

title: Original script provenance: Harpokrátēs
text: Original script for Harpokrátēs: 𓅃𓏤𓊪𓄡𓂋𓂧𓀔 Script: Egyptian hieroglyphs Transliteration: ḥr-pꜣ-ẖrd Steps: Written ḥr-pꜣ-ẖrd, 'Horus the Child', on the Horus-on-the-Crocodiles cippi and throughout Late Period texts The ꜣ of pꜣ is unwritten in this spelling — the normal convention The child determinative (A17) closes the name; Greek rendered it Ἁρποκράτης Sources: Horus-on-the-Crocodiles cippi (Late Period)

title: Original script provenance: Onuris
text: Original script for Onuris: 𓏎𓈖𓁷𓂋𓏏𓈐𓅆 Script: Egyptian hieroglyphs Transliteration: ỉn-ḥrt Steps: Written ỉn-ḥrt, 'He who brings back the Distant One', the standard theonym of Thinis Greek rendered the name Ἀνουρις / Ὀνουρις, whence the modern form Onuris Sources: Standard theonym of Thinis (Greek Ἀνουρις)

title: Original script provenance: Wyrd
text: Original script for Wyrd: ᚹᚣᚱᛞ Script: Anglo-Saxon Futhorc Transliteration: wyrd Steps: Wyrd is abundantly attested in Old English manuscripts (Beowulf, The Wanderer) — in Latin script with wynn (ƿyrd), not in runes No Futhorc inscription of the word is known; this rendering is a normalized phonetic reconstruction, not an attested inscription Sources: Beowulf / The Wanderer (manuscript attestations), normalized Futhorc reconstruction

title: Original script provenance: Cerēs

title: Original script provenance: Tōnatiuh
text: Original script for Tōnatiuh: Tōnatiuh Script: Colonial Nahuatl (Latin script) Transliteration: Tōnatiuh Steps: Nahuatl was recorded by Spanish and native scribes in Latin alphabets from the sixteenth century onward. Tōnatiuh is the sun deity; the name is attested in the Florentine Codex and colonial devotional texts. The macron marks a long vowel in scholarly Classical Nahuatl orthography. The Unicode restoration Tōnatiuh preserves the long vowel; there is no indigenous logographic spelling for the personal name. Sources: Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Karttunen, An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl

title: Original script provenance: Odùduwà
text: Original script for Odùduwà: Òdùduwà Script: Yoruba (modern Latin orthography) Transliteration: Òdùduwà Steps: Yoruba has been written in the Latin alphabet since the 1840s, with diacritics for tone and vowel quality. The underdot marks the open vowels /ɛ, ɔ/ and the postalveolar fricative /ʃ/; these are the obligatory phonemic marks. Tone marks (grave low, acute high, mid unmarked) are fully written in dictionaries but routinely omitted in everyday Yoruba writing. The owned Unicode form preserves the underdots and the tone marks the domain could carry; the fully tone-marked dictionary form is documented here. Sources: Abraham, Dictionary of Modern Yoruba, Ifá divination corpus

title: Original script provenance: Jǫrð
text: Original script for Jǫrð: ᛁᚬᚱᚦ Script: Younger Futhark Transliteration: Jǫrð Steps: The name Jǫrð is recorded in the Poetic and Prose Eddas, preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts. Younger Futhark runic inscriptions do not preserve the name directly; the runic spelling is a scholarly reconstruction. The normalized Old Norse form Jǫrð uses the letter ǫ (o with ogonek) for the rounded back vowel and ð (eth) for the voiced dental fricative. The Unicode restoration jǫrð.com preserves the normalized Norse spelling; the runic form is displayed as the original script. Sources: Poetic Edda, Prose Edda, Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic

title: Original script provenance: Animus
text: Original script for Animus: ANIMUS Script: Latin epigraphic capitals Transliteration: Animus Steps: The term is a Latin common noun and philosophical concept, not a theonym in the strict sense. PuniCodex treats it under the Greek pantheon bucket by convention, but its original script is the Latin alphabet. The restored form Animus preserves the classical spelling; the ASCII form animus is identical because no diacritics are required. Sources: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Cicero, De Natura Deorum and Tusculanae Disputationes

title: Original script provenance: Anima
text: Original script for Anima: ANIMA Script: Latin epigraphic capitals Transliteration: Anima Steps: Anima is a Latin noun meaning "breath, air, soul, life force". Its original script is the Latin alphabet; it is not attested in Greek letters. The PuniCodex restoration Anima is identical to the ASCII form because the classical spelling uses no diacritics. Sources: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Plato’s Latin reception in Cicero and Apuleius

title: Original script provenance: Clementia
text: Original script for Clementia: CLEMENTIA Script: Latin epigraphic capitals Transliteration: Clementia Steps: Clementia is a Latin abstract noun personified as a Roman virtue. The original script is the Latin alphabet; there is no Greek attestation for this concept as a deity. The PuniCodex restoration Clementia uses the classical Latin spelling. Sources: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Seneca, De Clementia

title: Original script provenance: Gravitas
text: Original script for Gravitas: GRAVITAS Script: Latin epigraphic capitals Transliteration: Gravitas Steps: Gravitas is a Latin abstract noun denoting weight, seriousness, and dignity. The original script is the Latin alphabet; the concept is Roman, not Greek. The PuniCodex restoration Gravitas preserves the classical spelling. Sources: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Cicero, De Officiis

title: Original script provenance: Bifrǫst
text: Original script for Bifrǫst: ᛒᛁᚠᚱᚬᛋᛏ Script: Younger Futhark runes Transliteration: bifrǫst Steps: The name Bifrǫst is recorded in the Poetic and Prose Eddas in medieval Icelandic manuscripts. Younger Futhark inscriptions do not preserve the name directly; the runic spelling is a scholarly reconstruction. ᛒ = b, ᛁ = i, ᚠ = f, ᚱ = r, ᚬ = ǫ (rounded back vowel), ᛋ = s, ᛏ = t. The Unicode restoration Bifrǫst preserves the normalized Norse spelling; the runic form is displayed as the original script. Sources: Poetic Edda, Grímnismál 44, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 15, Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic

title: Original script provenance: Máni
text: Original script for Máni: ᛘᛅᚾᛁ Script: Younger Futhark runes Transliteration: máni Steps: Máni is the personified moon in Norse mythology, brother of Sól. The runic spelling ᛘᛅᚾᛁ is a normalized scholarly reconstruction; no direct runic inscription of the name is known. ᛘ = m, ᛅ = á (long a), ᚾ = n, ᛁ = i. Sources: Poetic Edda, Völuspá and Grímnismál, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 11, Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic

title: Original script provenance: Sigurðr
text: Original script for Sigurðr: ᛋᛁᚴᚢᚱᚦᛦ Script: Younger Futhark runes Transliteration: sigurðr Steps: Sigurðr is the great dragon-slaying hero of the Volsunga saga and Poetic Edda. The runic spelling is a normalized reconstruction; ᚦ writes /ð/ and final ᛦ represents the nominative -r ending. ᛋ = s, ᛁ = i, ᚴ = k/g, ᚢ = u, ᚱ = r, ᚦ = ð, ᛦ = r (nom. ending). Sources: Poetic Edda, Fáfnismál and Sigrdrífumál, Völsunga saga, Prose Edda, Skáldskaparmál

title: Original script provenance: Sleipnir
text: Original script for Sleipnir: ᛋᛚᛅᛁᛒᚾᛁᛦ Script: Younger Futhark runes Transliteration: sleipnir Steps: Sleipnir is Óðinn’s eight-legged steed, born of Loki and the giant Svaðilfari. The runic spelling is a scholarly reconstruction; the name is not attested in runic inscriptions. ᛋ = s, ᛚ = l, ᛅ = æ (or e/æ), ᛁ = i, ᛒ = b, ᚾ = n, ᛁ = i, ᛦ = r (nom. ending). Sources: Poetic Edda, Grímnismál, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 42, Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic

title: Pronunciation: Apóllōn
text: Pronunciation of Apóllōn: /a.pól.lɔːn/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'ah-POL-lone' — stress the second syllable and hold the final 'o' roughly twice as long as English allows. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: A-: Short alpha, smooth breathing — the name opens without roughness, like light arriving. -pól-: Pi plus acute on short omicron. The pitch peak falls on the second syllable, a rising call that carries across distance. -lōn: Lambda, long omega, nu. The long final vowel sustains and resolves the name like a held musical note. Note: Apóllōn is dual-tier because the Greek Ἀπόλλων carries both stress (acute on the second syllable) and length (omega in the final syllable), and because two historically defensible restorations exist: Apóllōn with acute stress and Apollōn with macron-only length. Both forms are owned and both are philologically legitimate.

title: Pronunciation: Hádēs
text: Pronunciation of Hádēs: /há.dɛːs/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'HAH-dace' — the first syllable is pitched high and sharp; the second is long and level, like the floor of the underworld. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ha-: Rough breathing on short alpha — the name expires outward, like a breath seen in cold air. -dēs: Delta plus long eta, the long vowel that opens the name into the unseen. Note: Hádēs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἅιδης contains both stress (acute on the first alpha) and length (long η). The name literally means 'the Unseen,' and the acute on the first syllable gives it the force of a warning.

title: Pronunciation: Hekátē
text: Pronunciation of Hekátē: /he.ká.tɛː/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'he-KAH-tay' — the second syllable rises in pitch, and the final 'ay' is held long like the 'a' in 'say' stretched out. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: He-: Rough breathing on short epsilon — the name begins with an audible exhalation, like a breath across a threshold. -ka-: Kappa plus acute on short alpha — the pitch peak, a sudden calling note. -tē: Long eta, the final syllable that draws the name into the dark. Note: Hekátē is dual-tier because the Greek Ἑκάτη carries both stress (acute on alpha) and length (eta in the final syllable), and because two historically defensible restorations exist: Hekátē with acute stress and Hekatē with macron-only length. The form is etymologically debated, but both Unicode forms are orthographically legitimate.

title: Pronunciation: Níkē
text: Pronunciation of Níkē: /ní.kɛː/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'NEE-kay' — the first syllable rises in pitch like a shout; the second is long and clear. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ní-: Nu with acute on short iota — the name begins with a pitched cry of triumph. -kē: Kappa plus long eta — the final syllable sustains the victory. Note: Níkē is dual-tier because the Greek Νίκη carries both stress (acute on the short ι) and length (long η), and because two historically defensible restorations exist: Níkē with acute stress and Nikē with macron-only length. Both forms are owned and both preserve the goddess's essential meaning: Victory itself.

title: Pronunciation: Zeús
text: Pronunciation of Zeús: /zděu̯s/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'ZDEWS' — one syllable, beginning with a buzzing 'zd' and ending in a sharp 's', like the sound of distant thunder compressed into a name. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Zd-: Voiced affricate [zd] — the spelling Ζεύς preserves an archaic cluster, already simplified in some dialects. -eu-: Diphthong [eu], a bright gliding sound appropriate to the bright sky. -s: Final sigma; the nominative singular ending of an archaic stem *dyēu-s. Note: Zeús is Tier 1 because the Greek Ζεύς contains both stress (acute on the diphthong ευ) and length (the diphthong itself counts as long for accentual purposes). The acute falls on the only syllable, making the name a single pitched peak — the sonic image of a thunderbolt.

title: Pronunciation: Árēs
text: Pronunciation of Árēs: /á.rɛːs/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'AH-rays' — the first syllable is sharp and pitched high, like a command to charge. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Á-: Short alpha with acute pitch — the name shouts, a battle cry compressed into one syllable. -rēs: Rho plus long eta and sigma — the long vowel sustains the shout into a name. Note: Árēs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἄρης contains both stress (acute on the first alpha) and length (long η). The name sounds like a wound being named: short, sharp, and final.

title: Pronunciation: Aphrodítē
text: Pronunciation of Aphrodítē: /a.pʰro.dí.tɛː/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'ah-fro-DEE-tay' — the third syllable carries the pitch, and the final vowel is long and clear. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: A-: Short alpha — the name begins with an open, welcoming sound. -phro-: Aspirated phi plus rho, the breathy center that carries the name forward. -dí-: Delta plus acute on short iota — the pitched peak, bright and sharp. -tē: Long eta, the final syllable that sustains and resolves. Note: Aphrodítē is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἀφροδίτη contains both stress (acute on the short iota) and length (long η in the final syllable). The name's foam etymology makes the long final vowel sound like a wave receding.

title: Pronunciation: Athēnâ
text: Pronunciation of Athēnâ: /a.tʰɛː́.naː/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'ah-THAY-na' — the second syllable is pitched higher and drawn out; the final 'a' is long and pure. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: A-: Short alpha with smooth breathing — the name opens clearly, without roughness. -th-: Aspirated theta [tʰ], the sound of intellect: precise, sharp, clean. -ḗ-: Long eta with acute pitch — the stressed peak of the name, holding authority. -nā: Long alpha with iota subscript, the old nominative ending that gives the name its archaic dignity. Note: Athénā is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἀθηνᾶ contains both stress (acute on the long η) and length (η plus long alpha with iota subscript). The restoration Athénā preserves the acute stress; Athēnā is the macron-only variant. The form Athēnē changes the final letter and is therefore used only when the domain requires it.

title: Pronunciation: Dēmētēr
text: Pronunciation of Dēmētēr: /dɛ.mɛ́.tɛr/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'deh-MEH-ter' — stress the middle syllable; the final syllable is light and quick. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: De-: Delta plus short epsilon — the name begins with the sound of earth being struck. -mé-: Mu with acute on short epsilon — the stressed peak, like a seed breaking open. -ter: Tau-epsilon-rho, the mother-suffix (-τήρ) that marks her as a giver of grain. Note: Dēmētēr is Tier 1 because the Greek Δημήτηρ contains both stress (acute on the short ε) and length (long η in the first syllable). The name is transparently a compound: *dʰeh₁- 'grain' + *māter- 'mother.' Her Roman equivalent Ceres gives us 'cereal.'

title: Pronunciation: Hēra
text: Pronunciation of Hēra: /hɛ́.rā/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'HAY-rah' — the first syllable is sharp and pitched; the final 'a' is long and open. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Hē-: Short epsilon with rough breathing, pitched high — the name exhales authority. -rā: Rho plus long alpha — the final syllable opens broadly, like a queen's gesture. Note: Hēra is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἥρᾱ contains both stress (acute on the initial η) and length (long final alpha).

title: Pronunciation: Hermês
text: Pronunciation of Hermês: /her.ˈmɛːs/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'her-MACE' — the first syllable is quick and breathy; the second is long, level, and carries the accent. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Her-: Short epsilon with rough breathing followed by rho — the name begins with a rush, like a messenger arriving. -mēs: Mu plus long eta and sigma — the long vowel gives the name its final clarity. Note: Hermês is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἑρμῆς contains both stress (circumflex on the long η) and length (η). The circumflex form Hermês is the ideal; Hermēs is the macron-only LSJ convention. The name's boundary-marker etymology suits the god of thresholds.

title: Pronunciation: Hēphaistos
text: Pronunciation of Hēphaistos: /ˈhɛː.pʰaɪ.stos/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'HEH-fye-stoss' — the first syllable carries the accent; the middle has a breathy 'ph' and a bright diphthong; the final syllable is crisp. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Hē-: Long eta with rough breathing, carrying the acute pitch — the name begins with a forge-breath. -phai-: Aspirated phi plus diphthong αι — the sound of bellows and flame. -stós: Sigma-tau-omicron-sigma, the hissing final syllable of metal cooling. Note: Hēphaistos is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἥφαιστος contains both stress (acute on the long η of the first syllable) and length (η and the αι diphthong, which counts as long for accentual purposes). His name has no secure Greek etymology, reflecting his archaic, possibly non-Greek origins.

title: Pronunciation: Hestía
text: Pronunciation of Hestía: /hɛs.tí.a/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'hess-TEE-ah' — the middle syllable carries the pitch, and the final 'ah' is short and open. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: He-: Short epsilon with rough breathing — the name begins with a soft exhalation, like breath over a hearth. -sti-: Sigma-tau with acute on short iota — the pitched peak, calm and central. -a: Short alpha — the final vowel opens into the space of the home. Note: Hestía is Tier 2 because the original Ἑστία bears the acute stress only; the final alpha is short, so a single feature is preserved. The name is built on the PIE root *h₂wes-, 'to dwell,' making her literally the goddess of the dwelling-place.

title: Pronunciation: Poseidôn
text: Pronunciation of Poseidôn: /po.sei.dɔ́ːn/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'poh-SAY-done' — the second syllable is light, the third is long, pitched, and powerful. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Po-: Pi plus short omicron — the name plunges in with the sound of water striking. -sei-: Diphthong ει with no stress; the liquid middle syllable that carries the name across the wave. -dɔ́ːn: Delta plus long omega with acute pitch — the stressed peak that holds like a swell before it breaks. Note: Poseidôn is Tier 1 because the Greek Ποσειδῶν contains both stress (circumflex on the long ω) and length (ει diphthong and long ω). The circumflex form Poseidôn is the ideal; Poseidōn is the macron-only LSJ convention.

title: Pronunciation: Persephonē
text: Pronunciation of Persephonē: /per.se.pʰó.nɛː/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'per-seh-FOH-nay' — the third syllable carries the pitch, and the final 'nay' is long and solemn. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Per-: Pi plus short epsilon and rho — the name begins with a light, searching sound. -se-: Sigma-epsilon, the soft transition between worlds. -phó-: Aspirated phi with acute on short omicron — the stressed peak, like a cry in the dark. -nē: Long eta, the final vowel that opens into the underworld. Note: Persephonē is Tier 1 because the Greek Περσεφόνη contains both stress (acute on the short ό) and length (long η in the final syllable). The name's etymology is uncertain, which suits a goddess who moves between the known and hidden worlds.

title: Pronunciation: Promētheús
text: Pronunciation of Promētheús: /pro.mɛː.ˈtʰeu̯s/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'pro-meh-THEFS' — the middle syllable is long, and the final diphthong, which carries the accent, glides like the foresight the name denotes. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Pro-: Pi plus short omicron — the name begins with forward movement. -mē-: Mu plus long eta, the sustained middle of the name. -theus: Aspirated theta plus diphthong ευ plus sigma — the sound of forethought and divine knowledge. Note: Promētheus is Tier 1 because the Greek Προμηθεύς contains both stress (acute on the long η, realized as acute in our restoration) and length (η and the ευ diphthong). His name means 'Forethought,' the opposite of his brother Epimetheus ('Afterthought').

title: Pronunciation: Gaîa
text: Pronunciation of Gaîa: /ɡaɪ.a/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'GUY-ah' — the diphthong glides like the earth yielding; the final vowel is simple and vast. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Gai-: Gamma plus diphthong αι — the sound of the earth opening its mouth. -a: Short alpha — the final vowel is open and elemental. Note: Gaia is Tier 1 because the Greek Γαῖα bears a circumflex on the αι diphthong, which marks both stress and vowel length in a single sign. She is primordial: older than the Olympians, older than the Titans, the first power to arise after Chaos.

title: Pronunciation: Cháos
text: Pronunciation of Cháos: /kʰá.os/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: "KHAH-oss" — first syllable like "cat" with a breathy k, second like "oss" in "moss". Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ch-: Aspirated chi [kʰ], the breathy opening of a gap. -á-: Short alpha with acute pitch stress — the first sound to rise out of nothing. -os: Short omicron and voiceless sigma, a name that closes as it opens. Note: Cháos is Tier 2 because the Greek Χάος preserves only stress (acute on the first alpha), not length. There is no long vowel or diphthong. The accent marks the pitch peak of the primordial "gap" — a single prosodic feature, exactly what Tier 2 is designed to record.

title: Pronunciation: Tártaros
text: Pronunciation of Tártaros: /tár.ta.ros/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: "TAR-ta-ross" — three syllables, the first pitched high like a stone dropping. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Tá-: Voiceless tau with acute pitch on short alpha — the name strikes downward. -rta-: Rho-tau-alpha, a rolling descent into the second syllable. -ros: Short omicron and sigma, a name that ends in depth. Note: Tártaros is Tier 2 because the Greek Τάρταρος preserves only stress (acute on the first alpha), not length. The first syllable carries the pitch peak, appropriate for a name that denotes the deepest point of the cosmos. The absence of long vowels makes the name sound hard and abrupt — the acoustic opposite of the bright, sustained Aithḗr.

title: Pronunciation: Póntos

Note: Póntos is Tier 2 because the Greek Πόντος preserves stress (acute on the short ό) but no long vowel. The name means 'sea' but originally 'path' or 'crossing' — the sea as the route one takes, not merely the water itself.

title: Pronunciation: Hyperíōn
text: Pronunciation of Hyperíōn: /hy.pe.rí.ɔːn/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'hü-peh-REE-ohn' — round the lips for Hy- (the ü of German 'über'), strike the accent hard on -rí-, and let the final -ōn ring long. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Hy-: Rough breathing plus upsilon: a breathy /h/ before the close front rounded vowel /y/ — a sound English lacks, nearest to French 'tu' or German 'über'. -pe-: Unaspirated /p/ followed by a short, open /e/; light and quick, carrying no stress. -rí: A trilled /r/ closing on short iota, which bears the acute accent — the high pitch of the word falls here. -ōn: Long omega (ω), held roughly twice the length of a short vowel, closed by the final nasal; the length is part of the name, not an ornament. Note: Tier-1: the Greek original Ὑπερίων carries both a stress mark (the acute on the iota) and a long vowel (ω), and the restoration Hyperíōn preserves both — the í keeps the accent where Hesiod's auditors heard it, and the ō keeps the quantity of the omega. Both features survive in the Unicode form; the ASCII 'Hyperion' loses them.

Note: Lētō is Tier 1: the Greek original contains both length (ē and ō) and the circumflex pitch contour. The English 'Leto' preserves neither.

title: Pronunciation: Hēlios
text: Pronunciation of Hēlios: /hɛ́.li.os/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'HAY-lee-oss' — the first syllable rises like the sun; the rest is bright and clear. The name is built on the same root as English 'sun' and Latin 'sol,' one of the most ancient theonyms in the Indo-European family.

title: Pronunciation: Selēnē

The name shares a root with 'shine' across Indo-European languages.

title: Pronunciation: Ártemis
text: Pronunciation of Ártemis: /ár.te.mis/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'AR-te-miss' — the first syllable is sharp and high; the name is quick, like the arrow she looses. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ár-: Short alpha with acute pitch plus rho — the name opens like a bowstring drawn back. -te-: Tau-epsilon, the crisp release of the arrow. -mis: Mu-iota-sigma, the final syllable that lands silently, like a hunter's footfall. Note: Ártemis is Tier 2 because the Greek Ἄρτεμις preserves stress (acute on the first alpha) but no long vowel. She is the most important single-tier Tier-2 deity in the Greek pantheon: her acute alone carries the entire prosodic signature of the huntress's cry.

title: Pronunciation: Átlas
text: Pronunciation of Átlas: /át.laːs/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'AT-lass' — the first syllable is pitched high, as if lifting; the second is level and heavy. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Át-: Short alpha with acute pitch plus tau — the name begins with a strained upward effort. -las: Lambda-alpha-sigma, the final syllable that bears the weight. Note: Átlas is Tier 2 because the Greek Ἄτλας preserves stress (acute on the first alpha) but no long vowel. The name's short, heavy sound mimics the burden it describes: a single pitched syllable followed by the weight of the final syllable.

title: Pronunciation: Diónysos
text: Pronunciation of Diónysos: /di.ˈó.ny.sos/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: "dee-OH-nee-soss" — but the "y" is like French "u," and the second syllable carries the ancient pitch rise. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Di-: Short iota after delta — the first half of the name of Zeus (genitive Dios). -ó-: Short omicron with acute pitch stress; the name's prosodic peak. -ny-: Nu followed by front-rounded upsilon [y], the mysterious Nysa-element. -sos: Final sigma-omicron-sigma, a repeated sibilant like rustling vines. Note: Diónysos is Tier 2 because the Greek Διόνυσος preserves only stress (acute on the first omicron), not length. The upsilon remains short, and no macron appears in the standard restoration. The acute on ó marks the pitch peak of a name whose second element may come from beyond Greek itself.

title: Pronunciation: Médousa
text: Pronunciation of Médousa: /ˈme.doː.sa/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'MEH-doh-sah' — stress the first syllable, as the Greek acute marks; the middle ου is a long closed 'o' [oː] (a spurious diphthong), not 'oo'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Me-: Mu plus short epsilon — the name begins with a soft, warning sound. -dou-: Delta plus diphthong ου — the middle syllable that carries the hissing. -sa: Sigma plus short alpha — the final hiss that ends the name like a snake's warning. Note: Médousa is Tier 1 because the Greek Μέδουσα carries both stress (the acute on the first syllable) and a long vowel (the diphthong ου). The name means 'Guardian' or 'Queen,' an ironic title for a figure whose gaze turns men to stone.

title: Pronunciation: Krónos
text: Pronunciation of Krónos: /kró.nos/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: "KROH-nohs" — first syllable like "crow" without the w, second like "nose". Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Kr-: Voiceless velar stop [k] followed by rolling rho. -ó-: Short omicron with acute pitch stress — the peak of the Titan's name. -nos: Nu-omicron-sigma, a firm closing, almost a knell. Note: Krónos is Tier 2 because the Greek Κρόνος preserves only stress (acute on the first omicron), not length. The name's etymology is disputed; the acute marks the pitch peak, while the short vowels keep the name compact and hard, fitting a god whose story is one of cutting and devouring.

title: Pronunciation: Rhéā

She is the great mother of the Olympian generation.

title: Pronunciation: Pān
text: Pronunciation of Pān: /pán/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'PAHN' — one clean syllable; let the pitch lift on the á rather than hammering it, and keep the vowel open and pure. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Π-: unaspirated voiceless bilabial stop [p], like the p of English 'spin' — Attic π carried no burst of breath -ά-: short open [a] bearing the acute accent — a rising pitch, not an English stress-beat; the Arcadian by-form Πάων lengthens this vowel to ā -ν: dental nasal [n], tongue on the teeth, closing the single syllable Note: Tier 2 — a single preserved feature. The Attic name Πάν carries only an acute accent on a short alpha (stress without length); the long ā belongs to the Arcadian by-form Πάων, 'shepherd', which the restoration Pān honors instead. Either way the name keeps one distinctive mark, never both, which is exactly what Tier 2 certifies.

The name may be pre-Greek; its etymology from *ol-um- 'luminous' is speculative, so the pronunciation follows the attested Greek form rather than a reconstructed prototype.

title: Pronunciation: Athēnai

The aspirated [pʰ] is essential to the name; English 'Delphi' often loses the aspiration and the final diphthong quality.

text: Pronunciation of Valhǫll: /ˈwal.hɔlː/ Label: Old Norse Reconstruction Approximation: 'VAHL-holl' — stress the first syllable, pronounce the 'a' as in 'father', and hold the final 'l' slightly longer than English usually allows. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: V-: Voiced labiodental fricative [v], from earlier Proto-Germanic *w in initial position. -al-: Short open front [a] followed by alveolar lateral [l]; the first syllable is stressed. -hǫll: Voiceless glottal [h], short open-mid back rounded [ɔ], and geminated lateral [lː] written double. title: Pronunciation: Ragnarǫk
text: Pronunciation of Ragnarǫk: /ˈraɣ.naˌrɔk/ Label: Old Norse Reconstruction Approximation: 'RAGH-na-rok' — the middle consonant is a throaty 'gh', and the final vowel is a short, rounded 'o' like 'hot'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Rag-: Voiced velar or uvular fricative [ɣ] after the vowel in ragna, the genitive plural of regin 'gods, powers' -na-: Short [a] plus alveolar nasal [n], the genitive plural ending -rǫk: Short [ɔ] with o-hook (ǫ), the Old Norse rounded vowel; rǫk means 'fate, doom' — the familiar 'twilight' gloss belongs to the variant ragnarøkkr (røkkr, 'darkness', attested in Lokasenna 39) Note: Ragnarǫk is Tier 1: the o-hook (ǫ) preserves a distinct Old Norse rounded vowel — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The popular modern form Ragnarök normalises the ǫ to ö; both are registrable, but ǫ is the more conservative medieval spelling.

title: Pronunciation: Miðgarðr
text: Pronunciation of Miðgarðr: /ˈmiðˌɡarðr/ Label: Old Norse Reconstruction Approximation: 'MITH-garther' — the first 'th' is voiced like 'this', and the second 'th' in 'garth' is the same; roll the final r lightly. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Mi-: Short close front [i] with initial stress; mið means 'middle' -ð-: Voiced dental fricative [ð], the eth in mið; it is the soft 'th' of 'this', not the hard 'th' of 'thin' -garð-: Voiced velar stop [ɡ], short [a], and voiced dental fricative [ð] in garðr 'enclosure, yard' -r: Tapped or trilled alveolar [r], the masculine nominative ending Note: Miðgarðr is Tier 1: it preserves the voiced dental fricative ð (eth), a sound English lost in most positions — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. The compound is transparent: mið 'middle' + garðr 'enclosure'.

title: Pronunciation: Álfheimr
text: Pronunciation of Álfheimr: /ˈɑːlvˌhɛi̯mr/ Label: Old Norse Reconstruction Approximation: 'AHLV-haymr' — stress the first syllable like 'owl' without the w, then a quick 'lv-haymer' with a rolled final r. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ál-: Long stressed [ɑː] plus voiced alveolar lateral [l] and voiceless labiodental [f]; álfr means 'elf' -fhei-: Diphthong [ɛi̯] — a rising glide from open-mid to close front, the standard Old Norse ei sound -mr: Bilabial nasal [m] plus tapped or trilled [r]; final -r is the masculine nominative ending Note: Old Norse á is a long back vowel, and ei is a diphthong; the acute accent on Á marks stress and length together. The form Álfheimr is Tier 1 because it preserves the acute accent on Á — a distinctive diacritic the ASCII form loses.

title: Pronunciation: Jötunheimr
text: Pronunciation of Jötunheimr: /ˈjɔː.tunˌhɛi̯mr/ Label: Old Norse Reconstruction Approximation: 'YUR-tun-haymr' — start with a 'y' plus a tight, rounded 'ur', then 'tun' and 'haymer'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Jö-: Palatal approximant [j] plus long front rounded [øː] or [œː]; the ö arose by u-breaking of Proto-Germanic short *e before a following *u (*etunaz > jötunn) -tun-: Voiceless alveolar stop [t] plus short close back [u] and alveolar nasal [n] -heimr: Diphthong [ɛi̯] in heimr, 'home, world', with bilabial nasal [m] and tapped [r] Note: Jötunheimr is Tier 1: the ö preserves the broken vowel, a distinct Old Norse vowel — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The Proto-Germanic ancestor is *etunaz with short *e; in the attested Norse compound the vowel quality (front rounded) matters more than length for recognition.

title: Pronunciation: Helheimr
text: Pronunciation of Helheimr: /ˈhɛlˌhɛi̯mr/ Label: Old Norse Reconstruction Approximation: 'HEL-haymr' — a crisp initial h, then 'hell' and 'haymer' run together, with a light rolled r. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Hel-: Voiceless glottal fricative [h], short [ɛ], and alveolar lateral [l]; Hel is the hidden goddess of death -hei-: Diphthong [ɛi̯] — the same rising glide as in heimr, meaning 'home, world' -mr: Bilabial nasal [m] plus tapped [r]; the compound shortens heimr to heim- before the final r Note: Helheimr is a transparent Old Norse compound of Hel + heimr. It is Tier 2 because no vowel is marked long or stressed; the name relies on everyday Old Norse phonology. Modern English 'hell' descends from the same Germanic root but has lost the diphthong.

title: Pronunciation: Jǫrmungandr
text: Pronunciation of Jǫrmungandr: /ˈjɔrˌmun.ɡan.dr/ Label: Old Norse Reconstruction Approximation: 'YOR-mun-gand-r' — stress the first syllable, pronounce the 'or' like the 'o' in 'hot' with an r-color, and keep the final r light and trilled. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: J-: Palatal approximant [j], the y-glide as in English 'yes'. -ǫr-: Short open-mid back rounded [ɔ] plus trilled [r], the first syllable carrying stress. -mun-: Bilabial nasal [m], close back rounded [u], and alveolar nasal [n]. -gandr: Voiced velar [ɡ], open front [a], alveolar nasal [n], and trilled [r]. Note: Jǫrmungandr is Tier 1: the ǫ preserves the distinctive Old Norse rounded back vowel — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The first element is related to words for 'great' or 'universal'; gandr can mean monster, wand, or wolf, making the compound a 'mighty monster' or 'vast beast'.

title: Pronunciation: Týr
text: Pronunciation of Týr: /tyːr/ Label: Old Norse Reconstruction Approximation: 'TEWR' — start with a crisp 't', say the rounded 'ew' of 'few' while pursing the lips, hold it long, and finish with a light trilled r. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: T-: Voiceless alveolar stop [t], the same crisp t as in English 'stop'. -ý-: Long close front rounded vowel [yː], marked by the acute accent; pronounced like French 'tu' but held long and stressed. -r: Trilled or tapped alveolar [r], lighter than the geminated rr of Þórr. Note: Týr is Tier 1: the acute on ý marks stress on a distinctive long front rounded vowel — a diacritic the ASCII form loses. The registrable form preserves the Old Norse vowel quality and the god's name as recorded in the Eddas and skaldic verse.

title: Pronunciation: Þórr
text: Pronunciation of Þórr: /ˈθɔːrː/ Label: Old Norse Reconstruction Approximation: 'THORR' — begin with the breathy 'th' of 'thin', hold the 'o' long like 'awe', and trill the final r slightly longer than usual. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Þ: Voiceless dental fricative [θ], the thorn; it is the hard 'th' of 'thin', not the voiced 'th' of 'this' ó: Long open-mid back [ɔː] with acute marking stress and length rr: Long or geminated alveolar trill [rː], written double in Old Norse to show length Note: Þórr is Tier 1: the acute on ó marks stress and length on the first syllable, and the thorn Þ is a distinctive letter — features the ASCII form loses — while the geminate rr preserves the Old Norse long consonant. The English name Thor has lost both the thorn sound and the long rolled r.

title: Pronunciation: Óðinn
text: Pronunciation of Óðinn: /ˈɔːðinː/ Label: Old Norse Reconstruction Approximation: 'OH-thin' — hold the first vowel long like 'awe', then a soft 'th' as in 'this', and a crisp 'nin'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ó-: Long open-mid back [ɔː] with acute marking stress and length; the name derives from *Wōđanaz, 'the furious' -ð-: Voiced dental fricative [ð], the eth; it replaced Proto-Germanic *đ and gives the name its Norse colour -in-: Short close front [i] and alveolar nasal [n]; the participial/derivative suffix -n: Final alveolar nasal [n], geminated in Old Norse orthography as nn Note: Óðinn is Tier 1: the acute on Ó marks stress and length on the first syllable, and together with the distinctive letter ð these are features the ASCII form loses. The name descends from *Wōđanaz; the initial w- was lost in West Norse, giving Óðinn rather than *Wóðinn.

title: Pronunciation: Njǫrðr
text: Pronunciation of Njǫrðr: /ˈnjɔrðr/ Label: Old Norse Reconstruction Approximation: "NYORTH" — like 'nyore' with a short o, ending in the 'th-r' sound of 'father' plus a quick rolled r. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Nj-: Palatalized [n] plus [j] glide — the sea-god's name opens like 'ny' with a firm n. -ǫ-: Short open-mid back rounded vowel [ɔ], the vowel of *Nerþuz preserved in the Norse ǫ. -rðr: Trilled [r], voiced dental fricative [ð] as in English 'father', and a light syllabic final [r]. Note: Njǫrðr is Tier 1 because the Unicode restoration preserves the distinctive Norse vowel ǫ and the voiced dental fricative ð — distinctive letters the ASCII form loses. Old Norse stress is initial and strong, yet it is not encoded by an acute; the registrable form Njǫrðr records the name's characteristic Norse orthography. Reconstruction follows Cleasby & Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary (1874); Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (1910); and Ranke & Hofmann, Altnordisches Elementarbuch, 5th ed. (de Gruyter, 1988).

title: Pronunciation: Skaði
text: Pronunciation of Skaði: /ˈskɑː.ði/ Label: Old Norse Reconstruction Approximation: 'SKAH-thee' — stress the long open first syllable like 'spa' held long, then a soft 'th' as in 'father' and a short 'ee'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Sk-: Unpalatalized cluster [sk]; Old Norse keeps the hard [k] before the back vowel, untouched by the later Scandinavian palatalizations -á-: Long low back [ɑː]; the acute marks vowel length on the stressed first syllable -ð-: Voiced dental fricative [ð], the eth; the soft 'th' of 'father', never the hard 'th' of 'thin' -i: Short close front [i], the light nominative ending of the name Note: Skaði is Tier 1: the acute on á marks the long vowel [ɑː], and ð is a distinctive letter — features the ASCII form Skadi loses. The name is grammatically masculine in Old Norse though it belongs to a goddess, a fossil noted by the lexicographers, and is attested throughout the Eddic corpus (Grímnismál 11, Lokasenna, Gylfaginning, Skáldskaparmál). Normalization follows Cleasby & Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary (1874), s.v. Skaði; and Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (1910), s.v. Skaði.

title: Pronunciation: Rꜥ
text: Pronunciation of Rꜥ: /raʕ/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: 'rah-ʿA' — a rolled or tapped 'r', then a deep throaty 'ah' like the Arabic ع. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: r: Alveolar trill or tap [r], the first consonant of the solar god's name ꜥ: Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ], the ayin that closes the Egyptian root rꜥ a: Short open vowel [a], supplied by convention; Egyptian writing gave only rꜥ Note: Rꜥ is a Tier-1 restoration. Egyptologists vocalise the name as Ra or Rꜥa, but the hieroglyphs record only rꜥ. The ayin (ꜥ) is the defining non-English sound — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses; the acute variant Rá is a modern stress marker, not an ancient vowel sign.

title: Pronunciation: Wsjr

title: Pronunciation: Ḥr
text: Pronunciation of Ḥr: /ˈħaːru/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: 'HAH-roo' — the first syllable is throaty and drawn out, the second light and ascending, like a falcon rising. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ḥ-: Voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ], the same dry throat-sound that opens Heka and Hu. -aː-: Long stressed vowel; the name's peak, carrying the god's height and distance. -r-: Alveolar tap or trill [r], like a brief roll of the tongue. -u: Final short vowel, reconstructed from Coptic ⲟⲩⲣ (our) / ⲏⲣⲟ (hēro). Note: Horus is Tier 1 because the Egyptian Ḥr preserves the underdotted ḥ — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. The name is onomatopoeically apt: the throaty ḥ and the final u suggest a cry from far above. The Greek borrowing Hōros adds an omega, but the original Egyptian root is simply ḥr.

title: Pronunciation: Ꜣst
text: Pronunciation of Ꜣst: /ˈʔaːsət/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: 'AH-set' — begin with a slight catch in the throat (the alef), then 'set' with a crisp or silent final t. The variant 'EE-set' is also widely defended. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ꜣ-: Glottal stop [ʔ], the Egyptological alef (U+A723); at the beginning of the name it functions as a consonantal onset before the vowel. -aː-: Long open vowel in the first syllable; hieroglyphic ꜣst records no vowels, so the quality depends on Coptic and Greek evidence. -s: Voiceless alveolar fricative [s], as in English 'see'. -t: Voiceless alveolar stop [t]; the final -t is the feminine suffix, often unpronounced in later Egyptian and absent in Coptic. Note: This entry is the Egyptian goddess ꜣst (Aset/Iset), not the later Greek name Isis. Hieroglyphs record only ꜣ-s-t; the vowel evolution is reconstructed as Rūsat > Rūsaʾ > ʾŪsaʾ > ʾĒsə, whence Coptic ⲎⲤⲈ and Greek Ἶσις. The ꜣ is a glottal stop, and the final -t is a feminine marker often silent in speech. PUNICODEX uses the registrable alef ꜣ (U+A723) to signal the historic consonant; this is a Tier 1 restoration, the alef being a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. Sources: Allen, Middle Egyptian (2014); Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, s.v. ꜣst; Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache I, s.v. ꜣst; Hoch, Semitic Words in Egyptian Texts (1994), on the representation of Egyptian alef in Semitic transcriptions.

title: Pronunciation: Ḏḥwtj
text: Pronunciation of Ḏḥwtj: /tɨˈχuːtiː/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: tji-HOO-tee — the first consonant is like a 'dj' made against the hard palate, and the middle h is a dry throat-fricative. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ḏ: Palatalized voiced alveolar stop [ɟ] or affricate, written with d-dot-below; the first consonant of Ḏḥwtj ḥ: Voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ], the dotted h that follows the palatal d w: Bilabial glide [w], represented in writing by the quail-chick sign ty: Final consonants t-y, with the y indicating a palatalization or the Greek ending -is Note: Ḏḥwtj is Tier-1: the underdotted ḏ and ḥ are distinctive letters the ASCII form loses. Egyptian writing records only the consonants ḏ-ḥ-w-tj; the vowels are reconstructed from Coptic and Greek sources. The initial palatal ḏ and the pharyngeal ḥ are both non-English sounds preserved in the Unicode form.

title: Pronunciation: Ꜣmun
text: Pronunciation of Ꜣmun: /ʔaˈmuːn/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: ah-MOON — begin with a soft glottal catch, then a long 'moon' without the final glide. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ꜣ: Egyptological alef or reed-leaf, representing a glottal stop [ʔ] or a weak consonantal onset; the initial sound of the name jmn m: Bilabial nasal [m] u: Close back rounded vowel [u], supplied from Coptic Ⲁⲙⲟⲩⲛ and Greek Ἄμμων n: Alveolar nasal [n], closing the root Note: Ꜣmun is Tier-1: the initial Egyptological alef (Ꜣ) is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. The alef marks the consonant that Coptic and Greek sources vocalize as 'A'. Egyptian hieroglyphs record only j-m-n; the vowels are reconstructed from later witnesses.

title: Pronunciation: Ptḥ
text: Pronunciation of Ptḥ: /pəˈtaːħ/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: puh-TAHKH — the final consonant is a dry, breathy 'kh' made in the back of the throat, not the soft 'h' of English. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: p: Voiceless bilabial plosive [p], unaspirated as in Egyptian t: Voiceless alveolar plosive [t], unaspirated ḥ: Voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ], the dotted h that gives the name its throaty close Note: Ptḥ is Tier-1: the pharyngeal ḥ preserved in the Unicode form is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. The vowels are supplied by convention from Coptic and Greek transcriptions; Egyptian writing records only p-t-ḥ.

title: Pronunciation: Sḫmt
text: Pronunciation of Sḫmt: /saxˈmaːt/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: 'sakh-MAHT' — 'sakh' as in 'Bach' with an s, then 'maht' with a long 'ah' and a crisp or silent final t. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: S-: Voiceless alveolar fricative [s], as in English 'sun'. -a-: Short open vowel before the second consonant; vowels are not written in hieroglyphs. -ḫ-: Voiceless velar fricative [x], the 'kh' of Scottish 'loch'; written with h-breve (U+1E2B). -m-: Bilabial nasal [m], as in English 'moon'. -aː-: Long stressed vowel in the feminine syllable; the length is inferred from Coptic and from nominal patterns. -t: Voiceless alveolar stop [t]; the feminine ending, often silent in later speech and reflected as -i in Coptic Ⲥⲁⲭⲙⲓ. Note: The name is the feminine form of the root sḫm, 'to be powerful'. Hieroglyphs record S-ḫ-m-t; the vowels are reconstructed from Coptic Ⲥⲁⲭⲙⲓ and from Egyptian feminine-participle patterns. The ḫ is a voiceless velar fricative, not English 'k'. In PUNICODEX the Sḫmt spelling preserves the historic ḫ (U+1E2B) as a Tier 1 restoration — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses; the ASCII fallback is 'sekhm(t)'. Sources: Allen, Middle Egyptian (2014); Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, s.v. sḫm; Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache IV, s.v. sḫm; Hoch, Semitic Words in Egyptian Texts (1994), on Egyptian ḫ in Semitic orthography.

title: Pronunciation: Bꜣstt
text: Pronunciation of Bꜣstt: /buˈʔistit/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: 'boo-ISS-tee' — say 'boo', then a tiny catch before 'iss', ending with 'tee' (the final t is often silent). Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: B-: Voiced bilabial stop [b], as in English 'bone'. -u-: Short rounded vowel in the first syllable. -ʔ-: Glottal stop [ʔ], the Egyptological alef (ꜣ, U+A723) that Allen reconstructs before the stressed syllable in the earliest form. -i-: Short close front vowel in the stressed syllable. -s-: Voiceless alveolar fricative [s], as in English 'see'. -t: Voiceless alveolar stop [t]; the second -t marks the feminine suffix and was usually not pronounced in speech. Note: Allen (The Ancient Egyptian Language: A Historical Study, 2013, p. 74) reconstructs the earliest form as buʔístit or buʔístiat; by the first millennium the name had become *Ubaste and then Coptic ⲟⲩⲃⲁⲥⲧⲉ (Oubaste) /ʔuˈβastə/. The meaning of the name remains uncertain; the lexicon glosses it 'She of the ointment jar'. The final -t is a feminine marker often silent in speech, and the ꜣ represents a glottal stop. PUNICODEX uses the registrable alef ꜣ (U+A723); the double -tt- is orthographic. This is a Tier 1 restoration — the alef is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. Sources: Allen 2013, p. 74; Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, s.v. bꜣstt; Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache III, s.v. bꜣstt; Hoch, Semitic Words in Egyptian Texts (1994), for the phonological background of Egyptian alef and feminine -t.

text: Pronunciation of Mꜣꜥt: /maʔ.ʕaːt/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: 'mah-ʿAHT' — a soft 'm', a deep throaty 'ah' in the middle, and a crisp final 't'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: m: Bilabial nasal [m], the first consonant of the word mꜣꜥt ꜣ: Glottal stop [ʔ], Egyptological alef; some scholars vocalise this as a light 'a' glide ꜥ: Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ], the ayin that gives the root its throaty core -t: Voiceless alveolar stop [t], the feminine ending that turns the verbal root into the abstract noun 'truth' Note: Mꜣꜥt is a Tier-1 restoration of a consonantal Egyptian word. The Egyptological alef (ꜣ) and ayin (ꜥ) are both preserved, marking two different throat sounds that English lacks — distinctive letters the ASCII form loses. The final -t is the feminine abstract ending; the word literally means 'straightness' or 'rightness'.

title: Pronunciation: Rāma
text: Pronunciation of Rāma: /ˈraː.mə/ Label: Sanskrit Reconstruction Approximation: 'RAH-muh' — roll or tap the 'r', hold the first syllable long, and let the second syllable relax. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Rā-: Voiced alveolar tap or trill [r] plus long open [aː]; the macron marks length, giving Tier-1 status -ma: Voiced bilabial nasal [m] plus short open [a]; the second syllable is light and unstressed Note: Rāma is Tier 1 because the initial ā is long. The name is shared by several figures in Sanskrit literature, most famously the hero of the Rāmāyaṇa, but the Vedic Rāmas and Paraśurāma are distinct characters.

title: Pronunciation: Durgā
text: Pronunciation of Durgā: /ˈd̪ʊr.ɡaː/ Label: Sanskrit Reconstruction Approximation: 'DOOR-gah' — the first vowel is short and rounded like 'u' in 'put'; hold the final 'gah' long. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Dur-: Voiced dental stop [d̪] plus short close back rounded [ʊ], followed by voiced velar stop [ɡ]; the prefix dur- means 'difficult, hard to approach' -gā: Voiced velar stop [ɡ] plus long open [aː]; the macron marks length, giving Tier-1 status Note: Durgā is Tier 1 because the final ā is long. The name means 'she who is difficult to approach' or 'fortress,' a fitting title for the goddess who destroys demons and protects her devotees.

title: Pronunciation: Śiva
text: Pronunciation of Śiva: /ˈɕi.ʋə/ Label: Sanskrit Reconstruction Approximation: 'SHEE-vuh' — the first consonant is a sharp, high 'sh' made with the tongue near the hard palate, and the 'v' is light, almost like a 'w'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Śi-: Voiceless palatal fricative [ɕ], like an extra-hissing 'sh', plus short close front [i]; Śiva means 'the auspicious one' -va: Voiced labiodental approximant [ʋ] — softer than English 'v' — plus short open [a] Note: Śiva is Tier 1: the acute on Ś marks the palatal sibilant [ɕ], a sound distinct from both English 'sh' and Sanskrit retrophalatal ṣ — a distinctive diacritic the ASCII form loses. Sanskrit stress is pitch-accent based and not marked here; the acute is used to flag the palatal character of the initial sibilant.

title: Pronunciation: Viṣṇu
text: Pronunciation of Viṣṇu: /ʋɪʂ.ɳʊ/ Label: Sanskrit/Vedic Reconstruction Approximation: 'VISH-noo' — the first syllable has a crisp, tongue-tip sh; the second is short and resonant. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Vi-: Labiodental or dental approximant [ʋ] plus short [ɪ] — the prefix of pervasion, the sound that spreads. -ṣṇu: Retroflex sibilant [ʂ] plus retroflex nasal cluster [ɳʊ], from the root viṣ- ('to pervade, to work') — the name's active core. Note: The IAST form Viṣṇu marks the retroflex ṣ and the retroflex nasal ṇ. Etymologically the name means 'All-Pervading.' Devanagari विष्णु is the most common theistic spelling; in Vedic mantras the accent may fall differently depending on grammatical case.

title: Pronunciation: Kṛṣṇa
text: Pronunciation of Kṛṣṇa: /krsna/ Label: Reconstructed Sanskrit Approximation: Dialect: Confidence: generated Note: Broad IPA generated from the Unicode restoration Kṛṣṇa; review recommended before promotion to canonical.

title: Pronunciation: Gaṇeśa
text: Pronunciation of Gaṇeśa: /ɡɐ.ɳeː.ɕɐ/ Label: Sanskrit/Vedic Reconstruction Approximation: 'guh-NAH-shuh' — say the second syllable with a bright, held 'ay' sound and a soft, tongue-tip n. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ga-: Initial velar [ɡ] followed by short, open [ɐ] — the soft ground from which the name rises. -ṇe-: Retroflex nasal [ɳ] plus long [eː], a resonant, elevated syllable that distinguishes Gaṇeśa from common gana. -śa: Palatal sibilant [ɕ] (not retroflex [ʂ]) plus short [ɐ] — the śakti of sound and auspiciousness. Note: The IAST form Gaṇeśa marks the retroflex ṇ and the palatal ś. The acute-looking mark above the e is a macron in scholarly usage, indicating the long vowel ē that Sanskrit inherits from the diphthong ai. Devanagari गणेश is the everyday script of worship.

title: Pronunciation: Sarasvatī
text: Pronunciation of Sarasvatī: /sarasvatˈiː/ Label: Reconstructed Sanskrit Approximation: sah-RAH-swah-tee — the final ī long, the v soft as in verse. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Note: Sanskrit sarasvatī carries exactly one long vowel, the final ī; the restoration Sarasvatī keeps its single macron. The v of IAST is the labiodental व, which Hindi pronunciation softens toward w — hence the double life of the name as "Saraswati" in speech and "Sarasvatī" in scholarship. The IAST form is the owned one: the standard of the libraries she governs.

title: Pronunciation: Brahmā
text: Pronunciation of Brahmā: /brahmˈaː/ Label: Reconstructed Sanskrit Approximation: Dialect: Confidence: generated Note: Broad IPA generated from the Unicode restoration Brahmā; review recommended before promotion to canonical.

title: Pronunciation: Sūrya
text: Pronunciation of Sūrya: /ˈsuːr.jə/ Label: Sanskrit Reconstruction Approximation: 'SOO-ryuh' — hold the first syllable long and bright, as in 'sue' stretched out; the final 'yuh' is quick. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Sū-: Voiceless alveolar sibilant [s] plus long close back rounded [uː]; the macron marks length, giving Tier-1 status -rya: Alveolar tap or trill [r] followed by palatal approximant [j] and short [a]; the -ya forms a light final syllable Note: Sūrya is Tier 1 because the initial ū is long. In Vedic usage, Sūrya is the visible disk of the sun, while Savitṛ is the sun as the power that impels sacrifice and life.

title: Pronunciation: Ištar

Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Iš-: Close front [i] followed by voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] — the Akkadian rendering of the Sumerian divine name. -tar: Voiceless dental [t] and syllabic [ar] — the second element, possibly connected with 'morning star' or simply the borrowing of Inanna. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ašš-: Open [a] followed by a geminate voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃː]; the doubled š of the Assyrian theonym. -ūr: Long close back rounded vowel [uː] plus alveolar tap or trill [r]; the final vowel length is inferred from Neo-Assyrian and later Aramaic/Hebrew transcriptions. Note: The god's name is identical with the city and land of Assyria; from the Middle Assyrian period it is usually spelled Aš-šur. The doubled š indicates a geminate consonant, and the final vowel is commonly reconstructed long in Neo-Assyrian (Aššūr). Older or dialectal forms may have a short /u/. The PUNICODEX form Aššur marks the geminate sibilant without committing to vowel length. Sources: Chicago Assyrian Dictionary (CAD), George House Most High, Black & Green Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.

title: Pronunciation: Šamaš

The PUNICODEX form preserves the Akkadian sibilant š and the two short a-vowels. Tier 1: the caron on š marks a distinctive Akkadian phoneme — a distinctive diacritic the ASCII form loses. title: Pronunciation: Quetzalcōātl
text: Pronunciation of Quetzalcōātl: /két͡saɬˈkoː(w)aːt͡ɬ/ Label: Classical Nahuatl Reconstruction Approximation: 'ket-SAHL-KOH-wahtl' — the 'tl' at the end is one sound, the 'z' is like 'ts,' and the whispered 'l' in 'zal' is Nahuatl ɬ. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Quet-: Voiceless velar stop [k] plus [e], then the affricate [t͡s]. In Classical Nahuatl, qu before e/i is /k/ (not /kw/), and tz is /t͡s/. -zal-: Open [a] plus voiceless alveolar lateral fricative [ɬ] — the Nahuatl l is a 'whispered l,' not the English approximant. -cō-: Voiceless velar stop [k] plus long back rounded [oː]. Classical Nahuatl had no /u/ sound; the macron marks vowel length. -ātl: Long open [aː] plus lateral affricate [t͡ɬ] — final -tl is a single Nahuatl sound, not separate t + l. Note: Classical Nahuatl had no /u/; qu before e/i is /k/ and cu is /kw/. The long vowels ō and ā are preserved in the PUNICODEX restoration, and the final -tl is a lateral affricate [t͡ɬ], not English 'tuhl.' The [w] glide between ō and ā is common in natural speech but optional. Tier 1: the two macrons preserve reconstructed vowel length. Sources: Andrews Introduction to Classical Nahuatl, Karttunen An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl, Wiktionary Nahuatl.

Dialect: Confidence: canonical Note: Tēzcatlīpōca is Nahuatl for "Smoking Mirror": tēzcatl (mirror) + -tlī- + pōca (smoking). The ē and ī are long per Karttunen and Andrews, and the final ō of pōca is long — the macrons the restoration preserves — and the name belongs to the god of night, sorcery, rulership, and strife, whose obsidian mirror shows men themselves.

title: Pronunciation: Tlāloc
text: Pronunciation of Tlāloc: /ˈtɬaː.lok/ Label: Classical Nahuatl Reconstruction Approximation: 'TLAH-lok' — start with the Nahuatl lateral affricate 'tl', hold the first 'a' long, and end with a firm 'ok'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: tl-: Voiceless lateral affricate [tɬ], a single Nahuatl sound: 'tl' released with the tongue at the side teeth. -ā-: Long [aː], macron marking reconstructed vowel length. -loc: [lok], final syllable; the name has been glossed as 'he who is made of earth' or 'he who is the embodiment of the earth'. Note: Tlāloc is Tier 1: the macron on ā preserves reconstructed Classical Nahuatl vowel length, and the initial tl- is a single distinctive phoneme impossible in English.

title: Pronunciation: Cōātlīcue
text: Pronunciation of Cōātlīcue: /koː.aːˈtɬiː.kwe/ Label: Classical Nahuatl Reconstruction Approximation: 'koh-AH-tlee-kweh' — the 'tl' is one crisp sound, and the macrons stretch the o, a, and i into long vowels. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Cō-: Voiceless velar stop [k] followed by long open-mid [oː]. In Classical Nahuatl, c before back vowels is /k/; the macron marks vowel length. -ā-: Long open front [aː], a held vowel that distinguishes the first element of the compound. -tlī-: Lateral affricate [tɬ] plus long close front [iː]; the -tl is a single Nahuatl sound, not English t + l. -cue: Voiceless velar stop [k] plus rounded [we], the Nahuatl labiovelar sequence. Note: Classical Nahuatl vowel length is the key prosodic feature preserved here. The name is transparently composed of cōātl ('snake, serpent') and īcue ('her skirt'), a possessive form of cueitl 'skirt.' The final labiovelar [kwe] is not a diphthong in English terms but a velar stop followed by a labial glide. Tier 1: the three macrons preserve reconstructed long vowels in the first, second, and fourth syllables.

title: Pronunciation: Huītzilōpōchtli
text: Pronunciation of Huītzilōpōchtli: /wiː.t͡si.loːˈpoːt͡ʃ.tɬi/ Label: Classical Nahuatl Reconstruction Approximation: 'weet-see-loh-POCH-tlee' — the 'tz' is 'ts,' the 'ch' is as in 'church,' and the final -tli is one released sound. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Huitz-: Rounded [w] plus long close front [iː], then alveolar affricate [t͡s] — the beginning of huītzilin, the Nahuatl word for 'hummingbird.' -ilo-: Close front [i], alveolar lateral [l], and short [o]: the -il- tail of huītzilin plus the ligature -o- that joins it to ōpōchtli in the compound. -pōch-: Voiceless bilabial stop [p] plus long back rounded [oː] plus voiceless postalveolar affricate [t͡ʃ]; ōpōchtli means 'left-handed,' also associated with the south. -tli: Lateral affricate [tɬ] plus close front [i], the absolute suffix closing the noun. Note: The etymology is debated. The most widely accepted analysis takes huītzilin 'hummingbird' + ōpōchtli 'left/south,' joined by the ligature -o-, with a possible interpretation of the hummingbird as the soul of the warrior returning from death. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: O-: Open-mid back rounded vowel [ɔ] with low tone; the initial vowel is written without dot below in the lexical form. -ló-: Voiced alveolar lateral approximant [l] followed by close-mid back rounded vowel [o] with high tone. -dù-: Voiced alveolar stop [d] followed by close back rounded vowel [u] with low tone. -má-: Voiced bilabial nasal [m] followed by open [a] with high tone. -rè: Voiced alveolar tap or trill [r] followed by mid front vowel [e] with low tone. Note: Olódùmarè is Tier 1: the acute accent on ó preserves a high tone and the grave accents on ù and è preserve low tones, distinctive features the ASCII form loses. Tonal distinctions are crucial to Yoruba meaning.

title: Pronunciation: Dažbog
text: Pronunciation of Dažbog: /ˈdaʒ.boɡ/ Label: Common Slavic / East Slavic Reconstruction Approximation: 'DAHZH-bog' — crisp 'dah', then the 'zh' sound of 'measure', and end with 'bog' as in 'god' (which is what the word means). Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: D-: Voiced alveolar stop [d], as in English 'day'. -a-: Short open front [a], the first unstressed syllable in the compound. -ž-: Voiced postalveolar fricative [ʒ], the Slavic 'zh' sound written with a caron. -bog: Voiced bilabial stop [b], open-mid back rounded [ɔ], and voiced velar [ɡ]; means 'god'. Note: Dažbog is Tier 1: the caron on ž preserves the distinctive Common Slavic fricative, a feature the ASCII form loses. The h in the lexicon's ASCII form is silent, reflecting an older East Slavic spelling convention (Daždbog / Dadzbog) that was later simplified. We do not invent an etymology beyond the attested compound 'giving god'.

Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: s: Voiceless alveolar fricative [s], the first consonant of sꜥ 'perception, intellect' ꜥ: Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ], the ayin that gives the word its throaty closure a: Short open vowel [a], supplied by convention; the hieroglyphic spelling records only s-ꜥ Note: sꜥ is a Tier-1 restoration. title: Pronunciation: Šw
text: Pronunciation of Šw: /ʃuː/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: 'SHOO' — drawn out, breathy, like the sound of wind passing through a corridor. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Š-: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ], like English 'shoe' — the sound of rushing air. -uː: Long close back vowel, sustained like a drawn-out breath; the name itself resembles an exhalation. Note: Shu is Tier 1 because the Egyptian Šw preserves the caron-marked š — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. The name is an onomatopoeic masterpiece: šw sounds like the rush of air it names. Egyptologists debate whether the primary meaning is 'dryness', 'emptiness', or 'he who rises up'; the god contains all three.

text: Pronunciation of Varuṇa: /ˈʋɐ.ru.ɳɐ/ Label: Sanskrit/Vedic Reconstruction Approximation: 'VUH-roo-nah' — start with a soft 'v', keep the middle syllable light, and end with a tongue-tip-curled 'n' like an American 'r' pressed against the roof of the mouth. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: V-: Labiodental approximant [ʋ], softer than English v, followed by short open [ɐ]. -ru-: Alveolar tap or trill [r] plus short [u] — the syllable that names the rolling waters. -ṇa: Retroflex nasal [ɳ] plus short [ɐ]; the dot beneath the n marks the tongue-tip curl distinctive to Sanskrit. Note: Varuṇa is Tier 1 because the registrable form Varuṇa preserves the retroflex ṇ (a phonemic distinction central to Sanskrit) — a diacritic the ASCII form loses. The name is traditionally derived from the root vṛ- 'to cover, encompass,' fitting a god who covers the waters, the night sky, and the hidden deeds of humankind.

title: Pronunciation: Gaṅgā

Dialect: Confidence: canonical Note: Sanskrit gaṅgā carries the velar nasal ṅ of IAST — the nasal of the velum, /ŋ/, written with the dot above. The restoration Gaṅgā keeps both: the velar nasal and the long final ā. Hindi speech says "Ganga"; the scholarly form is hers. The ṅ is the velum's own nasal — the sound of ng in song — which plain English softens to n.

Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Pār-: Voiceless bilabial stop [p] plus long open [aː], followed by voiced labiodental approximant [ʋ] — softer than English 'v' -va-: Short open [a], the second syllable is light and unstressed -tī: Voiceless alveolar stop [t] plus long close front [iː]; the macron marks length, giving Tier-1 status Note: Pārvatī is Tier 1 because both the initial ā and final ī are long. title: Pronunciation: Kālī

Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Kā-: Velar [k] followed by long, open [aː] — a dark, resonant syllable that can mean 'black' or 'time'. -lī: Lateral [l] plus long [iː], a feminine ending that transforms the root into a goddess. Note: IAST Kālī uses a macron over both vowels to indicate length. The name is a feminine adjective: she is the Black One, the Time-One, the dark beyond gender. Devanagari काली is identical in form to the word for 'the feminine of time'.

title: Pronunciation: Typhōn
text: Pronunciation of Typhōn: /tyˈpʰɔːn/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: "tee-FOHN" — but the first vowel is like French "tu," and the second is long and breathy, like a storm that does not end quickly. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ty-: Short upsilon [y] — a rounded, front vowel like French "u" — the whirlwind's first breath. -phōn: Aspirated phi [pʰ] followed by long omega [ɔː] and nu; the name roars and sustains. Note: Typhōn is Tier 1 because the Greek Τυφῶν contains both stress and length: the circumflex over the omega marks a long vowel that also carries the pitch peak. The single character ῶ encodes both features, and the macron form Typhōn preserves the long vowel while implying the original stress position. The name sounds like what it describes: a long, smoky exhalation.

Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: P-: Voiceless unaspirated bilabial stop [p]; the rough breathing is absent in the Greek spelling. -ý-: Close front vowel [y], like French 'tu', with acute stress. -th-: Aspirated voiceless dental stop [tʰ], distinct from English 'th'. -ō-: Long open-mid back rounded vowel [ɔː], marked by the macron/circumflex. Note: Pýthōn is Tier 1: the Greek original carries both acute stress and a long vowel (ō). The English 'Python' flattens both features.

title: Pronunciation: Kírkē
text: Pronunciation of Kírkē: /kír.kɛː/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'KEER-keh' — high pitch on the first syllable, a trilled rho, and a long open final vowel; English 'SUR-see' has wandered far from the falcon's name. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Kí-: Kappa with a short iota under the acute — the pitch springs high, then the rolled rho snaps it shut, like a falcon turning on the wind. -kē: A second kappa released into the long open eta [ɛː] — the name ends wide and held, never the English 'see'. Note: Kírkē is the boundary case of the Greek list. The Greek Κίρκη carries both features the mechanical tier rule watches for — the acute pitch of the first syllable and the long final eta — and the restoration Kírkē preserves both against the Latinized 'Circe,' which shed them. This entry follows the catalog's Tier-2 assignment; a strict reading of the rule would promote her to the first rank, and her double signature is recorded here so the classification never hardens into doctrine.

Dialect: Confidence: canonical Note: Greek Κέρβερος is proparoxytone — the accent rests on the first syllable, exactly as LSJ prints it. The restoration Kérberos keeps that acute; the ASCII "Cerberus" is the Latinized form that lost it. The etymology is genuinely dark: the old comparison with Sanskrit śárvara ("spotted," one of Yama's two hounds) is famous but unproven, and Beekes (EDG) treats the word as likely Pre-Greek. Tier-2 by rule: the single feature preserved is the accent.

text: Pronunciation of Oṃ: /oːm/ Label: Sanskrit Reconstruction Approximation: 'OHM' — hold the open 'o' long, then let the sound dissolve into a hum that vibrates in the nose and skull. Note: Oṃ is Tier 1: the dot-under m (ṃ) preserves the anusvāra, a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The syllable is traditionally analyzed as containing the three sounds a, u, and m, representing the triads of waking-dream-sleep, creation-preservation-dissolution, and Brahma-Viṣṇu-Śiva.

The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Bāguà correctly shows the high level tone of 'eight' and the falling tone of 'trigram'.

title: Pronunciation: Tàijí
text: Pronunciation of Tàijí: /tʰaɪ̯˥˩ tɕi˧˥/ Label: Modern Standard Mandarin (Pinyin) Approximation: TIE-JEE — 'tai' like 'tie' with a sharp falling tone (high to low), and 'ji' like 'gee' with a rising tone. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: tài: Syllable with aspirated alveolar stop [tʰ], diphthong [aɪ̯], and Tone 4 (falling, ˥˩). The apostrophe-like aspiration is essential: Pinyin 't' is unaspirated [t], while 't' in IPA here is aspirated [tʰ]. jí: Syllable with unaspirated alveolo-palatal affricate [tɕ], high front vowel [i], and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). Pinyin 'j' before front vowels is always [tɕ], never English 'j'. Note: 太極 (Tàijí) means the 'Supreme Ultimate' or 'Great Extreme', the primordial source from which yin and yang differentiate in Neo-Confucian cosmology. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is tài (Tone 4) + jí (Tone 2), per the Hanyu Pinyin scheme (ISO 7098) and the Unihan Database (kMandarin). Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the component characters as 太 *l̥a[t]-s (GSR 0317d) and 極 *[g](r)ək (GSR 0910e). The Unicode restoration Tàijí preserves both citation tones.

title: Pronunciation: Wǔxíng
text: Pronunciation of Wǔxíng: /u˨˩˦ ɕiŋ˧˥/ Label: Modern Standard Mandarin (Pinyin) Approximation: WOO-SHING — 'wu' dips low and rises (or stays low in fast speech), and 'xing' rises like 'sheen' with a rising tone. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: wǔ: Syllable beginning with labio-velar glide [w], high back rounded vowel [u], and Tone 3 (falling-rising, ˨˩˦). In connected speech before a non-third tone, this is often realized as a 'half-third' low falling tone. xíng: Syllable with voiceless alveolo-palatal fricative [ɕ], high front vowel [i], velar nasal [ŋ], and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). Pinyin 'x' before front vowels is always [ɕ], like an extended 'sh' in 'she'. Note: 五行 (Wǔxíng) denotes the 'Five Phases' or 'Five Agents'—wood, fire, earth, metal, and water—the cyclical modes of transformation in Chinese cosmology, medicine, and feng shui. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading in this philosophical context is wǔ (Tone 3) + xíng (Tone 2), as given by the Unihan Database (kMandarin) and the Hanyu Pinyin scheme. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct 五 as *C.ŋˤaʔ (GSR 0058a) and 行 in the sense 'walk, conduct' as *C.[g]raŋ (GSR 0748a). The Unicode restoration Wǔxíng preserves the citation tones; note that 行 is disyllabically distinguished from the reading háng ('row, profession').

Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: xiān: Voiceless alveolo-palatal fricative [ɕ], palatal approximant [j], open-mid front vowel [ɛ], and Tone 1 (high level, ˥˥). The character combines 人 (person) with 山 (mountain), suggesting one who withdraws to the heights. The Pinyin restoration Xiān preserves the high level tone.

Dialect: Confidence: canonical Note: Māzǔ 媽祖 — "Maternal Ancestor" — carries the first tone on mā and the dipping third tone on zǔ; the restoration keeps both tone marks. Her personal name was Lín Mòniáng ("Silent Maiden"), but the world prays to the title: Grandmother of the sea. The third tone on zǔ dips and rises — the small valley in the name that Mandarin speakers sing without noticing.
